10875-at-sunwich-port-part-5-contents-ch:
W. W. Jacobs's At Sunwich Port closes in this fifth part, covering chapters twenty-one through twenty-five, with drawings by Will Owen. Gossip about preparations for his son's marriage reaches Captain Nugent through his sister, and hardens him against Jem Hardy, whom he nearly shows the door. When Hardy pays his third visit, the captain presses him for his methods and gets nothing.

Hardy's frank reply, that he is getting little out of it, only deepens suspicion of false pretences. Jacobs brings courtship, parental pride, and seaside gossip to a head here. Readers get the novel's final chapters, in which young love meets an old sailor's obstinacy.
15716-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
A weekly newspaper for boys and girls, dated April 29, 1897, and published in New York by William Beverley Harison. Each issue explains the news in plain words for young readers, with science and stories beside it. At five cents a copy, it kept children abreast of a fast-moving world. The tone is brisk, clear, and confident.

This issue leads with Greece and Turkey, where war clouds gather but the storm has not yet broken. The paper explains that the Powers do not agree, and that no Concert of the Powers truly exists. Greece's refusal of joint advice makes the split open. For a modern reader, the issue shows how American children first learned of a European crisis.
16509-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
The February 25, 1920 Punch leads its Charivaria column with news jokes. An American held to ransom in Mexico, an old lady crocheting asbestos ear-guards for Churchill, and a revue inventor advised to wait out the crime wave fill the column. The Poet Laureate keeps his head despite spring weather, and the Allies hint to Holland that they, not Holland, won the war.

The rest of the number follows Punch's usual weekly pattern, with drawings, rhymes, and brief comic items. Each joke is tied to that week's news, from Mexico to the ex-Kaiser's trial. Beside its February neighbors, this number stands out for its own set of news jokes and cartoons.
25033-report-of-the-chief-librarian-for-:
The Report of the Chief Librarian of New Zealand's General Assembly Library for 1924-25, laid on the table of the House of Representatives, records a year of careful stewardship. The Recess Library Committee, its constitution newly altered by both chambers, held three meetings under Speaker Charles E. Statham, though two lacked a quorum and only the third could confirm business. The report suggests the constituting rule may need slight alteration.

New accessions numbered 2,089, below the previous year's 2,700, which had included some five hundred volumes of the Herries bequest, now repaired, rebound, and shelved. Total catalogued holdings passed 109,705 on June 18, on a library vote of seven hundred pounds, only one hundred a year more than thirty years earlier. Chief Librarian Charles Wilson signs a report of economy, order, and modest growth.
30714-the-works-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Held here is volume twenty-five, the last volume, of the Swanston Edition of Robert Louis Stevenson's works, printed in London in 1912. The edition ran to twenty-five volumes, with two thousand and sixty copies printed and two thousand for sale. This volume holds Stevenson's letters, edited by Sidney Colvin, in parts eleven through fourteen, with thanks to Methuen for leave to use them.

Part eleven covers life in Samoa and the first year at Vailima, with letters to Colvin, Burlingame, Henry James, Rudyard Kipling, and Charles Baxter, among others. Later parts carry the Samoan years onward, through work, illness, and island life. Readers get Stevenson's voice at its most direct: warm, funny, and frank about writing, friends, and the far place he made his home.
5299-tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontain:
The twenty-fifth and final volume of La Fontaine's Tales and Novels gathers The Dress-maker, The Gascon. The Pitcher, To Promise is One Thing, to Keep it, Another, The Nightengale, and the Epitaph of Fontaine complete the volume. The Dress-maker opens with a cloistered nun and a lover in the neighbouring town, racking their brains to crown their love.

The youth must dress in woman's clothes to pass the convent door, a ruse often tried before that succeeds as of yore. Readers finishing the collection here get a last set of gallant tales, closing with Fontaine's own epitaph, in the verse that carried the whole work.
5928-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
The cave of Montesinos alone fills this Don Quixote installment, chapter twenty-two, on the grand adventure in the heart of La Mancha that Quixote brought to a happy termination. Many and great attentions were shown to Quixote by a newly married couple, who felt obliged to him for earlier kindness, before the cave descent began. What Quixote claims to have seen below becomes the chapter's marvel and its problem.

Here is the second part's most debated episode, as vision, dream, and boast blur in the cave's darkness. Sancho doubts, Quixote insists, and Cervantes lets readers judge. The single chapter suits readers following volume two, since its cave tale echoes through later jokes about enchantment, Dulcinea, and the truth of wonders.
7104-adventures-of-huckleberry-finn-chap:
This part of Huckleberry Finn opens at chapter twenty one, after sun up, with the raft still running and the king and duke turning out looking rusty. A swim perks them up. After breakfast the king sits on the raft's corner, boots off, britches rolled, legs dangling in the water, pipe lit, learning his Romeo and Juliet by heart. The duke drills him speech by speech, teaching sighs and a hand on the heart.

The king must not bellow Romeo like a bull, the duke insists. He must say it soft, sick, and languishing, since Juliet is a dear sweet mere child of a girl who does not bray like a jackass. Chapters twenty one to twenty five end with the frauds still rehearsing for river towns.
a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-papers: Franklin Pierce, son of a Revolutionary soldier who settled in New Hampshire, fills this fifth volume part compiled by James Daniel Richardson. Pierce's father served as sheriff and legislator, and the son rose to the presidency. The volume prints Pierce's messages and papers in the presidential series. It preserves the official record of his administration.
a-general-history-and-collection-of-voya: Volume three of Robert Kerr's voyages turns to the discovery of America and early conquests in the New World. Its opening chapter gives the history of Columbus as written by his son Ferdinand. Later chapters follow the first conquests across the Atlantic. Kerr presents the American story as part of his systematic history of navigation.

Volume six of Robert Kerr's voyages continues early English voyages of discovery to America. Its chapters open with the Cabots' discovery of Newfoundland in 1497 in the service of Henry the Seventh. A discourse by a papal legate on Sebastian Cabot's discoveries follows. Kerr gathers English American exploration into his systematic history.

Volume seventeen of Robert Kerr's voyages gives Captain King's journal of the return to the Sandwich Islands. Its sections describe the islands, their number, names, and situation, with Owhyhee in detail. Districts, extent, and island life fill the general account. Kerr's volume preserves Cook's Hawaiian story through King's careful journal.
achad-anatomy-of-the-body-of-god-1925:
Geometry crowns Achad's trilogy in The Anatomy of the Body of God, printed in 1925. Charles Stansfeld Jones here throws the Tree of Life into three dimensions. Will Ransom drew the plates that give the scheme its solid form.

The spheres and paths of the Tree become a body that can be turned, cut, and viewed from each side. Achad holds that the flat Tree hides truths the solid one shows plainly. The book is bold, strange, and wrought with great care throughout. It ends his bold reworking of the Kabbalah he learned from Crowley. Few occult books of its decade reach so far.
adventures-of-huckleberry-finn-chapters-:
Chapters 21 to 25 of Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn bring the king and the duke, the two frauds travelling with Huck and Jim, to an Arkansas river town. The duke drills the king in a mangled Romeo and Juliet and a Hamlet soliloquy pieced together from half of Shakespeare at once. they bill a Shakespearean Revival for the town's money.

The town answers with violence of its own: drunken Boggs is shot dead by Colonel Sherburn, who then faces down a lynch mob from his porch. A circus and the frauds' failed shows follow. then a richer scheme forms, as the pair plot to impersonate the English brothers of the late Peter Wilks and steal his family's gold. Huck watches the swindle take shape with growing shame.
almadel-sloane-3825:
The Ars Almadel survives here in a transcription of Sloane MS 3825, a seventeenth-century English manuscript. The Almadel forms Part Four of the Lemegeton, the Lesser Key of Solomon. Among the grimoires it counts as the gentlest high magic, concerned with good spirits rather than demons.

The art uses a wax tablet, the almadel, pierced and inscribed for the rite. Through it the magician addresses the angels of the four chorae, the quarters of the heavens. Colors, perfumes, and seals vary by quarter. The manuscript's own words guide the working step by step. Faithful transcription keeps a working magician's handbook readable in its original form.
anderson-dark-laughter-1925:
Sherwood Anderson published Dark Laughter in 1925, and it became the only bestseller of his career. Anderson had worked in Chicago newspaper rooms and Ohio factories, and both worlds meet here. The novel is also famous sideways: Hemingway's Torrents of Spring parodied its manner to break with Anderson's influence.

Bruce Dudley, a Chicago journalist, walks out on his wife and his job and drifts downriver under a new name. He takes factory work in Indiana and watches his employer's unhappy wife, drawn to the unforced laughter of Black workers around the plant. Anderson sets instinct against a tired, talkative civilization. The writing is loose and incantatory. Dark Laughter is his strangest popular success.
arcana-divina-paul-and-mary-mellon-colle: Arcana Divina, dated 1725, is an anonymous illustrated work whose Latin title means divine secrets. It belongs to the world of early eighteenth-century hermetic writing, where divine and hidden knowledge were set down together in one volume. The copy preserved here forms part of the Paul and Mary Mellon Collection. That is the great modern gathering of alchemy and early science books. In its company of rare illustrated works, this book now rests.
ars-paulina-sloane-3825:
The Ars Paulina, the Pauline Art, survives here in a transcription of Sloane MS 3825. It forms Part Three of the Lemegeton, the Lesser Key of Solomon. The seventeenth-century English manuscript teaches the art of the spirits who govern the hours of the day and night.

Angels of the hours, and of the signs of the zodiac, fill its tables. The magician calls them with seals, prayers, and a table of practice. Compared with the Goetia's demons, these are orderly celestial clerks. The transcription keeps the manuscript's working detail intact. Students of the Lemegeton need the Paulina to see the whole system: hell in Part One, heaven's timetable here.
arxiv-2509-00025:
Tai Vu, working alone, builds machine models in 2025 that read emotion from human speech. Speech emotion recognition is hard, since how feelings map to pitch, loudness, and energy in sound is still unclear. Vu tests three model families on the task: support vector machines, long short-term memory networks, and convolutional networks, which scan sound for local patterns.

Transfer learning, which reuses a model trained elsewhere, and data augmentation, which varies the training sound, help train on a small set. The best model is a ResNet34 network, a deep design with skip links. It reaches an accuracy near sixty-seven percent and a solid F1 score, a balance of hits and misses. Such tools could aid call care and health checks.
arxiv-2509-00225:
Sujan K. K. and N. S. Vidhyadhiraja study a sharp shift in how a solid carries current in 2025, in a changed Anderson model. Some solids act as metals, which pass current with ease. Others act as insulators, which block it. Which one a solid is can flip as the force that makes electrons repel each other grows.

At zero heat, that flip can be smooth, with scale-free traits near the threshold point. In the Hubbard model, such a point shows only above a warm end point in heat. The changed model instead holds a whole sheet of true zero-heat threshold points. With a solver that rescales the problem in steps, the team finds scale-free traits in how the solid resists current at low heat. The key exponents on the metal side and the insulator side fall in one shared range.
arxiv-2509-00825:
Alon Levi, with three co-authors, improves Quantum Likelihood Estimation. This hybrid algorithm identifies the Hamiltonian of a quantum system. The Hamiltonian is the rule that governs its energy and motion. The algorithm updates a weight distribution from measurement outcomes. It uses Bayesian inference to guide each update.

Efficiency varies greatly with parameter choices at each step. The team selects parameters dynamically to gain the most information. They choose the initial state, measurement basis, and evolution time per step. The goal is to maximize mutual information with the true Hamiltonian. A simulated annealing routine minimizes a quantum entropy measure. The optimized version needs far fewer iterations to converge. They also propose a general scheme for wider quantum learning problems.
arxiv-2509-01025:
Masked diffusion models build text by filling in blanked words in any order, not one word at a time from the left. Jaeyeon Kim, with seven co-authors, tackles a limit of these models: they cannot insert new words, so output length stays fixed. The team proposes a more flexible version of the model.

Their method adds blank tokens and then reveals them, so length can grow or shrink as needed. Tests show it matches the older models on text quality while tracking true length much better. On a maze task it solved far more cases, and the team also turned a large trained model into the new form in three days of fine-tuning.
arxiv-2509-01225:
Masahiro Kaminaga studies a Stark operator, which describes a charged particle in a steady electric field, combined with a sharp interaction on a surface. The surface is compact and only Lipschitz smooth, meaning it may have corners. The interaction strength can vary along the surface as any bounded function.

Kaminaga defines a class of solutions with piecewise regularity near the surface and proves the stated transmission conditions give a self-adjoint operator, the kind needed for sound physics. A boundary resolvent formula links the full problem to the free Stark case through one bounded operator. That formula shows the resolvent difference is compact, so the essential spectrum stays the whole real line when the field is present. The result gives a direct boundary method for such interface problems.
arxiv-2509-01325:
Frames are sets of signals that can rebuild a message even when some parts are lost. Gabor frames build such sets by shifting one window in time and frequency. Palina Salanevich and Nigel Q. D. Strachan study how robust these frames are. They test noise and erasures, which are lost measurements. They allow arbitrary sets of time-frequency shifts.

The pair shows a key pattern. Frame bounds for a random window behave much like those of frames with independent random entries. They give constructions of nearly tight Gabor frames that use few shifts. Uniform estimates cover the erasure case as well. Frames built from mutually unbiased bases stayed robust in tests. Erasure rates reached up to fifty percent. A Gabor frame from the Alltop window matched the best known set constructions.
arxiv-2509-01525:
Quantum dots are tiny traps that hold single electrons, and linking distant dots quickly remains an unsolved step toward large quantum machines. Mikel Olano and Geza Giedke model electron transfer between a moving dot, carried by a surface acoustic wave, and a static dot. Such transfer underpins schemes that shuttle electrons across a chip.

Their paradigmatic model derives the non-adiabatic terms, the parts that matter when motion is too fast for the electron to adjust smoothly, and discusses how they drive the two-state transfer. The analysis covers the electron's spin state and its effect on the loading probability, including the Rashba-Dresselhaus interactions, the main spin couplings in semiconductor electron gases. The work gives a clearer picture of a process tested in experiments but not studied in detail before.
arxiv-2509-01825:
Sonwabile Mafunda finds the largest possible edge counts for bipartite graphs under set limits. A bipartite graph splits points into two groups with edges only across groups. His limits fix the total points, the diameter meaning the longest shortest path, and the connectivity meaning how hard the graph is to split. The first part pins the top size under those three limits.

The second part sharpens a known bound for triangle free graphs when applied to bipartite ones. Proofs cover low edge connectivity values where the gain is largest. For higher values, past work shows the top size sits near a simpler bound anyway. His method differs from prior proofs and also names the graphs that reach the bound, so the bounds are sharp.
arxiv-2509-01925:
Kenta Suzuki constructs a time-like Janus solution in a curved space used for holography studies. Holography links a gravity theory in a volume to a field theory on its boundary. His solution is driven by a dilaton field, a scalar field that varies with time. It breaks a standard energy condition, yet he argues it still serves as a toy model.

The dual field theory reads as a global quantum quench, a sudden system wide change. A scalar operator couples to a time dependent source in that picture. He computes average values for that operator and for the energy stress tensor and finds they match the dual view. Entanglement entropy at late times and a hot version of the solution are also covered.
arxiv-2509-02025:
Junda He leads seven co-authors with CureFuzz, a curiosity driven tester for sequential decision systems. Such systems drive cars, robots, and traffic control, where learned unsafe behavior can cause crashes. Finding diverse crash triggering scenarios in black box testing remains an open problem. Their fuzzer rewards itself for novelty, pushing exploration toward fresh scenarios.

A seed selection step balances novelty hunting against crash hunting across many objectives. Tests on several decision systems find far more faults than the prior best method. The range of distinct crash scenario types also grows by a wide margin. Scenarios found by the tool can then repair the systems under test. The work gives safety teams a stronger pre-deployment check.
arxiv-2509-02225:
Jaime Collado-Montanez, L Alfonso Urena-Lopez, and Arturo Montejo-Raez argue for fundamental language models that split language skill from factual memory. Large models impress yet hallucinate, bias outputs, raise privacy issues, and cost heavily. Those flaws stem from fusing linguistic competence with memorized facts in one monolith. Their paradigm keeps models smaller and linguistically sharp while external tools supply facts.

Models from tiny to very large are scored on language competence, external knowledge, and internal knowledge. All improve with scale, but internal factual knowledge grows far faster than language skill. Size thus tracks memorization more than core language ability. Compact proficient models as foundations for tool augmented systems follow naturally. The path promises leaner, clearer, and more sustainable language technology.
arxiv-2509-03025:
Sohee Kim and 3 co-authors probed a 2025 weakness in large vision-language models, software that answers questions about images. Such models sometimes describe objects that a question mentions even when nothing like them appears in the picture. That habit produces confident but wrong answers.

Digging inside one model family, the team found a small set of neurons that fire in a telling pattern when a mentioned concept is absent. They built a detector on that pattern to judge whether each input word is truly grounded in the image. Guided by the detector, their fix rewrites prompts or swaps out ungrounded words while answers form. Tests across several models showed fewer invented objects, with the approach carrying over between systems.
arxiv-2509-03425:
Phuc Pham, Viet Thanh Duy Nguyen, and Truong-Son Hy introduced LINKER in 2025, a sequence-based model predicting how protein residues interact with parts of drug-like molecules. Knowing which residue touches which functional group, and by what kind of interaction, guides rational drug design. Earlier learning methods needed three-dimensional structures or mere distance labels, limiting their reach and biological meaning.

LINKER takes only protein sequences and a ligand's SMILES string, a text encoding of its structure, at prediction time. Training used attention supervised by real complexes, where interaction labels were extracted by functional group motifs. The model predicts biologically defined interaction types rather than simple closeness. On a standard benchmark its predictions aligned closely with expert biochemical annotations. That opens large-scale screening where no structure exists.
arxiv-2509-03825:
Where to place sensors so that unknown forces on a vibrating structure can be reconstructed sparsely, in the frequency domain, is the question in a 2025 research paper by Jeunghoon Lee. Force reconstruction works backward from measured vibrations to the loads that caused them. Bad sensor placement blurs that inference, because sensor readings end up carrying overlapping information.

Lee's strategy is built on the Gram matrix, a table of overlaps between responses, studied through its modal decomposition. Near a target frequency, a few modes dominate the matrix, and each mode's contribution reflects how its vibration shape correlates across space. Sensors placed near nodal regions, where correlation runs low, should reduce coherence in the response matrix and sharpen reconstruction. A greedy algorithm turns that insight into design: it picks locations one by one to minimise the Gram matrix's off-diagonal energy. Simulations and experiments show robust, accurate force estimates, beating heuristic layouts.
arxiv-2509-03925:
Rivu Bardhan and three co-authors construct Angel surfaces of every possible genus in a 2025 mathematics paper. An Angel surface is a complete minimal surface in ordinary three-dimensional space with exactly two ends: one catenoidal, like a soap-film hourglass, and one of Enneper type. Minimal surfaces minimise area locally, like soap films, and these examples carry the least total absolute curvature for their shape.

Earlier examples were built only numerically, by Weber, for particular cases. The authors prove existence for every genus at least one, genus counting the surface's handles, settling a question Fujimori and Shoda had posed. Their construction extends the orthodisk method of Weber and Wolf, which builds minimal surfaces from flat pieces. A central new idea is partial symmetry, introducing controlled symmetry rather than demanding it everywhere or nowhere. That control lets the construction tune both ends and the handles at once.
arxiv-2509-04125:
Tarik Zaciragic and two co-authors ask whether poker programs bluff, in a 2025 research paper. Bluffing, betting strongly on a weak hand, keeps human players unpredictable. Most computer poker work tracks win rates and ignores this behavior. The team let two well-known agents play Leduc Hold'em, a shortened poker game, against each other. One agent, DQN, learns from experience. The other, CFR, follows game-theory reasoning.

Game logs showed both agents did bluff, though in different styles and at different rates. Curiously, their bluffs succeeded at about the same rate, measured by opponents folding. Bluffing may belong to the game itself rather than to any one method, the authors suggest. Their code is public.
arxiv-2509-04325:
Nejc Košnik and two co-authors hunt for the high-energy origins of CP violation in lepton interactions in a 2025 physics paper. CP violation means nature treats matter and antimatter differently. The Higgs boson's couplings to leptons, its Yukawa couplings, might hide such effects, and colliders are probing their nature. Using effective field theory as a bridge, the authors ask which single- or two-field extensions of the Standard Model could generate the CP-violating versions.

Measurements then constrain those candidate origins from many directions: Higgs data, electric and magnetic dipole moments, flavor-changing lepton events, and electroweak precision tests. For the flavor patterns studied, precision measurements often beat dedicated collider searches in strictness. Model builders get a map of surviving options.
arxiv-2509-04425:
Rafael Aoude and one co-author, Andreas Helset, find a hidden simplicity in scattering calculations for spinning black holes in a 2025 physics paper. Heavy particle effective theory reframes a massive spinning object so that propagators, the lines inside calculations, linearize neatly and numerators exponentiate. Building on those two gifts, the authors introduce Kerr generating functions that describe any probe scattering off a Kerr black hole background at every loop order, meaning every level of quantum correction.

Tensor reduction, a painful simplification step, then reduces to taking derivatives with respect to spin. A first application computes how a neutron star raises leading nonlinear tidal effects in that background. Compact results cover several graviton helicity patterns, with a full four-loop answer for the leading tidal operators.
arxiv-2509-04725:
Photon pairs can carry hidden patterns that ordinary brightness measurements cannot see. Carlo Schiano, lead author with five co-authors, describe a way to shape those patterns in a 2025 quantum optics paper. Their method patterns the distinguishability of photons inside a quantum interference setup with a beam splitter.

By writing and editing correlations between the two output channels, they hide encoded information from conventional intensity measurements. The scheme extends easily to many-particle cases. The authors present it as a route to transmitting high-dimensional quantum information, with possible uses in quantum communication and imaging protocols.
arxiv-2509-04825:
Quantum gates for qubits and four-level qudits could be synthesised on the fly with light pulses and magnetic fields. A. F. Urquijo Rodríguez, lead author with two co-authors, propose a theoretical control protocol for that task in a 2025 paper. The setting is a microcavity quantum well system where excitons and charged trions couple to a photonic mode.

By tuning coherent light-matter interaction with the magnetic field, they steer populations of encoded states through unitary evolution. Their optimisation generates a single-qubit gate with very high reported mean fidelity. They also realise an iSWAP gate in the qudit case with high reported fidelity.
arxiv-2509-05325:
Late deliveries are hard to study because real shipping data stay locked away, so Liming Xu, Yunbo Long, and Alexandra Brintrup built a synthetic substitute in a 2025 dataset paper. SynDelay is generated by an advanced model trained on real records, keeping realistic delivery patterns while protecting privacy.

The data still carry some noise and inconsistency, which the authors treat as part of the challenge. They supply baseline results and scoring metrics as starting reference points, not as best possible claims. SynDelay is public through the Supply Chain Data Hub, an open effort for sharing supply chain data. Reproducible benchmarks like this let delivery prediction methods be compared fairly.
arxiv-2509-05425:
Translation quality across more than two hundred languages can be forecast without translating anything, Jessica M. Lundin and three co-authors show in a 2025 language technology paper. Their features are simple: how many tokens each language needs for the same text, token counts, and basic facts about family, script, and region.

Gradient boosting models trained on those features predict quality scores for a leading commercial system on the FLORES benchmark with surprising accuracy. Into English, broad language family traits dominate the forecasts. Into other languages, token fertility, the token count ratio, matters more. The findings offer a cheap way to estimate where translation will be strong or unfairly weak.
arxiv-2509-05625:
Erasing one narrow concept from an image generator, such as a single celebrity or character, without damaging neighbours. That is the aim of Kien Nguyen, Anh Tran, and Cuong Pham in a 2025 machine learning paper. Earlier erasure methods trade robustness against image quality, and narrow concepts sit close to concepts that must stay.

Their method, SuMa, first derives a subspace, a small direction set inside the model's representation, for the target concept. It then maps that subspace onto a reference one chosen to minimise the distance moved, neutralising the concept gently. Across subclass, celebrity, style, and instance erasure tasks, SuMa matched quality-focused methods on image quality and completeness-focused methods on removal.
arxiv-2509-05825:
Safer, sharper early drug trials are the goal of Locally Optimal Restricted Designs, proposed in a 2025 paper by Oleksandr Sverdlov and two co-authors. Phase I/II studies hunt for doses that are both effective and tolerable, so patients should never be sent to doses known to be overly toxic or useless. The designs build those ethical limits in from the start.

The team works out designs for a four-parameter model over a chosen dose range and studies how they shift when the range or target doses change. A nature-inspired search algorithm finds the designs quickly, without fixed assumptions about the model. Against a more heuristic rival, the restricted designs prove more efficient while respecting the safety limits. The method also suggests how to pick doses for the next study.
arxiv-2509-06225:
Filling in a missing multi-way table when the missingness itself depends on the values is the problem Maoyu Zhang and three co-authors formalize in a 2025 paper. Most tensor completion theory assumes entries vanish independently at random, but real data go missing for reasons tied to what they would have shown. Their generalized framework models the observation probability as a function of the underlying tensor.

The framework covers continuous, binary, and count data. An alternating maximization algorithm estimates the tensor, with non-asymptotic error bounds at each step under relaxed conditions on observation rates. A statistical test checks whether missingness really depends on values. Simulations and two real datasets demonstrate the approach for recommenders, imaging, and similar incomplete-data work.
arxiv-2509-07025:
Eduardo Lobo Lustoda Cabral, Paulo Pirozelli, and Larissa Driemeier introduce binary normalized neural networks in a 2025 paper whose title claims one bit is all we need. Modern neural networks keep growing, above all language models and large image models. Their size makes them hard to deploy, so researchers want models that use less memory and run more cheaply.

Their new layer type stores every parameter as a single bit. Weights in the kernels and the biases can each be only zero or one. Versions of the layer exist for the usual layer kinds, from fully connected and convolutional layers to attention, and each differs only slightly from its standard counterpart. To test the idea, the team built two models: one that sorts images into classes, and one language decoder. Their results suggest such models can work while using far less memory.
arxiv-2509-07225:
Ze Sheng and 7 co-authors describe a competition system in 2025 that finds and fixes software flaws on its own. Their team was one of seven finalists in DARPA's Artificial Intelligence Cyber Challenge, placing fourth in the final round. The system, called a Cyber Reasoning System, hunts vulnerabilities in real open-source programs written in C and Java.

During the contest, the system found 28 security flaws, including six zero-days, flaws not known before, and patched 14 of them. The full system is open source. Much of the report details its language-model parts and the strategies that guide them. The team also built a public leaderboard, drawn from the contest data, for ranking language models on finding and patching flaws. Together, the tools give other builders a benchmark and a working model for automated defense.
arxiv-2509-07425:
Sanyam Kaul and 3 co-authors speed up Hyperledger Fabric, a permissioned blockchain system for businesses, in a 2025 paper. Fabric checks, orders, and validates transactions in stages, but under heavy load its throughput drops and many transactions get rejected. Conflicts between transactions are often found only at the final commit stage, which wastes work done earlier.

The new dependency-aware design flags each transaction during endorsement as independent or dependent. The ordering service then builds blocks that favor independent transactions, and each block carries a directed acyclic graph, a chart of which transactions depend on which. Committers run independent transactions in parallel and dependent ones in graph order. Built into Fabric version 2.5, the system was tested under workloads with varying dependency levels, targeting higher throughput and fewer rejections.
arxiv-2509-07525:
Gianluca Amprimo and 7 co-authors release EHWGesture in 2025, a dataset for reading clinical hand gestures from video. Hand gesture recognition supports human-computer interaction. It also supports checks of hand dexterity in clinics. Dynamic gestures are hard to read, since they vary in space and time. Older datasets often lack varied sensor views, precise tracking, or a score for how well a gesture was done.

EHWGesture holds over 1,100 recordings, about six hours in all. They come from 25 healthy subjects who perform five gestures of clinical use. Two RGB-Depth cameras and an event camera record each session. A motion capture system gives precise ground-truth tracking of the hand. All devices are aligned in space and in time. The recordings are grouped by speed of execution, in classes that mirror clinical dexterity scores. First tests cover gesture naming, trigger detection, and action quality scoring.
arxiv-2509-07625:
Mingyang Feng and 3 co-authors pose a three-way version of influence maximization in a 2025 paper. Influence maximization picks seed users in a social network to spread a message widely, for marketing, rumor control, or finding opinion leaders. Most studies optimize spread alone, neglecting the interplay of cost efficiency and time pressure that real campaigns face.

The new problem optimizes influence, cost, and time jointly, and the authors give intuitive and empirical evidence that all three must be handled together. Their evolutionary variable-length search algorithm, EVEA, hunts for seed sets of flexible size. Across four real-world networks, EVEA beat all baselines, with up to 19.3 percent higher hypervolume and 25 to 40 percent faster convergence, while keeping a diverse, balanced Pareto front of trade-offs. Campaign planners could pick the spread, budget, and deadline mix that fits.
arxiv-2509-07925:
Knowing when a language model should not be trusted is the problem addressed by Tuo Wang and 5 co-authors in a 2025 paper. In high-stakes settings, a confident wrong answer is dangerous. Many uncertainty methods only look at token probabilities, the model's step-by-step word choices, and miss how meaning is structured across a whole answer.

Their framework, GENUINE, builds graphs from dependency parse trees, which map grammatical links between words, and pools them at several levels. Supervised learning then sharpens the confidence estimate using semantic and structural relationships. Tests reported in the study support the approach. Better uncertainty estimates let users and downstream systems decide when to accept an answer, double-check it, or hand the task to a person.
arxiv-2509-08025:
Legal search means finding past cases that a new case legally follows from, a task called entailment. Hoang-Trung Nguyen leads a team of 8 reporting their COLIEE 2025 competition entry in a 2025 research paper. The NOWJ team entered all five tasks of the legal information competition. Their system blends classic ranking methods with modern embedding models and large language models.

For the entailment task, a two-stage retriever first filters cases with lexical and semantic tools. A large language model then re-ranks them with full context. That pipeline took first place in its task. The team also performed robustly in case retrieval, statute retrieval, textual entailment, and judgment prediction. Their report is a practical reference for hybrid legal AI, showing where traditional search still earns its place beside generative models.
arxiv-2509-08125:
Allison Youngblood and 11 co-authors sketch a two-dimensional map of hydrogen gas in our local interstellar neighbourhood in a 2025 astronomy paper. A full census of gas within one hundred parsecs is hard because the warm, partly ionised medium has few good tracers. Ultraviolet absorption lines toward individual nearby stars remain the primary probe, and their sampling is patchy.

Hydrogen column densities measured toward 164 stars are interpolated into maps for separate distance shells. Sky-averaged values inside each shell summarise how the gas thins or thickens with distance. The local medium shapes the radiation and particles reaching the solar system, and it is the foreground every nearby-star observation must see through, so even a rough map has wide use.
arxiv-2509-09525:
Jialiang Huang and 14 co-authors introduce TrEnv-X in 2025, a system that lets serverless functions share execution environments across different functions and machines. Serverless platforms promise elastic computing, yet each function normally sits in its own local, dedicated environment. That habit wastes memory and slows fresh starts, shrinking the very elasticity the model advertises.

TrEnv-X joins platform, operating system, and remote memory pools reached through CXL or RDMA links. Its sandboxes can be repurposed and shared, and memory templates let state be restored quickly from the pool. Variants for microVM agent workloads add browser sharing and a page cache bypass. Tests show large latency cuts and sizable memory savings in both settings.
arxiv-2509-09625:
Mendel Nguyen and 1 co-author revisit confinement in lattice gauge theory in a 2025 theoretical paper. Standard instanton calculations in Yang-Mills theory run into trouble because instanton sizes are unconstrained, sending a key quantity off to infinity in the infrared. The same style of problem appears with monopole loops in the simpler U(1) lattice theory when their weak long-range interactions are ignored.

Nguyen and his co-author argue those interactions are no accident: they come from expanding a shorter-range link between current segments. Keeping them in the ledger proves the strongly coupled theory matches a lattice abelian Higgs model, free of the divergence. A mass gap appears, and confinement follows from monopole condensation, giving a cleaner picture of the mechanism.
arxiv-2509-09825:
Saran Vijayan and 1 co-author explore smooth families of critical quantum systems in a 2025 condensed matter paper, the second in a series on surface topological criticality. A conformal manifold is a whole surface of interacting Hamiltonians that each stay scale invariant, an unusual luxury in two-dimensional many-body physics. The setting covers topological surfaces and two-dimensional bulks alike.

When the number of fermion colours grows without bound, such a manifold appears as an exact solution, with its own set of marginal knobs. At large but finite colour count, fluctuations bend the flow gently inside the manifold, creating familiar stable fixed points. Those points group together through a hidden symmetry, and the flow's direction tracks a rise in a certain entanglement measure.
arxiv-2509-10125:
Madina Kojanazarova and 4 co-authors teach a graph network to mimic soft tissue in a 2025 medical paper. The network also gauges the force pressing on the tissue. Trainees need tissue that bends in a lifelike way. Planners need to feel forces through a screen. Classic finite element work gives fine results. It is slow, though, and fussy to set up. A learned stand-in promises the same give for less cost.

Their model reads sparse points on the surface. Each point is tagged with a profile of the layers beneath it. Messages pass in a way that respects rotations. Tests used silicone and bone-like phantom data. Tests also used synthetic finite element runs. The model matched a plain graph baseline on easy cases. It beat that baseline clearly on rotated scenes. It also won when point density changed. Its speed suits live use.
arxiv-2509-10225:
An elephant random walk remembers its past, and Krishanu Maulik, Parthanil Roy, and Tamojit Sadhukhan study a version with two memory channels in this 2025 probability paper. In the classic walk, the next step depends on one earlier step chosen at random. Here two bunches of past steps, drawn independently, both help decide the move.

Earlier physics work predicted, from variance estimates, a double change of regime: plain diffusive spreading, then faster superdiffusive spreading, then ballistic motion. The authors prove those predictions rigorously, with some corrections, and they find more structure along the way. A mildly superdiffusive regime appears at one boundary, along with a new second-order transition, and they map the walk's behavior in detail across all regimes.
arxiv-2509-10325:
Markku Kuismin proposes a fresh route to building statistical tests in this solo 2025 paper, based on rejection sampling. The method is meant to be intuitive, easy to code, and workable in any dimension, an appealing mix when standard test design gets stuck on hard distributions.

Three examples show the range. The test compares group means for paired or independent samples, checks whether a mean vector equals a fixed target, and judges whether data could come from a stated population distribution. In simulations, its power lands close to the best known unbiased tests in the settings where those exist. The third example doubles as a strong goodness-of-fit test, suggesting one simple sampling idea can cover many everyday testing jobs.
arxiv-2509-10425:
Evan Borras and Milad Marvian design a quantum algorithm for simulating open quantum systems in this 2025 quantum computing paper. Open systems leak energy into their surroundings and obey the Lindblad master equation. The best known simulation methods need a number of queries that grows like time multiplied by logarithmic factors in the precision.

For closed-system simulation, the optimal cost is known to add those terms instead of multiplying them, and whether open systems allow the same saving was open. The authors show the additive cost is reachable for a large class of dissipative Lindblad equations. Their construction rests on quantum trajectories, the random individual paths whose average reproduces the open system's behavior, turning a physics picture of noisy evolution into an efficient algorithm.
arxiv-2509-11225:
Youzhi Liang and Eyan Noronha present MEMBOT, a robot control design for sensors that keep dropping out, in this 2025 paper. Real robots often lose their observations to noise, blockage, or outright failures. Standard reinforcement learning assumes the world is fully visible and falters in that setting.

MEMBOT separates two jobs: inferring what the world state probably is, and choosing actions. A belief encoder, built from state-space and recurrent parts, learns offline across many tasks to reconstruct hidden state from sequences of past views and actions. Task policies are then trained by imitation on top of those beliefs. On ten manipulation benchmarks from two suites, MEMBOT kept about four fifths of its best performance even when half the observations vanished.
arxiv-2509-11425:
Md Mubtasim Ahasan and eight co-authors enrich speech tokenization in this 2025 speech processing paper. Neural codecs turn speech into discrete tokens. Most capture surface sound only. What the speech means and its context are missed.

Their system is FuseCodec. It fuses three streams. One carries sound detail. One carries semantic features from self-supervised speech models. One carries context from pre-trained language models. Three techniques do the joining. Features fuse inside the encoder. Tokens get supervision from pooled global signals. Context and speech tokens align in a local time window. On LibriSpeech, the codec beat known rivals on four scores: transcript accuracy, sound quality as heard, clarity, and likeness of speaker. A sibling system shows the tokens serve speech synthesis too.
arxiv-2509-11625:
Muhammad H. Ashiq and three co-authors guard people from models run on the wrong person's data. This 2025 machine learning paper names the threat test-time privacy. Open-weight models let anyone predict on personal data. Masking outputs cannot stop an adversary. The weights themselves can yield the harmful prediction.

Their goal is high uncertainty on protected inputs. Accuracy elsewhere must stay intact. The algorithm optimizes a Pareto balance of the two. A certifiable variant gives formal guarantees with no convexity assumed. A tight bound marks the trade-off. In image tests, uncertainty on protected inputs grew at least threefold. Accuracy drops stayed marginal. Model publishers gain a practical protection tool.
arxiv-2509-11725:
Mengyuan Ma and four co-authors refine camera-guided beam tracking for millimeter-wave networks. This 2025 communications paper is a companion to their distillation work. Fast users and blockages make millimeter-wave beams hard to align. Cameras on infrastructure can see trouble coming.

Their attention-enhanced model reads past image sequences. Convolutional networks and gated recurrent units do the reading. A temporal attention step weighs which past moments matter most. The model predicts the best beam now and for six future slots. Top-five accuracy passed ninety percent throughout. The design reaches nearly all of the state of the art's performance. Its computing cost is a small fraction. Sensing and beam training overhead fall as well.
arxiv-2509-11825:
Nonlinear filtering tracks a hidden signal through noisy data. The math behind it rests on equations whose basic soundness can still be in doubt. Fabio Bugini and three co-authors take a fresh route in 2025. They mix rough path ideas with probability.

The trouble spots are clear. One is models where the noise in the signal and the noise in the data move together. Another is cases where the signal's rules depend on what is seen. Past attacks needed heavy machinery. Or they needed smoothness terms that grow with dimension. The new rough approach gives filtering equations that are well-posed under terms that do not depend on dimension. Randomizing them brings back the classic Zakai and Kushner-Stratonovich equations. A rough form of the Kalman-Bucy filter also falls out. It is driven by a new rough Riccati equation.
arxiv-2509-11925:
Cell surfaces behave like thin films of flowing fluid. So Patrik Knopf and one co-author build a model in 2025 with two viscous mixtures. One lives in the bulk, the other flows on its boundary, each with its own motion. Earlier models coupled the chemistry across the surface but left the surface itself without full fluid equations.

The derivation leans on local mass balance, local energy dissipation, and Lagrange multipliers, and stays thermodynamically consistent by construction. Inside, a Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system runs in the volume; a matching one runs on the boundary surface, motivated by the classic fluid mosaic picture of cell membranes. The hard analysis sits in a new bulk-surface Stokes system. Its eigenfunctions form the Galerkin basis. That basis is what lets the authors prove global weak solutions exist.
arxiv-2509-12025:
David J. Fernández-Bretón gives two new proofs that there are infinitely many prime numbers in a 2025 mathematics paper. Primes are whole numbers divisible only by one and themselves, and Euclid already proved their infinitude long ago. The novelty here lies in the tools used to reach that old result.

Both proofs draw on Folkman's theorem, a result in additive Ramsey theory about patterns forced inside large sets of numbers. The paper can also be read as using Hindman's theorem, a closely related result. Fernández-Bretón adds his arguments to a growing body of work that derives the infinitude of primes from Ramsey-type theorems. The value is a fresh route to a classic fact, linking number theory with combinatorics.
arxiv-2509-12125:
Trams share streets with people, bikes, and cars, so early warnings matter. Ondřej Valach and Ivan Gruber present RailSafeNet in a 2025 paper on visual scene understanding for tram safety. The system works from a single camera video and aims to flag intrusions onto the track before an accident happens.

RailSafeNet combines semantic segmentation, which labels each part of the image, object detection, and a rule-based distance assessor. It finds the rails, locates nearby objects, and judges risk by comparing projected distances with the standard rail gauge. On the RailSem19 dataset, its segmentation and detection models scored solidly on standard accuracy measures. The authors say the approach needs little new annotation and can warn drivers in real time.
arxiv-2509-12425:
P-adic Hodge theory compares two worlds of numbers through certain period rings, and one of them, the de Rham period ring, has long been defined by concrete construction. In a solo 2025 paper in French, Pierre Colmez gives that ring a defining property instead: it is the universal thickening of the completed algebraic closure of the p-adic numbers.

The statement generalizes. For a reduced affinoid algebra, the relative version of the ring over the completed algebraic closure of that algebra is its universal thickening with coefficients in the base. Universal properties of this kind let other constructions be checked against a single characterization rather than a recipe.
arxiv-2509-12725:
When a giant star erupts, its companion can catch part of the outflowing wind. It can feed on that wind. Bhawna Mukhija and one co-author simulate that wind accretion in 2025. The binary is massive, and it is in a high mass-loss episode. The primary was born at a hundred solar masses. The companion is hot, at thirty to eighty solar masses.

The orbits run from roughly fifteen months to just over three years. The share of the eruption the companion captures varies across them. It depends on the period and the mass ratio. The simulations compress that dependence into one analytic formula. They also locate the period where a different channel takes over. There, overflow through the Roche lobe beats wind capture. Accretion cools the companion's surface, but gently. It stays in balance.
arxiv-2509-13025:
Raul Zaharia, Dragoş Gavriluţ, and Gheorghiţă Mutu survey GView, a system for binary forensics, in a 2025 paper. GView is an open-source tool for forensic analysis. It works visually, and it uses AI to strengthen its reasoning. It began with the practical needs of the security industry in mind.

Since then the system has grown. Large AI models now sit inside it, lifting its reasoning as a case develops and smoothing the daily work of forensic analysts. It also reasons with logic, through predicates and rules. That reasoning covers two things at once: the files under study, and the actions of the person using the tool. The point is to offer better suggestions. The survey reports where GView stands today. Its open design is presented as a bridge between hands-on forensic practice and academic research.
arxiv-2509-13425:
Julian Chrisnanto, Salsabila Alia and two co-authors model predator-prey dynamics in 2025 with USPIL, a unified physics-informed learner across scales. Ecological systems mix time cycles with spatial patterns and must obey conservation. Past models split those facets.

One network handles both ordinary and partial equation forms. Automatic differentiation enforces physics, while adaptive weights balance data fit and physics fit. On Lotka-Volterra tests, time cycles track near perfectly and 2D spiral waves track closely. Conservation holds within half a percent. Inference runs many times faster than numeric solvers. Parameter discovery and sensitivity reads come built in.
arxiv-2509-13525:
Romain Hardy, Tyler Berzin, and Pranav Rajpurkar present ColonCrafter in a 2025 paper on depth maps for colonoscopy videos. To rebuild the inside of the colon in three dimensions, a system must gauge depth from a lone camera. Past models for endoscopy tend to wobble from frame to frame, which breaks that rebuild.

ColonCrafter is a diffusion model, a kind of AI that builds outputs step by step from noise. It learns the shape cues of the colon from made-up video clips, so its depth maps stay steady over time. A style shift step keeps the true shape while making real clinic clips look more like the training clips. On a standard test set, the model beat both general and scope-specific rivals when used with no fresh training, the authors report.
arxiv-2509-13625:
Bishnu Bhusal and seven co-authors present a privacy framework for large language models in a 2025 paper. Prompts can carry sensitive records, and attackers have shown they can extract such details. The goal is to generate useful synthetic text from private examples while bounding how much any single record can leak.

Their method runs inference separately on private records, then merges the per-token output distributions under differential privacy, a framework with worst-case guarantees on leakage, all without fine-tuning the model. A blending step mixes private and public inference to recover quality. On in-context learning tasks, where models learn from examples in the prompt, the approach beat earlier private methods while keeping its formal guarantees.
arxiv-2509-13725:
Md Sabbir Ahmed and eight co-authors predict momentary anxiety from smartwatch data in a 2025 health paper. Social anxiety rises and falls through the day, but most studies miss those swings, which are exactly what timely, personalized phone interventions would need to catch.

The team followed socially anxious college students for about nine days with a custom smartwatch system and seven daily check-ins on current anxiety. A base model pretrained on more than ten thousand days of outside heart-rate data was transferred and fine-tuned, then combined with trait measures in a meta-learner. The pipeline detected anxious states with balanced accuracy near sixty percent, and the same recipe beat prior work on a separate holdout dataset.
arxiv-2509-13925:
Alexander Felski, Andreas Fring, and Bethan Turner build ghost-free versions of the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator in a 2025 physics paper. That sixth-order oscillator is the classic test case for higher-derivative theories. Such theories usually suffer from ghosts, runaway negative-energy modes. A version without ghosts would rescue the model as a healthy physical system.

The team find a six-dimensional Abelian Lie algebra behind the model's flow. They derive a hierarchy of conserved Hamiltonians governed by several compatible Poisson structures. Together these form a complete tri-Hamiltonian formulation generating the same dynamics. Positive-definite ones appear inside that hierarchy. The team also map the model onto coupled second-order systems in three dimensions. They state explicit conditions for ghost-free equivalence. Interactions, they note, generally break that shared structure.
arxiv-2509-14325:
Kira Lund, Anders Johansen and Oscar Agertz follow dust grains through a simulated galaxy in 2025, from birth in stars to life in a planetary system. Dust drives galaxy change and planet building. Grains found in meteorites carry clues to which stars made them.

Tracer particles track dust inside a fluid simulation of a Milky Way like disc galaxy. Nearly half the grains lost very little mass to heat erosion in the space between stars. Grains from supernovae were partly broken apart more than grains from ageing giant stars. Changing the supernova remnant model altered survival strongly. Results help link grain samples in the lab back to low and high mass stars in the early Solar System.
arxiv-2509-14525:
Peng Zhao and Xiaoning Wu prove that trapped surfaces can form in a gravity theory coupled to a spinor field, in a 2025 mathematical physics paper. A trapped surface is a region where gravity focuses light so strongly that not even outward light can escape, signaling black hole formation. Their system couples Einstein gravity to a massless left-handed Weyl spinor.

The proof makes no symmetry assumptions, which makes the result much harder and more general. Zhao and Wu build a semi-global solution using a double null foliation, slicing spacetime by two families of light fronts. They show that focusing of gravitational waves together with the spinor flux forces a trapped surface to appear. The result extends trapped-surface formation to matter described by spinor fields.
arxiv-2509-14925:
Konrad Nowosadko, Franco Ruggeri, and Ahmad Terra make reinforcement learning explain itself in a 2025 paper on mobile network resource allocation. Deep reinforcement learning performs well but hides its reasoning, which slows adoption in critical systems. Operators need to trust why a controller assigns spectrum and power the way it does.

The authors build the policy of a PPO agent from a self-explaining neural network, which produces local explanations as part of its own computation. A new aggregation method then rolls those local explanations into global ones operators can inspect. On the resource allocation task, performance lands within a small margin of the best deep learning method and well ahead of the deployed heuristic. The global explanations also agree strongly with two established explanation tools, supporting self-explaining policies for high-stakes control.
arxiv-2509-15125:
Arjun Berera and five co-authors build a warm inflation model from heterotic string ingredients in a 2025 cosmology paper. Warm inflation keeps the early Universe hot during its rapid expansion, thanks to friction between the inflaton field and other matter. Their model has two fields, an axion and a dilaton-like scalar, with mixed kinetic terms inherited from the string construction.

Gauge interactions create dissipation and thermal corrections acting on both fields. Numerical exploration uncovers regimes that behave like single-field inflation and others with genuine two-field dynamics. Workable solutions run mostly along the axion direction, while thermal effects block sustained dilaton-driven inflation across most of the parameter space. Near the end of inflation the dilaton can briefly matter. The dynamics thus naturally favor axion-driven warm inflation.
arxiv-2509-15325:
Ryan S. Yeung, David G. Black, and Septimiu E. Salcudean refine remote ultrasound by updating the patient model with live measurements in a 2025 medical robotics paper. Teleoperated ultrasound could bring expert scanning to remote communities, but sonographers need believable force feedback to press the probe correctly. Communication delays make direct feedback loops impractical, so the remote side works from an internal model of the patient.

A point cloud of the patient's surface is transmitted compactly and converted into a voxel volume carrying a potential field, from which contact forces and torques are estimated. The new method folds measured positions, forces, and torques back into that field model as scanning proceeds. A patient model that learns during the exam should make the sonographer's felt forces track the real contact more transparently.
arxiv-2509-16125:
Life-saving drugs sit at the cross of two forces: a patent holder with sole selling rights, and insurers who decide what care gets covered. Delia Coculescu, Maximilian Janisch, and Thomas Lehéricy model this clash as a step-by-step game. The maker sets a price, the insurer sets a premium, and people then choose whether to insure and whether to buy care if they fall ill.

People differ in how likely they think illness is and in the most they would pay. The authors prove that stable outcomes exist and that adding an insurer always lifts maker profits. Prices and uptake, though, can rise or fall, and insurance can even shrink access.
arxiv-2509-16225:
Fiber materials serve in fields from design to medicine, and their strength depends in part on how often fibers touch each other. Alex Keilmann, Claudia Redenbach, and Francois Willot extend a known fiber packing model so the number of fiber contacts can be set directly. They add an extra force to the packing process that pushes fibers into more contact.

Tests confirm the new packing hits its target values with good accuracy. Contact counts even rose past values theory had suggested as limits. More faithful contact counts could sharpen digital twin tests of how fiber systems bear heat and load.
arxiv-2509-16325:
Most AI chat tools demand your full attention, but a quieter style is possible: an agent that listens in and helps only when useful. Andrew Zhu and Chris Callison-Burch survey this overhearing style of agent, the first review to treat it as its own approach. Such agents might fetch facts during a medical visit or prep materials while teachers plan, without breaking the flow.

The survey builds a taxonomy of overhearing tasks from prior agent work and user studies. It lists best practices for builders and maps open gaps. The frame helps researchers design help that stays in the background until it earns its moment.
arxiv-2509-16425:
Simulating a whole neutrino detector in fine detail is the surest way to know what it can catch. Abigail Bishop, Alan Salcedo Gomez, and Marco Stein Muzio present updated simulations of the Askaryan Radio Array, five stations in South Pole ice that listen for cascades from the highest-energy neutrinos. Their work counts secondary particles and events seen by several stations at once, which older estimates handled loosely.

Those extras make up a large share of the detector's reach. The team aims to extend the study toward judging how visible such events would be in a real search. That guides how future hunts should be designed.
arxiv-2509-16525:
Anna Mazhar and Sainyam Galhotra tackle a trust problem in a 2025 paper on machine unlearning. Unlearning should erase the effect of some training records from a model. It should do so without full retraining. The hard part is checking that the effect is truly gone, even when it hides in linked features.

Their tool uses causal graphs and fuzz testing to hunt for leftover influence. On two benchmark networks, it ranks leftover effects with far higher accuracy than older checks. Older checks both passed bad models and flagged good ones. On real census data, the tool found effects that survived retraining. Such checks matter when people ask for their data to be removed.
arxiv-2509-16625:
Lorenzo Guerra and co-authors hunt intruders in network traffic in a 2025 security paper. Attacks change fast, and labeled examples of new attacks are scarce. Graphs can capture how hosts and flows link together. Prior graph methods, though, learned features apart from the hunt itself, which dulled their value.

Their system, GraphIDS, learns features and detection in one joined process. Features are tuned for the hunt from the start. On varied traffic benchmarks, scores came close to perfect on key measures. That strength held across datasets with different mixes of attacks. A joined design could help security teams spot fresh attacks sooner.
arxiv-2509-16825:
Jin Lee and co-authors build a neural operator with built-in clarity in a 2025 paper. Operators learn maps between functions, such as from a load to a field. A popular operator works in the frequency domain alone. That choice fails when behavior shifts from place to place. Their model, KANO, uses both frequency and space bases.

Tests show KANO handles place-based operators where the older model fails. On a quantum task, it rebuilt Hamiltonians in clean symbolic form. Its answers matched the truth to high precision. Its state error beat the rival by orders of magnitude. Clear, exact outputs could help science teams trust learned operators.
arxiv-2509-17525:
Matthew Burn and seven co-authors followed the radio afterglow of a star torn apart by a black hole. Their 2025 arXiv paper reports six years of monitoring of the tidal disruption event AT2019azh. Radio waves from such events reveal the outflow the black hole launched and the gas around it, but late-time radio behavior is rarely observed.

The team's data span well over a thousand days after the disruption. At each epoch they fit a physical synchrotron model to the radio spectrum, then model the fading as the outflow slows into the Sedov-Taylor regime. The fits pin down the density profile of the gas near the black hole, which comes out unusually flat. Unlike some events, AT2019azh shows no late re-brightening across the six years. A single ejection explains the whole curve, the authors find.
arxiv-2509-18025:
Gilles Bareilles and 4 co-authors present deep learning as the craft of building tame maths objects. Their 2025 note is an overview, not a new result. Tame geometry, also called o-minimality, studies shapes that avoid wild, endless wiggles.

Step by step, the note brings in the tools of that field. It then shows how they yield proof that a common training method settles, even when the task is rough and not convex. The tame frame fits many AI systems well, the authors argue. The note aims to give readers a shared set of ideas across three fields.
arxiv-2509-18125:
Harsha Koduri builds a learning system to assign nurses to patients in a hospital. The 2025 paper deals with tight staffing, where skill mix, patient need, tiredness, and care continuity all pull at once. Rule-based plans tend to miss that live, multi-limit mix.

The system, NurseSchedRL, learns by trial in a sim with real-like nurse and patient data. Masks block any assign that breaks hard limits, while attention weighs skill, fatigue, and place. A known policy method trains the agent. In sims, it beat rule plans and free learning on speed of assign, skill fit, and rest.
arxiv-2509-18425:
Vision language models read charts well when the charts are clean. Philip Wootaek Shin and four co-authors test what happens when charts are flawed. Their 2025 paper checks three top models on corrupted and partly hidden charts. Real charts often carry distortions, and real questions demand more than fact matching.

Accuracy dropped sharply under corruption or blocked regions. Errors grew more common: made-up values, misread trends, and mixed-up entities. Models stayed overconfident and gave smooth but baseless explanations. The team built CHART NOISe, a data set mixing damaged charts with exam-style questions. It adds a twist: models often contradict themselves when asked to confirm, then deny, the same claim. The paper also offers starter fixes like quality filtering. The testbed aims to make chart reading more robust.
arxiv-2509-18525:
The Sun sits inside a vast, thin bubble of hot gas carved by ancient supernova blasts. Guang-Ya Zeng, Guang-Xing Li, Bing-Qiu Chen, Ji-Xuan Zhou, and Martin G. H. Krause trace how that Local Bubble has expanded. Their 2025 paper uses motion data for young stars from the Gaia mission. Young star groups carry the imprint of the bubble's growth.

The team grouped young stars in three dimensions and found three associations with a wiggle-like velocity pattern. Their distances run from about 109 to 176 parsecs. Their outward speeds dip and then rise again with distance. That pattern matches a prediction for a recent re-acceleration of the bubble by a fresh supernova blast. The result supports the view of the Local Bubble as a still-evolving structure. Its growth shapes star birth nearby.
arxiv-2509-18625:
Symmetric polynomials carry operators that act on them like generalized derivatives. Houcine Ben Dali studies one such operator, a Jack version of the super nabla operator, in this 2025 paper. The operator was recently introduced for a rival polynomial family, the Macdonald polynomials. Ben Dali asks what its Jack analog looks like in a concrete basis.

He proves the operator has a differential form in the power-sum basis, built from two known operator families. The result flows from a broader formula for an operator that encodes the structure constants of Jack characters. A key step shows that one operator family, plus a rescaled version of the other, forms a Heisenberg algebra. The proof also leans on a fresh set of differential equations for that broader operator. The work links several active lines in algebraic combinatorics.
arxiv-2509-18725:
Divergences measure how far apart two probability patterns sit, and quantum versions multiply fast. Erkka Haapasalo studies the whole set of such measures in this 2025 paper. He works in a generalized algebraic setting that covers classical and quantum, single and multivariate cases. A special subset, called the test spectrum, turns out to organize the rest.

He shows the remaining divergences are captured as barycentres, weighted averages, of the test spectrum. The extreme points of the convex sets involved sit inside that spectrum, with few exceptions. For classical multivariate divergences, he characterizes the spectrum in full. The quantum case is wilder. Nearly all quantum divergences proposed so far land in the spectrum and are extreme. That, he argues, means quantum divergence variety is real: the proposals are genuinely independent, not rewordings of one idea.
arxiv-2509-18925:
Pierre Rouchon, writing alone, studies a quantum system made of a qubit linked to a cavity, a small space that traps light. The pair is watched through homodyne or heterodyne detection, which turns faint light signals into a stream of measured values. A stochastic master equation tracks how the state of the pair changes as those signals arrive.

Rouchon proves that the state settles, at a fast rate, onto a slow surface of states. That surface can be described by a simpler fake qubit, driven by the same input and output signals. Each part of the real system, qubit or cavity, can then be read off from the fake qubit through a fixed kind of map. The setup avoids flaws found in some past accounts, and it extends to larger atoms linked to many cavity modes.
arxiv-2509-19125:
Scientific papers pile up faster than anyone can organize them by hand. Kun Zhu and five co-authors build taxonomies, tree-like maps of topics, for research fields with help from large language models. Older methods cluster papers blindly or just ask a model to draft the tree, and both routes give trees that are muddled or too coarse. Their framework first has the model name the key aspects of each paper, such as method, dataset, and evaluation.

Papers are then summarized aspect by aspect, encoded, and clustered along each aspect to grow a coherent hierarchy. The team also built a benchmark of 156 expert-made taxonomies covering about 11,600 papers, the first naturally labeled dataset for this task. In experiments their method beat prior approaches on coherence, granularity, and how interpretable the trees are. The work points toward literature maps that stay useful as fields grow.
arxiv-2509-19225: Richard J. Mathar, writing alone, works out how one family of special polynomials can be rewritten in terms of another. Zernike polynomials are the standard language for describing distortions in optical systems, like telescope mirrors and the eye. Chebyshev polynomials are a simpler family prized for computation. The manuscript gives closed formulas for the coefficients that convert Zernike polynomials into sums of Chebyshev ones, for a few low cases. For larger cases it supplies a five-term recurrence that builds the coefficients step by step.
arxiv-2509-19325:
How much bad training data can a language model tolerate before it turns harmful? Jian Ouyang and two co-authors fine-tune a GPT-4o model on mixtures of correct and incorrect data, from ten to ninety percent correct. The wrong data come in two flavors, obviously wrong and subtly wrong, across coding, finance, health, and law. Bad data is known to cause emergent misalignment, where a model produces harmful or deceptive outputs far from the training topic.

Even modest contamination, ten to twenty-five percent wrong, badly damaged skill in the target domain, though moral alignment held up better. Models needed at least half their data correct to recover strong performance consistently. Even then they rarely matched the untouched base model, which showed near-perfect alignment out of the box. The authors warn that sloppy fine-tuning data carries a heavy cost in high-stakes fields.
arxiv-2509-19425:
Marcel R. R. Hughes and one co-author propose a new counting tool for a supersymmetric theory central to string theory's dictionary between gravity and quantum fields. The D1-D5 conformal field theory describes microstates of certain black holes. Standard indices, like the modified elliptic genus, go blind below the black hole threshold, returning trivial answers exactly where fine detail is wanted. Their new index is a one-parameter generalization that keeps that detail.

The formulation rests on a fresh treatment of symmetric orbifold theories using Schur-Weyl duality. Protection of the index is argued from the nature of exactly marginal operators in these theories. Below threshold, the index matches precisely between the gravity and field theory sides. Above threshold, it decomposes black hole microstates into distinct sectors that the old index cannot see. The authors offer it as a sharper probe of microstate structure.
arxiv-2509-19625:
Finding similar time series fast is easier when each series is shrunk to a short binary code. Juan Manuel Perez and four co-authors improve deep hashing, where a network learns those codes from labeled data. Turning smooth network outputs into bits loses information. Their fix maps data onto a sphere, where each class forms a directional cluster with a known shape.

A new loss term pushes those class clusters apart by the widest margin it can. That wider margin should keep meaning intact through the bit conversion. The authors test the model on standard time series tasks. Better codes mean quicker search in huge archives of signals, from health monitors to industrial sensors. The work refines a basic tool of data mining rather than replacing it.
arxiv-2509-19825:
Topological phases of matter hide in band structures, sorted by symmetry classes with discrete labels. Ken Shiozaki constructs a missing label for three-dimensional systems in class CI. Two symmetries frame the class: parity-time and parity-particle-hole. The first allows a real Berry connection, from which a spin-Chern-Simons action can be built.

The second symmetry pins that action to two values, yielding a clean two-valued invariant. The invariant adds across stacked systems and matches a known index where a simpler factorization exists. Lattice models show it separates phases that older indices cannot tell apart. A complete periodic table of topological phases needs every such label filled in. This work closes one cell of that table.
arxiv-2509-20125:
Matthew Teasdale and Dimitris Stamatellos wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on planet formation. Some giant planets orbit both stars of a binary pair on wide paths. They may have formed when a disc of gas around the pair broke into clumps. The paper asks how light such a disc can be and still break up.

The authors ran three sets of simulations with a smoothed particle hydrodynamics code called SEREN. One set used discs around a single star, and two used discs around binary pairs. They varied the binary separation, mass ratio, and orbit shape. Single-star discs needed a disc mass near a third of the star mass to fragment. Realistic binary discs fragmented at clearly lower masses. The authors conclude that giant planets can form this way more easily around binaries than around single stars.
arxiv-2509-20225:
Hui Wang and five co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on recommendation systems. Modern recommenders blend text, images, and other signals to model what users like. That blend also brings redundant and irrelevant information, which can hurt accuracy. Earlier methods either fused everything directly or split it with rigid designs.

Their framework, MRdIB, first squeezes the inputs through an information bottleneck that filters task-irrelevant noise. It then splits what remains into three parts: signals unique to one source, signals shared across sources, and signals that emerge only in combination. Separate learning goals keep each part in its role. The cleaned representations feed the recommendation model. Experiments across several strong models and three benchmark datasets showed broad gains. The authors present the framework as a versatile add-on for multimodal recommendation.
arxiv-2509-20425:
Wormholes sitting inside dark matter halos would bend passing waves in distinctive ways. Abdullah Guvendi and four co-authors compute those scalar-wave signatures in a 2025 arXiv paper. They start from a general static, spherical wormhole shape. The wave equation is recast into a form like the Schrodinger equation.

The rewriting separates the roles of gravitational redshift, spatial curvature, and angular momentum. An effective refractive index emerges that depends on position and frequency, encoding the throat shape and halo. The authors test three halo models, from the standard Navarro-Frenk-White profile to a condensate model. Near the throat, some wave modes are suppressed or become evanescent, fading instead of propagating. High-frequency waves behave like light rays, while low-frequency modes localize strongly. The framework is exact rather than perturbative, a first for this setting.
arxiv-2509-21025:
Deguang Zhong proves a theorem about well-behaved mappings on an unusual class of spaces in a solo-authored 2025 mathematics paper. The setting is Carnot groups of H-type, step-two geometries that appear in analysis on metric spaces. The mappings are quasiregular, a higher-dimensional cousin of quasiconformal maps.

Theorems of Reshetnyak type are prized because they certify the good analytic behavior of such mappings. Zhong establishes such a theorem for quasiregular values on these Carnot groups. The paper is brief and purely theoretical, extending a classical line of results from Euclidean analysis into sub-Riemannian geometry.
