Specialists in geometric function theory are its audience, particularly those tracking how far Euclidean regularity theory carries into Carnot group settings.
arxiv-2509-21125:
Voice assistants may answer the same question differently depending on whether the speaker sounds male or female. Junhyuk Choi and five co-authors build a dataset to expose that behavior in a 2025 paper, currently under review. They call the phenomenon acoustic-based gender differentiation in speech-aware language models.

Their dataset holds more than nine thousand speech samples in three categories: gender-independent, gender-stereotypical, and gender-dependent questions. Evaluating the LLaMA-Omni family, they find a paradox. Overall answers look near-identical across genders, yet the pattern is far from unbiased. On stereotypical questions, all tested models lean consistently toward male-oriented responses. The dataset gives developers a systematic way to audit voice systems for gender effects hiding under surface similarity.
arxiv-2509-21425:
Pole placement is a classic control design task: choose feedback so a system poles land at target values. Michael Sebek extends that task to quaternionic systems in a 2025 paper. Quaternions extend complex numbers and arise in attitude control. Single input, controllable, linear time invariant models are the setting. Companion forms and the Ackermann formula are the main tools.

Sebek defines a companion polynomial that annihilates its companion matrix. Spectra are described through right eigenvalue similarity classes, a quaternionic subtlety. Coefficient matching design is proved in controllable coordinates. A coordinate free Ackermann gain formula follows for real target polynomials. Scope and limits are stated plainly. Short cases show correctness, useful use, and numerical simplicity of the method. The gain can be set in closed form for real targets.
arxiv-2509-21625:
Editing audio from a plain description of the desired result is beyond current generative tools. Zitong Lan and 2 co-authors introduce a stereo editing framework in a 2025 paper. Past models need template like instructions and work only in mono. Declarative editing, where users state the outcome and leave operations to the system, is the target. Their system is called SmartDJ.

An audio language model decomposes a high level instruction into atomic edit operations. Adding, removing, or spatially relocating sound events are examples. A latent diffusion model then executes those operations on stereo audio. A data synthesis pipeline produces paired examples for training. Reasoning plus generation, the authors argue, unlocks flexible editing for immersive media and sound design.
arxiv-2509-21725:
Takuya Kanayama, Yuki Ito, Tomoyuki Tamura, and Masayuki Karasuyama tackle a hard kind of optimization problem in this 2025 paper. A bilevel problem hides one optimization task inside another. The inner task's best answer becomes a rule the outer task must obey. The authors study cases where both tasks are costly black boxes with no known formula.

They propose a Bayesian method that weighs what can be learned about both levels at once. One shared score measures the gain for the upper and the lower problem together. They also give a cheaper way to estimate that score in practice. Tests on standard benchmark problems show the method works well, and the paper was accepted at the UAI 2026 conference.
arxiv-2509-21825:
Data science work pulls files in many formats and often ends with an open question, not a single number. Jaehyun Nam and five co-authors present DS-STAR in this 2025 paper, an agent built for that kind of work. Earlier agents stumble on messy real workflows that span many sources. DS-STAR is designed to plan in steps, check its own work, and keep going.

The agent processes and joins data across mixed formats without a fixed script. It also goes beyond short answers, writing full research reports for open-ended questions. On four benchmarks, DS-STAR reached the best results, with the widest lead on hard questions that need many files at once. Its reports were also judged better than the strongest rival's in most head-to-head comparisons. The paper frames the design as a step toward agents that handle real analysis work end to end.
arxiv-2509-22125:
Ana Gjorgjevikj and five co-authors present FoodSEM, a language model specialized for food texts, in this 2025 paper. Its task is named-entity linking: tying food mentions in text to entries in formal food ontologies. General-purpose models and existing food systems both do this poorly, the authors note. FoodSEM was fine-tuned as an open-source model and links mentions to several ontologies, including FoodOn, a medical vocabulary, and the Hansard taxonomy.

The model reached state-of-the-art results on the task, with top scores on some ontologies and data sets. Comparisons against prompted versions of general models, with zero, one, or a few examples, underline the fine-tuned model's lead. Beyond the model itself, the team publishes food-annotated corpora recast in an instruction format suited to fine-tuning and evaluation.
arxiv-2509-22425:
Ke Xue and 5 co-authors pull one voice at a time from a noisy mix, guided by the speaker's face. Video cues like lip motion help, but most methods use them in a fixed, shallow way. Their network, CSFNet, works in two passes. A first pass makes a rough clean voice track. That track then goes back, with the video, into a speech reading model.

The loop yields richer meaning cues for a second, finer pass. Extra blocks encode who the speaker is and track sound patterns at several time spans. Tests on three standard sets and two noisy sets reached top scores, with clear gains from the loop.
arxiv-2509-22525:
Fabian Dawel and 14 co-authors keep an aluminum ion clock cold while it ticks. Single-ion optical clocks reach superb accuracy, but they need over a week of averaging to match it in precision. Longer probe times help, yet trap heating shifts the tick rate. The team cools the clock ion during probing, using a co-trapped calcium ion and a transparency effect.

The aluminum ion stays near its ground state of motion for any probe length. That holds the motion shift tiny and steady. The cooling light adds its own small shift, which the team says can be pinned down far better. The trick should transfer to other ion clocks and allow seconds-long probes.
arxiv-2509-22625:
Gustavo Jasso and Fernando Muro extend a correspondence between two classes of algebras to a Calabi-Yau setting. Their earlier work matched certain differential graded algebras with Frobenius algebras that repeat after a fixed twist. The match ran through cluster tilting objects in derived categories. This sequel proves a variant for algebras with a bimodule right Calabi-Yau structure, a symmetry between a structure and its dual.

A new cohomology theory supplies the key tool. It holds the obstructions to building minimal bimodule structures and to their uniqueness. As an application, they give the first known algebraic triangulated category with a triangulated Calabi-Yau structure that cannot be lifted to any bimodule version on its enhancements.
arxiv-2509-23225:
Tongue ultrasound helps speech research, but tracing the tongue contour live is hard. Alisher Myrgyyassov and 5 co-authors built UltraUNet for real-time segmentation. The images are noisy, variable, and costly to process. Their encoder-decoder stays light with squeeze-and-excitation blocks. Group normalization keeps small batches stable, and summed skip links cut memory.

The system runs at two hundred fifty frames per second. Ultrasound-specific augmentations, like blur and denoise simulation, harden training. Eight data sets tested accuracy and robustness. Single-set overlap scores were strong, and cross-set scores held up well. Uses span clinics, speech science, and motor disorder analysis.
arxiv-2509-23325:
Fine-tuning a non-robust pre-trained model for both accuracy and attack resistance can quietly fail. Jonas Ngnawé and 7 co-authors name that failure suboptimal transfer. A robust objective early in training blocks task adaptation, they find. In hard settings the result can be an outright transfer failure. Their fix is Epsilon-Scheduling, which ramps perturbation strength over training.

A new metric, expected robustness, scores performance across perturbation levels at test time. Six pre-trained models and five data sets frame the experiments. The schedule prevented suboptimal transfer across configurations. Expected robustness rose consistently with its use. The work opens the huge stock of non-robust models to robust tuning.
arxiv-2509-23525:
Spotting privacy risks in a new AI product is hard for builders with no privacy training. Hao-Ping Lee and 9 co-authors present Privy, a tool that walks practitioners through structured privacy impact checks. It helps them name the risks in a product concept and pick fitting fixes. A formative study with eleven practitioners shaped two versions: one powered by a language model, one built on templates.

Twenty-four practitioners tested the versions, and thirteen privacy experts graded the results. Assessments made with Privy were judged high quality, with apt risks and fixes named. The language-model version strengthened the effect. Users rated Privy useful and usable, and their comments show it easing blocks in awareness, drive, and skill.
arxiv-2509-23725:
Hard medical questions need more than facts; they need reasoning that can be checked step by step. Siqi Ma and 7 co-authors propose MedLA, a multi-agent framework where each agent builds its logic as an explicit tree. The trees follow syllogistic triads: a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion. That shape makes each inference transparent and lets agents align their premises directly.

Agents then discuss over several rounds, guided by a graph, comparing trees and fixing errors until they agree. On the tough MedDDx benchmark and standard medical question sets, MedLA beat static role-based systems and single agents. It also scaled across open and commercial model backbones.
arxiv-2509-23825:
Electric circuits move charge from sources to sinks; a new generative method moves probability the same way. Alexander Kolesov and 3 co-authors propose ECD2G, which generates discrete data by analogy with current flow. Samples from the source distribution act as current inputs, and target samples as outputs. A neural network learns the currents, which represent how probability should flow along circuit pathways.

To generate, one samples from the source and transports the samples along the learned pathways. The authors prove the transfer between distributions is guaranteed. Proof-of-concept experiments illustrate the method. They present the work as a first bridge between electrical engineering theory and discrete data generation.
arxiv-2509-23925:
A sterile neutrino with its own scalar partner could leave fingerprints in both gravitational waves and colliders. Qi Bi and 4 co-authors propose a complete extension of the Standard Model built on that idea. A gauge-singlet scalar gains a vacuum value, gives the sterile neutrino a Majorana mass through a seesaw, and mixes with the Higgs. With strong enough mixing, the early universe undergoes a strong first-order electroweak phase transition, radiating gravitational waves that observatories might catch.

The same mixing boosts sterile neutrino pair production at colliders through Higgs and scalar exchange. Small active-sterile mixing makes those neutrinos long-lived, so they decay at displaced vertices, a signature searches can target alongside the waves.
arxiv-2509-24325:
Free-viewpoint video of a dynamic scene is heavy to rebuild and store frame by frame. Jiaye Fu and 6 co-authors built ReCon-GS, a streaming framework based on Gaussian scene parts anchored at several levels. Anchors are placed in a density-adaptive way to capture how geometry deforms between frames, splitting motion into coarse-to-fine pieces.

A reconfiguration strategy rebuilds the anchor hierarchy on demand while keeping time consistency inside each level. A storage-aware step adjusts anchor density to trade fidelity against memory. On three data sets, training ran faster than rivals and synthesis quality rose. At equal quality, memory needs fell by over half against leading methods.
arxiv-2509-24525:
Simulating an open quantum system in many dimensions drowns in integrals over space and time. Hongfei Zhan and 2 co-authors attack both costs in the multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett model, a standard model of a system coupled to an environment. They follow the reduced density matrix as it evolves in real time.

A reformulated series plus a low-rank approximation halves the spatial dimension. A frozen Gaussian approximation then cuts the time-side integrals down to one and two dimensions, no matter the series order. Combined, the tricks form an efficient algorithm. Numerical tests, including a two-dimensional double-slit case, verify that the savings keep accuracy.
arxiv-2510-00025:
Nagai presents a full dual-basis picture of the classical analytic Bernoulli functions, modeled on the position and momentum descriptions of quantum mechanics. With the two sides joined by a transform playing the Fourier role. On the Hurwitz side the basis foregrounds even zeta values, while on the Clausen side odd zeta values come forward. And both families are also generated by one and the same Heisenberg-Weyl ladder operator in the note.

The bridge between the bases is the Poisson-Lerch transform. And the resulting explicit orthogonality relations isolate the even zeta values and the odd Dirichlet beta values in strictly separated channels of the system, with no mixing between them. Low-degree examples carefully confirm the rational evaluations the theory predicts, and appendices further connect the picture with selector kernels, Poisson summation, and oscillator analogies from quantum mechanics in umbral calculus.
arxiv-2510-00225:
Yue Meng, Fei Chen, and Chuchu Fan published this 2025 paper on teaching robots to follow timed instructions. Signal Temporal Logic is a formal language for tasks like visiting spots in order before deadlines. Its rewards are sparse and its demands stretch over long horizons, which defeats standard reinforcement learning. Their method, TGPO, breaks each logic formula into timed subgoals plus standing constraints.

A high-level planner proposes time budgets for the subgoals, guided by a learned critic. A low-level policy then learns to hit each subgoal with a dense, stage-wise reward. At run time the system samples several time plans and picks the most promising one. Across five test worlds, from navigation to a quadruped robot, TGPO beat the best baselines clearly. The average gain in task success was about thirty-two percent in the reported experiments.
arxiv-2510-00425:
Rishi Veerapaneni and eleven colleagues published this 2025 robotics paper proposing a shared protocol for fleets of unlike robots. Tomorrow's sites may mix dozens of robots from different makers, each with its own planner. The coordination problem is getting them through shared space without collisions. The authors recast Conflict-Based Search, a known planning algorithm, as a communication protocol.

The protocol asks each robot only for one planning function that respects given space-time constraints. A central planner then stitches individual paths into a collision-free whole. The robot's own solver can be almost anything behind that interface. The team demonstrates heuristic search, sampling, optimization, diffusion, and reinforcement learning planners working together. Tasks need not be simple start-to-goal trips, either, since the protocol accepts general independent jobs. The proposal reads like a standards pitch for the coming multi-vendor robot workplace.
arxiv-2510-00825:
Xu reports on the P371 experiment at CERN in this short 2025 arXiv paper about polarized antiprotons. Physicists routinely use polarized proton beams, but no practical source of polarized antiprotons exists yet. One simple hope is that antiprotons are born already polarized during production. An earlier experiment, P349, looked for that effect but gathered too little data for a firm answer.

P371 revisits the question at the CERN PS T11 beam line with an upgraded detector and longer beam time. The team will measure elastic antiproton-proton scattering, a well-understood reaction that reveals polarization through its asymmetry. They expect roughly a million scattering events within a few weeks of running. That sample should detect polarization down to the few-percent level, giving the first direct test of the production idea.
arxiv-2510-01025:
Tiblias and four co-authors at TU Darmstadt introduce a method for mapping how language models arrange concepts inside their hidden layers, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A leading idea says models encode each concept as a direction or structured shape in that space. Earlier studies found such shapes one feature at a time, by hand. Their tool, Supervised Multi-Dimensional Scaling, discovers these feature manifolds automatically for any model.

Using time reasoning as a test case, they found features forming circles, lines, and clusters. Days of the week, for example, sit on a ring, which matches how the concept itself cycles. The shapes stayed stable across model families and sizes, and they shifted in sensible ways when context changed. Probing experiments showed the models actively use these structures while reasoning, not merely store them.
arxiv-2510-01525:
Kim and Luedtke sharpen the math used to certify that tiny input changes cannot fool a binarized neural network. These networks store weights and activations as single bits, which suits cheap hardware. Checking their robustness becomes an integer programming problem, but the standard form is slow because its bounds are loose.

A new linear objective handles multi-class checks in a single solve instead of many. Fresh inequalities, drawn layer by layer from the network's own structure, tighten the problem further. Tests verified networks against larger input changes than earlier integer methods could manage in the time allowed. Stronger certificates support trusting compact models. Big loose constants in the old form were the main source of the slack. Recursive structure means each layer hands the next a tighter puzzle. Solvers either prove robustness or exhibit a fooling input. No middle verdict exists.
arxiv-2510-01725:
Rea and a large international team report on five distant exoplanet candidates in this 2025 astronomy paper. The candidates came from the TESS space telescope, and each orbits its star in more than a month. Long-period planets are hard to study because their transits are rare. The team followed all five with ASTEP, a telescope in Antarctica, plus other ground facilities.

Careful modeling and validation sorted real planets from impostors. Three candidates passed as genuine warm planets. Two are warm Saturns, one crossing its star every 104 days and one every 33 days or so. The third is a warm sub-Neptune with a period near 53 days. The other two candidates turned out to be eclipsing pairs of stars instead. Warm planets keep clearer traces of their formation, so these finds help fill a sparse region of planet catalogs.
arxiv-2510-02125:
Beger and six co-authors ask whether AI models truly reason abstractly or just mimic it in this 2025 paper. A top reasoning model recently beat human accuracy on the ARC-AGI benchmark. The team probed that claim with ConceptARC, varying text versus visual input, Python tool access, and reasoning effort. They also graded the plain-language rules models wrote to explain their answers.

With text input and medium reasoning effort, the best models matched or beat human accuracy. Their explanations told a weaker story. In only about half the text cases did the stated rules capture the intended abstraction. The rest leaned on superficial patterns that would not generalize. Visual input exposed a far bigger gap, with models performing dramatically worse than in text. Oddly, models often generated correct rules they then failed to apply. Accuracy alone, the authors warn, overstates how human-like current abstract reasoning really is.
arxiv-2510-02225:
Beck, Elmarassy, Sabbagh, Kreps, and Smith forecast flavor physics with polarized bottom baryons at a future collider in this 2025 paper. The FCC-ee would produce trillions of Z bosons in electron-positron collisions. Lambda-b baryons from those decays arrive polarized, unlike their unpolarized LHC counterparts. Polarization unlocks a much larger set of angular observables in their decays.

The team ran a toy angular analysis of the decay chain into a Lambda, a proton, a pion, and two muons. Simulated events used the IDEA detector concept and the full expected Z sample. Individual observables will not dramatically beat LHC precision on their own. Their sheer number, though, tightens global fits for new-physics effects across the decay. Polarization is the resource that makes the program possible. The study maps where a lepton collider's flavor reach genuinely exceeds a hadron machine's.
arxiv-2510-02325:
Shehab presents a prototype health assistant built from cooperating AI agents with privacy first. His 2025 paper describes a single investigator project. The system uses the Model Context Protocol to coordinate agents. Separate agents handle symptom checks, medication ideas, and appointments. A dedicated privacy layer guards every step. Role based access limits who sees which data. Field level encryption protects stored records. Tamper evident logs record each access for audit. The design tracks major rules like HIPAA and Canadian privacy law.

Patients can interact in English, French, or Arabic. The system explains its diagnostic reasoning openly. Shehab stresses that the platform is a research prototype. It is not a certified medical device. The point is to prove a design pattern. Agentic help, language access, and compliance can coexist. Clinics and startups could build on that pattern.
arxiv-2510-02425:
Wang, Isola, and Cheung show that simple prompts can wake latent senses in text only models. Their 2025 paper tests language models trained without any images or sound. Reading text still exposes models to how the world looks and sounds. The authors ask whether that hidden structure can be surfaced. One prompt type asks the model to imagine seeing or hearing. The model then predicts as if evidence from that sense existed. No picture or audio is supplied. Lightweight prompting reliably activated the matching representations.

Their tests compared model states against vision and audio encoders. Prompted states aligned more closely with the matching encoder. Seeing prompts and hearing prompts pulled different structures forward. The effect shows perception-like knowledge hiding inside text training. Symbol grounding may be less hopeless than critics feared. Prompt design becomes a tool for probing machine minds. Builders can borrow these states for multimodal tasks.
arxiv-2510-02525:
Marrow settles which subgroups form strong Gelfand pairs inside Suzuki groups. His 2025 algebra paper completes a classification problem. A Gelfand pair links a group to a subgroup with tidy representation rules. The strong version demands even cleaner behavior across all subgroups below. Suzuki groups form one family of finite simple groups. Marrow checks every candidate subgroup of these groups. For the larger Suzuki groups, the answer is stark. No proper subgroup forms a strong Gelfand pair at all. The proof rules out maximal subgroups first. Smaller subgroups then fall by a containment argument.

The smallest case behaves completely differently. The group with parameter two has exactly four strong Gelfand subgroups. They include the whole group and three named smaller ones. Computer checks verify that exceptional case easily. Classification results close whole lines of questioning. Algebraic combinatorics uses these pairs through Schur rings.
arxiv-2510-02625:
Feitelberg and co-authors fill missing table entries with a pretrained transformer that needs no tuning. Their 2025 machine learning paper presents a system called TabImpute. Missing data plagues tables in medicine, finance, and engineering. Fixes range from plain averaging to heavy generative models. Performance swings wildly across domains, so no default exists. TabImpute builds on a recent tabular foundation model. An entry-wise featurization speeds the method a hundredfold. Training used only synthetic data with realistic missingness patterns. A new benchmark, MissBench, grades imputers on forty two datasets. Thirteen missingness patterns stress each method.

Trained on fake data, the model still nailed real tables. It generalized across unseen domains without any fitting. Speed and accuracy arrived together for once. The team released the model, weights, and code openly. Data cleaning eats analyst time everywhere. A zero-shot default could become the standard first move.
arxiv-2510-02825:
Ghosh, Das, and Mukherjee explore a new kind of quantum sensor. Quantum sensors measure weak fields with extreme care. Their precision often jumps near a phase change, where a system flips state. The team studies a driven atomic model named after Lipkin, Meshkov, and Glick. Under steady pulses, the model can form a discrete time crystal. That phase repeats at twice the drive period. The flip into that phase is the sensing sweet spot.

The authors map the flip point with care. They track order, spread, and a spread measure called Fisher information. The critical drive error sits near a small fixed value. Near that point, precision grows faster than system size. That beats the standard quantum limit for plain sensors. Scaling checks confirm the exponents agree across measures. The work shows that time crystals are more than a curiosity. They may anchor a class of high-precision quantum sensors.
arxiv-2510-03325:
Di Somma and colleagues at the University of Pisa present a 2025 arXiv paper on reading ring laser gyroscope signals with neural networks. These devices sense Earth's rotation through a beat frequency in laser light. Classic methods need several seconds of signal before they can name that frequency. The team works with GINGERINO, a ring laser housed in an underground lab in Italy. Fast readings would let the device flag quakes and glitches as they happen.

Their network names the frequency from ten milliseconds of signal. In the working range of the device, its readings ran twice as sharp as standard methods. A second network sorted disturbances into classes like laser faults and seismic events. On test data, its calls on the seismic class were right nearly every time, with accuracy in the high ninety percent range. Faster, sharper sensing helps geophysics teams watch Earth motion in real time.
arxiv-2510-03525:
Mack and Genel present a 2025 arXiv paper counting how often three or more galaxies merge at once in simulated universes. Galaxy mergers drive much of cosmic evolution, and studies count only pairs. The authors mine the Illustris and IllustrisTNG simulations for systems caught in multiple mergers. They relate the multiple merger share to the total merger share across galaxy masses, eras, and merger definitions. Binary mergers dominate the totals everywhere they looked.

A power law links the two shares, with the multiple share scaling as the total raised to the five thirds power, times a factor one half to seven tenths. Toy models with steady or random merger timing predict fewer multiple mergers than the simulations show. Mergers thus cluster in time, a fingerprint of how cosmic structure grows in clumps. Observers can test the power law against telescope counts, and theorists gain a target for galaxy formation models.
arxiv-2510-03725:
Hallopeau and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper comparing two kinds of pretrained neural networks for mapping Rio de Janeiro's favelas from satellite images. Informal settlements grow and escape maps, yet services depend on knowing where they are. One contender family was pretrained on sets of images. The other, a remote sensing foundation model called CROMA, was pretrained specifically on satellite imagery of Earth. The question was whether specificity beats pretraining volume.

Both approaches detected favelas well and cost less to develop than traditional mapping methods. The satellite model, CROMA, outperformed its generic counterparts in their comparison. Pretraining on Earth's imagery apparently teaches features that transfer to textures. Because both model types learned from worldwide data, the approach should extend to settlements beyond Rio. City agencies could refresh settlement maps more often with such tools. Better maps support everything from sanitation planning to disaster response in communities that records miss.
arxiv-2510-03925:
Zare and colleagues wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on how a dark matter halo changes a black hole and its gas disk. Their black hole is the classic Schwarzschild type, wrapped in a King model dark matter halo. Dark matter adds gravity without light, so it should shift orbits, shadows, and heat near the hole. The team works through those effects one by one.

Raising either halo parameter pushes the event horizon outward and enlarges the black hole's shadow. The shadow sizes stay consistent with limits set by Event Horizon Telescope observations. For matter particles, they compute the innermost stable orbit and its energy and speed. They also work out how the halo changes the disk's energy flux, temperature, and brightness. The temperature curve hints at a stable leftover remnant when evaporation ends. The study maps how an unseen halo could leave fingerprints telescopes might detect.
arxiv-2510-04325:
Ogbuagu and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on FoilDiff, a diffusion model that predicts airflow around airfoils far faster than fluid dynamics. Designers iterate over airfoil shapes and flight conditions, and each full simulation is expensive. Their surrogate uses a hybrid denoising network: layers extract local flow features while attention captures global structure. Encoded Reynolds number, angle of attack, and geometry condition across wide operating ranges.

Against state-of-the-art models on the same datasets, FoilDiff cut mean prediction errors by as much as eighty-five percent. Its uncertainty was also better than existing diffusion-based models. The authors caution that diffusion models carry large parameter counts for a task. Efficiency gains and physics-informed hybrids remain necessary before routine deployment. Accurate, uncertainty-aware surrogates could still compress design cycles from days to minutes.
arxiv-2510-04425:
Bo Li, Ankang Sun, Zunyu Wang, and Yu Zhou wrote this 2025 paper on fair sharing with a packing twist. In their problem, each person values a bundle by the number of bins needed to pack or cover its items. Fairness is judged by the maximin share, the best amount a person can guarantee by splitting items and taking the worst bundle. That ideal share cannot always be reached, so the team studied two kinds of near miss.

One kind of near miss loosens what counts as a packed or covered bin. The other kind loosens the number of bins that must be packed or covered. For every model they studied, the team gave algorithms that reach a fixed fraction of the ideal share. Their result for chores improves the best bound known before. The model also covers groups of people, not just single agents, which widens its reach.
arxiv-2510-04825:
Eleanor Jones and Yuji Nakatsukasa wrote this 2025 paper on solving whole families of related linear systems quickly. Many tasks, from partial differential equations to kernel regression, pose the system at many parameter values. Solving each from scratch wastes the kinship between them. Their algorithm, SubApSnap, blends model reduction with randomized linear algebra. It solves the system at parameter values and stacks those answers as a snapshot.

Systems are then answered inside the world the snapshot spans. Subsampling trims the least squares problem down to a small one that carries the answer. The method never reads the matrix for a new parameter value. It generalizes a reduction algorithm used for nonlinear models. Under assumptions, the residual stays small for every parameter of interest. In one test the speedup passed twenty thousand fold on a system with ten million unknowns. Accuracy stayed good across their examples in equations, model reduction, and regression.
arxiv-2510-05225:
Dominic J. Williamson and Bence Hetényi design quantum error correction for sparsely connected hardware in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their lattice has maximum vertex degree three, like a honeycomb. Only nearest-neighbor gates and mid-circuit measurements are available. Dynamical Floquet codes fit such hardware naturally, because they measure checks in a repeating cycle.

The authors introduce several schemes that exploit the ancillary qubits cleverly. One resets all qubits every measurement cycle. Another swaps data and ancilla roles so two Floquet codes run simultaneously on one lattice. They show how to entangle that pair with a logical Clifford gate. Switching between the color code and the Floquet pair also performs color-code syndrome extraction. Numerical evidence shows a finite error threshold under circuit-level noise.
arxiv-2510-05325:
Valeriya Kirova and four co-authors read brain states from scanner data with simple models in this 2025 arXiv paper. They use Human Connectome Project fMRI recordings made during several cognitive tasks. Functional connectivity describes which brain regions activate together over time. The question is whether those patterns cleanly identify what a person is doing.

Even basic linear classifiers reached state-of-the-art accuracy at naming the task. Motor and language states were classified especially well, sometimes near perfectly. Feature rankings revealed a distinct set of crucial regions for each state. Few regions were needed for high accuracy, supporting functional specialization in the brain. Time structure mattered too: region pairs with uncorrelated signals carried the least information. The results favor interpretable classical methods for clinical-style brain decoding.
arxiv-2510-05725:
Hong and colleagues learn which masked token a diffusion language model should reveal next. Masked diffusion models fill blanks step by step, in any order. Which position to unmask next strongly affects the final quality. Their 2025 paper replaces rule-based schedules with a learned policy.

They cast denoising as a KL-regularized Markov decision process. A reference policy anchors the optimization, with guarantees of improvement and convergence. The learned policy provably lands closer to the data distribution than heuristic schedules. A tractable surrogate loss makes the framework practical to train. On Sudoku, where order is critical, it beats random unmasking by about twenty percent. It also beats the max-confidence rule by about eleven percent there. Occasional low-confidence picks can help when training nears optimality. Four benchmarks, including math word problems, confirm the pattern.
arxiv-2510-06025:
Raina and Schmah tackle out-of-distribution detection when training data are scarce, in a 2025 machine learning paper. A detector must flag inputs that differ from the data a classifier was trained on. Bayesian neural networks suit this task because they track the model's own uncertainty, not just its final answer.

The authors introduce a family of detection scores built from expected logit vectors, the raw outputs before a network assigns probabilities. They compare five Bayesian scores with four deterministic ones on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 image benchmarks. Training sets held no more than 5,000 examples in their tests. The Bayesian versions beat their deterministic counterparts across the experiments, and scores based on full logit vectors beat the better-known entropy measures. The findings give practitioners a stronger recipe for spotting strange inputs when data are limited.
arxiv-2510-06225:
Li and eight co-authors build a generalized framework for multi-agent social simulation in a 2025 computational social science paper. Language models energized agent-based social simulation, yet current systems scale poorly to diverse scenarios. Their code is rarely reusable because designs lack modularity.

The framework is modular and object-oriented, integrating base classes hierarchically. Researchers inherit those classes for common derived components, mixing only the pieces a scenario needs. A memory summarization mechanism filters raw agent memory, distilling salient events and interactions. The team customized one environment from these parts and simulated social media interaction. The simulation replicated real-world online social behaviors. Because scenarios assemble from reusable blocks, new studies skip starting from scratch. The authors will release the code and keep evolving it, lowering the cost of credible social simulation.
arxiv-2510-06425:
Gough and Yamasita give a new construction for anti-Wick ordering of bosonic fields in a 2025 mathematical physics paper. Ordering prescriptions organize creation and annihilation operators in quantum expressions. Anti-Wick ordering reverses the usual Wick arrangement. The anti-Wick map pairs each operator with a function of complex variables.

Their technique realizes the map as a two-step composition. First, the operator maps into a commutative sub-algebra of a doubled boson algebra. Doubling creates room for a commutative shadow of the quantum object. A partial conditional expectation then projects onto one factor. The composition recovers exactly the anti-Wick ordered operator. Building the map from standard operations replaces ad hoc combinatorics with structure. The construction applies to general boson fields, not only simple single-mode cases. Cleaner ordering machinery simplifies calculations passing between operator and function pictures.
arxiv-2510-06625:
Baskin, a single author writing as M. Y. Baskin, studies how listeners hear pitch in complex tones. The 2025 paper introduces a new spectrum method called MASP. Pitch estimation matters for music analysis and hearing science. Some tones fool standard algorithms, because their spectra hide the partials those methods expect.

MASP modifies a classic technique, the harmonic product spectrum, by smoothing with a global average. That change reduces the old method's sensitivity to missing partials. The result gives pitch estimates that match what listeners actually perceive. The same tool extends to judging musical consonance for pairs and triples of tones. A proposed harmonicity measure ranks those combinations in ways that match music theory and practice. That link suggests pitch and consonance may rest on a shared mechanism in hearing. Both, on this view, depend on how the ear reads a tone's spectrum.
arxiv-2510-06725:
Anirudh Lanka, Juan Garcia-Nila, and Todd Brun propose doing quantum logic with measurements alone. Their 2025 paper uses the quantum Zeno effect, where frequent measurement freezes a system's state. The setting is a quantum error-correcting code, which shelters fragile information. The authors rotate that protected space slowly by measuring a turning sequence of checks.

If the rotation is slow enough, the Zeno effect keeps the state inside the moving code space. Completing a full loop applies a logical operation, called a holonomy, to the stored data. The authors derive exactly which measurement sequence produces a desired operation. They also compute how long the procedure takes for a given success chance. Measurement can occasionally kick the state into a wrong subspace. They give a fix that steers the path back while keeping the intended operation. Conditions on the code ensure the scheme stays error-correcting throughout.
arxiv-2510-06925:
Armando Bellante, Stefano Vanerio, and Stefano Zanero ask how far quantum computers can compress sparse signals. Their 2025 paper studies sparse recovery, where a state is rebuilt from few dictionary pieces. The dictionary here is overcomplete and its pieces are not perpendicular. That freedom makes the reconstruction problem harder in general.

They first prove the general problem is NP-hard, so no efficient exact method exists for all cases. Then they build QOMP, a quantum version of the classic greedy matching pursuit algorithm. It stitches together quantum subroutines for inner products, maximum finding, and projections. A reset trick stops errors from piling up between iterations. Under standard assumptions about the dictionary, QOMP provably finds the exact support quickly. The team applies it to quantum tomography with such dictionaries. In favorable regimes, the query cost beats the best known classical methods quadratically. Sparse quantum sensing gains a principled algorithm, not just heuristics.
arxiv-2510-07125:
Guo and co-authors show how to load complex quantum states onto quantum hardware. Their 2025 paper uses matrix product states, a compact way to write down many quantum states. The hard part is turning that compact form into steps a real device can run. The team covers states in open chains and in closed rings. Closed rings matter for many physics models but resist older methods.

The authors turn each piece of the compact form into a gate for the device. Ring-shaped states need extra helper qubits and a lucky measurement step. They derive an exact formula for how often that step succeeds. Tests prepared the ground state of a magnet chain in ring form. The team also built excited states of a model of particle physics with high accuracy. Such loading tools are a key step toward quantum simulation of hard materials.
arxiv-2510-07425:
Andreev derives how electric fields couple to spin waves in magnetic materials that can also hold an electric polarization. The 2025 paper studies antiferromagnetic multiferroics whose ground-state spins form a cycloidal spiral. In such media, magnetization and polarization are linked, the magnetoelectric effect. Earlier work built the polarization from the parts of neighboring spins that sit at right angles. Andreev instead develops the case where the parallel spin part drives it. He adds the new term to the standard equation for spin dynamics and compares both routes side by side for ferromagnets and antiferromagnets.

From that base, he derives the dispersion relation for spin waves riding on the cycloidal order. Closed formulas give the material's electric susceptibility and permittivity. Two kinds of magnetic coupling between neighbors shape the outcome.
arxiv-2510-07925:
Westhäußer, Minker, and Zepf wrote this 2025 paper on personalizing long-term conversations with AI agents. Agents forget users between sessions, so every chat starts cold. Retrieval systems add context but do not build a picture of the person. The authors start from a unified definition of personalization and derive technical requirements from it. Their framework combines persistent memory with an evolving user profile at its center.

Multi-agent coordination and self-validation support the memory and profile. Three requirements guide the design: adaptivity, consistency, and tailored replies. Tests on three public datasets matched retrieval baselines while running more stably. A five-day pilot study added human evidence. Users noticed and valued the system's recall of earlier interactions. They also asked for more proactivity and sharper context use. The study offers early proof that durable memory makes agents feel genuinely personal rather than merely responsive.
arxiv-2510-08025:
Sigl wrote this 2025 astrophysics paper asking whether ordinary galaxies can explain the magnetic fields hinted at in cosmic voids. Voids are the emptiest regions of the universe, so any field there might be primordial. Gamma-ray cascades from distant blazars suggest void fields have a minimum strength. One candidate source is the sum of dipole fields from individual galaxies.

He argues they cannot reach. Intergalactic plasma screens magnetic fields, so galactic dipoles decay away instead of filling space. In real space the screening is exponential beyond a characteristic length. The surviving field falls short of observed lower bounds by many orders of magnitude. Sustaining the galaxy explanation would need a screening length of a few megaparsecs, which he calls implausible. Outflows and instabilities remain possible contributors.
arxiv-2510-08725:
Gorjan Alagic, Chen Bai, Christian Majenz, and Kaiyan Shi lay foundations for post-quantum security of block ciphers in a 2025 arXiv paper. Block ciphers secure everything from internet traffic to disk encryption as versatile building blocks. Quantum attacks on public-key cryptography drew intense study, while symmetric-key primitives stayed largely unexplored. A quantum adversary can query ciphers in superposition, changing the security game fundamentally.

Leveraging new techniques, the authors prove several standard constructions secure against quantum attack, for the first time. These include the FX key-length extension scheme and the tweakable block ciphers LRW and XEX. Most block cipher encryption and authentication modes are covered as well. Proofs work in the plain model and in the quantum version of the ideal cipher model, two standard adversary settings. The authors frame the work as initial steps toward rigorous post-quantum symmetric-key cryptography.
arxiv-2510-08825:
Sun and colleagues give language models a careful way to walk through a knowledge graph while answering hard questions, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Models answering from memory alone miss rare facts, invent details, and lag behind events. A knowledge graph stores facts as linked entities, but older ways of using one are brittle. Writing a full query up front demands knowing the graph's layout, and grabbing big chunks of it adds noise.

Their method, Search-on-Graph, moves one hop at a time. At each step the model first looks at which links actually leave the current entity, then chooses the next hop. That observe-then-navigate loop adapts to any graph layout and filters crowded nodes sensibly. Across six public benchmarks the method set new best scores with no fine-tuning. Gains were largest on Wikidata tests, improving on the previous best by about sixteen percent.
arxiv-2510-09425:
Gur Keinan, Rotem Torkan, and Omer Ben-Porat study an online matching problem in a 2025 arXiv paper. An algorithm must repeatedly match users to arms, meaning options, while respecting a limited budget over many rounds. Without structure, even computing the best matching is NP-hard, which makes learning while acting seem hopeless.

The authors exploit single-peaked preferences, a classic structure from social choice where each user's liking rises to one peak along a shared ordering of options. They give an efficient offline algorithm for the budgeted matching problem and lift it into an online method with a proven regret bound, using a PQ-tree technique to approximate the hidden order. When the single-peaked structure is already known, a second algorithm in the style of upper confidence bounds learns faster still, again with a proven bound on regret.
arxiv-2510-09725:
Nicolas Rouger and nine co-authors report an open science project on measuring transistor losses in a 2025 arXiv paper. The switching losses of power transistors are usually measured with the double pulse method. An alternative measures two switching cells in opposition, which is more accurate but indirect, harder to implement, and demanding in calibration and thermal management.

The team attacked the problem collaboratively, starting with a two-day hackathon that drew more than twenty participants, then continuing in monthly open sessions. Together they built an automated test bench covering how switching commands are generated, how measuring instruments are configured and controlled, and the hardware itself. The bench is developed in the open, and the paper shares both the technical work and the collaborative approach behind it. The authors present the project as a model for tackling complex experimental setups through open, distributed teamwork.
arxiv-2510-09825:
Mohsen Joneidi, the sole author, proposes Decomposer Networks in a 2025 arXiv paper, an autoencoder that splits a signal into meaningful parts. A classic autoencoder squeezes its input into one latent code. DecompNet instead keeps several parallel branches, each responsible for one readable component of the input.

Each branch receives a residual input: the original signal minus the outputs of all the other branches. That all-but-one rule forces the branches to compete, an idea unrolled from Gauss-Seidel block-coordinate descent into a network that can be trained. The competition yields lean, meaningful components rather than one tangled code. Joneidi positions the model against linear splitting methods and matrix factorisation, against deep unrolled methods, and against object-centric designs such as MONet and Slot Attention. He presents DecompNet as the first semantic model of its kind built on this residual update rule.
arxiv-2510-09925:
Usevitch, Juan Augusto Paredes Salazar, and Ankit Goel compute safe control inputs in this 2025 arXiv paper on control theory. Control barrier functions certify that a system stays in its safe region over time. Most work treats continuous time, but digital controllers act in discrete steps, so discrete-time versions matter.

The catch is that discrete-time barrier conditions can be nonconcave, which forces nonconvex optimization and blocks real-time control. The authors use matrix control barrier functions and convex optimization to get around that block. Convex problems solve fast and reliably, so safety checks can run at each control step. Their method aims to keep forward invariance guarantees without giving up real-time computation.
arxiv-2510-10825:
Rodrigo Rey Carvalho, Matheus Duzi, and Vinicius de Oliveira Rodrigues characterize covering properties of spaces built from the ends of infinite graphs, in this 2025 arXiv paper. End spaces and ray spaces encode the ways an infinite graph escapes to infinity. Covering properties describe how well a space can be covered by simpler pieces. The authors give combinatorial descriptions of several such properties: the Rothberger property, the Menger property, sigma compactness, the extent, and the Lindelöf degree.

Their results apply across ray spaces, end spaces, and edge end spaces. A headline result is that sigma compactness and the Menger property coincide for all these spaces. They also show these spaces are all D-spaces, a covering regularity notion. As an application, the results describe graphs with countably many ends and edge ends. The work links graph combinatorics with general topology.
arxiv-2510-11025:
Alexander Plakhotnikov studies boundary behavior of resolvent type operators near the spectrum, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The objects are a family of operators built from a self adjoint operator H, a rigging operator F, and a complex parameter z. As z approaches the real axis, where the spectrum of H lives, the resolvent factor can blow up. The question is when the full sandwiched operator still has a limit in the operator norm, the strongest sense of convergence for operators.

Plakhotnikov establishes conditions on H and on the rigging F under which this limit exists. The analysis pays special attention to separating two cases. In one, the limit point on the real axis belongs to the point spectrum of H, meaning it is an eigenvalue with an associated eigenvector. In the other, it does not.
arxiv-2510-11225:
Semantic parsers turn sentences into logical forms, but the standard score for them, Smatch, only measures how much two graphs overlap on the surface. Hayate Funakura, Hyunsoo Kim, and Koji Mineshima reassess that practice in this 2025 arXiv paper on natural language processing. They pair graph matching with theorem proving, checking whether a predicted formula logically entails and is entailed by the reference.

The comparison covers fine-tuned T5 models and few-shot prompting of GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, and GPT-5, under normalized and unnormalized targets. Models that score well on graph matching often fail to produce logically equivalent formulas. Normalizing the targets reduced incidental variability and improved well-formedness and logical adequacy. Errors grew with formula complexity and with coordination, prepositional phrases, and passive voice. The main failures involved variable binding and predicate naming. The authors argue for logic-sensitive evaluation and simpler normalized targets.
arxiv-2510-11625:
Electing a committee fairly is hard enough with full information; when voters cannot rank hundreds of candidates, asking everyone everything is not an option. Drew Springham, Edith Elkind, Bart de Keijzer, and Maria Polukarov study that communication problem in this 2025 arXiv theoretical computer science paper. Their voters live on a line: each voter's approval set is an interval of the real line, and voters belong to groups, each group drawing its interval endpoints from its own distribution.

The fairness target is Proportional Justified Representation Plus, a guarantee that any large enough group sharing an approved candidate gets its proportional share of winners. The authors give an algorithm that computes committees providing that guarantee by querying voters' preferences adaptively, needing only logarithmically many queries per voter in expectation. Strong proportional guarantees thus survive drastic communication limits.
arxiv-2510-11725:
Si Xie reports progress toward particle detectors built from superconducting microwires. These sensors register single photons and, potentially, charged particles with precise timing. Xie's 2025 arXiv paper describes beam tests of an eight-channel array made from tungsten silicide film. The tests ran at a CERN beamline, using hadron and muon beams at one hundred twenty giga-electronvolts. A silicon tracking telescope located each particle's hit to within about ten micrometers.

The tested sensor used a thicker film than the team's earlier device, and its efficiency rose as a result. Corrected for the gaps between wires, the array detected seventy-five percent of passing particles. Its timing precision was about one hundred thirty picoseconds across pixels. The study also reports the first efficiency measurement of such a sensor for muons. Xie points to future machines such as the FCC-ee and a muon collider as likely users of the technology.
arxiv-2510-12325:
Yang, Gu, and Liu propose a causal approach to multimodal recommendation that attacks two hidden biases, in a 2025 arXiv computer science paper. Recommender systems combine images, text, and interaction histories to personalize suggestions in e-commerce and advertising. The authors argue that latent factors such as brand style can drive several modalities at once and shape preferences, creating false links between features and tastes.

A second problem is interaction bias, where true preference mixes with noise from exposure effects and stray clicks. Their framework uses a dual channel cross modal diffusion unit to expose hidden confounders. Back door adjustment with layered matching and vector quantized codebooks blocks the confounding paths, while front door adjustment with causal topology rebuilding builds a cleaned causal subgraph. On three real world e-commerce data sets, the method greatly beat leading baselines. They also report that the causal structure keeps the system's recommendations fairly interpretable.
arxiv-2510-12425:
Chen and co-authors fill in missing entries of multidimensional data with an algorithm backed by a convergence proof, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Data arranged as tensors often have gaps. Recent completion methods combine global low rank structure with plug and play denoisers and work well empirically, but their convergence was unproven or rested on unrealistic assumptions about the denoisers.

Their framework rests on monotone inclusion, a general problem form that treats deep denoisers as general operators needing few restrictions. Generalised low rank priors with weakly convex penalties capture the overall structure. Building on the Davis Yin splitting scheme, their algorithm provably converges globally. In experiments it beat existing methods in scores and visual quality, most at low sampling rates. For image completion at a five percent sampling rate, its quality margin over the second best method was clear, and repeated for multispectral images and color videos.
arxiv-2510-12525:
Kypke, Ashwin, and Ditlevsen show that a simple model of three linked ice streams can surge chaotically, in a 2025 arXiv paper on ice sheet dynamics. Ice streams are fast flowing corridors within ice sheets. Thermomechanical coupling at the ice bed, where friction heats and lubricates the base, has long been theorized to produce build up and surge oscillations.

The authors build a model of three coupled streams arranged like a real branching system in northern Greenland, where one stream splits into two termini. The model displays both steady flow and build up surging oscillations, matching the qualitative behaviors expected. More strikingly, the variability can be chaotic. The chaos arises because the nonlinear coupling mixes three incommensurate frequencies, rhythms that never quite repeat together. This gives ice sheets containing such branching streams a mode of internal chaotic variability, generated by the ice itself rather than imposed by climate forcing.
arxiv-2510-12825:
Gschwind and colleagues build a system that turns plain language into data workflows in this 2025 arXiv paper. Tools such as IBM DataStage let users assemble ETL workflows visually. ETL means extracting, transforming, and loading data. But configuring each stage and its many properties is slow and demands deep tool knowledge.

Their approach, Classifier-Augmented Generation, first splits a request into smaller utterances, then uses a classifier plus stage-specific examples to predict the needed stages. Predicted stages are linked into branching workflows by edge prediction, and their properties are inferred from the matching sub-requests. Against strong single-prompt and agentic baselines, the system improved accuracy and efficiency while using far fewer tokens. The authors report detailed evaluations of stage prediction, layout, and property generation, and they describe the design as modular and interpretable.
arxiv-2510-13025:
Cheng and co-authors rethink Koopman learning through information theory in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Koopman operator turns nonlinear dynamics into linear evolution, but it is infinite-dimensional, so machine learning methods must find a good finite latent space. The authors argue the real difficulty is representation learning: latent variables often fail to balance simplicity against expressivity.

They connect that tension to the information bottleneck dilemma, where a representation should be compressed yet predictive. Latent mutual information encourages simplicity, but leaning too far collapses the latent space onto a few dominant modes. Von Neumann entropy counteracts the collapse by sustaining mode diversity. From this analysis they build a Lagrangian objective that trades the two off, plus an algorithm optimizing it. Across diverse dynamical systems the method beat existing Koopman learners, and plots of the learned manifolds matched the theory.
arxiv-2510-13225:
Puthenpurakal compares Grothendieck groups of a ring and its completion in this 2025 arXiv paper. For an excellent Gorenstein local ring that is an isolated singularity, the completion is a formal limit process. A natural map connects the ring's Grothendieck group, built from its modules, to the other group. Whether that map becomes an isomorphism after tensoring with the rationals was open.

Puthenpurakal proves the map is an isomorphism exactly when every maximal Cohen-Macaulay module over the completion can be realized as the completion of a module over the ring. This allows taking enough copies and adding free summands. A key step describes exactly which rational subspaces of the Grothendieck groups of triangulated categories arise, through dense subcategories. He also gives a test for Henselian Gorenstein rings in dimensions two and three, with many cases where the result holds.
arxiv-2510-13425:
Altuntas and colleagues argue that formal methods should play a larger role in climate model development. Their 2025 arXiv paper concerns Earth system models, vast codes that simulate climate processes. These models span millions of lines, many contributors, and varied hardware platforms. New graphics processors and mixed architectures make checking their correctness still harder.

Traditional checks lean on bitwise reproducibility, which new compilers or hardware often break. Expert review by eye is rigorous neither in coverage nor in timing, the authors note. They identify parts of Earth system models that suit formal specification well. They also propose abstraction methods for a framework tailored to climate models. A case study uses the CIVL checker to verify a bug fix in an ocean mixing scheme. The team aims at tools that domain scientists can actually use. Such tools would raise confidence in model results.
arxiv-2510-13725:
Li, Pull, and Ramsay design a two-sided type system that can prove functional programs go wrong, not just that they behave. Their 2025 arXiv paper complements ordinary typing, which only certifies the absence of errors. An untypable program might be buggy or merely beyond the system's reach. Proving incorrectness directly has lacked a clean type-theoretic home.

Their key move is letting types range over sets of final results, called normal forms. On that domain they define a complement operator that negates typing claims. The complement yields many refutation principles, including a type-level analogue of co-implication. With them, the authors certify that several Erlang-style programs genuinely fail. An expressive axiomatization of complement through subtyping turns out to be decidable. The whole system is proven sound and, unusually, complete for normal forms.
arxiv-2510-14125:
Waqar Muhammad Ashraf and co-authors build a neural-network optimization framework that keeps its answers inside the region where the network's training data applies, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Optimizers paired with data-driven plant models wander into domain-inconsistent solutions, operating points the model never saw and cannot judge, an overlooked failure mode in plant optimization.

They apply it to a combined-cycle gas power plant of about twelve hundred megawatts. The framework adds the data-driven domain as an explicit constraint inside a robust nonlinear optimization. It delivered optimal settings, improving energy efficiency by an average of over three-quarters of a percentage point. Scaling that gain across the global gas fleet, they estimate a carbon dioxide reduction of twenty-six million tonnes, with the largest shares in Asia and the Americas. They frame it as a near-term, scalable decarbonization pathway delivered by machine learning.
arxiv-2510-14725:
Al-Izzi and a large team of co-authors demonstrate, in a 2025 arXiv paper, free-standing filaments that keep changing shape on their own, with no tether and no outside controller. Active filaments drive propulsion and actuation in biology and soft robotics. Artificial versions usually stay robust only when externally controlled or anchored to a surface, which limits where they can work.

The team's trick is non-reciprocal interaction: the bending modes of a buckled beam are coupled anti-symmetrically, so action in one direction is not undone in the other. Ordinary snap-through buckling, where a beam jumps between two stable shapes, becomes a persistent cycle of self-snapping. The change is governed by a critical exceptional point, where the bending modes go unstable and merge at once. When the environment perturbs the filaments, they turn this cycling into useful behavior, including crawling, digging, and walking.
arxiv-2510-14825:
Poesia and Sampaio explore, in a 2025 arXiv paper, predictors that are made of readable code and decision trees instead of neural network weights. Classical models like decision trees are efficient and interpretable, but their quality depends entirely on hand-chosen input features. Neural networks learn their own features from raw data, at the cost of interpretability and specialized hardware. The authors ask whether language models can supply the features, keeping the predictor itself transparent.

Their LeaPR models stack features written as small programs, functions from a data point to a number, under a decision tree. Two learning algorithms are proposed. One adapts FunSearch to evolve features rather than predictors. The other extends the classic ID3 tree algorithm, generating features on demand when a leaf needs splitting. From chess position evaluation to image and text classification, the learned predictors often rivaled neural networks, with no network needed at prediction time.
arxiv-2510-14925:
Okutomi re-reads Kant's Critique of Pure Reason, in a 2025 arXiv paper, as an early theory of why reasoning systems become overconfident. For Kant, reason polices thought, keeping it within the bounds of possible experience. The author turns that picture into control theory: stable feedback on paper can still mislead in practice.

A composite instability index, H-Risk, combines four quantities: spectral margin, conditioning, time sensitivity, and innovation amplification. In linear-Gaussian simulations, higher H-Risk predicted sure-but-wrong errors even when the system was formally stable, exposing a gap between nominal and epistemic stability. Extended to large language models, internal fragility showed preliminary correlations with miscalibration and hallucination. Lightweight critique prompts modestly improved calibration in some small tests and worsened it in others. The author stresses the claims are early, but offers the Kantian lens as a principled way to diagnose overconfidence in reasoning systems.
arxiv-2510-15125:
Alexander Brady and Tunazzina Islam build an automated way to map the themes running through political advertising on social media. Their 2025 arXiv paper combines unsupervised clustering, which groups similar ads without preset labels, with large language models that name and refine the groups. Applied to Meta ads from the month before the 2024 United States presidential election, the method needs no seed topics or expert hand-labeling.

The analysis found voting and immigration ads dominating both spending and impressions, while abortion and election-integrity ads reached audiences beyond their budgets. Spending split sharply by viewpoint: conservative groups drove economic appeals, and abortion messaging divided between opposing coalitions. Brady and Islam also tagged ads with moral framing, finding, for example, that abortion ads leaned on liberty language while economic ads mixed care, fairness, and liberty themes. Targeting varied too, with younger Floridians seeing more housing ads.
arxiv-2510-15325:
Jonathan Bowden and Thomas Massoni prove that a geometric structure built from a foliation depends only on the foliation's topology, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A foliation slices a three-dimensional space into stacked surfaces, and a taut foliation has no dead-end leaves. Following work by Eliashberg and Thurston, the authors attach a Liouville structure, a kind of symplectic geometry, to a thickened copy of the space.

Their main result says foliations that are topologically the same yield matching Liouville structures, even if their smooth details differ. For the special case of flows with chaotic stretching, called Anosov flows, the result shows an older construction by Mitsumatsu is unchanged under orbit equivalence. The proofs rest on a careful smoothing scheme for rough conjugacies and a sharpened uniqueness result about contact structures near a foliation. An appendix by three other authors uses the smoothing to build new collapsed Anosov flows.
arxiv-2510-15525:
Weicen Dong and three colleagues map the magnetic phases of a two-dimensional magnet where a twist-promoting interaction is unusually strong. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, which cants neighboring spins and can create swirling textures. Topological magnons, spin waves with protected band structure, are prized for low-loss spintronic devices, but earlier work treated only weak versions of this interaction.

The team finds that strong interaction tips the ground state from simple ferromagnetism into a 120-degree noncollinear pattern, where spins point in three directions. Adding a magnetic field produces noncoplanar textures and a rich set of topological phases. Those phases can be read out through the anomalous thermal Hall effect, a measurable heat current. They also find that spin interactions in the strong regime let magnons hybridize with phonons, the lattice vibrations, creating mixed topological bands.
arxiv-2510-15625:
A dangling bond is an unsatisfied silicon atom that traps charge and disturbs electronic behavior. T. V. Pavlova and V. M. Shevlyuga examine single dangling bonds in this 2025 arXiv study. They work on silicon surfaces coated with chlorine or bromine, probed by a scanning tunneling microscope. The team observes a bond switching directly between positive and negative charge states. Notably, the neutral state plays no part in these observed transitions.

The switch happens when the bond and substrate fall out of equilibrium with each other. It ties to the charge neutrality level, where the bond changes from donor-like to acceptor-like character. The switching voltage also shifts with the bond's local electrostatic surroundings.
arxiv-2510-15725:
Old films are noisy and damaged, so software struggles to tell how the camera moved. Tingyu Lin and three colleagues improve camera movement classification for archival footage in this 2025 arXiv paper. They first unify modern datasets and the HISTORIAN collection into one balanced benchmark. Their model extends the Video Swin Transformer with directional grid motion encoding from optical flow. A small learnable fusion layer injects this motion signal late in the network.

Accuracy on modern clips rises from about eighty-two to eighty-six percent top-1. On World War II footage, accuracy improves from about eighty-three to eighty-five percent. Fine-tuning on modern data first adds over five points on historical material.
arxiv-2510-15825:
Lê Dũng Tráng, Juan J. Nuño-Ballesteros, and José Seade relate the topology of a Milnor fibre to a sliced version of itself for singular map-germs. A map-germ describes a holomorphic map near a point, here on a possibly singular complex variety. A second, well-behaved germ slices the first fibre, and the question is what the slice reveals about the whole.

Using stratified Morse theory, the three authors determine the fibre's topology up to homeomorphism from the slice and from Morse data of a perturbed restriction. That yields a general formula comparing the Euler characteristics of the two fibres. When the variety has only an isolated singularity, the difference formula becomes algebraic and easy to compute. It generalises the classical Lê-Greuel formula in two directions at once and unifies several known formulas as special cases.
arxiv-2510-15925:
Aleks Kleyn, writing alone, sets out the basic definitions for manifolds and Lie groups built over a Banach algebra. A chart is defined as a homeomorphism from a topological space into a convex set inside a power of the algebra. A simple manifold of a given smoothness class is one whose charts are linked by diffeomorphisms of that class.

A differential manifold is then a union of simple pieces whose overlaps are again simple. When such a manifold carries a group structure and the map sending a pair to the product with the inverse is differentiable, it is a Lie group in this setting. Kleyn equips the tangent module at the identity with a bracket product built from the group's structure coefficients, giving its Lie algebra. The note fixes the language for continuous transformation groups over general algebras.
arxiv-2510-16325:
Yuyao Zhang and Yu-Wing Tai present UltraImageGen, a framework for making images at ultra-high resolution from text. Top image models stall below two megapixels because their attention step grows far too costly as images grow. Sharp training data is scarce too. Their design splits the big picture into fixed local windows, where attention stays cheap.

A small, low-resolution copy of the image steers the whole, anchoring the layout so windows agree with each other. A light adapter, trained cheaply, links the global guide with the local detail work during cleanup. By reordering tokens window-first, the method runs dense, hardware-friendly math at any size. The result scales past eight thousand pixels across with more than ten times the speed and far less memory. Quality tests put it ahead, offering a practical path to poster-grade AI images.
arxiv-2510-16725:
Yongchun Bi and three co-authors prove stability tools for very large nonlinear systems whose rules change with time. Their target is integral input-to-state stability, which says a system's state stays controlled by its past inputs. The systems live in infinite-dimensional spaces and include terms that grow faster than linearly, a combination that resists standard methods.

The team first proves several comparison principles for ordinary differential equations with time-varying coefficients and superlinear terms. Those principles then support a local stability theorem in Banach spaces, using Lyapunov functions. In Hilbert spaces, they give conditions for such a function to exist and show how to build one. Two examples demonstrate the method in action.
arxiv-2510-17425:
Counting climate laws says little about what those laws actually push for, or what good they do. Aditi Dutta, writing alone, builds a number based measure of climate policy direction by reading official national policy documents with a multilingual language model. Each document is sorted by theme, such as cutting emissions, adapting to change, managing disaster risk, or covering loss and damage.

Dutta then links those theme scores to World Bank development data across countries and years. Policies centred on cutting emissions went together with higher national income measures. Disaster risk work linked to higher income and debt but lower foreign investment, while adaptation themes showed few measurable links. The framework offers a scalable way to compare climate governance between countries.
arxiv-2510-17625:
Jaehyup Seong, with Byungju Lee and two co-authors, improves satellite links for crowded beams in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their setting is a low Earth orbit satellite serving many users under shared beams. A method called rate splitting sends one common stream for all users plus private streams for each. Standard versions use one beam shape for the common stream, which limits quality when channel knowledge is poor.

The new design adds space time coding, meaning signals spread across antennas and time slots, to the common stream. Every user then gains full signal diversity, meaning protection against fading, regardless of load. An optimization routine balances power between common and private streams. The goal is raising the slowest user's rate. Simulations beat standard approaches clearly.
arxiv-2510-17725:
Haozhen Zhang and three co-authors built a new test for long-context language models. Their benchmark, AcademicEval, checks how well models write with very long inputs. Older tests use fixed lengths and costly hand labeling. They also risk leaking answers into model training data.

AcademicEval draws its tasks from real papers posted on arXiv. Models must draft titles, abstracts, opening sections, and related-work text. Sample answers come from a graph of co-author links. Fresh papers keep the test live and free of leaks. Results show models still struggle as tasks grow more layered.
arxiv-2510-17925:
George Ma, with eight co-authors, speeds up code completion by doing the hard lookup work before the coder asks. Retrieval systems that search a project at request time either return weak context or slow the tool down. SpecAgent instead explores project files during indexing and builds context that guesses future edits.

That early work hides the delay and improves the code the model writes. The authors also flag a leak in current benchmarks, where future context slips in and inflates scores. They build a clean synthetic test to avoid it. Tool builders get both a faster design and a fairer way to measure it.
arxiv-2510-18125:
Mohamed Warda and Ronojoy Adhikari find strange stability swings in a soft robot arm pushed by steady pressure under water. The arm bends, stretches, and shears like the Cosserat rods used to model it. Exact nonlinear equations, built with moving frames, govern its motion in the viscous fluid.

As pressure rises past a first threshold, the straight arm loses stability through an oscillating bifurcation. Push further, past a second threshold, and stability oddly returns. Nonlinear simulations confirm the pattern. Soft robot designers get a warning and a tool: pressure alone can switch a fluid-borne arm between calm and wobbling regimes.
arxiv-2510-18625:
Eric DeMarbre works with Jay Henderson, J. Felipe Gonzalez, and Rob Teather. They test how a controller should appear in extended reality. Participants selected targets in the tasks. Four display choices were compared. One showed a virtual controller. One showed a virtual hand. One showed both, and one showed neither. The tasks ran in two modes. One was full virtual reality. The other was mixed reality over the real room.

Performance came out much the same in both modes. Switching modes did not hurt basic task skill. Displays that mimicked the real controller helped in both modes. That is a practical design hint. Users judged their own performance in a distinct way in mixed reality. The scores did not match that feeling. The authors read this as a call for care. Mixed reality design needs its own focus on spatial awareness.
arxiv-2510-18725:
Josh McGiff and Nikola Nikolov make machine translation fine-tuning affordable for low-resource languages, using Irish as their test case. Adapting a huge multilingual model costs too much for many researchers, so efficient methods train only a small set of added parameters. The authors introduce two semi-supervised versions of that idea, SemiAdapt and SemiLoRA, designed to strengthen domain adaptation while staying cheap at inference time.

In their experiments, SemiAdapt beat even full-domain fine-tuning, while SemiLoRA matched or outperformed fine-tuning the entire model, a striking result for a method that trains only a fraction of the weights. Their embedding-based inference methods did especially well on larger and noisier text collections. All Irish translation models built in the study were released as open resources, aiming to lower the barrier for other low-resource language communities.
arxiv-2510-18825:
