Sparsity changes which split tests are cheap and which are dear. Fast split search keeps a stream tree fresh without falling behind the flow. The work was supported by Academy of Finland projects on machine learning.
arxiv-2601-12625:
Parisa Ansari Bonab, Elisabeth Andarge Gedefaw, and Mohammad Khajenejad work on safety for platoons of connected cars. Cooperative adaptive cruise control lets cars follow closely by sharing data. That connectivity opens a door to cyber threats, though. False data injection attacks can feed a car fake sensor values and break its control.

The team propose a control framework built to resist such attacks. It pairs a nonlinear controller with an interval observer. The observer gives robust state estimates even under measurement noise. Interval bounds tell the controller what range the true state must lie in. Control that stays safe inside those bounds can ride out an attack. The work serves the security of future autonomous traffic.
arxiv-2601-13125:
Denan Li, Chris Ahart, and Shi Liu chase a long gap in how heat marks a key change in a lead based crystal. The crystal is PbTiO3, a model case for matter that holds a built in electric lean. Its Curie point is the heat level where that lean fades.

Sums from first rules tend to land far below the lab value for that point. The team asks why. They run long atom path sims at fixed push, all from first rules. They also test fast sims that use machine learnt force fields drawn from the same first rules data. By set side by side, the two runs show which part of the gap is real and which is a flaw of the fast route.
arxiv-2601-13325:
Raz Lotan, Neta Elad, Oded Padon, and Sharon Shoham verify time traits of systems with no bound on state count. Their frame is deductive, built on well founded ranks. A rank map that must fall at each step can prove that a run ends or holds a trait. Check tasks are passed to SMT solvers, tools that test if a logic claim can hold.

Their new step is a cut from trait checks to end checks. A fresh tool of timers joins the ranks to make that cut work. With it any first order time trait can be recast as an end task. For proof tool teams, one strong end engine can then serve all traits.
arxiv-2601-13425:
Gian Sebastian Mier Bello and co-authors guard the truth of science data with a blockchain log. Big compute projects draw data from many sources. Some sets are so huge that a full copy is not real to make or keep. That scale makes a plain check of truth hard. A moved or marred file may pass unseen.

Their system logs a firm mark of each set on a chain. Any later copy can be checked next to the mark with no need to move the full set. If the marks part, the file is known to have changed. For big sim teams, the log gives trust in shared data at low cost.
arxiv-2601-13525:
Chunsheng Zuo and Daniel Khashabi show that to squeeze embeddings can help dense search fit a new field. Dense search uses learnt vectors to find docs by sense. It strains in niche fields, where the train mix parts from the target mix. Fit to a new field oft needs dear marks and re teach of query doc pairs.

Their find runs the next way from the norm. Squeeze of the vectors, to fewer dims, lifts fit to the new field. A smaller vector holds less of the old field's quirks. For search teams in law, care, or code, a cheap squeeze may beat a dear re teach.
arxiv-2601-13625: Zhenghui Li, Benchao Su, and Zhixiang Wu study the completed cohomology of quaternionic Shimura curves in 2026. These curves link to an indefinite quaternion algebra that is ramified at a prime p. The team uses methods first brought in by Lue Pan. They focus on the locally analytic vectors in that space. Such vectors are the parts that act in a smooth, calculus-like way. They often carry the key arithmetic data of the whole space.
arxiv-2601-13725:
Nikko John Leo Lobos studies spinning black holes through a lens of quantum gravity ideas in 2026. The frame is the Generalized Extended Uncertainty Principle, or GEUP. It adds two fixes to old rules: a smallest length at tiny scales, and large-scale fixes too. No full quantum gravity theory exists yet to test these ideas.

Lobos takes a metric-based path, working with the curved space form of the hole. He asks what traits such spinning holes would show in real data. Those traits are the phenomenology, the signs a telescope might catch. Clear signs would help future tests of quantum gravity.
arxiv-2601-14225:
Luke Coffman, N. L. Diaz, Martín Larocca, Maria Schuld, and M. Cerezo wrote this 2026 paper on quantum physics. It asks how a known tool for sorting quantum states works when states are drawn in quantum phase space. That tool splits a state into parts set by a symmetry group. Each part is a set piece called an irreducible representation.

Work before this paper showed that the split can show how much of a quantum resource a state holds. Phase space gives a second way to draw the same systems, so the group picture changes there. The authors study that change. Their aim is a clearer test for resource traits in the phase space view.
arxiv-2601-14325:
Li Tuobang examines universal rules in very large societies in this 2026 paper. It builds on the author's past research on the topic. The focus is the topological base that keeps shared rules in force. In graph terms, a small society can be a fully connected network, where all watch all.

In that small case, the paper finds two things can coexist. Absolute egalitarianism and the rule of law fit together through peer monitoring. The title frames the wider themes: scale, hierarchy, the cost of justice, and civilizational development. Readers get a theory of why shared rules need support as societies grow past the small scale.
arxiv-2601-14425:
Haley R. Stueber leads a team of thirteen authors on a distant galaxy cluster in this 2026 paper. The cluster is SPT-CL J2215-3537, at redshift 1.16. It is relaxed and has a cool core. Galaxy clusters serve as a unique laboratory for testing cosmological models. They also show astrophysics at the high-mass limit of structure formation.

Relaxed clusters are prized targets because their form and dynamics are simple. Past redshift one, though, very few such clusters have been identified. The team reports deep Chandra observations of this rare case. Readers get a close look at a calm cluster from when the universe was much younger.
arxiv-2601-14525:
Chenglei Si and five co-authors test automated AI research in this 2026 paper. Automated AI research holds great potential to accelerate scientific discovery. Yet current large language models often generate plausible-looking but ineffective ideas. A paper can sound right and still fail when run. Execution grounding may help, by forcing ideas through real runs.

Two questions stay open. Is automated execution feasible at all? And can models learn from execution feedback? The team's title states their stance: towards execution-grounded automated AI research. Readers get a study of whether running the code, and feeding back the results, makes machine-generated research more real.
arxiv-2601-14925:
Nicolás Arrieta Larraza and Niels de Koeijer work on cleaning up speech in small devices. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with single-channel speech enhancement, which lifts clear speech out of noise. Such tools run on embedded gear with tight limits on speed and power.

Many deep learning models have been put forward for the task in recent years. One recent model, ULCNet, ranks among the best of them. The authors present Fast-ULCNet, a faster and far lighter network in that line. The name itself points to the goal: low cost and low delay.
arxiv-2601-15025:
Marian Renz, Martin Günther, and co-authors report on the ExPrIS project, which helps robots read a scene. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with object recognition from sensor data. Deep learning has pushed the field far, but its answers can lack sense.

A purely data-driven system ignores what is already known about a place. ExPrIS tests a fix for that gap. Knowledge-level expectations, facts known ahead of time, serve as priors. Those priors guide how the robot interprets what its sensors report, so the labels it gives fit the scene it sees.
arxiv-2601-15325:
Chaojun Li and Hao Fang track communities in networks that change over time. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with dynamic community detection. The task shows how group structures in a complex network evolve, merge, and split as time passes.

A common tool is nonnegative tensor RESCAL decomposition. In its classic form, the decomposition rank must equal the count of communities, which limits the model's freedom. The authors add a multilayer perceptron to the method. That enhancement loosens the rank constraint and gives the model more room to fit the changing data.
arxiv-2601-15425:
Lucas G. Barão and J. E. Horvath explain odd changes in a young pulsar's spin. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with PSR B0540-69, a spinning neutron star. Its spin-down rate, the pace at which it slows, has shifted in ways that need a cause.

How a pulsar's crust and magnetic field lines move together is much debated. The question remains unsettled after fifty years of work. New evidence has begun to confirm parts of the theory. The authors tie the spin-down changes to a drift of the magnetic axis, the line through the star's magnetic poles.
arxiv-2601-15625:
Zhiwei Zhang and a large team make language models better at using tools in a 2026 arXiv paper. Models can call tools well in clean conditions. Real runs are messier. A tool call fails, and smaller models often loop. They repeat invalid calls instead of reading the error and fixing course. That brittleness blocks reliable deployment, since errors in tool use are inevitable.

Their method is called Fission-GRPO, per the title. It teaches models to recover from execution errors. Recovery is a distinct skill from first-try success. Training for it should make agents steadier across multi-turn tasks. The work speaks to anyone building agents that act through software. A model that can absorb an error and adapt is worth far more than one that cannot.
arxiv-2601-15725:
Joana Figueira, Jordi José, Rubén Cabezón, and Domingo García-Senz model a recurrent nova's blast wave in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their system is U Sco. Recurrent novae erupt more than once. Their outbursts return on short timescales, from one to about a hundred years. Such pace demands extreme conditions. The white dwarf must accrete mass at a very high rate. Its mass sits close to the Chandrasekhar limit.

The star also starts with very high luminosity, the authors note. The study follows how the ejecta interact with two partners. One is the accretion disk feeding the dwarf. The other is the secondary star in the system. Those collisions shape how the eruption looks and fades. Modeling them helps observers read real nova light curves.
arxiv-2601-16125:
Tingyu Song and coauthors build a fine test for search by pic plus word change. Their 2026 preprint deals with composed image search. In that task, a query joins a base pic with a word change. Past tests use few query types. They miss the wide needs of real search by users.

The team builds a new test from real image edit cases. Edits give clear base pics, changes and true end pics. Fine groups let teams see where a model fails by type. A rich test can guide search tools to real world strength. The work stems from edits, not made up query sets.
arxiv-2601-16525:
Yi-Jie Wang, Geng-Dong Zhou, Hyunsung Jung, Seongyeon Youn, Seung-Sup Lee, and Zhi-Da Song study a quantum puzzle in graphene. Flat sheets of carbon, twisted at a magic angle, show odd traits. Pairs of charges form, and gaps open in strange ways. Small flaws in the sheet may drive these traits. Their 2026 preprint builds a theory for such flaws.

The flaws carry both spin and valley marks. The team maps the flaw to a known Kondo type task. They then solve that task with a tool called bosonization. The work splits into two clear cases. In one, a valley pair rules the flaw. In the next, a plain lone state rules it.
arxiv-2601-16625:
Krishanu Sengupta and coauthors sum trace flaws and bulk drag in ion clash flows. Their 2026 preprint deals with hot gas from heavy ion hits. The gas grows in a boost firm way named for Bjorken. It may sit far from rest in its first steps. Three count laws for grains are all tested in the sums.

The team solves the Boltzmann flow maths in a loose frame. Trace flaw and drag marks shift as the gas nears rest. Those marks shape how wave and flow data are read. Firm far from rest maths aids reads of real clash data. The work links grain laws to flow marks.
arxiv-2601-16725:
The Meituan LongCat Team presents a vast new open model in a 2026 tech report. The model holds 560 billion weights in a mix-of-experts frame. In that frame, just part of the net wakes for each task. The model was built for deep thought steps. It was also built to act as an agent with tools.

The report says the model tops open peers on agent tests. Those tests span search, tool use, and mixed thought with tools. The team also notes strong skill in messy, real-world scenes. Noise and odd inputs do not throw it off much. The full weights are free for firms and labs to use.
arxiv-2601-16925:
Jaideep Kalani, Saptarshi Datta, Ganesh Tambve, and Prabhakar Palni test thin sensors for fast particle hits. Such sensors, called LGADs, time hits to tens of trillionths of a second. Hard radiation zones need that speed to sort hits. Their 2026 preprint studies ultra-thin 4H-SiC forms of the sensor. The films run less than fifty microns thick.

A sim tool named WeightField2 models the films' acts. Thin films react fast but give small signals. The team weighs that trade for harsh zones. Good thin sensors could serve collider and space work. They may also serve fast scan tools in care.
arxiv-2601-17025:
Muhammad Pervez and a team of seven co-authors expose loan apps that prey on low-read users. Phones spread fast in new markets, but read skill lags. That gap breeds risk in app use. Crook loan apps abuse the yes-click that should guard users. Their 2026 preprint traces how that abuse plays out.

Users tap yes with no true grasp of terms. Fees and data grabs then drain their funds. Low-read users bear the brunt of the harm. The work names the tricks that fool such users. It can guide laws and app store checks. It may also guide plain-word consent design.
arxiv-2601-17125:
Ewoud Wempe, Simon White, Amina Helmi, Guilhem Lavaux, and Jens Jasche weigh the dark mass in and near our galaxy pair. Our Galaxy and Andromeda form the Local Group. Dwarf galaxies trail them as small kin. Most mass there is dark, not gas or stars. It must be read from how seen things move. Their 2026 preprint builds that read from dwarf paths.

Gravity's pull on dwarfs betrays the hid mass. The team maps where that mass sits and how much. Such maps test how groups of galaxies form. They also set the stage for our pair's far fate. Andromeda and our Galaxy will meet in time.
arxiv-2601-17325:
Rajat Adak and Pragya Verma set bounds in hypergraph theory. A hypergraph lets one edge hold many vertices at once. It is linear when each pair of vertices shares at most one edge. The Turán number asks how many edges such a graph can hold while it avoids a banned family. The authors study that count when the host is linear.

They focus on trees as the banned shapes. Sharp bounds sort sparse from dense in a clean way. Such results guide network and code design, where hypergraphs model group links. They also test proof tools in extremal combinatorics. Each new bound trims the space of graphs that builders must check.
arxiv-2601-17425:
Benjamin Moseley, Kirk Pruhs, Marc Uetz, and Rudy Zhou prove a hardness result for job scheduling. The setting is stochastic jobs on parallel machines. Run times are not fixed; they follow chance laws. The goal is to cut the expected weighted sum of completion times. It is a classic problem with two decades of work on near-best methods.

The authors show the problem is hard in a strong sense. That caps what any algorithm can promise. Hardness proofs save teams from hunting for tools that cannot exist. They steer work toward smart trade-offs and special cases. Plant and cloud planners both face this task. Knowing its true depth shapes what software can claim.
arxiv-2601-17525:
Andrés Mora Martínez and Gérliz M. Gutiérrez-Finol present a kinetic Monte Carlo platform for electron flow through chiral molecules. Chiral molecules lack mirror symmetry, like left and right hands. Their shape can filter electron spin as charge passes. Room-temperature spin filtering is a prized trait. It could power practical spintronic devices.

An expandable platform lets users model many molecules and setups. Monte Carlo methods track random hops that rule such flow. Good models cut the need for slow lab trials. They also show which traits drive the filter effect. Spintronics promises fast, low-power logic. Tools like this help find molecules that can deliver it.
arxiv-2601-17625:
Yuhan Xie and co-authors present BrainDistill for implantable brain-computer interfaces. Large transformer decoders now beat older methods on BCI tasks. They are too big and power-hungry for implants. Implants must run cool and small inside the body. BrainDistill uses task-specific knowledge distillation. A big teacher trains a small model for one task.

A lean decoder that keeps accuracy could reach real patients. Motor decoding turns brain signals into movement commands. That can restore control for people with paralysis. Distillation tuned per task squeezes size where it counts. The work targets the gap between lab scores and bedside use. Power limits, not accuracy, are the wall it attacks.
arxiv-2601-17725:
Eunok Bae, Jeonghyeon Shin, and Minjin Choi cut circuit costs in Grover's search algorithm. Grover's method gives a quadratic speedup over brute-force search. It serves as a subroutine in many quantum algorithms. Combinatorial problems have huge search spaces. For them, shrinking the effective search space is natural. The authors use constraint-aware initialization to do that.

Starting the search inside the feasible zone wastes no steps outside it. Fewer circuit resources mean less noise and cost. Near-term quantum machines are short on both. Constraint-aware starts could widen what Grover's method can solve today. The work links problem structure to circuit design. That link is where practical quantum gains will come from.
arxiv-2601-17925:
Tristan Langhorne, Erik E. Domenech, Juan Oliveros Gonzalez, and Richard A. Klemm work out the wave patterns for a five-sided quantum box. Their 2026 preprint also covers a thin microstrip antenna of the same pentagonal shape. Wave functions say where a particle in the box is likely to be found. For square, triangular, and disk shapes, those functions are known and rest on two quantum numbers. The pentagon is harder, since its sides do not tile in a simple way.

The authors derive the general wave functions for the regular pentagon case. The same math serves two fields at once. Physicists use it for confined particles, while engineers use it for antenna design. Filling a gap in the set of solved shapes has value in both worlds.
arxiv-2601-18125:
Mohammad Hadi Nezhad, Francisco Enrique Vicente Castro, and Ivon Arroyo study how people reason about privacy while chatting with bots. Their 2026 preprint deals with conversational agents. Users often share sensitive facts with such agents, which raises real privacy concerns. Privacy judgments depend heavily on context, so blanket warnings do little good. The authors examine how users think and act about privacy during chatbot use, with the aim of supporting real agency.

Agency here means users can act on their privacy choices in the moment. Support must arrive inside the chat, not in a policy page no one reads. The study maps the gap between what users fear and what they do. That map guides kinder, clearer privacy design.
arxiv-2601-18325:
Pavel Exner studies how small local changes can trap quantum states along a leaky curve. His 2026 preprint deals with a class of singular Schrödinger operator models. In these models, a particle interacts with the space along a curve that leaks into the plane. If the curve has a periodic shape, the spectrum has a continuum with a threshold. Exner shows that local perturbations of the curve can create a discrete spectrum below that threshold, even when the changes average to zero mean.

A zero-mean change that still binds states is a subtle effect. It matters for waveguides and nanostructures modeled by such curves. The result warns designers that average shape is not the whole story.
arxiv-2601-18425:
Emanuel Pfarr, Radu Timofte, and Frank Werner study the math that sits under tools which build images from noise. Those tools run a rule that adds noise in small steps, then learn to walk the steps back. Each step is a guess, and the size of the step sets how far each guess can stray. Most past proofs of truth dealt with the plain first grade of step.

The team push the proofs to higher grades of step, which should cut the stray for the same count of steps. They ask how the end stray grows with step size and step count for each grade. Firm bounds help teams pick a step plan with eyes open. A good plan can give the same image worth for less time on the chip.
arxiv-2601-18525:
Eleonora Grassucci and three colleagues tackle a flaw in how smart tools join sight and text in one space. The lead tool in that field learns to place a shot and its tag close if they match. In spite of that training, the shots and the tags still sit in two half-split zones of the space. That split is known as the modality gap.

A split space can blur fine picks, since a tag may sit far from a shot it fits. The team show that to close the gap does more than tidy the map. It lines up groups of like things across sight and text as well. That line-up should help tools find the right shot for a tag, and the right tag for a shot. It may also make the shared space a fairer base for new tasks.
arxiv-2601-18825:
Shahab Shahidi and Sedigheh Farahzad put forth a new way to view the stuff whose pull makes up most of what we call matter in maths of space. In their view, the dark stuff that speeds the growth of space is not a thing on its own. It is a mix of heat traits of the plain stuff we know. That is a bold shift: the dark side would be a face of the plain side, not a next kind of thing.

They show their view stands apart from past views that join stuff and shape in one sum. In their view, the push books of plain stuff and of dark stuff each stay shut and true on their own. That trait is a strong check: many joins fail it. The view thus makes a clean claim that tests can weigh.
arxiv-2601-20125:
Yuetian Chen and seven colleagues study a privacy risk in diffusion language models, a newer kind of text model. These models predict masked words using context from both sides, unlike standard models that write one word at a time. The risk is a membership inference attack, where an attacker guesses whether a given text was in the training data.

The authors present the first systematic study of this risk for fine-tuned diffusion models. They note that the many ways to mask text give attackers far more chances to probe the model. Their findings matter for anyone who fine-tunes such models on private text.
arxiv-2601-20625:
Yao Wen, Luping Xiang, and Kun Yang tackle resource allocation for immersive volumetric video in extended reality. Streaming a full three-dimensional scene is far heavier than flat video. It demands ultra-low motion-to-photon latency, since any lag between head movement and the updated view breaks immersion and can cause sickness.

Conventional edge designs render each frame in step with user motion, which strains compute. The authors propose a playback framework built on open radio access networks that jointly orchestrates radio, compute, and content resources. Coordinating all three could make volumetric streaming practical on real networks.
arxiv-2601-20825:
Julia Lieb and Michael Schaller construct a family of error-correcting codes with strong distance properties. Their 2026 paper concerns convolutional codes with optimal column distances. A convolutional code protects a stream of data by mixing nearby symbols. Column distances measure how well errors can be caught early in the stream. Codes with the best profile are called maximum distance profile codes.

Building those best codes usually demands very large finite fields. Large fields make coding and decoding costly. Codes with optimal column distances take a different deal. They maximize the column distances for whatever field is given, large or small. The authors present a construction of such codes. They also cover how to decode them. The result gives code designers strong protection without the price of huge fields.
arxiv-2601-21025:
RuiKang OuYang, Louis Grenioux, and José Miguel Hernández-Lobato propose a new loss for training energy-based generative models. Their 2026 paper works with score-based generative models. Such models usually learn the score, the gradient that points toward likely data. An alternative uses a series of time-dependent energy-based models. There, the score comes from the negative input-gradient of the energy. That route has its own training hurdles.

The authors introduce a diffusive classification loss for this energy-based path. Framing training as classification can stabilize learning. It can also sidestep costly sampling during training. Better energy-based models widen the toolkit for image and data generation. They also connect to physics, where energies are native language. The paper offers a fresh objective for a classic model family.
arxiv-2601-21125:
Ataru Tanikawa and a large team of co-authors report a compact family of three stars found by accident. Their 2026 paper describes a hierarchical triple main-sequence star system. The system is cataloged as Gaia DR3 1010268155897156864, or TIC 21502513. The team calls it G1010 for short. It consists of a primary star and an inner binary. The pair and the primary orbit each other in a tight hierarchy.

The discovery came while searching for binary stars with compact objects. Such hunts survey many ordinary systems along the way. A compact triple of normal stars is a valuable bycatch. Its orbits test how triple systems form and stay stable. The primary's mass is pinned near that of the Sun. The paper gives the community a new, well-measured triple for dynamical studies.
arxiv-2601-21225:
Tianyi Xu and eight co-authors build a tougher multilingual test for math reasoning. Their 2026 paper introduces MGSM-Pro. Large language models have made substantial progress in mathematical reasoning. Benchmarks for multilingual evaluation lag behind English in difficulty and recency, though. GSM-Symbolic recently showed high variance in scores across versions of the same question. That warning sign was measured only in English. The authors extend the probe across languages.

MGSM-Pro offers a simple strategy for robust multilingual evaluation. It varies problems systematically so luck and memorization show up. Models must solve the math, not recall an answer key. Fair multilingual tests matter for the billions who learn in other languages. The benchmark can reveal whether reasoning skill truly transfers. It raises the bar for claims of global competence.
arxiv-2601-21525:
Meet Doshi and seven co-authors improve how text is squeezed into a single vector for search and ranking. Encoders usually collapse a passage into one vector using a special token or a plain average. Both routes can blur the fine detail that search depends on.

Their method pools around landmark tokens instead. Landmarks anchor the summary at the most telling spots in the text. A better summary vector lifts search, clustering, and reranking at once. The work matters wherever one vector must stand in for a whole document, from web search to company archives.
arxiv-2601-21725:
Liangze Jiang, Zachary Shinnick, Anton van den Hengel, Hemanth Saratchandran, and Damien Teney warm up language models on abstract data before real text. Standard practice starts pretraining straight on huge web corpora. The authors test a gentler start, much as people learn basic logic and math before deep reading.

Models first see structured, abstract data with clear patterns. Only then do they move to rich semantic material. The warm start may ease the later learning, the way drills ease a new sport. If the effect is real, cheaper early training on synthetic patterns could cut the cost of building capable models.
arxiv-2601-21825:
R. Esteban Goetz and Anh-Thu Le study light created when intense laser pulses strike matter. In high-order harmonic generation, atoms emit light at multiples of the driving frequency, but the emission normally stops at a cutoff energy. Their 2026 preprint analyzes cases where the spectrum reaches beyond that usual cutoff.

The extension comes from a two-color process. Extreme ultraviolet light first knocks an electron out and leaves a hole in the ion's core. The infrared field then drives loose electrons back to recombine with that hole, releasing higher-energy light. Understanding these spectra matters for building tabletop sources of extreme ultraviolet and soft X-ray light. Which are used to film electrons moving inside atoms and molecules.
arxiv-2601-22025:
Daniel Commey warns that improving a prompt can quietly make a language model application worse. Testing such applications differs from traditional software testing. Outputs are stochastic, high-dimensional, and sensitive to small changes in the prompt or the model behind it.

Commey presents an evaluation-driven workflow with four stages: Define, Test, Diagnose, Fix. Each round of prompt edits is checked against defined tests before it ships, turning prompt tweaking into a repeatable engineering loop. His 2026 preprint stresses reproducibility, since a fix that cannot be retested is just a hope. Teams shipping chatbots and assistants need exactly this discipline as prompts become production code.
arxiv-2601-22125:
Kunpeng Song and Ahmed Elgammal teach diffusion models to be creative, not just accurate. Creative image generation aims at pictures that are novel and high-quality, pushing past the boundaries of what already exists. The authors tie creativity to a measurable quantity.

In their 2026 framework, an image's creativity relates to how improbable its existence is, judged in the embedding space of the CLIP vision-language model. Images that sit in unlikely regions of that space count as more original. Steering generation toward those regions, while keeping quality, gives artists and designers a dial for novelty. The work also gives creativity research a concrete handle instead of a purely subjective label.
arxiv-2601-22225:
Mariam Bouhmadi-López and co-authors test whether a modified theory of gravity can ease cosmology's sharpest disagreement. Local and early-universe measures of the Hubble constant, which sets the universe's expansion rate, do not agree. Late-time changes to gravity are one proposed way to close that gap.

The authors work in teleparallel gravity. It rebuilds gravity from torsion rather than curvature. They study its f(T) extension as a minimal, controlled change to general relativity. They confront the models with baryon acoustic oscillation data from the DESI survey. Their 2026 preprint checks whether this corner of modified gravity can move the Hubble tension at all.
arxiv-2601-22325:
Paula Mellado, Xavier Cazor, and Andres Concha study small rings of magnetic rods twisted like a wreath. Their 2026 preprint varies the twist between stacked polygons and watches the spin patterns shift. The rods act like tiny compass needles that push and pull on each other.

As twist grows, the patterns turn chiral, with a clear handed twist. They range from closed swirls to spiky, hedgehog-like spreads. Such shapes hint at new ways to store or steer signals at tiny scales. The work also gives a clean test case for twist-driven magnetism.
arxiv-2601-22425:
Elin Bergeaas Kuutmann, for the ATLAS team, sums up hunts for two kinds of new particles at the Large Hadron Collider. Vector-like quarks and leptoquarks sit at the heart of many plans to extend the standard model. Their 2026 report notes that the known model, while strong, stays incomplete.

The new particles could help explain why masses span such a vast range. They could also explain odd quirks in how some particles decay. ATLAS hunts for their marks in clash data. A find would rewrite particle physics; a blank hunt still trims the space of live theories. The report gathers the latest bounds.
arxiv-2601-22525:
Tracy Bergemann and Tim Hanson adapt interim trial checks to the win ratio, a popular way to grade treatments. The win ratio compares each treated patient with each control on a ranked mix of outcomes. Their 2026 preprint brings in group sequential methods, which let a trial stop early on firm evidence.

The mix can join time, yes-no, and count outcomes in one score. Early stops save patients and funds when a treatment clearly wins or fails. Sound interim math is a must for such stops to be trusted. The work gives trial teams a checked tool.
arxiv-2601-22625:
Haixia Liu and Ruifan Huang protect just the labels in regression data, with a prior in hand. Labels often hold the sensitive fact, while inputs may be safe to share. Their 2026 preprint, RPWithPrior, works under label differential privacy, a firm bound on what one label can reveal.

The team weave a prior belief into the private release, to keep accuracy high at the same privacy cost. Good private regression serves health and social data, where labels are touchy. The work seeks the best trade the math allows. It is a careful balance of two goods.
arxiv-2601-23025:
Grégoire Le Lay and Adrian Daerr watch thin streams of fluid dance in a narrow cell. A rivulet flows inside an air-filled Hele-Shaw cell, a thin gap between plates. Bends across and along the stream can travel as waves, though both fade in their setup.

They then shake the system with a steady, uniform acoustic tone. On this simple setup, forcing brings out rich motion from a single filament of fluid. Small systems like this reveal how vibration can steer flows in microfluidic devices. Acoustic forcing, uniform in space and harmonic in time, drives the dancing motion on this deliberately simple system.
arxiv-2601-23125:
Helena Cobo studies a special polynomial tied to the Weyl algebra and a chosen polynomial raised to a power. The b-function encodes deep information about singularities and differential equations linked to that polynomial. Here it is taken with respect to weights, which grade the variables by importance.

The work examines properties of this weighted b-function for the annihilating ideal, the set of operators killing the power. Such functions govern algorithms in computational algebra. They also connect geometry, through the singularities of the polynomial's zero set. Weights on the variables change the b-function's behavior, and the annihilating ideal fixes which operators are under study.
arxiv-2601-23225:
Rajib Mostakim, Reza T. Batley, and Sourav Saha make deep reinforcement learning cheaper for small devices. Learning systems increasingly run where resources are tight. The usual multilayer perceptron approximator wastes parameters, because its bias fits smooth value functions poorly.

Their separable neural architecture matches that smooth structure better. A better fit means fewer parameters, faster learning from fewer samples. Efficient learning matters for robots and controllers that must adapt on modest hardware. Capacity-limited regimes are where the mismatch bites hardest, wasting scarce parameters on structure the value function never had. Separable architecture is the proposed remedy, reshaping the approximator around the smoothness of value functions.
arxiv-2602-00125: Soumyadip Sarkar presents MiniTensor, an open source tensor library built for minimalism, correctness, and speed. It offers a familiar PyTorch like Python API, while heavy code runs in a Rust engine. The core covers dense tensors, broadcasting, reductions, matrix products, reverse mode differentiation, a compact set of neural layers, and standard optimizers. Its install size is only a few megabytes, orders smaller than PyTorch and TensorFlow, while keeping the essentials for CPU research and development.
arxiv-2602-00425: Siyuan Wang and team propose segment attribution for selective learning of long reasoning traces. Large models perform strongly by making long chains of thought, yet only a small fraction of traces matters. Such redundancy grows after tuning, as models copy verbose patterns. The authors use integrated gradients to score token influence on final answers, aggregating into two metrics. Strength measures magnitude, and direction consistency captures whether token scores in a segment are all positive, all negative, or mixed. From those metrics, they propose selective learning on informative segments.
arxiv-2602-00525: David Angel Alba Bonilla and colleagues build a classical-quantum framework that tells calcium fluoride from erbium-doped calcium fluoride using first-principles optical descriptors. Clusters are modelled with density functional theory and its time-dependent form, and optical excitations are turned into absorption spectra. A classical support vector machine beats quantum variants on test accuracy, while a hybrid quantum neural network with a 3-qubit feature map performs strongly. The results show dopant-induced fingerprints give a feature space for benchmarking quantum learning models against classical baselines.
arxiv-2602-00625: Shuo Dong and colleagues investigate thermoelectric transport in a triangular triple quantum dot system linked to two reservoirs under linear response. Using hierarchical equations of motion, they compute thermopower and the thermoelectric figure of merit, analysing how interaction schemes among the three dots affect it. At low temperatures, easing of the geometric blockade speeds heat current growth far more than electric current growth. The effect lifts thermopower to a remarkably high figure of merit.
arxiv-2602-00725: Uwe Kähler and colleagues work on the n-sphere with the Dirac operator, bounding the best constants in two Lieb-Thirring analogues. Their bounds then improve a known result for the n-sphere: the upper bound on the classical Lieb-Thirring constant. The improvement thus concerns the classical constant in higher dimensions, using the two Dirac analogues as its source.
arxiv-2602-00825: Kedar Karhadkar and colleagues prove that smooth interpolators of noisy data can overfit harmfully. Generalization error stays above a positive constant even as sample size grows without bound. They study functions in Sobolev spaces that perfectly fit noisy training data, where smoothness bias picks approximately norm-minimizing interpolators. The result holds for every p from 1 to infinity, unlike prior work limited to the Hilbert case p equals 2 via kernel methods. Their proof finds harmful neighborhoods of training data with Sobolev inequalities.
arxiv-2602-00925: Hayato Chiba obtains non-principle Kovalevskaya exponents from principle ones using a commutable vector field. He studies groups of Laurent series solutions for a quasi-homogeneous vector field with a commutable vector field. A family is principle if it includes m free parameters, and non-principle if fewer than m. Starting from a principle family, he gives an ordered way to obtain a non-principle family.
arxiv-2602-01025: Kaiyuan Cui and co-authors build UltraBreak, a jailbreak trick for vision-plus-text models that works across many models and goals. Old tricks tuned on one open model tend to stick there and fail on closed ones. UltraBreak reins in the image trick with warps and smoothing, while loosening the text goal to a sense-based aim. Its loss lives in target text space, so its tricks carry over. In tests it beat past jailbreak tricks time and again, showing why loss smoothing helps tricks travel.
arxiv-2602-01325: Kai Hu and co-authors build a single region-of-interest squeeze frame with a generalized Gaussian law. Region-based squeezing spends bits unevenly by sense weight, warping latent spreads into sharp peaks with fat tails that plain Gaussian laws fit badly. Their rate-distortion frame backs a generalized Gaussian law with bendy shape knobs, steadied by smooth differentiable tricks and a live lower bound against train-test drift. COCO2017 tests show top region rebuilds and downstream jobs like segmentation and object spotting.
arxiv-2602-01625: Nobuyuki Okuma proposes a steady state skin effect for matter built from bosonic Bogoliubov de Gennes systems, whose spectral theory carries non-Hermiticity. Realizations stayed classical or artificial, but Okuma adds parametric pumping terms to edge states of a Hermitian Chern insulator, creating non-Hermiticity without dissipation. The design stays largely independent of microscopic details. Under open boundaries, Green function analysis finds a steady state with the skin effect, and corner buildup shows quadrature anisotropy, a bosonic quantum signature. The result links non-Hermitian matrix math to quantum systems.
arxiv-2602-01825: Mingyuan Xu and colleagues learn decision policies from offline multi site data. They study robust MDPs with group linear structure: sites share a feature map, and transitions and rewards are linear in those features. Feature wise uncertainty sets preserve robust Bellman recursions while keeping cross site structure. Their algorithm uses pessimistic value iteration with per site ridge regression, worst aggregation, and a data dependent pessimism penalty from design matrix diagonals. Clustering pools similar sites, and under partial coverage they prove a suboptimality bound, without strong state action rectangularity assumptions.
arxiv-2602-02125: Chen Hao Xia and colleagues learn and predict the Hamiltonian matrix of large structures with equivariant graph networks. That dodges the costly build. Where a unit cell repeats, atom counts shrink. That trick fails for amorphous materials. They model valence change memory cells, hitting a Mean Absolute Error of three point three nine to 3.58 meV. Swapping the DFT Hamiltonian of VCMs for the predicted one, they find good agreement between both curve sets. Their work opens a path past DFT limits.
arxiv-2602-02225: Shad Ali models emission of short gamma-ray bursts and gravitational waves from binary mergers in a report spanning three parts. The first part treats short bursts from mergers surrounded by strong magnetic fields, with rapidly spinning magnetized neutron stars as the field source. The second part reviews black hole interiors, tracing information and evaporation from initial to final phases through entropy variation. The final part studies black hole configuration entropy and thermodynamic phase transitions under modified gravity, comparing results with charged anti-de Sitter black holes.
arxiv-2602-02325:
S. F. Pate and 3 co-authors address a measurement problem in spin physics in a 2026 arXiv paper. Experiments with polarized beams or targets, where particle spins point in a chosen direction, measure a quantity called transverse single-spin asymmetry. That measurement gets hard when polarization changes over time or differs between spin states. Unequal data amounts and detector blurring add further trouble.

The authors give general methods for extracting the asymmetry in two ways. One groups data into bins, and the other uses an unbinned likelihood method that weighs each event directly. Both can undo detector smearing, a step called unfolding, and both can subtract background events. The result is a flexible toolkit for experiments facing messy, uneven running conditions.
arxiv-2602-02425:
Amaru Caceres Arroyo and 5 co-authors repurpose protein language models to design fitter proteins without expensive sampling, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Protein fitness optimization searches a vast space of variants where high scorers are extremely rare. Many methods underperform or need costly gradient-based sampling at design time.

Their framework, CHASE, compresses embeddings from a pretrained protein language model into a compact latent space. Those embeddings carry evolutionary knowledge learned from natural sequences. A conditional flow-matching model, trained with classifier-free guidance, then generates high-fitness variants directly, with no predictor steering the sampling steps. CHASE reached the best reported performance on AAV and GFP design benchmarks, two standard protein engineering tests. Bootstrapping with synthetic data improved results further when real data was scarce.
arxiv-2602-02525:
Liam Hebert and 2 co-authors make the case for pretraining social media models on community norms without task labels, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Discussion transformers model conversations as graph structures and show promise for fighting hate speech and misinformation. Their progress is throttled by dependence on high-quality human-labeled datasets, which are expensive and narrow.

The authors advocate a shift from task-specific fine-tuning to unsupervised pretraining grounded in community norms. Such pretraining could ease data scarcity across many downstream tasks at once. It could also make model decisions interpretable, by exposing the social norms the system used. The paper is a position piece rather than a system report. It maps opportunities for AI for social good that follow once norms become the organizing signal for social media modeling.
arxiv-2602-02625:
Md Motaleb Hossen Manik and 1 co-author study how AI agents police each other on an agent-only social network, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Agents increasingly share information and instructions in common spaces, yet almost no evidence exists on how they regulate one another without humans or central moderation. The network, Moltbook, hosts OpenClaw agents exclusively.

The dataset covers about thirty-nine thousand posts and fifty-seven hundred comments from nearly fourteen and a half thousand agents. A lexicon-based risk score measures action-inducing instruction sharing, which appeared in about eighteen percent of posts. Instruction sharing is therefore routine in this environment. Most responses were neutral, but posts containing actionable instructions drew significantly more norm-enforcing replies cautioning against risky behavior. Toxic responses stayed rare in both conditions. The authors read this as selective social regulation emerging without human oversight.
arxiv-2602-03025:
Tool-calling agents that stall during training are the problem for Haitian Zhong and 5 co-authors in a 2026 paper. In multi-turn tool use, rewards are sparse and exploration is costly. A standard recipe can stall when every rollout in a group scores all zero or all one, leaving no useful learning signal.

Their method, RC-GRPO, steers exploration with discrete reward tokens placed in the prompt. A first policy learns to produce trajectories of distinct quality on demand. During reinforcement learning, varied reward tokens diversify each group. Tests on a Berkeley function-calling benchmark followed. Performance improved consistently, and one setup surpassed all closed-source models tested.
arxiv-2602-03425:
Fine-tuning flow-based image models with reinforcement learning can sharpen results, but it often adds hallucinated details that clash with the prompt. Xiaofeng Tan and 9 co-authors study that failure in a 2026 paper. They blame limited exploration during sampling rollouts and a trajectory imitation effect that warps the model's underlying vector field.

Their framework, ConsistentRFT, answers with two parts. A dynamic granularity rollout schedules different noise sources to balance global meaning against local detail. A consistent policy gradient method keeps the updated policy close to a stable prior, protecting cross-step consistency. Experiments report large drops in both low-level and high-level perceptual hallucinations, plus better out-of-domain behavior than rival methods.
arxiv-2602-03525:
Membership filters answer one question fast: is this item probably in the set, with a small controlled chance of a false yes. Antoine Limasset introduces ZOR filters in a 2026 paper, a deterministic relative of XOR and fuse filters. The older designs build quickly, but their peeling construction can fail by chance, forcing awkward restarts.

ZOR keeps construction deterministic: its peeling simply drops a small fraction of keys instead of restarting on failure. A compact auxiliary structure stores the leftovers, restoring false-positive-only behavior. In experiments the abandoned share drops below one percent at moderate sizes, so overhead lands within about one percent of the theoretical minimum. Queries stay as fast as fuse filters, apart from an auxiliary check on negative answers.
arxiv-2602-03625:
A segmentation model trained on video game screenshots fails on real streets because the visual styles differ. Estelle Chigot and 3 co-authors treat the fix as a sequencing puzzle in a 2026 paper. Style transfer can repaint synthetic images realistically, but choosing which operators to apply, and in what order, is a huge combinatorial search.

Multi-objective genetic algorithms evolve the pipelines, balancing structural coherence against style similarity to the target domain. To keep evolution fast, candidate pipelines are scored on individual image pairs rather than whole distributions. The evolved Pareto front is then judged with distributional metrics and real segmentation performance. Tests move from the game GTA5 to real datasets, with emphasis on adverse weather conditions.
arxiv-2602-03725:
Pricing exotic financial derivatives by classical Monte Carlo is provably decent but slow, and quantum algorithms promise a quadratic speedup. Dylan Herman and 7 co-authors extend the proven territory in a 2026 paper. End-to-end quantum speedups had only been shown for the simplified Black-Scholes model, not for the messier models traders actually use.

The team identifies a property they call fast-forwardability in the underlying stochastic equations. It yields quadratic speedups for the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model and a variant of Heston's stochastic volatility model. For general models they build a quantum Milstein sampler, enabling quantum multilevel Monte Carlo speedups. Improved integration analysis cuts resource requirements, and a final critique identifies barriers blocking quantum PDE solvers from the same speedup.
arxiv-2602-03825:
Robots deployed with human oversight learn from interventions, often by simply learning to avoid triggering them. Ethan Pronovost and 2 co-authors examine what that avoidance objective really does in a 2026 paper, from a geometric angle. Intervention avoidance, they show, constrains policies to one face of the occupancy measure polytope.

That picture explains when the method works. Informative ones pin down a unique solution, while weak ones leave many feasible policies, plenty of them suboptimal. The authors define Robust Intervention Learning, built to perform well however informative the interventions are. Their algorithm, Residual Intervention Fine-Tuning, blends the corrections with a prior policy to choose among feasible solutions. It provably improves on the prior and wins empirically, above all when interventions are sparse.
arxiv-2602-03925:
Superconductivity usually means pairs of electrons condensing together. Zhi-Qiang Gao and 3 co-authors argue that groups of four can condense first, on their own, in a 2026 theory paper. Their platform is a featureless Mott insulator, a material that blocks current despite having mobile electrons, given extra symmetry and then doped.

They build a bilayer Hubbard model whose insulating phase carries the needed symmetry. Large-scale numerical simulations find the four-electron superconducting phase in one symmetry case and ordinary pairing in another. The work maps the surrounding normal states and sketches the finite-temperature picture, giving experimentalists a concrete place to look.
arxiv-2602-04125:
Platforms allocating exposure with bandit algorithms can play favorites unfairly. Qingwen Zhang and 1 co-author develop fairness-respecting contextual bandits in a 2026 paper. Uniform merit fairness requires that preferential treatment always track merit, in every context and round, not just on average.

Their algorithms nearly achieve perfect fairness while keeping regret at the minimax level among fair policies for linear rewards, and near it for smooth rewards. Lower bounds price fairness exactly for linear rewards: regret grows by a logarithmic factor. Adversarial corruption of rewards degrades the guarantees in a quantified way, separating regret robustness from fairness robustness.
arxiv-2602-04325:
Nonreciprocal interactions, where influence runs one way, make patterns with no equilibrium analogue. Yuta Tateyama and 5 co-authors map those patterns in a two-field Swift-Hohenberg model with circular symmetry in a 2026 paper. Special higher-codimension points order the whole phase diagram.

Computer runs and path following explore the full equations, while a one-mode reduction and normal form study near a special bifurcation give analytic grip. Uniform, patterned, moving, standing, and modulated wave states connect through the bifurcation structure the authors chart. Organizing centers let one diagram explain many pattern-forming systems at once.
arxiv-2602-04725:
Neville Mathew and 4 co-authors benchmark cuffless blood pressure estimation from fingertip light signals in a 2026 paper. Photoplethysmography, which tracks blood volume changes optically, is easy to collect, making it attractive for large-scale cardiovascular screening without an inflatable cuff.

Earlier evaluations lacked rigorous controls and used mixed-quality datasets. The authors built a standardized benchmark subset from two clinical databases, with over one hundred thousand high-quality signal segments from healthy adults. Leading models were tested against international accuracy standards. None met those standards as originally designed. Adding patient details such as age, sex, and body mass index improved every model. One modified model cut its error substantially and approached the standard limits.
arxiv-2602-04825:
Achilles Machumilane and Alberto Gotta model packet loss for dual connectivity in future 6G satellite networks in a 2026 telecommunications paper. Dual connectivity sends traffic over two paths at once for throughput and reliability, but paths through low Earth orbit satellites have very different delays.

Delay mismatches can reorder packets, trigger congestion control unnecessarily, or drop real-time traffic that arrives too late. Fixes such as duplication, switching, and network coding each carry costs in resources, delay, or computing. The authors build a mathematical framework for average end-to-end packet loss when channel loss follows a Markov chain model. It covers combining duplication with switching, and network coding separately. The metrics support optimal policies for later comparison with learned models.
arxiv-2602-05025:
Isabel Agostino and Thibaut Mastrolia study a control task driven by self-exciting chance in this 2026 mathematics paper. The chance comes from a Hawkes process, where each event makes more events more likely for a while. The controller can act in a sharp, forceful way and wants the best time and way to step in.

In continuous time, the task boils down to a variational partial differential equation with gradient limits, a hard thing to compute with head-on. The authors instead build a discrete-time form cast as a Markov decision process. They then prove its value tends to the continuous one under the right rescaling. So discrete optimizers are nearly best for the first task. An application to power plant investment under cyber threat, modeled with an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, shows the theory with simulations.
arxiv-2602-05125:
Rubrics, lists of criteria for judging open-ended answers, now steer both LLM judges and the reward signals used in fine-tuning. William F Shen and 8 co-authors tackle rubric quality in this 2026 machine learning paper. Home-grown rubrics often miss important dimensions, blur separate ideas together, point the wrong way, or repeat themselves, and each flaw degrades judging and training alike.

Their framework, RRD, refines rubrics in a recursive loop: split coarse criteria into fine, discriminating ones, then filter out the misaligned and redundant, with weights that stop correlated criteria from dominating. On two judging benchmarks it lifted accuracy for both GPT-4o and a large Llama judge, by up to about 18 points. Used as a reward source in fine-tuning on chat data, it produced far stronger learning signals than earlier rubric baselines, and the gains carried over to health and general benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-05325:
Robot dexterity training usually demands hours of teleoperation, a slow and costly route. Jiacheng Fan and 6 co-authors present RoboPaint in this 2026 robotics paper, a pipeline that turns human demonstrations into robot training data instead. Standard capture rooms film volunteers with many cameras, a sensor glove tracking 29 degrees of freedom, and tactile channels.

Geometry and force guide a tactile-aware retargeting method that maps each human hand state onto a robot dexterous hand. A photorealistic simulator renders the resulting trajectories into the training set. Retargeted motions won about 84 percent of trials across ten manipulation tasks. Vision-language-action policies trained only on generated data averaged about 80 percent success on pick-and-place, pushing, and pouring tests. The authors present the pipeline as a scalable, cheaper replacement for teleoperation with minimal performance loss.
arxiv-2602-05825:
Generative AI often answers a vague design brief in ways the user never intended. Lena Hegemann, Xinyi Wen, and 3 co-authors present ToMigo, a tool that exposes the model reading of intent. Intent is drawn as a design concept graph: nodes hold choices about purpose, content, or style, and edges explain how the choices link.

Applied to graphic design, ToMigo infers intent from reference images and text. A schema of node and edge types, derived from a pre study, guides a multimodal model to build graphs that stay faithful to the user and coherent as a whole. Users can then inspect the reasoning and edit the graph directly. In user studies, the tool earned high alignment ratings and captured most intentions well. Participants reported greater control, and they valued features such as editable graphs and reflective chat for developing their design ideas.
arxiv-2602-05925:
Hash tables sit inside nearly every program, and Gábor Melis argues that fixing one hash function for the table whole life is a mistake. General purpose functions such as Murmur spread keys well and run fast, but they ignore the actual key distribution, which limits how evenly buckets fill. Tailoring a function to an assumed distribution risks disaster when the assumption fails.

Perfect hashing sits at the other extreme: optimal for a known, fixed key set, but costly and static. The author proposes adapting the hash function online, to the keys currently stored, with minimal overhead and no change to the hash table interface. Experiments show better bucketing and faster hashing together. The conceptual claim is that adaptivity is necessary for the best performance, not a luxury. It reframes hashing as a learning problem over the live key set.
arxiv-2602-06025:
Agents built on large language models need memory beyond one context window, but most systems build that memory offline, without knowing the question it must serve. Haozhen Zhang and ten co-authors present BudgetMem, a runtime memory frame that routes each question with its budget in mind. Memory modules come in low, mid, and high tiers, and a small neural router trained with reinforcement learning picks the tier per module.

The team studies three ways to build tiers: method complexity, inference behaviour, and module model size. On LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and HotpotQA, BudgetMem beats strong baselines when performance matters most, and draws better accuracy-cost frontiers when budgets tighten. The analysis shows which tiering axis wins under which regime, giving agent builders a dial, not a guess, for trading memory cost against answer quality.
arxiv-2602-06125:
When a gravitational wave passes a black hole, it scatters, and computing that scattering precisely matters for future detectors. Yilber Fabian Bautista and 3 co-authors build the needed framework inside worldline quantum field theory, a method that treats the black hole as a particle following a path. They leave out spin to keep the case clean.

The team proves that, with no energy loss, their scattering matrix links directly to the classic phase shift from black hole perturbation theory. Working through the math, they match that phase shift up to a stated order. They also describe a fast way to generate the needed diagrams and explain the two-loop integrals involved.
arxiv-2602-06625:
As language models increasingly grade each other's answers, Bo Yang and five co-authors ask how fair and steady those judges really are. Such judges can be rigid, favor long or well-formatted answers, and contradict themselves when the grading style changes. The team treats judging itself as a skill that can be trained and corrected.

They build a dense training set that teaches rubric use, bias control, and consistency, then train in stages that move from basic alignment to preference tuning and reinforcement. On internal and public benchmarks, their judge agreed more with human grades and showed fewer format-driven biases than much larger general models. The authors plan to release their data and models openly.
arxiv-2602-06825:
Yuming Li and eight co-authors improve how diffusion image models are aligned with human preferences. Methods like GRPO treat every prompt and every denoising step the same, but samples differ greatly in learning value, and some moments in the denoising process matter more than others. The authors find that attention entropy, a measure of how spread out the model's attention is, serves as a useful double signal.

Changes in entropy between the current and base policy flag high-value prompts, while entropy peaks across denoising steps mark moments of high-value exploration. Their method, AEGPO, uses both signals: it budgets rollouts toward promising prompts and explores selectively at critical steps rather than everywhere. On text-to-image tasks it converged faster and aligned better than standard GRPO variants.
arxiv-2602-07025:
Daniele Savietto and six co-authors study why vision-language models stumble on multi-object visual tasks. They may invent elements that are not there, or fail to pick the most similar objects among distractors. Those slips mirror a human limit known as the binding problem, yet the inner mechanisms in artificial systems are little known. The team studies the geometry of inner representations in three open-weight model families.

They compare ways to pull out concept vectors, directions in latent space that encode visual concepts. Steering tests check those vectors: they can reliably shift model behavior, even making it see a red flower as blue, in simple and in natural tasks. Overlap in geometry between vectors lines up strongly with specific error patterns. That gives a quantitative frame for how inner representations shape visual failures, and hints at targeted fixes.
arxiv-2602-07125:
Searching across text and images breaks down when a query needs unstated thinking, such as sorting out a vague reference or a combined setting.  Jianrui Zhang and five co-authors argue the fault often lies in the data: a single embedding step is forced to reason and compress at once, which invites false matches.

Their method moves thinking out of that step.  A strong vision-language model writes dense captions for images in the collection, clears up ambiguous references in queries. Rewrites long instructions as short retrieval constraints, and the retriever is then trained on these enriched representations.  The result is a retrieval system aimed at queries that need real thought before matching.
arxiv-2602-07825:
Cutting health gaps means asking what would happen under what-if steps, and which factors may fairly define the gap itself. John W. Jackson and three co-authors survey gauging plans for causal split analysis, a method built on future results that lets analysts specify fair factors.

Allowing some factors and excluding others makes results more open and real, but tangles gauging, for instance by needing density models. The paper reviews ready plans, offers new ones, and clarifies how causal split differs from standard econ split methods. Gaps teams get a guided tour that should make a strong but rare method easier to adopt right.
arxiv-2602-08325:
Some flows remember their past, and the math for them involves fractional derivatives that are costly to compute. Liangcai Huang and two co-authors design a second-order time-stepping scheme for a tempered fractional advection-dispersion equation. That equation models spread with memory in moving fluids, and their arXiv paper leans on a sum-of-exponentials trick to approximate the awkward convolution kernel.

Graded time meshes handle the sharp behavior near the start, and a half-step time scheme joins a spatial finite-difference method. Compared with the classic approach, the new method keeps the same accuracy while cutting storage sharply. Storage falls from a product of grid sizes to a product with the small exponential count, and compute time drops likewise. Proofs of solvability, stability, and accuracy back the scheme, and numerical trials confirm the gains.
arxiv-2602-08525:
Calcium tungstate is a promising host for erbium-based quantum memories, but stored states leak through interactions with lattice vibrations. Mikhael T. Sayat and ten co-authors map those vibrations with neutron scattering and density-functional perturbation theory. Their arXiv paper traces phonon bands up to 130 milli-electronvolts, with a gap between 60 and 80.

Symmetry analysis picks out eight modes that link straight to erbium crystal-field operators. A low-energy mode at 9.1 milli-electronvolts looks dominant for phonon-assisted spin-lattice relaxation. Readers get a microscopic picture of the phonon bath in this host crystal, plus a basis for engineering quieter environments for quantum memories.
arxiv-2602-08625:
Many-language models support dozens of tongues, but deploying one for just a few wastes capacity. Muhammad Naufil asks whether these models contain dedicated attention heads for single languages that could be pruned away. His arXiv paper explores that question for many-language models beyond translation-only systems.

Prior work probed language-specific heads in translation models, but many-language models handle diverse tasks, and no comparable study existed for them. The paper investigates whether removing heads tied to unwanted languages preserves performance on target languages. Readers get early evidence toward leaner deployments that keep only the languages they need.
arxiv-2602-08825:
Some hard problems are too slow or costly to solve directly, so scientists train a stand-in model, called a surrogate, to mimic them. Tomohiro Harada and two co-authors argue that a good stand-in must be judged on more than accuracy alone. Their 2026 paper introduces PTME, a checklist covering precision, time, memory, and energy use.

They test the idea on a real task: arranging traffic lights across European cities for the best flow. Several stand-ins are built and scored on sampling, data size, and resource use, then put to work in new decision-making routines. The authors present PTME as a guide other fields can borrow when weighing speed against trust.
arxiv-2602-08925:
Research tools promise open participation, yet blind and low-vision scholars face daily barriers as charts and images dominate workflows. Omar Khan and one co-author, writing as blind and low-vision researchers themselves, survey 57 peers and interview 15 more about how they cope. Nearly one in five cannot independently review literature or judge visual outputs, delegating work to sighted colleagues or leaning on AI retrieval to cut fatigue.

Participants describe lost autonomy, physical strain, and frustration with tools whose makers respond with gestures rather than fixes, even costing them deserved credit. The paper closes with design recommendations that treat accessibility as core to good research, not an add-on. Its title quotes a participant's blunt verdict on professional tools.
arxiv-2602-09025:
When a massive star explodes, does the nuclear equation of state change the outcome? Aleksandr Rusakov and three co-authors run full three-dimensional simulations to late times for a nine-solar-mass star, comparing the SFHo and DD2 equations of state. DD2 is stiffer with a lower effective nucleon mass, giving a puffier protoneutron star at lower central density.

That softness ripples outward: mean neutrino energies, final explosion energy, and recoil kick all drop, while convection, neutrino light curves, and gravitational-wave signals shift in diagnostic ways. The faster SFHo explosion also yields slightly more neutron-rich ejecta with a weak rapid-capture process. A broader multi-progenitor survey is the planned next step.
arxiv-2602-09125:
Gravity waves are now routine, but their quantum nature stays unproven. Kristian Toccacelo and three co-authors show that new single-graviton detectors could do more than count quanta: they could reveal the quantum state of the passing wave. Spotting odds tell apart squeezed, in-step, and thermal glow, three unlike quantum kinds.

The full second-order link function, which encodes the wave's quantum stats, can be read directly at the device, independent of how weakly gravity couples. Building on quantum-optics tricks, that opens the door to full mapping of Gaussian gravity states. The work turns a foundational curiosity into a practical measurement program.
arxiv-2602-09225:
Neural networks that learn the same task can still organize knowledge differently, and comparing them is tricky because units can be reordered or rotated without changing what the network does. Shreya Saha and two co-authors introduce barycentric alignment, a framework that quotients out those nuisance symmetries to build a shared embedding space across many models. Unlike summary similarity scores, it compares representations stimulus by stimulus.

That fine grain reveals which inputs drive models together or apart, and which input properties predict convergence across vision and language families. The same framework builds shared spaces for brain representations across people and visual areas. It also aligns unimodal vision and language models so well that image-text scores track human cross-modal judgments, nearing contrastively trained models.
arxiv-2602-09525:
Manish Yadav and three co-authors probe whether dark energy changes over time, using a new transition form for the Om diagnostic in a flat expanding-universe model. Their 2026 paper fits the model to Hubble data, supernova data, and local calibration data with Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, hunting deviations from the standard cosmological model. The Om slope flips from negative to positive, with the flip redshift differing by dataset combination.

That flip suggests dark energy evolving from a quintessence-like phase toward a phantom regime. The combined fit yields a Hubble constant near the local calibration value, supporting the model's viability, and a universe age of roughly thirteen to fourteen billion years across dataset combinations. The deceleration-to-acceleration transition falls at moderate redshifts, marking dark energy's recent rise to dominance. The parametrization captures smooth cosmological change across epochs.
arxiv-2602-09725:
Remote key-value cache reuse fetches cached key-value data for identical contexts from remote storage, avoiding recomputation and speeding language model inference. Liang Mi and five co-authors note that it shines in high-speed networks but fades in bandwidth-limited cases. Recent compressed-transmission studies help, yet heavy decompression eats the reuse gains. Their 2026 paper offers KVCodec, an efficient, widely deployable fix using GPU-native video codecs.

A codec-friendly tensor layout packs the key-value cache into a highly compact video format for fast sending. An efficient fetcher runs sending, decoding, and restoring of packed caches in a pipelined way, cutting resource contention, masking network swings, and reaching minimum time-to-first-token. Tested across diverse GPUs from high- to low-end, KVCodec cuts time-to-first-token by up to three and a half times while keeping lossless accuracy against state-of-the-art methods.
arxiv-2602-10325:
Large multi-band surveys estimate abundances for millions of stars nearly as accurately as low- to medium-resolution spectroscopy. A 2026 paper led by Jihye Hong, with six co-authors, uses iron and carbon estimates from J-PLUS DR3 and S-PLUS DR4 to identify carbon-enhanced metal-poor stars in the Milky Way. Together they cover sixty-two hundred square degrees. After quality cuts and evolutionary corrections, about six point four million stars yield about one hundred five thousand CEMP candidates, roughly twice Gaia's XP count.

Photometry shows carbon abundance splits CEMP stars into two main groups, CEMP-no and CEMP-s, matching spectroscopic studies. Morphological Groups I through III in the Yoon-Beers diagram are recovered, plus the new Group IV, shown distinct even in photometric data. Frequency counts confirm the CEMP fraction rises toward lower metallicity, with CEMP-no stars dominating the lowest-metallicity regime.
arxiv-2602-10525:
George Pu and eight co-authors study what happens when long-horizon workflow agents face vague instructions in a 2026 paper. Steady agents must notice ambiguity and ask for clarification, but research has lacked a scalable way to create and measure ambiguity across arbitrary workflows. Progress stalled on bespoke examples.

Their pipeline, LHAW, transforms any well-specified task into controllable underspecified variants. It removes information along four sizes: goals, constraints, inputs, and context, each at configurable severity. Unlike methods that rely on a model's own ambiguity judgments, LHAW checks its variants independently. The system lets teams measure how clarification conduct degrades as tasks lose information, task by task.
arxiv-2602-10725:
Gergely Csáji and Thánh Nguyen stabilize kidney exchange with altruistic donors in a 2026 paper. Pooling patient-donor pairs across hospitals creates transplants no single center could arrange, but cooperation unravels when coalitions can profitably withdraw. Monetary transfers, which could restore steadiness, are unavailable in this setting.

Their fix, the supplemented core, lets the platform draw on donors who signed up freely to steady the exchange. Such a donor supplies one extra kidney while bringing no patient of their own, which gives the platform a useful non-cash tool. In worst-case compatibility graphs the required donor count can grow linearly with market size, but under a standard random-compatibility model a logarithmic number suffices. Calibrated simulations find donor-free stable exchanges in virtually all markets.
arxiv-2602-11025:
Headsets can now overlay digital help on the real world, yet most still need hands or controllers. Liuchuan Yu and two co-authors present Reality Copilot, a voice-first assistant for mixed reality built on large multimodal models. Speech becomes the main control, freeing hands and eyes for the task at hand.

The system reads physical context, creates realistic 3D content, and pulls live facts on request. It also reaches beyond the headset, drafting context-aware text and exporting created assets for use elsewhere. The paper maps the design space for voice-led human-AI teamwork in mixed reality, rather than claiming one finished product for all settings.
arxiv-2602-11125:
A swarm of robots must spread out evenly while travelling as little as possible. Animesh Maiti and four co-authors study that min-sum uniform coverage problem on a line segment and on a circle. Robots are identical, silent, memory-free, and move under a fair asynchronous scheduler.

For the line, the authors give a fixed distributed recipe that reaches even spacing at minimum total travel. For the circle, they map exactly which starting layouts make the problem unsolvable under this robot model. Every other layout gets a fixed recipe that also achieves minimum total travel. The results settle when cheap, oblivious swarms can spread optimally.
arxiv-2602-11325:
Simulator-based inference breaks when data contain outliers from faulty instruments or human error. Ayush Bharti and three co-authors propose a method that is both amortized and provably robust, a combination prior methods missed. It rests on generalized Bayesian inference and a neural approximation of a weighted score-matching loss.

A carefully chosen conditional density model simplifies inference further, removing the need for Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. Hardness falls to a small fraction of current leading methods. The paper targets sciences and engineering where simulators are routine but data are dirty, offering inference that is fast, reusable across data sets, and resistant to extreme values.
arxiv-2602-11525:
Quasi-periodic swings in X-ray binaries can probe black hole spacetime. R. H. Ali and three co-authors analyze wobble and epicyclic swings in a rotating regular magnet black hole, where a nonminimal coupling setting and magnet charge shift the three basic rates. A relativistic wobble model plus Monte Carlo sampling constrains mass, spin, magnet charge, and coupling from five X-ray binaries.

Gyroscope wobble rates for a stationary observer are also examined. Theory results show the regular charged black hole suppresses wobble rates compared with the Kerr case. The work shows how swing data can test whether astrophysical black holes match Kerr expectations or carry regular, magnetically charged structure.
arxiv-2602-11825:
Air pollution health and climate effects hinge on particle traits like toxicity and water uptake, yet measuring those traits takes complex instruments or costly models, so labeled data are scarce. Fei Jiang and eight co-authors estimate them from routine readings such as pollutant concentrations and weather conditions. The mapping is noisy in an input-dependent way, a heteroscedastic regression setting where noise levels vary with the input.

With a limited labeling budget, choosing which samples to measure matters. Standard active learning leans on predictive doubt, but under such noise that signal mixes fixable model doubt with built-in data noise, wasting budget on noise-dominated regions. The proposed CAAL design separates the two: a decoupled training objective steadies doubt estimates, and a confidence-aware picking rule weights model doubt by predicted data noise as a trust signal.
