Tests on several datasets beat raw visual features and fusion methods.
arxiv-2603-12925: Eva-Maria Schön and co-authors teach agile requirements engineering through a stakeholder simulation run by generative AI. Active user input is a chronic weak point in agile practice. Students interview AI personas with a shared meta-prompt. They then document requirements with story mapping or impact mapping. A group talk follows, where the class reflects on tool limits. Over several terms, the meta-prompt kept the course free of any single model provider.
arxiv-2603-13525: Miguel Alcocer, Ana Isabel Gómez, and Domingo Gomez-Perez link two ways to validate ring-oscillator random number generators. Such generators need strict statistical checks to be fit for cryptographic use. One tool is the Mauduit-Sárközy correlation measure, which bounds pseudorandomness on paper. The other is Maurer's Universal Statistical Test, which gauges entropy from data. No prior work had tied the two metrics to each other. Their framework links Maurer's Z-score to the second-order correlation value, and both to Markov chain transition rates.
arxiv-2603-14025: Nichele and Benatti extend the Alicki-Lindblad-Fannes entropy to open quantum systems as a gauge of information flowing back from the environment. Older back-flow measures use only the reduced dynamics of the system itself. Their version leans on the full joint picture, which makes it stronger. For a qubit hit by a classical spin chain, they derive an exact formula tied to environment correlations. One extreme case gives zero entropy production, as in reversible finite systems.
arxiv-2603-14225: Catalan and co-authors study how software engineers think while working with agentic coding assistants. Heavy reliance on AI can dull judgment, and agents that act alone raise the stakes. Their formative study tracks engagement and sense-making during real tasks with one assistant. Engagement falls steadily as tasks go on, they find. Current designs give weak support for reflection, checking, and meaning-making. The authors point to richer interaction modes and thinking prompts as fixes.
arxiv-2603-14525: Modzelewski and co-authors build MALINT, a dataset on disinformation and malicious intent. Most English datasets flag false claims but ignore the intent behind them. MALINT is the first human-labeled English corpus built with expert fact-checkers for intent. The team tests 12 models on intent labels, from BERT to Llama 3.3. They also test an inoculation idea drawn from psychology. Adding intent analysis to model reasoning boosts zero-shot detection, they find. Tests span six datasets, five models and seven languages.
arxiv-2603-14725: Lee and co-authors trace UV-driven phase shifts in a chromonic liquid crystal to molecular damage. Disodium cromoglycate solutions form isotropic, nematic and columnar phases by heat and strength. Past work saw UV light turn nematic samples biphasic, with slow recovery. Chromatography and mass spectrometry name the breakdown products here. Those products disrupt how DSCG aggregates stack together. Isotropic and biphasic zones then widen in the phase map. Tiny chemical changes steer the whole assembly, they show.
arxiv-2603-14825: Han and co-authors defend vision-language models from jailbreaks by projecting out a bias direction. Safety tuning often trades away skill on plain visual tasks. A cross-modal bias direction shows up across datasets here. Weak coupling between the language backbone and visual encoders breeds it. That direction drags down both safety and utility scores. Their method projects features onto the null space of the bias. One forward pass does the whole defense. Safety and utility rise together across benchmarks, they report.
arxiv-2603-14925: Zhang and co-authors split anime illustrations into production layers with workflow-aware decomposition. Raster edits tangle line, color and shading in one flat file. Object segmentation misses the staged craft of anime drawing. Their frame targets line art, flat color, shadow and highlight layers. Light layer embeddings guide the split for each stratum. Layer-wise losses supervise each output sheet. A built dataset mimics the standard anime production workflow. Clean, coherent layers emerge in their tests, they report.
arxiv-2603-15425: Fattebert and co-authors introduce EDB-bounded datalog, a way to bound the size of intermediate results in recursive queries. Given any datalog program, their algorithm rewrites it so each rule carries a conjunctive query that over-covers its output. From those adornments they define a width, based on edge-cover measures. Width yields worst-case size bounds for every derived predicate, polynomial in the input size. The same bounds give output-sensitive complexity limits for the whole program. The approach also yields a semi-decision test for datalog boundedness.
arxiv-2603-15525: Rafferty and co-authors present CARPA, a tool that makes synthetic chest X-rays with clinical traits edited in a set way. Real datasets miss many useful trait mixes, which caps model reliability. CARPA changes the trait list while holding the anatomy fixed, then renders faithful images. Fine-tuning on these images beat older methods across seven network backbones on a held-out MIMIC-CXR test. Precision and recall rose, doubt fell, and scores were better calibrated. Two radiologists judged the images realistic and in clinical agreement.
arxiv-2603-15825: Seo and co-authors search for leaking ultraviolet light from distant Lyman-alpha galaxies. The ODIN survey supplied 7,498 emitters at redshift 4.5. Strict cleaning for interlopers and neighbors left 851 galaxies. Forced photometry on deep u-band images measured their Lyman-continuum flux. The team flags 12 gold and 39 silver leaker candidates. Stacking the full clean sample shows no mean signal. Expected flux likely sits below the detection limit, they note. Big samples still pay off by surfacing single strong leakers.
arxiv-2603-15925: de Campos, Krebs, and Gottschalk fix ordering glitches in generative inverse design. Design tools learn maps between parameters and target traits. Plain conditional flow matching reacts badly to coordinate order and scale. Training then wobbles across runs and layouts. Their Diagonal Flow Matching anchors designs to noise and labels to zero. The learning task becomes provably blind to coordinate shuffles. Round-trip error drops far below flow and invertible baselines. Two doubt scores flag shaky candidates. Abstention and out-of-distribution spotting follow from those scores.
arxiv-2603-16125: Ahn and co-authors settle the magnetic ground state of rutile RuO2 by Monte Carlo. The crystal was floated as an altermagnet candidate. Density-functional answers split on whether bulk RuO2 orders magnetically. Fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo gives a sharper verdict here. Clean bulk RuO2 lands nonmagnetic in their runs. The best antiferromagnetic rival sits 23 meV per formula unit higher. A 3 percent squeeze flips the balance toward antiferromagnetism. Strain tuning thus explains clashing past reports, they argue.
arxiv-2603-16225: Laverick and co-authors link qubit entanglement to energy. Each qubit's internal energy splits into coherent and incoherent parts. For a pure, separable pair, the coherent parts are at their peak. As entanglement grows under energy-preserving local steps, coherent energy falls. That drop, the coherent energy deficit, matches a known entanglement measure. For mixed states, the deficit splits into quantum and classical parts.
arxiv-2603-16425: Jadhav and co-authors map the magnetic field of a dark cloud, G351. Infrared data show active star birth inside the cloud. Two dense clumps, c1 and c2, anchor the filament. Planck data put field lines across the filament's long axis. SOFIA telescope data reveal an hourglass field shape toward c1. Field strength averages about 147 microgauss across the filament. It peaks near 0.8 milligauss at c1. Gravity and magnetic energy look comparable there.
arxiv-2603-16525: Shang, Kosack, and Humensky estimate backgrounds for very-high-energy gamma-ray telescopes. Wide sources leave too little empty sky in the field of view. Standard background methods then break down. Their STOICS method mines OFF-run cosmic-ray event patterns. Singular value decomposition compresses those patterns to low dimension. Cosmic-ray-like events in ON runs then predict the gamma-like background. VERITAS archive tests show the modeling holds across varied conditions.
arxiv-2603-16725: Zhang and co-authors use deep learning to read electronic structure from photoemission spectra. Such spectra map energy and momentum across four dimensions. Getting model parameters out of them is slow work done by hand. Their neural net speeds that step up a great deal. They test it on two oxide families, nickelates and manganites. The fits beat classic by-hand fitting on Fermi surfaces and band shapes. Labs could run the same checks the same way. The team aims at self-running discovery pipelines.
arxiv-2603-16925: Sindu and Hamaekers predict many epoxy polymer properties at once with a distilled learning framework. Epoxy polymers are widely used, but curated datasets are scarce and their structure is complex. Their method trains single property Gaussian process models as teachers. A unified neural network student then learns from all teachers together. The target property is fed in as an input, so the student can exploit links between properties. Features come from SMILES strings through RDKit. The authors report better accuracy than conventional models.
arxiv-2603-17025: Gupta and co-authors improve targeted sound detection, the task of finding one chosen sound in a mixture. A reference clip of the target sound is given. Older systems build a separate embedding for the reference and pair it with a mixture encoder. This team instead uses a shared encoder for the two inputs. The shared space aligns them and simplifies the design. They report a segment level F1 score of 83.15 percent and accuracy of 95.17 percent on URBAN-SED. They call it a new state of the art.
arxiv-2603-17125: Binnie, Sumray, and Yim introduce the chordal distance transform, a new invariant for geometric loops. They embed a circle in Euclidean space and record the distance between every pair of points on it. This gives a function on a Möbius band. The persistent homology of its sublevel sets is invariant under isometry and reparametrization. For smooth and piecewise linear embeddings, they characterize the critical points of the transform. They also show how the idea extends to features built from three or more points.
arxiv-2603-17325: Tran and co-authors present MedSAD-CLIP, a supervised adaptation of CLIP for medical anomaly detection and segmentation. CLIP based detectors often work with global features and weak supervision, giving coarse localization. Their model uses token patch cross attention to exploit fine grained text and visual cues for sharper lesion maps. Light adapters and learnable prompt tokens adapt the encoder to medicine while keeping its semantic alignment. Across brain, retina, lung, and breast benchmarks, the model beat prior state of the art methods.
arxiv-2603-17625: Li and co-authors present S-VGGT, a way to scale feed-forward 3D foundation models. Global attention costs grow quadratically with input length, which caps scene size. Token merging saves little and adds search overhead instead. S-VGGT splits frames into a few subscenes through a dense scene graph. Each part shares one reference frame, so parts run in parallel without alignment steps. The trick stacks with token-level speedups, they report.
arxiv-2603-17825: Cheng and co-authors study massive activations inside video diffusion transformers. These rare spikes sit in a few fixed hidden dimensions. Their size peaks at first-frame tokens and at frame borders, mostly early in denoising. A VAE encoding quirk leaves those spots with less content, they trace. The spikes act as dampers on residual updates at each token. Their STAS steering method retunes them and lifts video quality.
arxiv-2603-18225: Kota and co-authors pair a diffusion model with DeepONet to predict stress in soft, stretchy solids. UNet nets smooth out sharp stress peaks; DeepONet nets miss peak heights. Their hybrid splits shape from scale: the diffusion part draws the stress map, and DeepONet sets the low and high ends. Tests use sets with one hole and with many polygonal holes. The pair beats each part alone and UNet by one to two orders in error.
arxiv-2603-18325: Rajaraman and co-authors prove that autocurriculum helps models learn to reason with less cost. In autocurriculum, a model picks training problems based on its own current performance. For supervised fine-tuning, it needs exponentially fewer reasoning examples than fixed training. Teacher effort lands on prompts where the model now struggles. For reinforcement learning, it splits compute cost from reference model quality, leaving the latter as a near-fixed burn-in cost.
arxiv-2603-18625: Zou and co-authors probe where vision-language models fail at spotting AI-made videos. Their GenVideoLens benchmark holds 400 deceptive fake videos and 100 real ones. Experts scored each clip on 15 authenticity dimensions. The dimensions span perceptual, optical, physical, and temporal cues. Eleven models were tested. Models handle perceptual cues fairly well but struggle with optical consistency, physical contact, and temporal cause. Smaller open models sometimes beat big closed ones on single cues. Time shuffling tests show models barely use temporal information.
arxiv-2603-18725: Żychowicz and co-authors build a first-principles theory of slow spin relaxation in single-molecule magnets. Slow relaxation comes from axial anisotropy that blocks spin flips. Their linear response theory for open quantum systems yields the a.c. magnetic response directly. Paired with density functional and wavefunction methods, it runs fit-free. They apply it to three cyanide-bridged polymers with ytterbium, terbium, or dysprosium. The method matches both low-temperature direct relaxation and high-temperature Orbach behavior for all three compounds.
arxiv-2603-18925: Saoulis and co-authors improve earthquake source estimates when Earth's inner structure is not known for sure. Standard fits often assume a simple bell shape for model error. They show that this shape breaks down under small shifts in a layered Earth model. Their method uses simulation-based learning to model the errors as they truly fall. Two forms are offered, one guided by physics and one end-to-end learned. Tests show the old shape biases results and understates doubt, most at short periods.
arxiv-2603-19125: Gibbon and Vincenzi challenge the lore that no math link ties the Navier-Stokes equations to the multifractal model of turbulence. They build a theory joining the model to Leray's weak solutions of the flow equations. A derived inverse scale acts as a bridge between the two views. It links to the Reynolds number through a local scaling exponent. Gradient norms of varied powers match power to exponent. That range falls where thermal noise may make the equations fail.
arxiv-2603-19225: Agrawal and co-authors build FinTradeBench, a test of financial reasoning for language models. It holds 1,400 questions on NASDAQ-100 stocks over ten years. Items cover firm basics from filings, trading signals from prices, and mixed tasks that join both. A core set of 400 items was checked by experts. Models do far worse on trading questions than on basics. Tests with search and tools show that weak math and poor evidence choice drive most failures.
arxiv-2603-19525: Orendain and co-authors introduce homotopy lattice gauge fields, a richer form of gauge field on a lattice. Standard lattice fields track parallel transport along paths only. The new fields also track transport along homotopies, or deformations, of those paths. On two- and three-dimensional bases, this extra data fixes a principal bundle over the base space. It also yields formulas for topological charge on two-dimensional bases. A second part will use the field space for quantum field theory.
arxiv-2603-19825: Ngo and co-authors recast FrameNet semantic role classification as a problem of analogy. They define analogies over pairs of lexical units and frame elements. A pair counts as a valid analogy when both sides share a semantic role. A light neural network trains on these pairs and converges fast. No role labels enter the training at all. Roles are recovered at test time by sampling and analogical transfer. The method beat prior best results while staying cheap to run.
arxiv-2603-20425: Singh and Gajbhiye present ZeroHungerAI, a tool for food security policy in data-scarce regions. Policy there rests on sparse data and fragmented text reports. Their system mixes socio-economic indicators with policy text embeddings. A transfer-learned DistilBERT model supplies the contextual learning. On 1,200 samples across 25 districts, accuracy reached 91 percent. That beat classical SVM by 13 percent in their comparison. Fairness tuning cut the demographic parity gap to 3 percent. The design aims at scalable, bias-aware policy support.
arxiv-2603-20625: Zheng and co-authors name a new attack on AI agents that use checkpoint restore. After a restore, an agent writes tool calls afresh rather than word for word. Servers treat these new calls as brand new requests. This gap allows duplicate payments and reuse of spent credentials. They call such tricks semantic rollback attacks. Two classes are shown: action replay and authority resurrection. Their fix, ACRFence, logs effects that cannot be undone. It then forces replay or fork choices on restore.
arxiv-2603-20925: Wang and co-authors propose profit driven red teaming to stress test AI agents in economic settings. Agents now act on outside inputs that rivals can shape for gain. Fixed prompt attack lists miss such adaptive pressure. Their protocol trains an opponent to maximize profit from scalar outcome feedback alone. It needs no judge model or attack labels. They test it on four classic economic interactions. Agents that look strong against static attacks prove easy to exploit. Rules distilled from the failures then block most of them.
arxiv-2603-21325: Hakobyan constructs the dynamical symmetry of the quantum Calogero model. The model has particle exchange and sits in a confining Coulomb field. The symmetry is governed by the algebra so(N+1,2), deformed by Dunkl exchange operators. Its invariant sector comes from the Dunkl angular momentum tensor and a modified Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector. A twin form of the Hamiltonian, with a linear spectrum, is written through the smaller conformal algebra so(1,2). The wave functions fall into lowest weight multiplets of that algebra.
arxiv-2603-21525: Baten and co-authors release BOxCrete, an open-source tool that forecasts concrete strength and optimizes mix designs. Most prior AI work on concrete used private data and closed code. BOxCrete trains on a new open dataset of over 500 strength tests from 123 mortar and concrete mixes. Gaussian process regression predicts strength growth across five curing ages and reports uncertainty too. The tool also balances strength against embodied carbon in a multi-objective search. Its dataset and code are meant as a shared base for the field.
arxiv-2603-21625: Waite counts permutations by how many times a fixed pattern occurs inside them. For a chosen family of patterns, Waite shows the count with r occurrences is asymptotically n to the r times the count that avoids the pattern entirely. This settles part of a conjecture by Conway and Guttman. The work focuses on a case that generalizes the pattern 231. Waite also uses the asymptotics to prove that certain ordinary generating functions for these counts are neither rational nor algebraic.
arxiv-2603-21725: Wang and colleagues propose CurvZO, a sparse zeroth-order method for fine-tuning language models with less memory. Such updates use only forward passes, saving memory, but they can converge slowly or prove unstable. CurvZO tracks curvature signals online from scalar feedback, uses them to pick which parameters to perturb each step, and adjusts its perturbation budget over time, cutting variance. Tests on OPT and Llama across varied tasks found gains of up to 4.4 accuracy points and up to twice the speed.
arxiv-2603-21825: Chen and co-authors turn a smartwatch into a badminton stroke coach. Skilled feedback is hard for amateur players to get, so the team built BadminSense around wrist motion and vibration signals. Interviews with experienced players shaped four design needs. The team collected strokes from twelve skilled amateurs, labeled by type, quality score, and shuttle contact point. BadminSense segments and classifies strokes, grades their quality, and locates the impact. It reached 91 percent stroke accuracy in tests, and a user study backed its value for practice.
arxiv-2603-21925: Chen and co-authors build a retrieval system that answers eye care questions straight from clinical guideline pages. Each page is an evidence unit, retrieved as an image, so tables and flowcharts stay intact. Routing and filtering add outside evidence only when it helps. Queries are split, rewritten, retrieved, reranked, and reasoned over, with answers citing the exact pages used. On the hard part of HealthBench, the system beat GPT-5.2 by about thirty percent in overall score. Ablations credit the reranking and routing steps.
arxiv-2603-22125: Cai and co-authors present DA-VAE, a plug-in that compresses the latent space used by diffusion models. Simply adding channels per token tends to blur latent structure. DA-VAE instead keeps the first channels from a pretrained VAE. Extra channels then carry the fine detail from higher resolution input. A detail-alignment step keeps the wider space close to the original structure. With light fine-tuning, Stable Diffusion 3.5 makes 1024 by 1024 images with four times fewer tokens.
arxiv-2603-22525: Roy and co-authors probe the safety of neural operator digital twins used in nuclear plants. These models rebuild full flow and heat fields from sparse sensor readings in real time. The team attacks four designs with gradient-free search, changing under one percent of inputs. Tiny, plausible tweaks at boundary sensors drive error from near one percent to well over a third. Every winning single-point attack slips past standard anomaly checks. The authors trace the risk to how sharply each design concentrates its sensitivity.
arxiv-2603-22825: Hasan and co-authors study ground-state fields in two-color QCD at nonzero matter density. They run lattice simulations with Wilson gauge and fermion actions. Two improved topological charge operators are built and calibrated for the task. Four gradient flow actions are compared. Results show a finite-volume crossover near the expected phase boundary. Chromo-electric and chromo-magnetic field strengths dip, then recover past vacuum values. A field-strength gap measure grows steadily with chemical potential. Sigmoid fits confirm the phase boundary location.
arxiv-2603-23025: Kushwaha and Suyama revisit limits on the primordial curvature power spectrum from black hole counts. Primordial black holes form when large density bumps collapse after horizon entry. Their abundance caps how large early curvature bumps could be. The authors derive limits for narrow and broad spectrum peaks. They compare Press-Schechter and peak theory routes, plus window and transfer choices. Non-spherical collapse raises the inferred spectrum size a lot. For broad peaks, the two formalisms disagree. Theory uncertainty remains the key limit, they stress.
arxiv-2603-23125: Alwasiak and co-authors describe a system for the TREC 2025 DRAGUN track on news trust. The track asks tools to help users judge online news. Their system tackles both question generation and trust reporting tasks. Language models draft critical questions, filtered for sense and diversity. Query expansion methods, including chain-of-thought, fetch evidence from a news corpus. A re-ranker and a language model judge then clean the set. Top evidence is woven into short trust reports with citations. Expansion and re-ranking lift both relevance and domain trust.
arxiv-2603-23325: Yokota continues his study of geometric data sets, now with pyramids. Two distances live on these sets: observable distance from measure concentration, and the box distance. The first is non-separable, while the second is complete yet also non-separable. He carves out a subclass of L-compact sets tied to 1-Lipschitz functions. That subclass is both complete and separable under the box distance. He builds a compactification of it from L-pyramids. A limit formula gives the observable diameter of those pyramids.
arxiv-2603-23425: Jung and seven co-authors present Wayfinder, a tool that tunes an operating system for one app on its own. Hand tuning takes rare expertise, and the setting space is huge. Many settings are invalid, and each test run is slow. Wayfinder pairs an automated benchmarking rig with a neural search. The search learns live which knobs move the target metric and which break the system. A model trained on one app can seed work on a related app. On two systems and four apps, gains reach 24% in speed.
arxiv-2603-23725: Soukhovei and five co-authors print robot skins that carry large-area touch sensors. Wide sensing skins help robots spot nearby obstacles, but curved links fight flat mounts. Their method grows a skin from CAD that hugs a link's unflattenable shape. Pockets in the skin hold circuit boards of any size at fixed spots. Sensors thus need no fresh calibration before use. A skin on a Franka arm builds point cloud views of clutter around it from flight-time imagers.
arxiv-2603-24225: Cea and co-authors bring large deviation theory to monitored quantum many-body systems. Glassy classical systems show coexisting dynamical phases, and hints of the same exist in monitored quantum systems. Past methods could not run a full large deviation analysis there. Their tensor network framework fills that gap. With it, they find a series of first-order dynamical phase transitions in trajectory space. The method also yields the conditioned quantum states themselves. That allows a microscopic look at each phase and how phases coexist.
arxiv-2603-24325: Terfloth and co-authors test whether explanations of technical objects should cover both structure and purpose. Dual Nature Theory says understanding needs both the architecture of a thing and its relevance. In an experiment with 104 participants, trained explainers described the board game Quarto! in three ways: structure only, purpose only, or both. The two single-focus styles gave equal understanding. The integrated style raised enabledness, the ability to use the knowledge, over both. Comprehension scores did not differ. The authors link integrated explanation to agency.
arxiv-2603-24925: Miao and co-authors present GraphER, a graph-based reranking method for retrieval-augmented generation. Semantic search can miss evidence scattered across sources, leaving answer sets incomplete. Agentic iterative retrieval is slow, and stored graphs add upkeep. GraphER instead uses the data's own structure to define proximity beyond semantic similarity. It builds a graph at query time and ranks candidates with graph-based signals. Tests on table, multi-hop, and long-document retrieval show gains in completeness. No extra graph infrastructure is needed.
arxiv-2603-25025: Wang and Zhang tackle a cost choice in physics simulators: how much past data each forecast step should see. Neural PDE simulators roll a field forward from a fixed window of past frames. Picking that window by full search is pricey, and theory-based picks may miss what helps rollouts. Their method, SAKE, first draws a small candidate set from physical traits of the system. It then picks the knee point by real rollout scores. Across eight PDEBench families, SAKE is the strongest cheap picker at matched budget.
arxiv-2603-25125: Wang and Li merge two routes to single photons in a driven two-qubit cavity system. One route bends energy levels so a second photon is blocked. The other uses quantum paths that cancel. Each alone trades brightness against purity. By tuning one qubit and the pump field, they find settings that keep both strengths. Those settings come with hyperradiance, a boosted glow from linked emitters. The effect survives uneven couplings, which makes it a practical path to clean single-photon sources.
arxiv-2603-25925: Gao and Dubé study how to personalize math game levels for children. Good game-based learning needs many quality levels matched to each player's skill. Their framework uses AI to sort levels that players create. They gathered 206 levels from experts and advanced players in a game's Creative Mode. A classifier reads level features and predicts which levels are valid. Four models were compared, and random forest did best, they report. The authors say such sorting could help games tailor levels to each learner.
arxiv-2603-26425: Nottebaum, Dunnhofer, and Micheloni design vision backbones for plain CPUs rather than parallel hardware. Most backbone research targets devices that run many operations at once. CPUs gain more from a balance of total operations and hardware-efficient speed. The team tests grouped convolutions and smaller kernels, which cut operation counts while keeping CPU efficiency high. Their CPUBone family reaches state-of-the-art speed-accuracy trade-offs across many CPU devices. The gains also carry to downstream tasks like object detection.
arxiv-2603-26525: Prieto-Viertel and co-authors project demand for health, education, and housing in Austria through 2050, split by citizenship. Public debate often blames foreign nationals for strain on welfare services. Their structural demographic model tests that claim across migration scenarios. Ageing among Austrian nationals drives health demand 4.7 times more than immigration does. Migration accounts for all net housing growth, mostly in cities, while school demand shrinks under every scenario. Foreign nationals use services in line with their population share.
arxiv-2603-26625: Ayhan, Duruk Mutlubas, and Tang prove well-posedness for a generalised Camassa-Holm equation with freely chosen orders. The momentum order and the power of the nonlinearity can both be set as high as one likes. Local existence comes from Kato's semigroup method, with commutator bounds and a fractional Leibniz rule handling the nonlinearity head-on. The phase space matches the classical Camassa-Holm threshold. A conserved quantity then lifts the local result to global existence for the same class of data.
arxiv-2603-26725: Spera proves that capability safety can be written exactly as propositional Datalog evaluation. The target is the monadic, ground, function-free fragment of first-order logic. His earlier capability hypergraph frame lacked fast incremental upkeep and a decision test for audit surface containment. The equivalence is tight: hypergraphs match this fragment and nothing beyond it. That match lets results from Datalog research transfer to capability safety at once. It also opens routes to incremental checks as systems change.
arxiv-2603-26925: Gaitsgory and co-authors introduce a canonical filtration on the space of automorphic functions. The setting is the everywhere unramified function field case of the Langlands program. The filtration is transferred from the spectral side of the classical Langlands conjecture. There, it comes from coherent singular support. The authors propose several conjectures tying this filtration to another one. That second filtration arises from the analytic spectrum of Hecke operators acting on complex-valued functions. The work links a support-based notion to a Hecke-based one.
arxiv-2603-27425: Elorreaga and co-authors complete a study of split behavior in linear systems. They treat equations whose parts grow or shrink at a set rate. Three traits are at play: dichotomy, noncriticality, and expansiveness. The authors prove when these traits amount to the same thing. They also extend a classic Floquet theory result. The new test gives a full condition for dichotomy. Group theory tools drive most of the proofs. The work closes a line begun in an earlier paper.
arxiv-2603-28125: Giergiel and Surówka realize a programmable spin ice model on a superconducting quantum annealer. Spin ice hosts odd excitations that act like magnetic monopoles, but their quantum behavior was hard to reach. The team maps each lattice spin to one physical qubit and builds dipolar couplings across more than 400 sites. Tuning quantum fluctuations, they watch Dirac strings and monopole plasmas move in real time. The monopoles spread faster than plain diffusion, a sign of coherent motion.
arxiv-2603-28225: Jaiswal, Hellum, and Heiberg use sensor data and machine learning to spot accidents on a smart bridge in Norway. Human inspections are slow and can miss or misjudge damage. Their system learns from live iBridge sensor streams and flags odd events as they happen. A density-based clustering model, DBSCAN, beat the rival models they tried at catching the accident case. The setup could warn operators fast when something goes wrong.
arxiv-2603-28425: Leonenkova and three co-authors present DiPA, an attack that fools face recognition cameras with a patch shown on a phone screen. Printed patches are the usual route; a screen patch deploys fast and needs no print-friendly smoothing. An ensemble of face models makes the patch transfer to unseen commercial systems. In a live demo, the attack hid authorized users from a working camera in real time. It beat older physical attacks on success rate and confidence drop.
arxiv-2603-28525: Haghighat and Nouri build an exactly solvable model where a non-Hermitian Klein-Gordon field feels an inverse-square pull. The purely imaginary, scale-free potential turns the field equation into a known spectral problem. Demanding purely outgoing waves at the center picks one physical version and tames the fall-to-center flaw. The decay states then form a log-periodic ladder with complex energies. Their spacing is set only by the anomaly exponent, giving quantized dissipation.
arxiv-2603-28625: Elgouhary and El-Wakeel combine reinforcement learning with Pure Pursuit control for autonomous racing. Pure Pursuit is simple and fast, but its lookahead distance is hard to set. Short values corner well yet can shake on straights. Long values are smooth but cut corners poorly. Their agent uses Proximal Policy Optimization to set lookahead online from speed and curvature data. Training ran in the F1TENTH Gym simulator, with deployment in ROS2. On unseen tracks, the learned method set the best lap times. It also transferred to a real car.
arxiv-2603-28825: Ercole uses game theory to assess the limits of AI in healthcare, through a stylized inpatient capacity problem. He describes three deployment forms: tools that reduce effort, systems that improve observability, and interventions that change incentives. The first two can improve performance within current behavior patterns. They do not, in general, change which actions are individually rational, so existing equilibria absorb them. Interventions that change how local actions map to downstream risk can shift stable behavior. Ercole argues that expected system gains should depend on whether a deployment changes incentives.
arxiv-2603-29025: Li and co-authors test whether language models truly condition on hidden constraints in decisions. Asked about walking to a car wash 50 metres away, most models say walk and forget the car must go too. Standard accuracy tests can mislead, since cautious answers score well with no real reasoning. The team instead checks if decisions change when the constraint is removed. Tests span log-probability sweeps, a 500 prompt stress test, and a human validated paired benchmark. Constraints nudged decisions rather than governing them. Prompting fixes largely vanished under paired scoring.
arxiv-2603-29325: Mameda and co-authors study baryonic vortices in rotating nuclear matter. They work within chiral perturbation theory. Two vortex types appear: local and global. Both carry baryon number as a topological charge. In a local vortex, charged pions condense at the boundary with a phase winding. A global vortex instead winds the neutral pion condensate. Global vortices are usually dropped for their diverging energy. Finite size in a rotating frame cures that divergence. The two states compete as rotation and size vary.
arxiv-2603-29425: Baker studies Poincaré duality spaces built from the Joker module. The Joker is a famous module in algebraic topology, due to Adams and Priddy. It is known to arise as the cohomology of a connected space. Baker attaches one extra cell to that space. The result is an eight-dimensional Poincaré duality space. He uses obstruction theory to show it carries a PL structure. Smoothability stays open. Its cohomology is also realized by a homogeneous space.
arxiv-2603-29525: Ye studies pulse control of one superconducting qubit where simple models fail. Decoherence stems from multilevel dynamics plus structured noise. The study couples waveform building to hierarchical equations of motion. Noise takes the form of 1/f pure dephasing with memory. Here, filter-function forecasts lose their grip. Y-CPMG pulse trains break their scaling law and partly revive coherence. X-CPMG trains keep clean power-law scaling. Waveform style left no mark on the scaling at all. The results give tests that lab work can check.
arxiv-2603-29625: Svegborn and Tavakoli study one-way quantum tests where the receiver picks no settings. A quantum edge there needs two things: shared entanglement and measurements that adapt to the message. For classical messages, they find the smallest setup with such an edge. High-dimensional entanglement makes the edge largest. In the next setup up, CHSH-type nonlocality can power the edge. That setup suits certification experiments well. With quantum messages read first, the edge grows larger still. Non-projective read-out proves essential for that gain.
arxiv-2603-29825: Marx, Pilipczuk, and Pilipczuk give a sampling method for pattern problems in H-minor-free graphs. They draw a random induced subgraph with a tree decomposition of modest width. Any fixed pattern of size k survives whole with a stated chance. Each bag then holds few pattern vertices. This yields fast randomized algorithms for tasks like directed k-path and H-packing. A stronger form covers distance-d neighborhoods too. That widening handles partial domination and distance-constrained problems.
arxiv-2603-29925: Egorov bounds the vertex counts of right-angled hyperbolic polyhedra in dimensions five to twelve. These finite-volume shapes have both ideal and finite vertices. He uses orthogonal gluings to set fresh low-dimension bounds. One result forces at least three ideal vertices in dimension five. Another forces at least four finite vertices in dimension seven. Double counting and recurrence steps then lift both bounds. The gains reach dimension twelve, the highest where such polyhedra exist.
arxiv-2603-30025: Li, Panchendrarajan, and Zubiaga move retrieval into the first stage of fact-checking. Pipelines first judge whether a claim can be checked against outside evidence. Past work decides from the claim sentence alone. Their ContextClaim system finds entity mentions and queries Wikipedia for background. A language model compresses that material into short summaries for a classifier. Gains appear in several setups across Twitter and debate corpora. The summaries also lift a downstream FEVER verifier's F1 score.
arxiv-2604-00025: Hakim asks about an odd pattern: on 7.7 percent of problems, larger language models trail smaller ones despite far more parameters. Tests of 31 models across 1,485 problems identify the cause as extra verbosity adding errors. Causal tests show this reflects fixable prompt design rather than basic skill limits. Brief responses lift accuracy by 26 points and shrink gaps by up to two-thirds. Key, brevity limits reverse rankings on math and science tests, with large models gaining leads over small models. These flips prove large models possess better skills that prompts mask.
arxiv-2604-00125: Lella and McDonald turn lectures from a September 2025 training school in Annecy into expanded notes on hunting weakly interacting slim particles. The notes cover axion dark matter and axion-like particles probed with neutron stars, superradiance, and white dwarfs. They also treat astrophysical searches for high-frequency gravitational waves with compact objects. A set of practical exercises accompanies the notes for students working through the material.
arxiv-2604-00225: Almuallem and four colleagues propose an asymmetry score for pupil design, linking imaged intensity to the inbound wavefront. Earlier work showed that breaking pupil symmetries allows wavefront recovery from one image, but gave little guidance on making better pupils. Their study shows that greater asymmetry improves recoverability. They also map trade-offs in pupil design, including light throughput under noise, backed by large simulations and bench experiments.
arxiv-2604-00725: Agbeti-Messan and colleagues compare linear-time state-space models, especially Mamba, with Transformer and BiLSTM recognizers for reading old newspapers. Their benchmark uses Luxembourg historical newspapers with verified gold-standard labels, plus tests on Fraktur and Antiqua lines. All neural models reached low error rates near 2 percent, but Mamba matched their accuracy. It also cut inference time roughly in half and scaled memory far more slowly.
arxiv-2604-00925: Wu and team ask whether Lyman-alpha light from astrospheres can be seen and mapped, using a 3D model of stellar-wind bubbles. Charge exchange between charged wind bits and cold gas between stars fills the bubble with neutral hydrogen, whose resonant scatter makes the light. Judged against Hubble limits, sharp light in space could pin down bow-shock gap, wind symmetry, and tail shape. That makes Lyman-alpha bubble finding a hopeful case for Hubble and the future Habitable Worlds Observatory.
arxiv-2604-01025: Liu and team introduce lightweight in-training probes for large language models, replacing generative evaluation with downstream performance monitoring during training. Simple metrics like training loss often diverge from task outcomes, while generative evaluation can take about an hour per checkpoint. Their probes read internal representations of checkpoints and predict downstream success probability, or pass@1. On OLMo3-7B checkpoints across tasks, the probes predict performance with average AUROC above 0.75, generalize from earlier to later checkpoints, and cut latency from about an hour to about 3 minutes.
arxiv-2604-01325: Laudy proposes a digital-twin route around a core headache of causal inference: nobody ever sees what would have happened to the same person under the other treatment. Instead of estimating that missing outcome statistically, his Digital Twin Counterfactual Framework simulates it. The simulator faces a five-level validation ladder, each rung unlocking richer quantities to estimate. Average and subgroup effects become testable against observed data, while individual-level effects stay tied to unobservable dependence assumptions, with bounding tools making that gap plain rather than hiding it.
arxiv-2604-01925: Vedula and colleagues probe bias in large language models with ImplicitBBQ, a benchmark that signals identity through traits rather than names. Name-based tests link weakly to many groups and cannot cover age or class, while models hide stated-identity bias. Across 11 models, implicit bias in vague contexts ran over six times explicit bias, with caste worst and gender least. Safety prompts and reasoning barely dented the gap, yet few-shot prompting, which cut implicit bias by 79 percent, left caste bias four times any other dimension.
arxiv-2604-02325: Röthl and colleagues link dopant layout to full response curves in a lead free perovskite. While most work tracks average zirconium content in barium titanate, they generate many nanoscale layouts, from layers and rods to dots and lamellae, and encode each with a compact code. Hamiltonian dynamics compute polarization and strain loops, and an autoencoder learns to predict whole loops from layout codes. The design maps show layout alone strongly shifts loop shape, energy storage and switching behavior.
arxiv-2604-02725: Colombo-Murphy and four colleagues use gravitational tides to probe what pulsar companions are made of. Short-period, low-eccentricity companions evolve strongly under tides, so modeled tidal traits such as apsidal motion and deformability can be matched against pulsar timing for four systems. The comparison aims to place tight limits on the chemical and structural makeup of these dense, exotic objects and clarify their history.
arxiv-2604-02825: Lv and six colleagues offer a method to measure electric-charge transport across high-energy nuclear collisions using an energy scan of isobaric systems. Nuclei with equal mass but different atomic number let charge differences emerge through a double-ratio technique that cuts systematic errors. The scan spans beam energies from 19.6 to 200 GeV. Simulations of ruthenium and zirconium collisions show midrapidity charge difference falling exponentially with rapidity gap, with slopes that vary a lot by model. Charge and baryon transport are compared, and baryon transport shows distinct patterns.
arxiv-2604-02925: Nandakumar conjectures that the largest solid wrappable by a given sheet of paper is always non-convex. Paper may be folded or wrinkled but never stretched or torn. For any convex solid that a sheet can wrap, he claims some non-convex solid holds strictly more volume and the same sheet can wrap it. The paper discusses related work, a key subquestion about the sphere, and several further directions.
arxiv-2604-03025: Forbes analyses UK income from 2000 to 2023 using HMRC percentile data for pre-tax and post-tax income. He fits a prefactor-adjusted kappa-generalised distribution and simulates income populations by inverse transform sampling. The bottom 40 percent appears to gain share, while the 50th to 90th percentiles lose share. The top 10 percent stays broadly stable, and the top 1 percent gains pre-tax share. Simulated 2023 incomes show matching tax rises on high earners must exceed four times rises on lower earners.
arxiv-2604-03225: Wu and colleagues ask whether image super-resolution can succeed from visual data alone, without a text-to-image model underneath. Their VOSR system draws semantic guidance from the low-resolution input itself, replaces the usual unconditional branch with restoration-oriented guidance, and distills a multi-step model into one step. It trains at under a tenth of the usual cost while matching or beating text-based rivals on quality.
arxiv-2604-03425: Gong and colleagues scale encrypted transformer inference across many graphics cards, where long inputs exceed single-card memory. Their AEGIS system places data by ciphertext links so communication happens only when app needs demand it, with the rest hidden behind compute. Communication falls about 58 percent in feed-forward layers and 81 percent in attention, with a scaling rate near 97 percent on four cards.
arxiv-2604-03825: Ali Enayat proved new proof-theoretic theorems about axiomatic theories of truth over set theory, using mostly model-theoretic methods. The theories sit over Kripke-Platek set theory and stronger systems, especially Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory. The results sharpen what is known about truth theories built on these foundations. The work treats several theories, comparing their strength across the hierarchy of set-theoretic foundations.
arxiv-2604-04325: Fang and colleagues introduce MINT, a multi-turn medical diagnosis benchmark of 1,035 cases with labelled evidence. Testing 11 language models reveals three habits. Models rush to answer early, with over 55 percent of answers locked in within two turns. Wrong-to-right revisions outnumber right-to-wrong flips by about 11 times, showing unused self-correction. Striking lab results trigger early answers even when models are told to wait. The authors advise delaying the diagnostic question and holding back striking evidence until later turns, which cuts early answers and lifts accuracy.
arxiv-2604-04525: Maese and colleagues present G-EDF-Loc, a 6-DoF localization framework on a direct CPU-based pipeline. The system uses G-EDF, a continuous, lean 3D distance field. It models the Euclidean Distance Field with a Block-Sparse Gaussian Mixture Model and adaptive splits, ensuring C1 continuity across blocks and cutting boundary artifacts. Analytical map gradients, maintaining Eikonal consistency, enable high-fidelity reconstruction and real-time location. Large-scale tests show G-EDF-Loc matching state-of-the-art methods, with resilience under odometry loss or absent IMU priors.
arxiv-2604-04625: Kheti, Ghosh and Dash present a 1-bit reconfigurable intelligent surface built from three layers with a stackup and an air gap cutting dielectric losses on low-cost FR4. Each unit cell uses a PIN-diode-based biasing network simplifying control while keeping distinct ON and OFF states within 20 degrees. A phase-gradient code steers beams up to 30 degrees in anechoic and noisy settings. An Arduino interface drives the surface, which shows reflected gain of about 9 dB over a 30-degree range. The design works from 3.38 to 3.67 GHz for 5G n78.
arxiv-2604-05225: Korkmaz, Goksuluk, and Karaismailoglu present fastml, an R package through redo, redoing prep inside each redo. Leakage arises when scaling, filling, or other changes are estimated before redo, lifting seen scores. It supports redo, blocks risky setups, audits recipes, and has boxed runs and notes. A test pitting global against fold-local scaling shows prep inflates seen scores versus guarded redo. fastml matched tidymodels on held-out scores while cutting work, and ran lasting models through one panel.
arxiv-2604-05425: Kurban and nine colleagues test whether planet-mass companions on ultrashort orbits around pulsars and white dwarfs could be heard in continuous gravitational waves. Comparing measured systems against space-detector sensitivity curves, they find fourteen sources clearing a signal-to-noise ratio of 5 within four years of observing. Near-term missions like LISA would likely miss them, but future observatories such as DECIGO and BBO could catch them.
arxiv-2604-05625: Benoist proves singular cohomology with finite coefficients of a finite-dimensional Stein space matches étale cohomology of its Stein algebra. It follows that every integral cohomology class comes by pullback from an algebraic variety, and classes in degree two or higher vanish outside a nowhere dense closed analytic subset. The bridge links complex-analytic and algebraic cohomology.
arxiv-2604-05825: He studies the Hodge-to-de Rham spectral sequence for integral projective curves with local complete intersection singularities. Degeneration at the second page holds exactly when every singularity is a quasihomogeneous plane curve singularity. The same condition governs the Hochschild-to-cyclic sequence, tying both degenerations to one local property.
arxiv-2604-06325: del Toro and Bavaresco study machines that lift quantum states and channels to purifications and dilations from a few copies or uses of black-box input. In the probabilistic setting, purifying two inputs of different rank with nonzero chance already rules out linear positive maps. This point restores the no-go result for universal probabilistic purification from finite copies. In the approximate setting, they rank strategies by minimum average error and give a general error bound. Pure-output strategies win at large environment size; append-environment strategies win when small.
arxiv-2604-06525: Ji and Lan extend self-tuning acceleration to noisy composite convex optimization. The deterministic auto-conditioned gradient method hits accelerated rates with no line searches or Lipschitz knowledge, but its noisy extension stayed open. Older self-tuning noisy methods miss accelerated rates or lean on narrow rules: bounded domains, bounded gradients, known horizons, or sub-Gaussian noise. Their stochastic AC-FGM adapts to the Lipschitz constant, horizon, and noise level, picks stepsizes and batch sizes adaptively, and hits optimal iteration and sample complexity under standard variance rules.
arxiv-2604-07725: Maheswaran and 18 colleagues present Squeeze Evolve, a way to evolve model answers with no outside checker scoring them. Strong models handle only the stages where added skill matters most. Cheaper models cover the rest, which curbs collapse toward narrow answers and keeps costs down. Across math, coding, and vision tests it beats single-model evolution on cost versus skill, cuts API cost up to about threefold, and on discovery tasks matches methods that use checkers.
arxiv-2604-07925: Lapenna, Fioresi, and Gharesifard analyze rank decay in Sinkhorn doubly stochastic attention. Standard row-stochastic focus weakens signals across layers, sinking rank toward uniform token vectors and packing focus into entropy collapse. Doubly stochastic focus acts as entropy control, evening the spread and lifting test scores. The team studies rank collapse across network depth and shows Sinkhorn doubly stochastic tables preserve rank better than standard softmax row-stochastic ones. The analysis shows why even focus keeps signals alive in deep models.
arxiv-2604-08125: Lin and three colleagues present PolySLGen, an online framework for group speaking-listening replies. Human-like replies matter for natural group chats between humans and built AI. Current methods handle single modes or speaking-only replies in pairs, unfit for real social scenes, and miss silent cues and complex group dynamics key for engagement and chat flow. Given past talk and motion from all, it makes a future reply for a target person, including speech, body motion, and speaking state score.
arxiv-2604-08625: Laitinen Imanov and two colleagues recast benign overfitting, where fitting noisy data exactly stays statistically harmless, in transport geometry. Rank rules for covariance spectra prove fragile under tiny shifts, so they measure log eigenvalue moves in units of sample size n. Exact variation formulas and size free stability bounds follow, showing benign overfitting survives every shift whose local transport cost grows slower than n.
arxiv-2604-08725: Álvarez-García and Ruehle show that Coxeter invariant functions behind the Type IIA prepotential are eigenfunctions of a Laplace-Beltrami operator built from the Coxeter bilinear form. The Gromov-Witten series thus reads as waves on the Coxeter quotient of the moduli space, with summing up as spectral decomposition. For dihedral groups, this split explains why modified Bessel, ordinary Bessel, and Jacobi theta functions appear for hyperbolic, elliptic, and parabolic rotations.
arxiv-2604-08925: Yan and four colleagues design multi-stream downlink precoding for massive antenna satellite systems in low Earth orbit. Precoding shapes the signals before they go out. They use delay and Doppler precompensation to keep signals in step, then model interference between satellites and compensation errors. Majorization theory pins down the optimal precoder structure under total power limits, and a Lanczos step cuts complexity. Simulations show designs using average channel data nearly match designs using instant channel readings when antenna counts are high enough.
arxiv-2604-09325: Bonnet-Weill, Ehrlacher, and Nenna propose a reduced-order model for parameter-dependent transport problems using model order reduction. They constrain primal and dual high-fidelity models to small subcones or subspaces, yielding a linear program with few degrees of freedom. Clear conditions guarantee at least one solution, and two a posteriori error bounds limit the error against the high-fidelity problem. One bound needs nonlinear terms, computed fast via empirical blending, and tests cover a 1D example and color transfer, compared with Sinkhorn.
arxiv-2604-09425: Ghosh, Babu, and Agarwal ask whether vision language models need to process image tokens through model stacks. Vision language models join visual coders with large language models, handling dense image tokens at large cost. The authors show visual pictures rapidly converge to a bounded-complexity regime, with entropy settling and inner size shrinking. Once settled, visual pictures become largely shared between layers, showing limited further change in deeper stages. Depth-wise cutting shows need is task-dependent: single-token guesses stay robust, but multi-token output needs sustained visual access.
arxiv-2604-09625: Dang, Mitrovi, and Granitzer test web-scale unlabelled text and model annotations for multilingual hate-speech detection. From OpenWebSearch.eu texts in English, German, Spanish, and Vietnamese, they first continue pretraining BERT models on unlabelled text. That step gains about 3 percent average macro-F1 across sixteen benchmarks. Gains run larger where resources are scarce. Four open models then generate synthetic labels under three ensemble rules. A LightGBM meta-learner wins. Those labels lift a small model 11 percent on pooled F1, but a larger one only 0.6 percent.
arxiv-2604-09725: Cui and three co-authors give a curvature-flux picture of Dirac-node topology via the non-Hermitian Zeeman quantum geometric tensor. Unlike the Hermitian tensor, the Zeeman tensor splits by index exchange into normal and anomalous metric-curvature sectors. The anomalous sector holds two parts: an imaginary symmetric metric-like tensor and a real antisymmetric curvature-like tensor. In a two-dimensional Dirac system, that curvature forms a radial flux field dual to the winding field, turning the winding number into a Gauss-type flux invariant.
arxiv-2604-09825: Al Sayem and six co-authors present the first lab showing of a thin-film lithium tantalate electro-optic modulator with high bandwidth. The device operates at 1 micrometre, in the near-infrared band. It shows a half-wave voltage of 2.4 volts, less than 2 decibels of electro-optic roll-off up to 50 gigahertz, and stable direct-current bias operation.
arxiv-2604-10225: Hedges asks when a prescribed ergodic measure is the unique equilibrium state of a continuous potential. For actions of infinite discrete amenable groups on compact spaces, a local entropy condition characterizes the property. The measure is uniquely attainable when this entropy function is weak-star upper semicontinuous at the zero measure. Entropy semicontinuity at the measure alone does not suffice. He builds a shift space with entropy upper semicontinuous at every ergodic measure, yet continuous at a fixed-point measure that is no equilibrium state of any potential.
arxiv-2604-10625: Wiggins asks whether a geometric effect from classical reaction dynamics also appears for quantum wavepackets squeezed in phase space. In the classical picture, passage through a bottleneck depends on local width scales. Using a Weyl-symbol treatment of the quantum normal-form bottleneck, he derives an exact transmission baseline for a simple saddle model. He then evaluates anharmonic variants with strict energy conservation. As squeezing grows, transmission collapses: the bath absorbs the reactive energy, a quantum suppression effect matching the classical width picture.
arxiv-2604-10825: Bugaud introduces CheeseBench, testing large language models on nine classical rodent behavior paradigms, spanning six cognitive dimensions. Each task follows peer-reviewed rodent protocols, and agents must discover goals from ASCII observations and reward signals, like a rodent in an unfamiliar apparatus. Evaluating six open-weight models from 3B to 72B, the best reaches 52.6 percent average success on ASCII input, against 32.1 percent random and 78.9 percent rodent. Scaling beyond 7B yields diminishing returns, longer context hurts, chain-of-thought hurts, and vision-language helps at 7B but hurts at 32B.
arxiv-2604-10925: Zhang and five colleagues propose Malleable Prompting, an interactive technique for controllable generation, turning preference phrases in plain prompts into GUI widgets. Users struggle to state subjective tastes like tone, style, and emphasis precisely through prompting alone. Widgets let users set choices to steer generation, while showing each control's influence on output. A decoding algorithm shifts token probabilities during generation from preference phrases and widget values. In a user study, Malleable Prompting helped participants hit target tastes more precisely and felt more controllable and clear than prompting alone.
arxiv-2604-11025: Jiang and six colleagues address the grounding paradox in image thinking. There, multimodal models invoke tools such as zooming and cropping. To gain a detail, a model must ground attention on the correct region. Knowing the correct region presupposes having observed that detail. Grounding errors are rarely self-corrected within one trajectory. Once a wrong region is inspected, reasoning builds on that observation and the error propagates. The authors propose test-time scaling over perception, treating perception as the scalable unit of inference. It allocates compute, starting with gated exploration.
arxiv-2604-11225: Javorek and four colleagues ask whether general vision-language models can recognize isolated signs without task-specific training. Testing several open and proprietary models zero-shot on the WLASL300 benchmark, they find open models far behind classic supervised classifiers, though they capture partial alignment between signs and text. Larger proprietary models score much higher, pointing to scale and training diversity as decisive.
arxiv-2604-11325: Brea Rodriguez reports the first observation of the charmless purely baryonic decay of a Lambda-b baryon into a Lambda, a proton, and an antiproton, using the full Run 2 LHCb dataset. A simultaneous fit to long and downstream track categories gives a signal significance of 5.1 sigma including systematics. The relative branching fraction, measured against a similar Lambda-K-K mode, is 5.13 times ten to the minus two in the region where the hadron-pair mass sits below 2.85 GeV.
arxiv-2604-11425: Rendell-Bhatti and four colleagues study phase transitions in neopentyl glycol, a barocaloric crystal proposed for solid-state cooling. They watch the crystal with polarized light images and infrared heat maps, and compare with heat data. They compare pure material with a version doped with 1 percent pentaerythritol. The doped crystal shows less supercooling and less thermal hysteresis, which they link to greater inner disorder and more seeds forming. The findings point toward low-lag barocaloric materials for efficient solid-state refrigeration.
arxiv-2604-11725: Terao gives a faster approximation method for linear matroid intersection. The task is finding the largest set of columns independent in two given matrices. His method lands within a factor of one minus epsilon of optimal, in time set by the number of nonzero entries plus the optimum size raised to the matrix-multiplication exponent. The same approach handles the weighted version, improving on earlier algorithms by Harvey and by Cheung, Kwok, and Lau.
arxiv-2604-11825: Jin, Liu, Lukacova-Medvidova, and Yuan ask whether quantum linear programming can beat standard methods for the measure-valued form of nonlinear partial differential equations. That form becomes a linear program, but one cursed by many dimensions. Some quantum methods, including the quantum central path method, gain up to a polynomial advantage over the standard interior point method. For dissipative weak solutions, meaning expected values of the Young measure, no advantage appears, while random equations can still gain up to polynomially.
arxiv-2604-12025: Dalal and five colleagues propose WiseOWL, a method for choosing ontologies to reuse, scoring options instead of relying on gut feel. It rates four metrics: docs breadth, meaning match via vectors, shape links, and layered balance. Outputs are scaled 0 to 10 scores with usable feedback. Built as a Streamlit app, it ingests OWL format, converts to RDF Turtle, and offers live charts. Tests across six ontologies, including Plant, Gene, and Dublin Core, show good results.
arxiv-2604-12125: Dognini designs pay-as-you-go social security systems that stay balanced by linking the design to general equilibrium theory. His backward method finds optimal monetary equilibria for overlapping generations of varied households, making the design usable for countries in demographic transition. Because household budgets balance at equilibrium prices, these systems resemble notional accounts systems. Brazil, China, India, Italy, and the United States show the design from 1950 to 2070.
arxiv-2604-12225: Lai studies noisy networks wobbling around a stable, noise-free steady state, tracing non-equilibrium effects to connection symmetry and noise covariance. He sets out matching rules for equilibrium motion and studies non-equilibrium steady states through probability currents and drift against a potential surface. Overdamped Brownian motion turns out to be a special case of the general noisy network, and a general fluctuation-dissipation relation follows.
arxiv-2604-12425: Michele De Vita, Julian Wiederer, and Vasileios Belagiannis spot distribution shift in path prediction for self-driving cars. Shifts between training and test scenes can make forecasts fail in new settings. Their method trains a decoder with no labels to predict the second half of a path from its first half. The size of the last layer's gradient then scores how shifted a scene is. The predictor itself stays untouched. Shift detection improves on two driving data sets. The method also flags crashes early for a planner in a simulator.
arxiv-2604-12725: Malik Amir and Sourangshu Ghosh refine covariance asymptotics with curved geometry. Fisher results capture only first-order geometry of efficient estimators. Curved models deviate from those in finite samples. The team views a set as a curved manifold with Fisher-Rao metric. A second-order fix refines the leading term. A tensor splits into intrinsic, extrinsic, and extra parts. The extrinsic part is non-negative, and the full correction is stable under reparameterization. It vanishes for full exponential types. Singular models are handled via resolution.
arxiv-2604-13125: Sajja adds behavioral fidelity as a third test for synthetic tabular data. It asks whether generated data preserves the timing, sequence, and structure patterns real detection systems rely on. She defines four fraud patterns covering event timing, bursts, multi-account graph motifs, and velocity-rule triggers, and proves row-independent generators cannot reproduce the graph motifs or the positive burst fingerprint. Benchmarking four generators on fraud datasets, all fail badly, with composite degradation from 24.4 to 39.0 times on IEEE-CIS and up to 99.7 times on Amazon data.
arxiv-2604-13325: Dallas and five colleagues improve safety filters for self-driving systems by sampling paths that barely avoid a crash. They describe those edge paths with Pontryagin's Maximum Principle and use them to guide data collection for learned Hamilton-Jacobi reachability. The learned Control Barrier Value Function then blocks unsafe actions directly. Tests in shared-control race cars show faster learning, fewer failures, and better safe-set recovery, with wall times around 3 milliseconds.
arxiv-2604-13425: Yifan Li and four colleagues propose VibeFlow, a self-taught tool for editing video colour and light while keeping shape and timing intact. Old tools need costly training on fake paired data, but VibeFlow taps the physical sense inside pre-trained video generation models. A perturbation pipeline that splits structure from colour lets it mix shape from source videos with light and colour cues from reference images. Residual velocity fields and a structural consistency rule then protect shape and timing across relighting, recolouring, and day-night shifts.
arxiv-2604-13625: Ju and Tong study random reaction-diffusion equations, in a space built over continuous functions. Standard methods break down here. The Galerkin method gives no energy estimates for exponents above two. Mild-solution theory lacks the spatial smoothness for a direct Ito formula. The authors prove a critical regularity estimate for the stopped process. That justifies the Ito formula here. It yields explicit energy estimates, dissipativity bounds, global existence and uniqueness, and exponential decay.
arxiv-2604-13725: Feng and six colleagues test context compression for repository-level coding tasks, where long multi-file inputs bury key context, overflow windows, and slow inference. They sort eight methods into three groups: token sequences, latent vectors, and visual tokens. At fourfold compression, latent-vector methods beat full-context scores by up to 28.3 percent in BLEU, filtering noise rather than merely truncating. Visual and text compression also cut end-to-end latency by up to half at high ratios.
arxiv-2604-13825: Nicolau describes contractive analytic self-mappings of the unit disc. These are maps whose hyperbolic derivative stays uniformly below one. He describes them by Aleksandrov-Clark measures and inner-outer factorization. Contractive inner functions, he shows, match a mixing property of boundary values. In short, contraction tames maps near the edge. The disc here is the unit disc in the plane. Further results cover edge behavior of these inner functions.
arxiv-2604-14225: Gieg and three colleagues run numerical-relativity merger simulations that include muons and muonic reactions for two standard equations of state. Neutrinos ride a gray truncated-moments scheme with an implicit-explicit integrator, and new full-kinematics rates plus kernel-based opacities keep neutrino interactions sound. Matter-radiation equilibration comes through a novel two-timescale approach, and muon and non-muon runs agree on remnant, disk, and outflow. Electron fractions, speeds, and heat differ by under about 6 percent, while muons cut ejecta masses by at most about 17 percent.
arxiv-2604-14525: Salla, Amancherla, and Saravanan study whether language-model answers to related queries agree. They define case-file consistency as a belief state that holds together across linked queries, and build a 390-instance benchmark labeled entailment, contradiction, or unknown. Metrics cover satisfiability rate, contradiction density, and revision cost for whole cases. A solver-aided method extracts claims, checks global satisfiability, and repairs via counter-cases, lifting case consistency from 56 to 94 percent across four domains while keeping per-query accuracy.
arxiv-2604-14825: Zhao, Yang, Budiu, and Misailovic present Nautilus, a tensor compiler turning algebraic specs of tensor operators into tiled GPU kernels. Its lowering design applies high-level, expression, and tile optimizations jointly. An auto-scheduler finds optimization chains while keeping tile-optimizer structure. Nautilus is the first full compiler to start from a math-like attention description and discover FlashAttention-3-like kernels. On five transformer models and 150 configs on GH200 and RTX 5090 hardware, it beat leading compilers by up to 23 and 42 percent, matching cuDNN kernels on many long-sequence setups.
arxiv-2604-15225: Perca and colleagues build UrbanClipAtlas, a visual analytics system for finding events in long urban videos. Recordings from street intersections are cut into short clips, described by a vision-language model, and indexed for semantic search. A knowledge graph maps entities from model answers onto a domain taxonomy, then matches them to detected objects and paths. The combination supports event and scene retrieval with grounding and verification for analysts.
arxiv-2604-15525: Wang, Chakraborty, and Shanbhag introduce exponentially-shifted Gaussian smoothing for zeroth-order optimization, whose estimate moments grow linearly rather than quadratically with dimension. The estimate stretches to decision-linked cases with densities known or unknown in closed form, still linear in dimension. Their method covers nonsmooth strongly convex, convex, and non-convex cases with better dimension scaling in iteration counts and new high-chance guarantees.
arxiv-2604-15825: Kevin Michael Frick asks how fast pricing algorithms can learn to collude, testing average-reward soft actor-critic algorithms in a repeated Bertrand duopoly with two symmetric firms, logit demand, and fixed marginal costs. The algorithms reach collusive prices within 50,000 periods, and in 36 percent of runs, learned punishments make one-period cheating unprofitable, so high prices become mutual best responses. Where punishments fail, profitable deviations are typically only hundredths of a percent.
arxiv-2604-16025: Alexandrou and three colleagues find scalar and tensor Lambda-to-proton transition form factors from lattice QCD. The factors matter for semileptonic hyperon decays under Standard Model extensions with scalar and tensor interactions. Using twisted mass fermions at the physical pion mass, they give the complete factors as functions of momentum transfer squared. They examine impact on searches for non-standard interactions through the muon-to-electron decay-rate ratio, where scalar and tensor terms enter and are helicity-enhanced. Comparison with recent measurements tightens constraints on non-standard interactions.
arxiv-2604-16225: Bogdanović, Dimitrijević Ćirić, and Szabo build cubic scalar field theory on lambda-Minkowski space. They use Batalin-Vilkovisky methods and harmonic analysis. The result is two different noncommutative theories. One theory is braided. It shows usual ultraviolet divergences, and no UV/IR mixing. The other theory is standard. It relates plane-wave and cylindrical harmonic decompositions. It confirms the planar equivalence theorem. It also shows periodic UV/IR mixing, where non-planar correlators are mostly ultraviolet finite but turn non-analytic at exceptional momenta.
arxiv-2604-16325: Chen and eight co-authors present UniMamba, a unified time design that joins state-space motion with focus. Transformer methods capture time patterns through focus but pay squared cost, while state-space models like Mamba handle long contexts well but lack clear pattern spotting. It joins a Mamba variate-channel coding layer, boosted with FFT-Laplace transform and TCN, a spatial-temporal focus layer, and a forward time layer. Tests on eight benchmarks assess its prediction accuracy.
arxiv-2604-16425: Lazebnyi and colleagues present a pipeline for collecting and merging web data that keeps working when pages change. Hybrid scraping handles static pages and pages that load late, results land in MongoDB, and language models pull entries into a fixed JSON form. A two-stage check compares embeddings from several model outputs at different temperatures, plus consistency rules, to catch invented facts. Experiments reported high accuracy on key fields and held up when page layouts changed, suiting news aggregation and near-real-time monitoring.
arxiv-2604-16525: Bochniak and colleagues derive fusion rules for anyonic quasiparticles in fractional quantum Hall fluids from microscopic data. They build on the idea that topological traits hide in the DNA of candidate wave functions. That DNA is the pattern of orbital occupations across a few lowest Landau levels. Extending Schrieffer's counting argument, they introduce classes of topological excitations. This framework gives one route to fusion rules for Abelian and non-Abelian excitations. It explains topological features from first principles in fermionic and bosonic systems.
arxiv-2604-16625: Du and colleagues propose AdaExplore, a tool for kernel making through self-learning. Most methods treat each problem alone, with no saved know-how, hurting special tongues like Triton. AdaExplore learns from run feedback in two stages: failure tuning and varied search. Tuning makes tasks and turns repeat failures into a memory of rules, keeping outputs valid. Search sorts kernels as a tree, mixing small local tweaks with larger remakes beyond optima. On KernelBench Level and Level, it hits 3.11 times and 1.62 times speedups in steps, gaining with more work.
arxiv-2604-16825: Liu and colleagues open the spatial messy-wide Langevin equation, a data-driven method for coarse-grained dynamics in heterogeneous systems. Unlike mean-field ways, it uses a variational Bayes framework with a random field prior to split static spatial disorder from stretchy friction. Number results show standard rules fail where the new method extends long-time motion from short paths. It captures the odd diffusion switch and regains group statistical traits of messy systems.
arxiv-2604-16925: Liu and three colleagues challenge one-size-fits-all denoising for low-dose PET scans. A single model averages across dose levels and blurs dose-specific noise. Their residual approach learns the noise directly from low-dose images instead of predicting clean images, outperforming single-dose and dose-conditioned models on multi-dose data from two medical centers.
arxiv-2604-17025: Zhang confronts a control gap in safety-critical engineering with language models, where even rare missed rule breaks make a system undeployable. Current setups suffer from sycophantic compliance, fading context attention, and unstable self-correction. His Convergent AI Agent Framework moves workflows from open-loop generation to closed-loop fail-safe determinism through atomic decomposition, harness-as-asset records, and locked semantic gradients. Ablations show no single pillar closes the gap alone.
arxiv-2604-17125: Turgut and Gümüş audit a published CASCADE evaluation, a fully local layered defense against prompt injection in the Model Context Protocol. Across three configurations on a frozen 5,000-sample corpus, the headline depends on the decision convention. The false-positive rate swings from about 12 percent to about 2 percent depending on whether referrals count as positives. Corpus construction also shapes results, with wrappers alone identifying labels. The local review model changes no binary outcome while converting 1,492 referrals into denials.
arxiv-2604-17225: Saha, Lakshmanan, and Ng propose MACE, a multi-agent framework for verifying claims from tabular data documents. A Planner drafts reasoning strategies, an Executor lays out computation steps, and a Verifier checks the logic. Each agent works zero-shot with chain-of-thought prompting, avoiding elaborate fine-tuning, and the traces stay interpretable. MACE tops two datasets and matches the best models on two others, while hitting 80 to 100 percent of best performance with far smaller models — 27 to 92B parameters against 235B.
arxiv-2604-17425: Kang, Suk, and Chung speed up the design of meta-optics, the tiny structures that steer light for imaging and color routing.
