Since the property remains desirable, the survey explores conditions such as countable compactness, pseudocompactness, and pseudocompleteness, checking in which cases a general complete uniform space qualifies. The result is a map of how far metric-space intuition carries into the uniform setting, and where it stops.
arxiv-2605-18525: Lena Hansen and fifteen co-authors wire solid state artificial atoms to a tiny light guiding channel so they act in step. Each added emitter lifts the order of photon correlations the setup can show, with emitter count setting the pattern. From two emitters acting together, the team records true three photon correlations while weaker photon number signals stay muted. Adding a third emitter tuned to the same frequency marks the start of many body behavior in waveguide light matter physics.
arxiv-2605-18625: Ilkka Mäkinen, Hanno Sahlmann, and Waleed Sherif study, in a 2026 paper, the near-kernel sector of the Hamiltonian constraint. They work in the one-vertex model of quantum reduced loop gravity. Using variational Monte Carlo with neural quantum states and spin cutoffs to 1001, they find near-kernel states in three classes. Low-cutoff solutions do not factorize across three edge freedoms, while larger cutoffs yield two factorized branches in different spin regimes. One branch matches reduced Thiemann coherent states with near-unit fidelity, evidencing emergent semiclassical organization.
arxiv-2605-18725: Haoyu Zhang probes chaotic spacing in the D1D5 CFT, by looking at lifting matrices at second order in low energy sectors close to BPS states. In the large N flat diagram limit, mixing between one cycle and many cycle states fades out, and spectra split by symmetry look Poisson like. At finite N, diagrams beyond the flat limit switch that mixing back on between unlike cycle patterns. Once that mixing returns inside each symmetry sector, levels push apart as random matrix theory expects.
arxiv-2605-18825: Shaoke Fang and five colleagues improve prefix caching by evicting blocks on meaning, not recency. Cached key-value states save repeated prefill work, but least-recently-used rules treat all tokens alike. Token types differ hugely in reuse, by up to seven hundred fifty-six times across prompts. SAECache routes blocks to task queues, learns reuse values from eviction feedback, and tunes itself online. It lifts time to first token by one point four to two point seven times over production baselines.
arxiv-2605-19525: Aigner, Simsen and Waurick prove global solutions exist for coupled partly time-varying evolution inclusions. It joins a Cauchy problem with a compact resolvent generator and a slope-ruled equation. It covers time-varying Schrödinger-Debye inclusions with variable powers and extends to wave-heat and Maxwell-parabolic systems. They extend a Vrabie approach to the time-varying case with semigroup tools plus a new result for usable selections. Links must be Hausdorff-continuous with bounded, convex, closed values and weakly steady in one variable.
arxiv-2605-19625: Filmus, Moran and Nesterova study rebuilding an unknown point from approximate linear queries, a setting spanning remote sensing and privacy-sensitive inference. Their goal is the optimal reconstruction error from query count, dimension and noise. In the infinite-query limit the error converges to an exact value like the Bayes optimal error in supervised learning. With fixed dimension the excess error decays doubly exponentially, while with growing dimension exponentially many queries prove necessary and enough. The key core generalizes Jung's 1901 theorem to a robust variant for near-extremal bodies.
arxiv-2605-20325: Mayrhofer and three co-workers make outlier spotting for multi-variable curve data both sturdy and explainable. They tie random processes with separable covariance to matrix forms, then apply a matrix-variate Minimum Covariance Determinant estimator with a trimmed Mahalanobis semi-distance. Outlier scores are split into time-coordinate shares via Shapley values, with a cut that brings exponential cost down to linear. Simulations and real cases show the approach keeps its key traits.
arxiv-2605-20425: Shen and four co-workers present AgentCo-op, a retrieval-based builder of multi-agent workflows for open science. It joins reusable skills, tools and outside agents into runnable workflows via typed artifact handoffs, then repairs failing parts locally from execution evidence. In genomics case studies it coordinates agents for spatial transcriptomics and single-cell multiome analysis without redesign or global search. Across six benchmarks in coding, math and question answering it tops four and cuts per-task cost versus multi-agent baselines.
arxiv-2605-20525: Mohammad Abbasi and fourteen colleagues built NeuroQA, a benchmark for answering questions about three-dimensional brain scans. It holds 56,953 question-answer pairs from 12,977 people across twelve datasets. Coverage spans ages five to 104 and five clinical areas, from Alzheimer disease to brain tumours. Careful answer balancing cut text-only guessing on closed questions from over 80 percent to 44.6 percent.
arxiv-2605-20725: Jingyang Mao, Ningkang Peng, and Yanhui Gu propose holistic reliability propagation for learning with noisy labels in media classification. Most methods merge outside annotations and model predictions into one reliability weight, though the two sources can fail in their own ways. Their method estimates separate reliabilities for the given label and the pseudo-label, without forcing them to sum to one. Reliability-aware Mixup and beta-gated contrastive positives then route each signal to its own objective.
arxiv-2605-21125: Xixiang He and colleagues diagnose advantage collapse in Group Relative Policy Optimization, where uniform rewards inside a group yield near-zero advantages and stalled learning. Their Advantage Collapse Rate measures the share of batches with ineffective gradients and predicts stagnation across models from half a billion to fourteen billion parameters. Their AVSPO extension injects virtual reward samples guided by that rate, cutting collapse by roughly three fifths and lifting accuracy.
arxiv-2605-21625: Aditya Chetan and co-authors present Flat-Pack Bench, a benchmark testing fine-grained spatio-temporal understanding in large vision-language models through furniture assembly. Existing benchmarks favor coarse tasks like action segmentation, captioning, and retrieval, and lean on entities easy to name in words. Their multiple-choice questions, paired with visual prompts marking relevant parts, test temporal ordering, state localization, part mating, and tracking. State-of-the-art models struggle markedly on these fine-grained tasks.
arxiv-2605-21825: Haichao Miao and co-authors present an end-to-end agent harness for AI visualization co-scientists. Such systems design custom visual analysis apps from data plus a high-level task description. Coordinated agents and specialized skills handle analysis, planning, setup, implementation, interface checks, and task evaluation. Each stage leaves documents guiding later work. Validated on IEEE SciVis Contests across science and engineering fields, the system produces functional single-page apps with verified linked-view behavior, tailored to experts' tasks from data and targets alone.
arxiv-2605-22125: Aldarawsheh and co-authors build a neural network sorter that identifies magnetic states in spin dynamics simulations. Hand-made features and manual inspection often fail on subtle or complex spin textures. Their EfficientNetV1B0 model sorts nine magnetic states, including ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic forms such as AFM skyrmions and AFM stripe domains. Spin layouts come from atomistic runs with the Spirit code, turned into RGB images with VFRendering for sorting.
arxiv-2605-22225: Esmerian and co-authors predict collision outcomes for silicate dust grains in space using molecular dynamics. They target threshold velocities for shattering and vapor loss plus resulting grain sizes, key inputs for grain population models. Runs evolve every atom in grains of radius 5 to 50 angstroms at 0.1 to 20 km/s, for glassy SiO2 and a Draine and Hensley silicate. Shattering thresholds reach about 6 km/s for both materials, about twice a canonical value. The work quantifies how shattered and vaporized mass fractions and product sizes depend on impact velocity.
arxiv-2605-22325: Ali and colleagues work on radio nets that link rescue teams after a disaster. Nodes must find each other across many hops. Old rules often stop too soon. That leaves the neighbour map half built. The team offers MR-DMCA, a clock method that confirms each neighbour by position. Its stop rule waits until the full map is built. In a hard test with 20 nodes and 20 channels, it found all neighbours. It cut link-up time by up to 76 percent over one rival method.
arxiv-2605-22625: Bandekar and others simulate brain like hardware from spin orbit torque devices, building a fully linked artificial neural net from domain wall motion in magnetic nanotracks. A 3 nanosecond current pulse drives wall motion that mimics the ReLU activation of a neuron, while notched tracks pin walls at steps that serve as stable synaptic weights. The design also shows a threshold delay effect in which each release depends on earlier ones, echoing synaptic adaptation. With quantized weights, the net scores about 95 percent on MNIST and about 62 percent on Fashion MNIST.
arxiv-2605-22725: Fornasiero, Kaplan, and Matthews prove tight links in the theory of geometric fields. Stability matches strong minimality here, simplicity matches rank one, and rosiness matches a trait called surgical. With a prior result of Hrushovski, this identifies stable fields with bounded algebra as algebraically closed fields plus constants. Generic derivations, they show, preserve simplicity or rosiness just when they commute.
arxiv-2605-23025: Cardoso do Nascimento and four coauthors present World Machine, a world-modeling design for time series. It uses a transformer with latent states that adapts to different amounts of observed data and context. That beats classic transformers, whose cost grows with the square of context length. Tests on a synthetic Toy1D dataset show the approach works, show skills missing from classic transformers, and isolate each training part's role. The design aims at predictive understanding and controllable simulation of settings.
arxiv-2605-23425: Parkavousi and Saha show that one-sided, nonreciprocal surface tension rewires how defects move in conserved scalar fields under the nonreciprocal Cahn-Hilliard model. Surface tension alone yields defects that flicker in and out: system-wide target patterns form, collapse, and regrow from a chaotic defect state. When bulk and surface effects combine just so, a mosaic-wave state appears, with coherent traveling waves inside domains walled by moving dislocations. The large-scale fluctuations fall in the anisotropic Kardar-Parisi-Zhang class.
arxiv-2605-23525: De la Varga and colleagues restore observability in grids, where scarce and mixed monitors struggle to track states as distributed resources join the grid. Their framework generates pseudo-measurements with a neural network while keeping the exact nonlinear AC power flow model in a classical weighted least squares estimator. Unlike prior methods that build pseudo-measurements apart, theirs couples both parts end to end, with the estimator as a network layer for implicit differentiation. Tests on IEEE 30-bus and 33-bus systems beat leading methods across loads and monitor layouts.
arxiv-2605-23625: Bönsel, Kunst, and Roccati study atom-photon bound states in fractal lattices, seeded by emitters. Via the photonic Green's heat kernel, they show far-field localization length scales as detuning to minus one over walk dimension. That scaling is governed by anomalous diffusion, not translational invariance or band-edge effective-mass ideas. Diagonalization on Sierpiński gaskets, pyramids, Vicsek graphs, and carpets confirms the law once the bath turns Laplacian-like. Near-field amplitudes vary, with nested fractals matching resistance scaling as carpets deviate.
arxiv-2605-23825: Bladon and Bent test whether geopolitical bias in language models comes from pre-training or post-training. They use seven model pairs from seven labs, on a forced-choice probe over 28 country pairs in English, French, and Chinese. They find bias originates in post-training rather than pre-training. The shift is strongest in Alibaba's Qwen 2.5: the base model is neutral on China-favourability, while the chat variant shows a large positive shift. The findings suggest geopolitical preferences are actively shaped during post-training, not inherited from internet data.
arxiv-2605-23925: Imran and Bulathwela name a blind spot in automated tutoring: systems that praise a right answer even when the student's reasoning is wrong. Drawing on real answers from the Eedi maths platform, they find that most such misses cluster in just two question types, where faulty working happens to land on the correct number. A tuned T5 model caught 57 percent of cases against 84 percent for a leading language model. The best model still raised about four false alarms per true catch, so solo screening at class scale looks unworkable.
arxiv-2605-24225: Wang and three co-authors introduce ECo-MoE, a model of robot evolution co-optimizing latent design vectors with control experts gated by each decoded body plan. Training one policy per robot wastes effort, while one universal controller yields timid bodies. So this middle path keeps ancestral knowledge in a modular frame where plans switch circuits on and off. One expert module can be overhauled for new body types without disturbing the rest, and pretrained experts can plug in, steering evolution toward desired shapes, called evo by demo.
arxiv-2605-24625: Toufiq Musah and colleagues introduce ULF-Synth, a 2026 system for boosting ultra-low-field MRI, which is portable but noisy and low-detail. It builds true-to-life ultra-low-field images from high-field volumes to create large paired training sets. A spatial-frequency goal favors fine anatomy. The approach works across encoder-decoder, rival, and diffusion models, and trained only on synthetic data, it carries over to real 64mT scans. It lifts downstream brain segmentation and wins higher reader favor in a blinded reader study.
arxiv-2605-24725: Shengyang Wu and Vladimir Dvorkin synthesize dynamic power-grid models that protect source-grid privacy without losing quality. Real grid models aid blackout and shock analysis, yet their release risks exposing sensitive transmission, generation, and load settings. Their algorithm adds privacy noise to hide original settings, then tunes the perturbed settings so model dynamics stay statistically matching with the source grid. The privacy guarantee uses differential privacy as its yardstick. On frequency dynamics of the IEEE 30-bus system, stricter privacy degrades quality, yet tuning greatly improves the built models.
arxiv-2605-25025: Josef Berman and Oren Gal steer sixteen micro-robots through a pulsing artery in a 2 millimeter channel, coupling a Navier-Stokes solver with policy learning. The swarm must advance upstream, save energy, and move smoothly, with conflicting gradients resolved by PCGrad surgery; without it, energy and smoothness collapse. Policy scores run six and a half to seven on progress, around 0.64 on energy efficiency, and around 0.98 on smoothness. They beat brute-force baselines by over 8 units. Training reveals unprogrammed throttling formations, a cycle-synced ratchet using flow reversals, and tailored approaches.
arxiv-2605-25225: David Olivieri and Antonio Pérez Rodríguez recast a popular way of probing language models as field physics. They treat the model's leftover signal across layers and word positions as a field. An intervention then becomes a small source dropped into that field. Sensitivity maps then forecast how a patch will shift behavior, and related math tracks how effects spread downstream. Tests on GPT-2-style models show the forecasts hold locally, giving experimenters a principled map for choosing where to intervene.
arxiv-2605-25525: Mingxu Zhang and colleagues tackle forgetting when a language model learns task after task. Dense updates smear concepts across shared dimensions, so guarding old knowledge tends to block new learning. Their SAE-FD method anchors updates in the sparse features of a pretrained sparse autoencoder, which separates concepts and allows tighter, less disruptive regularization. Across two benchmarks and three model designs, it beats older regularization methods, reaching about 53 percent average accuracy with only slight backward transfer.
arxiv-2605-25925: Li, Yu, Wang and Gu analyse spin-dependent forces and fine structure in negative-parity baryons with one heavy quark. Baryons are three-quark particles, and their energy levels split under competing strong-force effects. The authors apply the relativised quark model rigorously to the three-quark system for the first time, a step earlier work found unfeasible. Their calculation reproduces measured levels with an average deviation below five mega-electronvolts. That precision reveals how each strong interaction shapes level order, splitting and mixing.
arxiv-2605-26025: DeChant, Geelen, McQuarrie and Guilleminot approximate huge nonlinear systems with a moving basis. A fixed low-dimensional basis must swell in rank to track shifting physics, a snag called the Kolmogorov barrier. The authors trace the basis along a geodesic path on the Grassmannian manifold, a space of subspaces. Splitting shape drift from state change keeps rank low. Costs stay independent of full state size, and tests on transport flow and a turbulent wake bear the method out.
arxiv-2605-26325: Tobias Jaeggi, David Gregory Black, and Septimiu Salcudean present Directionality-Aware Reslicing, a method that rebuilds ultrasound volumes and re-slices them with direction in mind. Current re-slicing ignores that a structure looks different from each new angle, which matters when remote experts preview scans over limited links. Their fast GPU code re-slices in real time from any viewpoint, giving true previews. Tested by image likeness metrics and a user study, it beats current methods on likeness and realism against ground truth.
arxiv-2605-26425: Melvyn B. Nathanson opens a new class of problems on additive h-bases for n. In additive number theory, a finite integer set A is an h-basis for n when every number from 0 through n equals a sum of exactly h members. Repeats are allowed. The seventh installment in his problems series lays out questions on these bases and their kin. The problems are shaped, in part, to invite attack by artificial intelligence.
arxiv-2605-26625: Ibon Gracia and three others plan robot motion that stays safe under random disturbances of unknown shape. They frame safety as chance constraints for linear or linearizable systems among oddly shaped obstacles. From recorded trajectories they learn a Wasserstein ambiguity tube that likely contains the state distribution, then grow a sampling tree inside it. Learning several slim tubes instead of one fat tube cuts caution and scales better, while a bandit checker speeds checks without losing completeness. Cluttered tests beat current leaders under strict safety limits.
arxiv-2605-27125: Evangelista and Santos study gravitoelectromagnetism in Weyl form via a gauge symmetry on a tensor. They derive and decompose the propagator via Barnes-Rivers into spin-2, spin-1, scalar parts, with spin-2 and scalar active. It takes a form like the linear gravity propagator. The Lorentz gauge fits it and yields gauge-free results, while de Donder leaves gauge-tied terms. For fermions and EM, they derive currents matching energy tensors, so it couples to matter like gravity, and they verify the Ward identities.
arxiv-2605-27425: Jose Luis Rosales builds a quantum-inspired setup for routing in quantum key distribution networks. The network becomes a random graph whose routing follows a Hamiltonian covering delay, key rate, crowding, risk, and capacity. A random annealer and a tensor-network model explore the options together, linking network control with statistical physics.
arxiv-2605-28225: Jan Sikora, Paweł Lenartowicz, and Hubert Plisiecki compare feeling words across cultures, past word-for-word translation. Their supervised meaning-gradient method tracks affect words in Polish, English, and French embeddings. Valence looks mostly shared, while arousal and dominance show patterned contrasts, some from corpus quirks, not culture, so readings need care.
arxiv-2605-28425: Markus Weißenhofer and five colleagues show how driven lattice vibrations can steer the topology of magnon bands, the wave excitations of ordered magnets. Linearly polarized phonons leave the spectrum unchanged, but circular and elliptical phonons carrying angular momentum open and tune gaps at Dirac points. Gap size and Chern numbers follow the phonon angular momentum directly, so handedness selects the topological phase. Applied to monolayer chromium triiodide, the work presents driven lattice motion as a broad route to Floquet control of magnetism.
arxiv-2605-28625: Julien Lalanne and five colleagues introduce Random Process Flow, a flow-matching method for generative models of random fields from a single seen field. Only sparse readings are on hand, so the method learns a hidden signal code with random Fourier parts, askable anywhere. A Bayesian posterior built by Gaussian-process fit in the source space makes high-quality samples. Tests show true samples with tuned uncertainty even at fast changes, thin data, or many axes, suiting scarce-data rebuilds.
arxiv-2605-29125: Johannes Kellendonk and Reem Yassawi ask when the Ellis semigroup fully captures a dynamical system. The semigroup gathers facts about a system, mixing algebra, shape, and motion, and it stays unchanged when systems are matched by conjugacy. Yet two systems that are not conjugate can still share the same semigroup, so it is not always a complete test. The authors find a class of minimal systems inside which this cannot happen. Within that class, the Ellis semigroup alone tells matched systems apart from unmatched ones.
arxiv-2605-29225: Jiahao Huang et al. present BenchTrace, testing reflection and controlled evolution in agents. Self-growing agents improve by looking back on misses, but testing counts only task scores and relies on agents' own runs, without set misses. BenchTrace uses 1,821 episodes across six tasks, with reflection tests on finding misses and growth tests on dodging. A failure avoidance rate metric counts the share dodging the failure. Qwen3-32B and GPT-4.1 fall below 30 percent on reflection, with diagnosis the bottleneck, and evolution lifts dodging but suffers loss and bad transfer.
arxiv-2605-29625: Arturo Valdivia and Paolo Burelli explore co-creation in which children and models build stories through a physical board game. Most co-creation research studies adults with AI in digital settings, leaving young players aside. Their multi-agent framework aims for narratives suited to young players. It uses a Writer-Editor loop: one model writes stories while another judges them and returns feedback. A simulation study shows this loop steadily improves perceived story quality. The findings suggest a few refinement steps may yield high-quality output in interactive storytelling.
arxiv-2605-29825: Pascal Baumgart and four colleagues test whether photons from two trapped calcium ions interfere as identical particles. They generate Raman photons with few-nanosecond pulses and study how spontaneous scattering to the starting state disturbs Hong-Ou-Mandel interference. The mean count of such back-decays emerges as a measurable single-emitter quantity tracking how sharp two-emitter interference runs. The work ties a simple per-emitter number to the visibility achievable when photons from identical emitters meet. It clarifies one limit on indistinguishability for trapped-ion photon sources.
arxiv-2605-30125: Claudio M. Salgado and five colleagues map the thermodynamics of the quantum spin-5/2 Blume-Capel model in transverse and random crystal fields. Its Hamiltonian mixes neighbour exchange with lengthwise and transverse anisotropy. With a Bogoliubov mean-field approach, they derive the state function and the magnetization law. Most ranges give second-order transitions with no tricritical point, though some positive anisotropies yield a first-order jump in the ordered phase. Negative transverse anisotropy favours order and raises critical temperature, while positive anisotropy lowers it.
arxiv-2605-30225: Pernille Matthews, Lena Krieger, Tommaso Amico, Artur Zimek, Thomas Seidl and Ira Assent present ExDBSCAN, explaining DBSCAN cluster assignments with counterfactual reasoning. Clustering groups points by similarity with no labels, and supervised tools do not transfer. ExDBSCAN is a density-aware post-hoc method giving usable counterfactuals with validity guarantees. It generates counterfactuals from a weighted graph, using a physics-style model that pushes candidates apart for diversity while pulling them toward the instance. On 30 tabular datasets against four baselines, it wins with perfect validity and diverse close counterfactuals.
arxiv-2605-30325: Shihao Han, Hao Yang, Xinting Hu, Xiaofeng Mei, Yi Jiang and Xiaojuan Qi present Veda, a distilled sparse attention method for video diffusion. They show quality depends not on sparsity ratio, but on the fit between the sparse mask and attention's tile geometry. Veda formulates tile selection as a reconstruction problem from attention, combining tile scoring with head-aware tiling to cut error and mismatch. A hardware-efficient tile-skipping kernel converts sparsity into speedups. On one model, Veda achieves about fivefold speedup and about tenfold attention speedup.
arxiv-2605-30525: Paul Almasan and three co-authors present GRAPHWAVE, a neural graph-driven signal solver hinging on ray tracing rules. The model uses a digital signal area to build a point cloud and extract a matching graph of the radio area. By applying neural message passing over the matching graph, it infers well radio-related values, e.g., caught signal strength, in a 3D area. They showcase GRAPHWAVE as a radio area digital twin, showing it can learn from fake and real-world data with fast run times.
arxiv-2605-30625: Huynh and van der Schaar choose measurement times for learning probability paths from sparse snapshots, a core problem in single-cell biology where sampling destroys cells and sequencing costs run high. Targets live in infinite-dimensional Wasserstein space, where standard Euclidean metrics fail and current interpolations lack uncertainty estimates. Mapping snapshots into a tangent space via linearized optimal transport, they build a Gaussian-process surrogate for the probability path and an acquisition policy that picks times to minimize uncertainty. Their policy beats uncertainty-blind baselines on synthetic and real data.
arxiv-2605-30825: Khalafi, Ribeiro, and Ding build a frame for making diffusion models forget chosen data while keeping other skills intact. Forgetting means staying close to the base model under strict split rules, using two KL forms and a likelihood rule. They prove strong duality for all three forms, name the best targets, build paired solvers, and beat weight-based rivals on keep-versus-forget trade-offs, with the likelihood form keeping held ideas best.
arxiv-2606-00225:
Piro and co-authors compare two kinds of cosmic flashes in one clean BeppoSAX set. The set holds 96 true gamma-ray bursts caught by two tools on the craft. Soft bursts, called X-ray flashes, sit next to rich and plain bursts. The team asks if these groups share one root.

Counts split the set into 36 flashes, 40 rich bursts, and 20 plain ones. Shape traits of the bursts look much the same across groups. Peak energy drives most of the gap in their spectra. Some bursts show a soft herald well before the main flash. Near nine in ten bursts leave an X-ray afterglow. Light and radio glows show up far less. Shared traits point to shared roots, with jet traits setting the gaps.
arxiv-2606-00625:
Nguyen and co-authors frame flaw replays for soft tools as set recipes a machine can check. Flaw replays are core work for guards, code crews, and class rooms. A replay can rot as its soft world ages out of reach. Their frame, NICE, builds on the Nix pack world.

A replay in NICE is a pack of set parts. VM forms for NixOS, a script for the exploit run, and check claims form the pack. Those claims give hard proof the flaw was hit in the run. Share, check, and long-run use all gain from that form. Tests span 19 real flaws in more than one class. Marks span user, system, core, and art tools as targets. Tight recipes and tests come out of the frame in use.
arxiv-2606-00725:
Fang, Shao, and Wu extend a classic trick for the maxcut problem in this 2026 maths paper. Maxcut asks how to split a graph's nodes into two sets so the weight of edges between them is as large as can be. Hadlock once turned maxcut on planar graphs into a simpler form. Graphs in that class lie flat with no crossed edges.

Their tools are an Eulerian-spanning set and a coboundary operator. With them, the conversion works for general graphs with weights that are zero or more. The pair of tools opens new paths to maxcut algorithms past the planar class. As one gain, they give a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm for k-contraction apex graphs. For graphs with crossing number k, their method matches the best known run time for this weight range.
arxiv-2606-00925:
Hossain and co-authors build a security test for agent skill stores in this 2026 paper. Open platforms let anyone publish reusable skills that agents run on demand. A bad actor can hide harmful acts inside a skill that looks tame. Static checks alone struggle to catch such traps.

Their benchmark, SkillVetBench, vets skills in two stages. Stage one reads each skill's text spec for hidden malicious intent. Stage two runs flagged skills in a watched sandbox and logs what they truly do. The cases come from confirmed bad skills in the live OpenClaw system, some from the ClawHavoc campaign. Semantic and signature baselines miss up to 89 percent of the bad skills, they report. The misses hide in plain-language instructions and cross-part logic. Runtime attacks cluster in a few high-power tools, like exec and file writes. Execution traces give the audit proof that text checks cannot.
arxiv-2606-01325:
Khial and co-authors pick radar detectors on the fly for drone search. Drones with radar hunt targets through occlusions. Human targets show signs like respiration micro-motion. Radar statistics shift as the drone moves through scenes. No fixed processing strategy stays best for long. Their setup keeps a library of specialized detectors. Search becomes online policy selection over that library. Regret measures the gap to the best policy per scene.

In-scene noise and inter-scene drift both matter here. The Stochastically Extended Adversary frame captures both regimes. SEArch is a light optimistic selector built on it. It runs onboard in real time on tight hardware. A windowed variant restarts to adapt faster. Tests cut regret by up to 30 percent.
arxiv-2606-01825:
Jia and co-authors improve search for a person from a text query. A user types a phrase about how a person looks. The system must find that person's photo. Models based on CLIP lean on whole-image traits. Short captions leave fine details sparse and weak.

Their ROGLE method joins global and local matching. It mines region-to-sentence pairs on its own. That step removes the need for costly hand labels. Global contrast training is fused with region-level fit. The team also builds the P-VLG benchmark data set. It holds over 100,000 marked regions with long captions. The authors report strong gains in fine-grained search.
arxiv-2606-02025:
Townsend builds a classifying category for locally compact locales. Locales are point-free versions of topological spaces. The work starts with an internal category in a cartesian one. A construction assigns principal bundles over each object. Morphisms are principal bundles of a related core groupoid form.

The assignment is shown to form a stack of categories. Such stacks are called lax-geometric in the paper. Two sufficient conditions for that property are given. They prove the locally compact locale functor is lax-geometric. Sheaves over a locale supply the categories involved. The result gives a classifying setting for these bundles. It extends geometric logic tools to this setting. Category theorists and locale specialists are the main audience.
arxiv-2606-02225:
Thom studies prime endomorphisms of the free group on two generators. Endomorphisms map the group into itself in structure preserving ways. Prime ones are singled out for study here. The work asks how common non-prime endomorphisms are. Density is measured on a logarithmic scale.

Thom proves lower and upper bounds for that density. The non-prime density lies between three quarters and 27/28. Equivalent bounds govern how fast a key probability decays. The chance that a random endomorphism is non-prime decays exponentially. Rates are pinned between the stated bounds. The results align with a heuristic argument by Ian Agol. Group theorists gain sharp limits on prime maps. The free group of rank two is the test case.
arxiv-2606-02325:
Jyothish S and Narasimhan study a hard routing puzzle on graphs, the Steiner tree problem. A graph gives points joined by edges. A set of special points, called terminals, must all join in one tree. The tree may use only a few extra points. A terminal Steiner tree adds one more rule. Every terminal must sit at a leaf of the tree.

The authors ask when such leaf-constrained trees exist. They sort out how hard the problem is on varied graph classes. The base problem has been known as NP-complete since 1977. They also show uses of the problem as a black box in other tasks. One result gives a fast method when the terminal count is the fixed parameter. The work maps both the limits and the usable paths for this problem.
arxiv-2606-02825:
Avelino and co-authors build a high-bandwidth backplane for wideband radio telescope correlators. Wideband correlators need accurate, scalable backends. Throughput must stay high while timing alignment stays stable across many signal chains. A co-designed backplane is their answer. It extends the Control Readout System FPGA platform. The Canadian Hydrogen Observatory and Radio-transient Detector, CHORD, guides the requirements.

Each backplane hosts up to four CRS boards. One crate joins four backplanes for sixteen modules. That gives 128 digitized inputs per crate. Links run at 25 gigabits per second per lane. An on-backplane shuffle network interconnects the boards. Validation shows robust high-speed link performance. Timing alignment stays stable below sampling level. Thermal and power behavior holds across environmental changes. The design scales from one crate to many without firmware changes. Next-generation interferometers gain a phase-consistent digital foundation.
arxiv-2606-02925:
Fischer, Gauger, and Kusch extend the one-shot method for design optimization to problems with inequality constraints. The one-shot approach solves design and state equations together. It suits tasks governed by costly steady-state systems. Past versions handled extra equality constraints well, but inequalities were largely missing.

The team adds slack variables inside a doubly augmented Lagrangian form. After the slack variables are eliminated, nonsmooth terms remain that depend on the active set. The coupled one-shot matrix structure survives. The gradient system keeps a clean form like the equality case. To handle the nonsmooth switches, the authors use generalized second-order subdifferentials in the sense of Clarke and Rockafellar-Wets. They derive explicit positivity conditions. Those conditions ensure all admissible generalized Hessians stay positive definite, which gives strict local optimality. The authors close with an outlook on preconditioners built from generalized Hessian approximations.
arxiv-2606-03125:
Khandelwal, Basistha, Jolotia, and Pareek ask how wide a neural network must be to proxy AC optimal power flow. Such proxies can speed grid work, but no clear rule sets their size. They seek the least width that still tracks the true solution map well.

Their algorithm, Loss-Guided Neural Densification, grows the network step by step. It adds neurons only when the current size stops improving. Tests span several IEEE grid systems. The grown networks matched published baselines while using up to ten times fewer neurons per layer. Small size is not just a saving here. Grid work is safety-critical, and formal checks of a network grow hard as it grows. A lean proxy is far easier to verify. The authors present the method as a way to find the right size from the loss curve itself, rather than by guesswork or habit.
arxiv-2606-03225:
Xia, Yang, Li, and Wang speed up reverse nearest neighbor search in high dimensions. A reverse search returns all points that count a query among their own k nearest neighbors. Past methods gather nearby points as candidates, then check each one. Two flaws hurt them. Many nearby points are not true results, and the check needs each point's k-nearest radius, computed online at high cost.

Their index, HRNN, takes a unlike route. Nearby points act as proxies: a query's results are often found through the results of its near points. The index also stores high-grade radii offline, so checks skip costly rebuilds. It joins a navigation graph, a ranked neighbor graph, and reverse-neighbor lists. Tests show throughput up to ten times past methods. The index scales to ten million vectors and supports append-only updates. The work targets fast search in very large vector stores.
arxiv-2606-03825:
Sieberling, Runwal, Panda, and Kim add dynamic short convolutions to the Transformer toolkit. Attention, feed-forward layers, residuals, and normalization made Transformers dominant. Short convolutions offer a local bias that attention lacks. Static versions use fixed filters. Dynamic versions make filters depend on the input, raising expressivity while keeping locality.

On hard associative recall tasks, dynamic convolutions on keys, queries, and values beat static ones. Language modeling from 150 million to 2 billion parameters shows the same edge. Standard Transformers and static-convolution variants both trail. Scaling fits imply a solid compute advantage over matched Transformers. Gains extend to linear RNNs and mixture-of-experts models. Custom Triton kernels keep training cost manageable. The primitive looks scalable, hardware-friendly, and broadly useful. Architecture designers get a new building block with measured returns.
arxiv-2606-04025:
Sheldrake and Scheffler argue that software needs a biomimetic rebuild. Dominant coding models suit one human mind guiding a local machine. That old base leaves modern systems with heavy path dependence. Forcing them to host neural AI creates a deep mismatch. The mismatch is between probabilistic and symbolic ways of working.

Patching it with bigger harnesses around language models adds cost, they argue. Their Software 4.0 answer is an autopoietic heterarchy. It joins human intelligence, neural AI, and a reflective symbolic base. Software becomes a self-regulating network, not inert code. It checks, changes, and evolves its own structure. Recognitive is their language and platform that puts this design into form.
arxiv-2606-04125:
David Pankaczy and Conrard Tetsassi Feugmo benchmark in 2026 eleven physics-informed neural network designs on a notoriously stiff problem: the coupled equations governing ions and electric potential in a lithium cell. Such networks need no mesh, but they often fail where layers turn razor-thin.

The eleven configurations fall into four strategy families, chiefly differing in how competing training losses are weighted. Errors against a trusted finite-volume reference spanned a wide range across designs. One scheme, balanced residual decay rate, matched the accuracy of the much heavier neural tangent kernel approach on concentration fields while taking far less time. Loss-landscape shapes backed the ranking. The team released its implementation openly for reuse on other stiff coupled systems.
arxiv-2606-04225:
Bart Rosenzweig and Jonathan Stanfill answer a question posed by V Maz'ya in 2026. It concerns a heat-like equation built from a logarithmic Laplacian on a circle.

The operator is nonlocal: each point feels the whole circle at once. That makes even basic questions, such as whether smooth solutions exist, hard to settle. The pair exploit links to a classical problem about cavities and to known formulas for the operator's eigenfunctions. They show the solution extends in a clean way and derive exact sums for its parts. One sum involves Bernoulli numbers, a classic sequence. The work gives a rare exact handle on a nonlocal equation.
arxiv-2606-04425:
Yuanbo Xie leads a team naming in 2026 a new attack class against AI agents: cross-session stored prompt injection. Agent systems keep persistent state, memories, files, and tool records that survive between sessions, and hostile instructions planted there can fire long after the attacker has left.

Modeled on stored cross-site scripting, the attack extends prompt injection across time, persisting and activating in later sessions, and across space, spreading from the chat into the agent's stored state. The team formalizes the attack's lifecycle, builds a taxonomy of persistence channels and incorporation mechanisms, and releases a sandbox toolkit for evaluation. Their conclusion reframes agent security: the hard problem is governing how outside information gains authority inside persistent state, not just filtering inputs.
arxiv-2606-04525:
Ledneva, Nuridinov, and Kuznetsov build a common yardstick for genomic foundation models, in a 2026 arXiv paper. They argue that today's comparisons cannot be trusted. Benchmarks are fragmented. Each model reports on its favorite tasks. So claims of superiority are rarely comparable. Their benchmark, GENEB, evaluates frozen representations from 40 genomic models. It covers 100 tasks in 13 functional categories under one probing protocol. It includes settings with only a few labeled examples.

Aggregate leaderboards prove unstable. Rankings swing sharply across task categories. Larger scale brings only modest and inconsistent gains. Alignment of architecture and pretraining with a task often outweighs raw parameter count. It replaces a single league table with a diagnostic profile. The profile shows where each genomic model actually works.
arxiv-2606-04725:
Gondosiswanto and Pulsipher make nonlinear model predictive control fast enough for harder real-time problems by exploiting repetition, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their framework uses a parametric interior-point formulation that reuses structure-dependent computation across re-solves.

Symbolic factorization in the sparse Cholesky solver, for example, is done once and reused. On distillation column and two-dimensional heated plate benchmarks, against state-of-the-art CPU and GPU configurations, the framework cut total NMPC run times by more than a factor of ten. The gains come mainly from reduced per-iteration solve times, with GPU execution reducing them by up to 94 percent against the baseline.
arxiv-2606-05125:
Si-Cong Ji and colleagues test the quantum physics of the inverted harmonic oscillator in this 2026 arXiv paper. When a quantum system passes an unstable fixed point, its dynamics reduce to this oscillator, which stretches one quadrature while squeezing the other. That grows large quantum states out of tiny zero-point fluctuations. The same mathematics describes how inflation stretched quantum ripples in the early universe.

The team realized the dynamics with a Bose-Einstein condensate on an AtomChip, using radio-frequency dressing to flip the confinement into the inverted form. Phase-space imaging let them follow the full Wigner function of the evolving state. They observed sub-vacuum squeezing of 10.6 decibels, give or take 1.3 decibels. Time-reversing the evolution tested whether the process runs coherently in reverse. Matter-wave interference between the two daughter clouds confirmed coherence far beyond the initial expansion.
arxiv-2606-05425:
Ziad Ghanem returns to the Ize Conjecture in this 2026 arXiv paper, replacing a disproved claim with an exact test. The conjecture claimed that every irreducible representation of a compact Lie group admits a maximal isotropy subgroup with an odd-dimensional fixed-point space. Ghanem defines Ize pairs: a group and representation where some maximal isotropy subgroup makes a dimension difference odd.

He proves this dimension-parity test captures the obstruction to a nontrivial change of the degree at maximal orbit types, the point where bifurcation guarantees live or die. Combining the test with a mod-2 equivariant spectral flow yields local and global bifurcation guarantees without Burnside ring arithmetic.
arxiv-2606-05525:
Kuangshi Ai and colleagues present SciVisAgentSkills in this 2026 arXiv paper, reusable skill packages that make coding agents good at scientific visualization. General-purpose agents can write code, but scientific visualization demands tool-specific expertise: long multi-step workflows in tools such as ParaView, napari, VMD, and TTK, each with its own assumptions and idioms. The skills encode that knowledge: environment needs, tool usage patterns, and domain heuristics.

The team evaluated the skills on two agent harnesses using SciVisAgentBench, a benchmark of 108 expert-designed tasks. Adding the skills improved mean task scores across the suites. Structured procedural knowledge, not just a stronger base model, drives reliable work. Token-efficiency benefits were real but depended on the harness and setting used. The authors caution that skills should be studied together with the harness that runs them, not as portable magic. The skills are publicly available.
arxiv-2606-05725:
Shuze Liu, Guo, and Dong catch model theft from API traffic with a strikingly plain tool in a 2026 arXiv paper. Extraction attackers query a hosted model to clone it; each query alone looks harmless. The team watches windows of traffic instead. Queries are embedded as points of meaning, and the window's spread is compared with past benign traffic. A maximum mean discrepancy test flags windows that drift too far.

Thresholds come only from benign-versus-benign checks, so no attack examples are needed. Fourteen attacker-normal pairings tested the detector. Five adapted rival systems served as baselines. The simple test kept false alarms near a third of one percent. It caught every pure-attacker stream and reached about ninety-five percent balanced accuracy overall. Mixed traffic, where attackers hide among normal users, also gave way. The authors call plain distribution testing the baseline to beat.
arxiv-2606-05825:
Alutto, Zino, Johansson, and Fontan model how leaders emerge from opinion exchange in a 2026 arXiv paper. In real groups, people with firm views often gain sway. Lasting sway, though, demands staying near the group's drift. The team extends the Friedkin-Johnsen model of opinion dynamics. Leadership becomes a moving trait: each person's openness to influence evolves by a game-like rule.

Decisive yet socially coherent opinions build leadership in the model. Drifting away from the collective state bleeds it away. The coupled math tracks opinions and leadership feeding each other over time. The authors prove sufficient conditions that sort agents in advance. Under those conditions, some agents must emerge as leaders and others as followers. The results give network designers a first map of who will lead. They also suggest how seeding views might steer that outcome.
arxiv-2606-05925:
Guangyu Wang and a twenty-five-author team argue biomedicine needs models that simulate futures, not just label data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Today's biomedical AI mostly recognizes static patterns in scans, sequences, and records. Clinicians and biologists instead ask what happens next: after a drug, a mutation, a surgery. Biomedical world models would learn hidden states from molecule to patient scale. Intervention-conditioned dynamics would let users rehearse actions in simulation before touching a real system.

The authors sketch roles across the field. World models could serve as data engines, environment simulators, and planning substrates. Virtual cells, organoids, virtual patients, and surgical rehearsal are the flagship applications. None of it works without data infrastructure, honest benchmarks, safety limits, and governance. The paper maps those requirements rather than claiming a finished system. Closed-loop discovery, where simulation proposes experiments that refine the model, is the endgame.
arxiv-2606-06125:
Riccardo Poiani, Martino Bernasconi, and Andrea Celli study online contract design in this 2026 arXiv paper at the boundary of economics and learning theory. In a principal-agent problem, a principal offers payments tied to outcomes to persuade an agent to exert costly effort. Here the principal repeats the interaction over many rounds, without knowing each agent's private cost type or seeing the actions taken. Learning relies only on each round's outcomes.

For agents who either act or do not, the authors prove tight regret bounds, where regret measures the loss against the best fixed contract known in hindsight. Against adversarial type sequences, regret grows with the two-thirds power of the number of rounds, independent of the number of outcomes. When one hidden type stays fixed, an explore-then-commit strategy using stochastic binary search improves the rate to roughly the square root of the rounds.
arxiv-2606-06225:
Anh Truong and co-authors solve the cold start problem for a streaming service's recommendations in this 2026 arXiv paper. Collaborative filtering recommends content from patterns in what similar users watched, but a brand new title has no watch history at all. Tubi's production system also needs an embedding, a numeric fingerprint, for new content the moment it arrives. The team reframes cold start as filling in missing links in a device and content graph.

Their architecture, Shallow RHS, is deliberately asymmetric. The device side reads watch history through graph message passing to absorb collaborative signals. The content side stays shallow and builds its embedding only from the title's intrinsic features, never from interactions it may not have. After training, that content encoder maps any new title into the collaborative space, and retrieval finds warm surrogate neighbors for it. Online experiments showed gains for both new content and new devices.
arxiv-2606-06325:
Julia Blyumen and Eitan Farchi price data products where no money changes hands in this 2026 arXiv paper. Inside a company, teams trade datasets through internal platforms, and ordinary pricing fails twice over. Data is non rival, since one team's use does not consume it, and no market sets a price anyway. Managers still need to know which offerings deserve investment and attention.

Their metric values a data product purely from user choice behavior, modeling attention and preference as staff pick among offerings. They show the metric is a cooperative game whose Shapley value, a fair division rule from game theory, has a closed form. The formula rewards uniqueness and discerning use instead of raw popularity. That steers creators toward distinctive long tail products rather than more copies of what everyone already downloads. Worked examples show the valuation matches economic intuition while staying equitable.
arxiv-2606-06525:
Ziheng Geng and co-authors let language models do a structural engineer's paperwork in this 2026 arXiv paper. Analyzing a 3D frame, the skeleton of beams and columns in a building, normally means hours of manual model building. Their framework takes a plain language description instead. A team of agents handles it: one parses the problem into structured data. Others lay out floors and place nodes, girders, slabs, and columns. The last agents assign supports and loads and emit scripts for SAP2000 analysis software.

The key enabler is representation. An irregular 3D frame is projected onto a 2D plan of gridlines, with a matrix recording how many stories rise from each grid cell, so the geometry stays consistent and machine readable. On ten representative 3D frames, the system averaged ninety percent accuracy across repeated trials. The authors present it as a step toward trustworthy automation of routine engineering modeling.
arxiv-2606-06725:
Outlining the heart muscle in ultrasound scans is slow hand work, yet it is needed to measure how well blood feeds the muscle. Gonzalez and co-authors borrow a trick from large language model design in this 2026 arXiv paper. Neural scaling laws, rules that predict how a model's error falls as it grows, let them pick the right network size before full training.

Working with a public heart scan set and a contrast ultrasound set from twenty five patients, the team found that trends measured on small data slices predicted full scale performance well. Their chosen networks matched or beat the best published results with far fewer parameters, in one case two hundred forty times fewer. The automatic outlines also produced blood flow measures that agreed closely with those of a senior cardiologist, suggesting the sizing method suits small medical data sets.
arxiv-2606-07125:
Red giant stars ring like bells, and their tones reveal how fast their cores spin. De Vries and co-authors simulate those tones directly in this 2026 arXiv paper. The tones are mixed modes, waves that behave partly like sound and partly like buoyancy waves. They matter because they may carry angular momentum outward through the star.

Two dimensional hydrodynamic simulations followed a red giant of about one point three solar masses. Two runs cut the star's surface layer at different depths. Frequencies matched linear theory excellently for pressure dominated modes. Gravity dominated modes disagreed slightly in one frequency band. Surprisingly, the largest kinetic energies sat in slow modes below fifty microhertz, not near the expected peak. The deeper run produced surface velocities comparable to empirical predictions. Those slow, energetic modes are hard to observe yet may dominate momentum transport inside the star.
arxiv-2606-07225:
Ermolina, Danilkin, and Vanderhaeghen jointly analyze two particle collision processes to pin down exotic charm states in this 2026 arXiv paper. The data come from the BESIII experiment, where electrons and positrons annihilate into a J/psi particle plus pion or kaon pairs. A Dalitz plot, a map of how energy is shared among the three outgoing particles, reveals intermediate states. The analysis covers collision energies from about 4.1 to 4.4 giga-electronvolts.

Their model combines two resonant structures with a smooth background and treats pion and kaon scattering with a method that enforces consistency with scattering theory. One shared parameter set described both total production rates and mass distributions measured by BESIII. A purely resonant picture failed, so the background term proved necessary. From the fit they extracted mass and width values for three exotic states, including the charged Zc(3900) candidate.
arxiv-2606-07325:
Kim derives fundamental limits on forecasting how a probability distribution evolves, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting treats each distribution as a point in Wasserstein space, a geometric space where distance measures the work to reshape one distribution into another. Given finitely many noisy past snapshots, how accurately can any method estimate a future distribution? Kim assumes the flow changes smoothly, bounded by an adiabatic condition on its velocity field.

The central result is a minimax lower bound, the best worst-case error any estimator must suffer, blending temporal and spatial difficulty. It interpolates between an irreducible extrapolation cost, present even with a perfect record of the past, and the spatial estimation curse that worsens with dimension. Matching upper bounds are proved for the smoothness case and in a translation submodel. For smoothness the upper bound remains conditional, which Kim flags as an unresolved problem for the field.
arxiv-2606-07525:
Allein and Moens reconstruct the middle steps of causal claims in text, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Writers state a cause and its effect while leaving the intermediate events unstated, assuming readers share the knowledge. That gap matters when causal claims are wrong, correlational, or deployed to mislead, as in climate debates. The authors treat each cause-effect pair as the endpoints of a causal graph. They use language models to infer the missing links, comparing whole-graph generation against building graphs from discovered causal chains.

Chain-based methods either aggregate many inferred chains or expand chains through iterative search. Wisdom-of-the-crowd variants combine models' knowledge, either after generation or during inference. To judge quality without ground-truth graphs, they evaluate inferred relations against a database of over 1,500 validated causal pairs. That database check is proposed as a cheap evaluation transferable to domains where causal graphs are never available.
arxiv-2606-07625:
Huang and co-authors quantify how much city buildings shelter each other from the wind, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Shielding by upstream buildings controls urban drag, the resistance cities exert on airflow, yet it is barely measured in practice. Their large-eddy simulations reproduce the University of Bristol campus, 110 buildings of height, shape, and orientation, under 24 wind directions, so each building faces shielding conditions. Campus drag varied little with direction, while individual building drag swung widely.

About a fifth of the buildings accounted for four fifths of drag, led by a few large structures. To characterize shielding, the authors introduce two dimensionless ratios: the distance to the nearest upstream obstacle scaled by its height, and that obstacle's height relative to the target building. Together they separate near-wake from far-wake, sheltered from exposed. The framework suits any city, pushing shielding-aware definitions of effective frontal area and drag coefficients.
arxiv-2606-07725:
Teutschmann and colleagues pretrain GNSS-FM, a reusable base model for satellite positioning time series, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Stations in global navigation networks record daily ground movement, revealing slow tectonic drift, seasonal shifts, and sudden earthquake steps. Labelled examples for training are scarce, even though unlabelled records are abundant and free.

GNSS-FM learns without labels by predicting masked parts of its own compressed codes, an approach adapted from speech modelling. It was pretrained on records from more than seventeen thousand stations worldwide, feeding in both displacement and day-to-day change. Analysis of its learned codebook shows it separates the main signal types, including seismic offsets, steady drift, and seasonal cycles. Fine-tuned afterwards, it beat strong task-specific baselines at both ninety-day forecasting and locating seismic steps, suggesting this label-free training suits such data well.
arxiv-2606-07925:
Vijayaraghavan and co-authors summarise hardware code with a search procedure borrowed from game-playing AI, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Engineers write chips in hardware description languages such as VHDL and Verilog. Good summaries of what a module does are scarce, slowing maintenance and reuse. Language models can draft summaries, but a single greedy pass often misses the code's actual function.

Their system, RoSum-Mcts, explores summary candidates with Monte Carlo tree search, the lookahead strategy behind strong game agents. A composite reward guides the search, combining functional correctness, how well the summary covers the local content, and fluency. A verification loop checks candidates against the code. On the VHDL-eval and Verilog-eval benchmarks it beat baseline summarisation on standard quality metrics. It also proved robust to variable renaming, a cosmetic change that degraded baseline summaries sharply. Treating summarisation as search, not one-shot generation, is the main lesson.
arxiv-2606-08125:
Derya Acar, Metin Azmaz, Vural Cam, and Ömer Küçüksakallı rule out a family of polynomials from a rare club, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A polynomial is arithmetically exceptional if it permutes a finite field's elements for infinitely many primes. In one variable the exceptional polynomials are fully classified: built from linear maps and Dickson polynomials. The question here concerns generalised Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind, a multivariable family attached to the root system A2.

The verdict is negative: these polynomials are not arithmetically exceptional. The wider question is which such maps can shuffle a finite field perfectly. The proof studies the norms of certain cyclotomic elements, special numbers tied to roots of unity. Tracking those norms shows the permutation behaviour cannot persist across infinitely many primes. Negative results matter as much as positive ones: each family excluded sharpens the boundary of what such behaviour is possible.
arxiv-2606-08225:
Salman and colleagues propose an adaptive filter that handles two difficulties at once in this 2026 arXiv paper. An adaptive filter adjusts its own coefficients to track a signal, and many real systems are sparse, meaning most coefficients are zero. Separate methods exist for sparse systems and for impulsive noise, sudden large spikes that corrupt measurements, but combining both strengths in one algorithm was an open gap. Their design, called DP-SAF, updates cheaply, with cost proportional to filter length.

Two gain matrices do the work. One scales each step in proportion to coefficient size, so large coefficients learn faster. The other pulls small coefficients toward zero, most strongly for inactive taps, sharpening the sparsity. A sign-error update, which uses only the direction of the error, adds resistance to impulsive spikes. Simulations under random impulsive noise showed steadier final accuracy than rival algorithms, at matching or better speed.
arxiv-2606-08825:
Cheng, Jin, and Zhang ask when a molecule's 3D shape improves property predictions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Drug hunters predict properties like solubility from molecular structure. The cheap input is a 2D fingerprint, a summary of which chemical fragments a molecule contains. The expensive input is a conformer ensemble, the set of 3D shapes the molecule folds into, summarized by statistics from their Distribution Kernel Operators. They ran roughly 1,000 experiments across 13 model setups and 16 prediction targets.

The answer is selective. Conformer statistics cut prediction error on solvation properties, which depend on how molecules meet water: error fell 11 percent on the ESOL benchmark and 13.5 percent on FreeSolv. They gave no benefit for electronic or steric tasks. The gains grew for large, flexible molecules and with more training data, pointing to a physical cause. Still, end-to-end 3D neural networks beat fingerprints by 21 to 42 percent, far beyond what ensemble features add.
arxiv-2606-09125:
Chen and colleagues show that AI models which see images can leak private information in ways text-only models cannot, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multimodal models process text and pictures together. A photo may contain a name or medical detail, and the model can repeat it, or retain it in memory. The team built MM-Privacy, a dataset assessing such risks across tasks, split into disclosure risks, leaking image content, and retention risks, leaking stored content.

Evaluating several models, they found leakage: models exposed sensitive data embedded in images and held in memory. A striking factor was task inconsistency: a model could guard information in one framing and spill it in another, so single-task tests overstate protection. Mitigation is harder here, because safeguards must track information across modalities and turns. The authors release the dataset and code to spur defenses.
arxiv-2606-09225:
Buil and colleagues bring software containers, cloud packaging, to microcontrollers that could never run Docker, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multi-tenant chips run several apps with varying permission levels, useful for IoT devices. Current tools for such hardware lack runtime configuration: scheduling policies and each one's access to host resources are fixed at build time, limiting use in dynamic deployments.

TinyContainer is middleware with per-container scheduling and fine-grained access control through metadata describing each container's rights. A runtime layer supports multiple runtimes. The team tested CS4WAMR, a small WebAssembly runtime, on RIOT OS, across IoT boards with various Cortex-M chips. Regulating access and host services cost an overhead of up to 4 ms per call. A TinyML demo showed the value: containers hold data and model weights, delegating inference to native host services, so untrusted code never touches the model, and permissions change while the device runs.
arxiv-2606-09325:
Thomsen and colleagues show that the bewildering variety of spectra from stars torn apart by black holes reduces to one knob: how ionized the debris gas is, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Tidal disruption events flash as a star's remains accrete, and their optical spectra fall into four classes: hydrogen-dominated, helium-dominated, mixed, and featureless. The mixed class shows Bowen fluorescence lines, rare in other sources and long unexplained. The team built the first unified radiative transfer model covering all four classes, simulating optically thick, outflowing envelopes.

The controlling parameter is the ratio of injected luminosity to envelope mass, which sets the ionization state. As ionization decreases, the classes emerge in sequence: featureless, helium, Bowen, hydrogen. Electron scattering in the thick outflow explains the extreme line widths directly. The model also reproduces links with luminosity and black hole mass, and why each event's class stays stable.
arxiv-2606-09425:
Veena and her many co-authors hunt for methanol masers where gas streaming along the Milky Way's bar crashes into its centre in this 2026 arXiv paper. Masers are natural amplifiers that beam out intense microwave emission from excited molecules. The target region is where inflowing gas meets the Central Molecular Zone.

Using the Yebes forty-metre telescope, the team searched for class I methanol maser lines near thirty-six and forty-four gigahertz, alongside thermal emission and archival survey data. They found widespread emission at the lower frequency across several parsecs. The brightest source ranks among the most luminous galactic class I masers known, with an isotropic luminosity just under a thousandth of the Sun's output. Because the masers trace an extended high-velocity gas feature, the authors link them mainly to shock-processed gas at the bar interface, not only to local star formation.
arxiv-2606-09525:
Nadya Yuki Wangsajaya, Haeun Yu, and Isabelle Augenstein trace how language models learn their habits of using provided context during instruction fine-tuning in this 2026 arXiv paper. A model's decision to trust a supplied passage depends on traits like its length, fluency, and similarity to the question.

The authors tracked sensitivity across the successive stages of instruction tuning: supervised fine-tuning, direct preference optimisation, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Experiments covered four models and three datasets. Supervised fine-tuning consistently made models favour contexts that are easy to understand, meaning long, fluent passages closely matching the query. Later stages could either reinforce or undo those preferences, depending on the training dataset's own balance of characteristics. Context use is reshaped at every stage, so dataset design decides how robustly a system uses the evidence it is given.
arxiv-2606-09725:
Jhonny Velasquez Olivera, Christo Thomas, and Walid Saad untangle the factors inside data with a symbolic twist in this 2026 arXiv paper. Disentanglement means splitting a sample's traits, like shape, hue, and pose, into clean parts. Past tools leaned on smooth number codes and tuned losses. This team treats the code as a bundle of symbols instead.

Their tool uses holographic reduced representations, vectors that can be bound and summed like tied notes. Each latent unit is itself a vector, and units add up to form the whole code. An unbinding step peels one symbol-value pair from the bundle. Tests with latent walks and standard scores matched rival methods. A theory side shows unbinding yields near-free pairs, and caps how many clear concepts each slot can hold. The codes also shook off noise well, losing sense in a slow, graceful way.
arxiv-2606-10125:
Pourhabib tackles the cost of labeling cases for text-to-SQL systems, which turn natural language questions into database queries, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning. Few-shot prompting with a bank of annotated cases is the dominant approach, but expert annotation is expensive and the bank's quality governs quality of answers. He casts choosing which cases to label as a bounded design problem over the small manifold of query meanings.

His stratified greedy algorithm maximizes a heteroscedastic mutual information objective, which accounts for the uneven reliability. He proves the goal stays submodular and roughly monotonic, giving a constant-factor approximation guarantee. A spectral bound shows the guarantee degrades gently, not badly, when the assumed kernel diverges from the true data-generating process. In tests, the strategy sharply reduces tagging effort while keeping high retrieval accuracy for the downstream system.
arxiv-2606-10425:
Kim and Kim study when a partial differential equation still has exactly one solution in this 2026 arXiv paper in analysis. The equations are second-order evolution equations, describing how a quantity changes over time, and their coefficients can degenerate, vanish, or blow up. Standard theory demands the coefficients stay locally integrable, their accumulated size near any moment finite. This paper drops that demand, allowing blow-up even at the starting and ending times.

The key that makes this possible is a zero initial condition: the system starts from nothing, so singular behaviour at the start has nothing to destroy. Working in weighted Lp spaces, the authors prove existence and uniqueness of weak solutions for exponents from one upward. Open problems remain, including uniqueness for bounded solutions.
arxiv-2606-10725:
Shakhmatova and colleagues mine discharge reports to predict atrial fibrillation in this 2026 arXiv paper on medical informatics. Atrial fibrillation is the commonest heart rhythm disorder, but risk scores lean on factors, age and hypertension, that nearly every cardiology patient has. The team studied 17,562 cardiology patients without prior fibrillation; 1,438, or 8.19 percent, developed it during follow-up. A language-processing pipeline turned discharge reports into 73 features, feeding models predicting risk over twenty-four months and the whole follow-up.

The full model reached a ROC area of 0.735 for the twenty-four-month target; a 13-feature simple model, Pre-AF 13, scored 0.725, against 0.53 to 0.64 for four scores. A linear 9-feature bedside score separated patients whose two-year incidence ran from about 7 to about 36 percent. Age and left atrial volume carried the most weight. Routine hospital text, mined well, stratifies risk better than the scores clinicians use.
arxiv-2606-10825:
El Asri and colleagues improve diffusion policies for robot control in this 2026 arXiv paper. A diffusion policy, which plans actions by gradual denoising, is usually trained by copying demos and cannot beat them. Direct reinforcement learning on such policies is awkward, since each action comes from a multi-step process. MODIP instead plans inside a learned world model with model predictive control, then trains the policy on the planned paths as fresh targets.

Two choices keep it fast: a terminal state value replaces policy-dependent action values, and critics train on policy-independent targets. On D4RL and RoboMimic tasks, MODIP lifts diffusion policies beyond plain copying and matches or beats both RL fine-tuning methods and strong model-based baselines such as TD-MPC2. The authors note that all tests use state vectors, not images.
arxiv-2606-11025:
Ping and co-authors introduce a 2026 arXiv method for fine-tuning flow matching models, the generators behind many image and video tools. Online reinforcement learning, where a model improves from scored trial outputs, can raise quality, but PPO-style ratio clipping limits updates using a noisy single-sample estimate of how far the policy moved.

Flow-DPPO swaps clipping for a divergence proximal constraint built on the KL divergence, an exact distance between old and new policies that is cheap here because each step is Gaussian. An asymmetric mask blocks only updates that both leave the trusted region and break the divergence limit. Across several base models, Flow-DPPO earned higher rewards, forgot less, and stayed stable over many passes where clipping degraded. Paired with CPS sampling, it reached 92.6 percent on a GenEval2 image test, ahead of the 84.5 percent scored by Flow-GRPO in the same setting.
arxiv-2606-11525:
Shen, Chuck, Feng, and Huang diagnose why contrastive learning struggles with robot manipulation in a 2026 arXiv paper. Contrastive Reinforcement Learning has succeeded at goal-conditioned tasks like locomotion, but it falters on interaction-rich manipulation. The authors argue the difficulty is object-centric interaction: contacts and grasps switch the underlying dynamic modes. They model manipulation as a piecewise-smooth Markov process, showing mode changes create reachability structures standard energy functions represent poorly.

Their fix, Interaction-weighted Resampling, resamples around phases before, during, and after interactions, so representations capture the complexity near contacts. Across two-dimensional control, manipulation, and robot air hockey, it improves sample efficiency and performance over prior methods, by about 19.8 percent on average in simulation. A sim-to-real pipeline yields the first real-world goal-conditioned robot air hockey agent that scores goals, raising success from twenty-five to sixty percent.
arxiv-2606-11725:
Mayur Abhisheki and Prasanta Kumar Das test a model of the infant universe in this 2026 arXiv paper on cosmology. Inflation is the brief burst of rapid expansion thought to have smoothed the early cosmos. Their model uses an inverse-tangent potential, a curve describing the energy driving inflation. After inflation ends, reheating converts that energy into hot matter, and its details are usually guessed.

Using Bayesian inference, weighing evidence for parameter values, they confront the model with Planck and ACT satellite data. Where reheating's character stays fixed, preferred settings imply reheating temperatures spanning a huge range and durations of a few to a few dozen e-folds, units of expansion. A dynamical version, where the decay rate evolves, tightens things sharply. Demanding inflation and reheating agree restricts the spectral index, how clumpiness varies with scale, to a narrow band.
arxiv-2606-11825:
Fabio Cavalletti and Andrea Mondino prove a new singularity theorem in this 2026 arXiv paper on mathematical relativity. The classic Hawking-Penrose theorems show that spacetime must contain incomplete paths, interpreted as singularities, under broad conditions. Their engine is a focusing hypothesis: gravity pulls bundles of paths together strongly enough, usually expressed through a starting surface's mean curvature.

The authors replace that local hypothesis with a condition on asymptotic volume growth, how the volume of space expands far from a compact starting surface. Under the strong energy condition, a uniform positive lower bound on their new expansion invariants forces past timelike incompleteness. They also give an explicit upper bound on how far the past can extend. The theorem is proved not only for smooth spacetimes but also for non-smooth Lorentzian length spaces, with no differentiability assumed. Companion results include an area comparison theorem and a volume-based singularity theorem.
arxiv-2606-11925:
Zsolt Robotka and four colleagues manufacture training data for sign language translation in this 2026 arXiv paper. Translation systems need parallel sign video and text pairs for fine-tuning, but such data is scarce, especially for rare vocabulary. Starting from a gloss-annotated corpus, where glosses label individual signs, they cut training videos into per-gloss clips using forced alignment.

A large language model, anchored to the corpus, invents new gloss sequences and matching sentences; synthetic videos are assembled by sampling clips for those sequences. Counterintuitively, polishing clip transitions for smoothness hurts, while abrupt boundaries seem to help training implicitly. In a strict controlled comparison, five recent methods gained at most about one BLEU point over baseline. Augmentation gains nearly three BLEU points, with no change to model architecture or training protocol. The authors also warn the synthetic data harms vision-language pretraining despite improving its own objectives.
arxiv-2606-12325:
Dúcz settles how few colors a certain geometric pattern needs by coloring all of it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The fractional chromatic number of the plane asks how few colors paint the plane so equal-distance points differ, allowing colors to be shared fractionally. Earlier work pushed the lower bound to four using a twenty-seven-point unit-distance graph inside the Moser lattice, a four-dimensional grid of points. That graph's geometric fractional chromatic number is exactly four. Whether four colors suffice for the whole lattice stayed open.

Dúcz exhibits geometric four-colorings of the entire Moser lattice, proving the bound tight for lattice graphs. Geometric means the coloring respects distances: isometric point sets receive matching color patterns. The same colorings extend to the Moser ring, a larger structure. The result explains why computerized searches inside this lattice stalled at four: nothing better was there to find.
arxiv-2606-12525:
Davenport and co-authors derive how bound states of particles drift through crystals, and find the rule needs replacing, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Excitons and trions are composite excitations: an electron bound to a hole, or to two partners. Single electrons feel Berry curvature, a geometric field that bends their motion sideways. The team asks what geometry governs composites.
