The region combines visual features with higher-level information such as speech sounds, actions, and meanings. Its apparent specialization for spelling therefore emerges from those interactions. It does not come from built-in tuning to letters. The authors show how the account explains normal reading, developmental dyslexia, and the effects of damage to the region.
europmc-pmc3257625:
Claudia Luevano-Contreras and Karen Chapman-Novakofski reviewed dietary advanced glycation end products and aging in this 2010 article in Nutrients. These compounds, called AGEs, form when sugars react with proteins without enzymes, both in cooked food and inside the body. Levels rise with age and are higher in several chronic diseases of aging.

The authors summarize two decades of work measuring AGEs in foods and in people, and the mechanisms by which some tissues get damaged while others are spared. Animal and human studies link AGEs to heart and blood vessel disease, Alzheimer's disease, and diabetes complications. Diets low in AGEs improved wound healing, insulin resistance, and heart outcomes in several studies. Such diets also extended lifespan in animals. The paper closes with suggestions for future research.
europmc-pmc3257725:
Maddalena Rossi, Alberto Amaretti, and Stefano Raimondi reviewed folate production by probiotic bacteria in this 2011 article in Nutrients. Folate is a vitamin many people lack, and certain gut bacteria can make it. The authors assessed which probiotic groups genuinely produce the vitamin, aiming at folate-enriched fermented foods and supplements that manufacture folate inside the colon.

The verdict differs by genus. Most lactobacilli cannot synthesize folate at all and actually drain it from fermented dairy products, though one species is an exception when a building block is supplied. Several bifidobacteria strains do produce and release folate, in widely varying amounts. Rats fed folate-producing bifidobacteria showed higher blood folate, and a human trial found more folate in feces, proof of production in the body.
europmc-pmc3338325:
Blacquière, Smagghe, van Gestel, and Mommaerts reviewed fifteen years of research on a popular insecticide class and bees, in a 2012 article. Neonicotinoid sprays and seed coatings control crop pests effectively, but they can also reach pollinators. The review gathers evidence on three fronts, contamination levels found in the field, harms seen in bees, and whether official risk assessment handles these chemicals properly.

Residues in plants, bees, and hive products generally sat below levels that kill or chronically harm bees outright, though data were thin and gathered for few crops. Lab studies found real effects on foraging, learning, and memory at sublethal doses, while field studies at realistic doses found none. The authors judge the existing risk scheme for systemic chemicals usable for these insecticides, and call for field realistic tests with molecular markers to sharpen future assessments.
europmc-pmc3377625:
Orenstein and colleagues examined arteries from children lost to Kawasaki disease in 2012 to explain its complex damage to blood vessels. Among children in rich countries, it is the leading source of heart disease that begins after birth. Earlier accounts described one bout of artery inflammation followed by healing, which fit the illness poorly.

Studying dozens of autopsy and transplant specimens, the team separated three linked processes. A brief, self-limited attack destroys the artery wall early and can form bulges that clot or burst. A longer inflammation follows, converting wall cells into scar-like builders that slowly narrow the channel. Untangling the three steps reshapes how doctors think about treatment timing.
europmc-pmc3460225:
Morris proposed in 2011 a smarter way to pool genome-wide association studies across ethnic groups. Such pooling finds the spots behind complex traits and zooms toward the causal variant, but most data came from European-descended groups. Mixing populations helps, because their local DNA correlation patterns differ, yet their genetic effects may also differ in ways standard pooling handles badly.

The new method expects similar effects in closely related populations while allowing distant groups to diverge. Across many simulated scenarios it beat both fixed-effect pooling, in raw power and in pinpointing the causal spot, and random-effects pooling when relatedness was modeled well. The payoff is sharper maps of trait genetics drawn from the whole species, not one branch of it.
europmc-pmc3464725:
Fan and co-authors reviewed the role of cardiac fibroblasts in heart disease for Fibrogenesis and Tissue Repair in 2012. Fibroblasts are the most common cells in heart muscle, and their main job is building the support matrix around other cells. When they grow too active, that matrix builds up as stiff scar tissue called fibrosis, which harms heart function.

The review covers where these cells come from and how their numbers rise in disease. Fan's group explains how fibroblasts both make and break down the matrix, guided by enzymes and their blockers. Lessons from mouse models with altered matrix proteins fill much of the paper. The authors show why these once ignored cells now sit at the center of heart research.
europmc-pmc3491025:
Most protists are single cells that sit outside the animal, plant, and fungal kingdoms, and their true diversity is still largely unknown. In 2012 Jan Pawlowski leads the CBOL Protist Working Group, which sets out a DNA barcoding plan for them. A barcode names a species from one short, standard stretch of DNA.

No single barcode fits groups this varied, so the plan works in two steps. A shared first barcode, the same across all eukaryotes, sorts a sample. Barcodes tuned to each group then fix the finer name. Protists serve as disease agents, water-quality signs, and records of past habitats, yet few have formal names. A shared two-step system could open that hidden wealth to orderly listing.
europmc-pmc3552825:
Gut microbes may help set the body's estrogen levels, and Roberto Flores leads a nine-author cross-sectional study testing that idea in 2012. Outside obesity, little was known about what drives non-ovarian estrogen levels, which matter for breast cancer and bone loss. The suspected route is recycling through the gut and liver.

Fifty-one NIH epidemiologist volunteers, 25 men and 26 women, gave urine and stool samples. The team measured estradiol, estrone, and 13 metabolites, plus fecal enzyme activity and microbial diversity from gene sequencing. Results support, for the first time in human volunteers, the long-standing theory that the intestinal microbial community shapes systemic estrogen levels.
europmc-pmc3556525:
Simon Harris and colleagues reported a descriptive study in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2013 on a suspected MRSA outbreak in a Cambridge hospital. The setting was a special care baby unit, where routine tests and antibiotic profiles had left a possible outbreak unconfirmed. Their question was whether reading the full genome of each strain could show how the bacteria spread.

Sequencing widened the picture sharply. Infection control staff had flagged twelve infants over six months in 2011, but genome data linked twenty-six related cases in all. Spread had occurred in the baby unit, among mothers on a postnatal ward, and out in the community. The outbreak strain proved to be a new type, close to a known hospital lineage. The paper shows sequencing resolving transmission that older methods missed.
europmc-pmc3556625:
Mark Little and a large international group published a systematic review and meta-analysis in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2012 on low-level radiation and circulatory disease. High radiation doses were already linked to heart and vessel disease, yet the risk at work-level doses stayed disputed. The authors set out to gather the published evidence and estimate what it could mean for whole populations.

Their search covered peer-reviewed studies since 1990 on whole-body exposure below set dose limits. Pooling the results supported a link between low and moderate doses and deaths from circulatory disease. Estimated extra population risk ranged from 2.5 percent per sievert in France to 8.5 percent in Russia. The authors note wide differences between studies, mainly for non-heart outcomes, as a limit on firm conclusions.
europmc-pmc3607725:
Joshua Cobb and colleagues argued for a phenotyping upgrade in crop science in Theoretical and Applied Genetics in 2013. Breeding progress rests on linking genes to traits, and genotyping has raced ahead while trait measurement, phenotyping, stayed slow and rough. Their paper sets out what next-generation phenotyping must do: measure more accurately, at every level from cell to field, with automation and remote sensing cutting cost and labor, across seasons and environments.

The data flood that follows needs its own plumbing. It needs shared vocabularies so data sets merge, storage and access systems, sounder experiment design, and statistics that pull real signal from weather and plot noise. The authors call for standing teams of biologists, computer scientists, statisticians, and engineers, much as genotyping was industrialized decades earlier. Rice work from one author's program grounds the general case.
europmc-pmc3630325:
Stan Floresco, writing alone in Frontiers in Neuroscience in 2013, revisited how dopamine in the prefrontal cortex shapes flexible behavior. The standard story came from working memory research: dopamine acting at D1 receptors follows an inverted-U, where too little or too much impairs performance. Studies of behavioral flexibility, the ability to change strategy, told a messier story across receptor types and tasks.

Set-shifting, for instance, needs D1 and D2 receptors cooperating, and extra stimulation of them did not wreck it the way the curve predicts. Decisions weighing cost against uncertain reward were pushed in different, sometimes opposite, directions by the two receptors. Floresco argues the single curve should give way to a family of functions, one per cognitive operation, with reduced or excessive dopamine helping or harming depending on the job at hand.
europmc-pmc3665925:
A free program that sorts people by ancestry gets a user's guide from Porras-Hurtado, Ruiz, Santos, Phillips, Carracedo and Lareu in a 2013 Frontiers in Genetics overview. The program, called STRUCTURE in the text, groups samples by shared patterns of gene variation using a stepwise probability method. It can also place a person of unknown origin into the best-fit group. The overview covers its two main ancestry and frequency models and its chief uses in human genetics.

Worked cases show how changing the main settings shifts results on one uniform human data set. Uses span disease gene hunts, population genetics and forensic work. Helper programs are covered too: CLUMPP and distruct, and STRAT for disease studies. A step-by-step guide runs with the article. The aim is plain: informed setting choices, not defaults taken on faith.
europmc-pmc3667625:
A small molecule lifts a brake on memory in mice, Sidrauski and a large team report in a 2013 eLife study. When cells are stressed, a switch in the protein-making machinery slows most protein building while letting a few stress messages through. That brake, part of the integrated stress response, also limits how memories settle. The team screened for compounds that block one stress sensor, and found a molecule they named ISRIB that undoes the brake's effects at very low dose.

In living mice the molecule sharpened both place memory and fear-linked learning. Memory settling, the authors say, is held back by this stress brake by design, and releasing it boosts learning. The finding points to a new route for probing memory faults and, in time, perhaps for treating them.
europmc-pmc3678125:
Whole-brain behaviour can be simulated on a computer built for the job, Sanz Leon and six colleagues present in a 2013 Frontiers in Neuroinformatics article. Their platform, The Virtual Brain, models large-scale brain network dynamics for primates. It joins a data framework, for making, storing and sharing model inputs, with a simulation core written in Python. Personal settings can be built from one person's own brain data, a feature aimed at disease work.

With a personal model, users can test what happens when parts of the system sicken, and try ways to counter the change. The platform talks to common toolboxes and can run through a web browser with rich graphics, or as a standalone library for scripting. The article lays out the theory under the platform, its main parts and likely uses.
europmc-pmc3679525:
A plant hormone switches genes on in waves, Chang and a large team show in a 2013 eLife study of Arabidopsis, a small test plant. The hormone is ethylene, a gas that steers many growth and ripening processes. How one signal coordinates so many growth paths was unclear. The team mapped where the master switch of the pathway, a protein called EIN3 in the text, binds DNA, and read gene activity over a timed course of gas treatment.

Gene switching came in timed layers under the master switch's control. Its binding tuned whole cascades of further switches, including a feedback loop that reins in the ethylene pathway itself. Links ran out to nearly all other hormone growth pathways, tying them into one web. The major plant growth networks, the authors say, are cross-regulated through this single timed response.
europmc-pmc3681325:
One gene fault gives a family a disease with feet in two camps, Kiely and a large team report in a 2013 Acta Neuropathologica study. The British family carries a fault called G51D in the SNCA gene, whose protein, alpha-synuclein, clumps in Parkinson disease. The proband's father and sister both developed drug-responsive parkinsonism in their late thirties, in a dominant inheritance pattern. Brain tissue from the proband was examined after death in full detail.

Nerve loss ran widest in frontal and temporal cortex, deep brain nuclei and brainstem spots. Clumps of the fault protein filled nerve cells across the brain. A second clump kind sat in support cells, matching the hallmark of a kin disease, multiple system atrophy. The case may teach how one protein's biology sets the shape a disease takes.
europmc-pmc3767825:
Sharmila Vaz and co-authors made a methodological case in PLoS ONE in 2013 for a different way to judge test-retest reliability. Clinicians rely on standardized tools, and to read change in a patient they must know how much of a score shift is real. Common reliability numbers, such as correlation coefficients, are unitless ratios that can hide large measurement error.

The authors argue for the repeatability coefficient, also called the smallest real difference. It is computed in the same units as the tool itself and marks the boundary of the smallest true change the tool can detect. Using examples from an earlier study of a social skills scale in schoolchildren, they show cases where a fair correlation still leaves error too wide for safe decisions. Knowing the error in real units, they say, sharpens clinical judgment.
europmc-pmc3847225:
Miriam Reiner, Christina Niermann, Darko Jekauc, and Alexander Woll review long-term gains from physical activity in BMC Public Health in 2013. Diseases such as heart disease and type 2 diabetes cost health systems more each year. One-time surveys link activity to better health, but proof over many years is what counts.

The team kept only studies that tracked healthy adults for at least five years. Activity showed a good long-term link with every outcome they checked: weight gain, obesity, heart disease, diabetes, and memory loss diseases. Yet long studies proved scarce for such a key question. The review calls for more long tracking work, since short studies cannot show whether active habits guard health across a lifetime.
europmc-pmc3867325:
Balázs Győrffy, Pawel Surowiak, Jan Budczies, and András Lánczky present an online survival tool in PLoS One in 2013. Non-small cell lung cancer still kills most patients fast, and gene markers tied to outlook could guide care. Their tool lets any user test a gene's link to survival in pooled past data.

The system merges gene activity and survival data from ten public study sets, over a thousand samples in all. Users pick a gene and get survival curves, risk ratios, and significance scores at once, split by cancer subtype if wished. As a check, the team retested known markers and found the strongest ones ranked as before. Fresh candidate genes also surfaced. The free tool turns months of data work into minutes.
europmc-pmc3872725:
Brain signal software is presented in Frontiers in Neuroscience in 2013 by Alexandre Gramfort and a team of co-authors. MEG and EEG read the faint magnetic and electric signals of brain activity. Turning those signals into maps of where the brain fired takes skill in physics, statistics, and code.

Their package, MNE-Python, wraps that skill in free, open code. It covers the full path from raw data cleaning to source maps, statistics, and links between brain areas. All tools share one clean style and full guides, so users can script their own pipelines. The code plugs into the main Python science libraries and allows reuse even in paid products. The paper invites labs to build on a shared base rather than each coding alone.
europmc-pmc3878225:
Carl-Henrik Heldin wrote a solo review on PDGF signals in tumors in Cell Communication and Signaling in 2013. PDGF is a growth factor that drives growth, survival, and movement in support-type cells. It guides embryo growth and adult tissue repair, yet too much of its signaling can feed tumors.

Overactive PDGF receivers, by excess amount or by mutation, can drive tumor cell growth directly. The factor also acts on vessel support cells and scar-type cells around tumors, which help the tumor thrive. Blocking the signal has already helped patients with a few rare tumors. Trials now test whether the same block helps common cancers. The review sums the biology and the clinic record to date.
europmc-pmc3879625:
Alexander S. Hebert and a team of co-authors report a speed feat in Molecular & Cellular Proteomics, with the record dated 2014. Their title says it in full: the one hour yeast proteome. Reading all of a cell's proteins used to take days of machine time.

Better sample prep, faster liquid sorting, and a new hybrid mass spectrometer did the trick. The machine scans at great speed and catches many peptide pieces per second. In a run of just over an hour it matched tens of thousands of peptides and named near four thousand yeast proteins, at a strict error bar. The team argue that faster scans could soon bring full human protein reads down to a few hours, a shift for drug and disease work.
europmc-pmc3899025:
An infection survey report in The Lancet in 2013 comes from Pam Sonnenberg and a team of co-authors. Control programs for sexually transmitted infections need sound counts of how common each infection is and who takes up testing and care. The report draws on Britain's third national sex survey, done after new national strategies.

Adults gave interviews, and a subset of younger adults gave urine samples tested for four infections: chlamydia, a wart virus, gonorrhea, and HIV. Rates are broken down by age and sex and set against behavior and background factors. Uptake of testing, vaccination, and care is charted the same way. Changes since the first survey in the early 1990s show where strategies bit and where gaps persist.
europmc-pmc3905725:
Patricio Grassini, Kent M. Eskridge, and Kenneth G. Cassman sort crop yield trends in Nature Communications in 2013. Future food supply hinges on how fast cereal yields can keep rising. Many forecasts assume yields grow by a steady percentage each year, like interest. Past trends may not back that shape.

Their framework fits past yield paths with straight-line gains, which mean the percentage rate of gain shrinks over time. Clear plateaus, flat spells or sharp slowdowns, show in major cases such as rice in eastern Asia and wheat in northwest Europe. Those plateau cases cover a large slice of world output of the three main cereals. The authors urge forecasters to test trend shapes with sound statistics before projecting food futures.
europmc-pmc3965125:
James Dunbar and colleagues introduce SAbDab in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. SAbDab is the structural antibody database. Antibodies are the immune system's targeting proteins. They are also a growing class of medicines. Every published antibody structure is gold for design work. Yet those structures sat in general archives. No antibody-specific notes came with them.

SAbDab gathers all public antibody structures in one place. It annotates them in one shared scheme. Each entry lists the experiment details. It names the genes behind the antibody. It pairs the heavy and light chains correctly. It gives the target antigen and binding strength, where known. Users can filter by these fields. They can also filter by shape traits, such as loop form. Whole sets, or the full database, can be downloaded.
europmc-pmc3993125:
Daniela C. Ifrim and ten co-authors study how human monocytes can be set for stronger or weaker later responses, in Clinical and Vaccine Immunology in 2014. Monocytes are blood cells of the innate immune system. A first dose of a fungus, or of a fungal wall part called beta-glucan, makes them respond more strongly later, an effect called trained immunity.

A first dose of a bacterial product called lipopolysaccharide does the reverse, leaving the cells muted, a state called tolerance. The team tested many signals from bacteria and viruses at varied doses. Which program followed depended on the signal type and its dose. Training needed two named signal paths inside the cell, and lasting effects rested on chemical marks on the DNA packaging. The work shows innate cells can gain a kind of memory, tuned by what they first meet.
europmc-pmc3998225:
Jerome Sarris, Adrienne O'Neil, Carolyn E. Coulson, Isaac Schweitzer, and Michael Berk make the case for lifestyle medicine in depression, in BMC Psychiatry in 2014. Rates of depression seem to have risen over three decades. Drugs and talk therapy remain the first-line care, yet daily habits tied to the illness get little weight in treatment.

Strong evidence now links several changeable habits to depression. The authors survey exercise, diet, sleep and rest, social contact, and mindfulness practice, plus cuts in smoking, drinking, and drug use. They also flag newer areas with thinner evidence, such as city living, pollution, and heavy technology use. Lifestyle medicine joins health promotion with clinical care, aiming to lift body and mind together. Hard proof for combined, multi-habit programs over the long term is still thin, so they call for trials that test several changes at once rather than one at a time.
europmc-pmc4001325:
Iris Jonkers, Hojoong Kwak, John T. Lis, and Kevin Struhl track how the cell's message-making machine moves along genes, in eLife in 2014. The machine, RNA polymerase II, copies DNA into RNA. Its speed shapes how much message a gene yields. In many genes the machine pauses soon after it starts, and release from that pause is a key control point.

In mouse stem cells, the team blocked the machine at start or at pause release with two drugs, then watched it move. Both blocks stopped nearly all genes, so pause escape is a near-universal step. Paused machines proved fairly stable, lasting a good while at thousands of genes. Once moving, the machine sped up sharply as it crossed a gene, yet slowed at exons, the parts kept in the final message. Gene makeup and marks on the DNA packaging helped set speed.
europmc-pmc4009425:
Brian B. Avants, Nicholas J. Tustison, Michael Stauffer, Gang Song, Baohua Wu, and James C. Gee present a rebuilt image alignment framework, in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics in 2014. Alignment, called registration, warps one medical image to match another so they can be compared. Their toolkit, ITK, is a public set of tools for image work.

Version four unifies two kinds of warp: simple shifts and rich, free-form bends. The same quality measures and search tools now serve both, and warps can be chained in any order. The tools use multi-core chips when present and set scaling across unlike settings, such as turn versus slide, on their own. That cuts the hand tuning that older versions demanded for each new image pair. The authors frame the release as a shared base for fair tests and repeatable research in image registration.
europmc-pmc4148225:
Steven W. Cole, writing alone, reviewed human social genomics, the study of how daily life circumstances change gene activity. His review appeared in PLoS Genetics in 2014. Conditions such as city living, low status, isolation, and social threat have been tied to altered activity of hundreds of genes in white blood cells and diseased tissue.

Across kinds of adversity, a shared pattern appears: inflammation genes turn up while antiviral and antibody genes turn down. Brain pathways that translate social threat into this pattern have been mapped in part. Work is also starting on the gene patterns of thriving, not just hardship. Cole highlights two frontiers: network analyses of socially sensitive genomes, and near-real-time feedback of gene readouts to help individuals tune their own well-being.
europmc-pmc4170925:
Nida Iqbal and Naveed Iqbal reviewed the HER2 protein and its role in cancer in Molecular Biology International in 2014. HER2 sits on the cell surface and, when paired with a partner, switches on signals that push cells to grow. Too much HER2 appears in about 15 to 30 percent of breast cancers and 10 to 30 percent of stomach cancers.

High HER2 levels mark cancers that grow fast, but they also give doctors a target. Drugs aimed at HER2 have sharply improved outcomes in breast and stomach cancers that test positive for it. The same drugs have disappointed in other cancers with high HER2, such as ovary and lung. The review covers where HER2 shows up, how it is tested, and which targeted treatments exist.
europmc-pmc4188125:
Guillermo Arango Duque and Albert Descoteaux reviewed macrophage signal proteins in Frontiers in Immunology in 2014. Macrophages are immune cells that eat germs and dead cells, and they steer the body's response by releasing small signal proteins called cytokines. Those signals can push a macrophage toward attack mode or calm repair mode.

The review explains what the main macrophage cytokines do in infection and immunity, then follows how the cell packages and ships them out. Multi-protein machines guide each cytokine from where it is made to the cell's exit ports, in steps fine-tuned in space and time. When secretion goes wrong, chronic inflammation or allergy can result. Some germs survive by sabotaging the shipping lines, a trick the authors detail for several pathogens.
europmc-pmc4210525:
Mark G. Ehrhart, Gregory A. Aarons, and Lauren R. Farahnak built a workplace survey scale in Implementation Science in 2014. Clinics often fail to adopt proven treatments, and the climate of the workplace, whether staff feel the new practice is expected and supported, helps decide success. No tested scale measured that climate directly.

The team wrote items from past research and expert advice, then surveyed 630 clinicians in 128 work groups across 32 mental health agencies in the United States. Factor analysis settled on six dimensions: focus on evidence-based practice, training support, recognition, rewards, hiring for the practice, and hiring for openness. A second half of the sample confirmed the structure. The scale, named the Implementation Climate Scale, showed sound reliability and validity for group-level use.
europmc-pmc4213225:
Ching-Lan Cheng, Yea-Huei Kao Yang, and four co-authors checked heart attack records in Taiwan in the Journal of Epidemiology in 2014. Taiwan's national insurance database is a popular research source, but studies built on it are only as good as its diagnosis codes. The team tested the code for acute myocardial infarction, a heart attack, against real hospital charts.

They matched 341 database cases from 2008 to discharge notes at one medical centre and reviewed 338 charts in full. Clinical and lab evidence confirmed 297 cases, giving a positive predictive value of 0.88. Codes for heart procedures, stents, and blood-thinning prescriptions matched charts over 90 percent of the time, and other diagnoses agreed in 95.9 percent of cases. The authors judge the database sound for heart attack research.
europmc-pmc4213725:
Robert Nunan, Keith G. Harding, and Paul Martin examined animal models of stubborn wounds in Disease Models and Mechanisms in 2014. Most cuts heal without thought, but chronic wounds in people with diabetes, obesity, or poor circulation can linger for months. Nearly all fall into three groups: leg ulcers, diabetic foot ulcers, and pressure ulcers.

Healthy wound healing is well mapped in animals, yet chronic wounds are not, because lab models rarely copy the human condition faithfully. The article walks through the best current models and names what each one misses. It then sets out how models could be improved, by combining age, poor blood flow, infection, and metabolic disease in one animal. Better models, the authors argue, are the route to treatments that work in the clinic.
europmc-pmc4230325:
David T. Ting and a team of eleven co-authors read single tumour cells caught from the blood in Cell Reports in 2014. Pancreatic cancer spreads through the bloodstream, carried by circulating tumour cells shed from the main tumour. Comparing those rare travellers to the tumour they left can reveal what the journey selects for.

In a mouse model, the team fished out single circulating cells without relying on surface markers and read their gene activity one cell at a time. The travellers clustered apart from the primary tumour: they divided slowly, carried a stem-cell-linked gene, and showed both epithelial and mesenchymal traits. Strikingly, mouse and human circulating cells alike switched on genes for matrix proteins normally made by surrounding tissue, including SPARC. Silencing SPARC in cancer cells cut their migration and invasiveness.
europmc-pmc4237825:
Samantha Kaufhold and Benjamin Bonavida reviewed a master switch of cancer spread in the Journal of Experimental and Clinical Cancer Research in 2014. Snail1 is a gene controller that, when switched on, reprograms stationary epithelial cells into wandering mesenchymal ones, a change called EMT. Tumours hijack that program to invade and seed new growths.

Snail1 works chiefly by shutting off E-cadherin, the glue protein between epithelial cells, while raising fibres such as vimentin. High Snail1 marks cancers with poor outlook, and it also helps tumours resist chemotherapy and immune attack and keep a stem-like pool. Signals from the PI3K and Wnt pathways govern where in the cell Snail1 sits and how long it lasts. The authors argue blocking Snail1 could both slow spread and re-sensitize tumours to drugs.
europmc-pmc4245825:
Ziheng Yang and Bruce Rannala removed a crutch from species delimitation in Molecular Biology and Evolution in 2014. Deciding where one species ends and another begins, using DNA alone, usually starts from a guide tree the researcher supplies. A wrong guide tree can drag the answer with it.

Their Bayesian method infers the species tree and the species boundaries together, with no guide tree required, under the multispecies coalescent model that allows gene trees to differ from the species tree. Simulations with six populations and three true species showed the method is conservative: strong support for a split is trustworthy, and power grows with older splits and more genes. Reanalysis of cavefish and horned lizard data found the method sure about boundaries even where the tree itself stayed fuzzy.
europmc-pmc4269925:
Alexandre Dias Lopes, Luiz Carlos Hespanhol, Simon S. Yeung, and Leonardo Oliveira Pena Costa review which injuries runners get most often. Their systematic review appeared in Sports Medicine in 2012. Many studies had counted running injuries, but no clear list ranked the main ones by how often they occur.

The team searched five databases and kept studies that reported rates for set injury types. Knee pain syndromes, shin pain, Achilles tendon pain, and foot arch pain stood out among the most common problems, though rates varied widely between studies. The review gives clinicians and coaches a firmer base for prevention plans, and it shows where study methods need to match up.
europmc-pmc4303825:
Michael A Conlon and Anthony R Bird review how food and daily habits reshape the gut microbiota and, through it, human health. Their narrative review appeared in Nutrients in 2014. New DNA tools had just revealed how varied gut communities are from person to person, and how fast they can change.

Carbohydrates are the best studied lever, while the effects of fats and protein remain less clear. Both brief diets and lasting eating patterns move the microbial profile, and what infants are fed may leave marks for life. The review also weighs activity, smoking, and other lifestyle factors. It gives a broad, careful account of a field where much is promised and much remains unproven.
europmc-pmc4443025:
Sergio Ferreira, Mychael Lourenco, Mauricio Oliveira, and Fernanda De Felice reviewed amyloid-beta oligomers in Alzheimer's disease in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2015. Alzheimer's is the most common dementia in older people, and cases keep rising worldwide. The amyloid-beta peptide, which clumps into the plaques found in patients' brains, has long been a prime suspect in memory loss.

Evidence gathered over about fifteen years points to a smaller, dissolved form: clusters called oligomers that float free rather than sit in plaques. These clusters attack synapses, the junctions where brain cells pass signals, and so may drive early mental decline. Many basic questions remain open, including the clusters' exact makeup, which cell receptors they bind, and which signals they trigger. The review sums up progress on each and the treatment ideas that follow from it.
europmc-pmc4533825:
Abdel Aziz Taha and Allan Hanbury tackle how to grade 3D medical image outlines, in BMC Medical Imaging in 2015. Segmentation marks out organs or tumors in scans, and progress in the field depends on scoring those outlines against truth. Scores clash in practice: the same metric may carry several definitions, and old code crawls on whole-body scans.

The pair review 20 evaluation metrics drawn from the literature and give each a fuzzy form, for outlines that assign partial membership rather than hard borders. They explain each metric's traits to guide sound choices. Their free tool computes all 20 fast and with low memory, even on very large volumes such as whole-body MRI or CT.
europmc-pmc4591525:
Jonathan W. Mueller and four co-authors review the sulfate switch that turns steroids up and down, in Endocrine Reviews in 2015. Steroids travel poorly in blood, so the body sulfates them, attaching a sulfate group for the trip. Target cells import the sulfated forms through dedicated transporter proteins, then enzymes called sulfatases clip the sulfate off, usually waking the steroid up.

Because nearly every steroid, from cholesterol to estrone, can ride this system, its tuning shapes the whole endocrine network. The review maps where the sulfating and desulfating enzymes sit, how they are regulated, and how their interplay sets local steroid action. Faults in the system feed steroid-driven cancers, polycystic ovary syndrome, and a skin disorder called X-linked ichthyosis.
europmc-pmc4595525:
In 2015, Monique Maas and colleagues' study on judging treatment response in rectal cancer appeared. After chemotherapy combined with radiation, some tumours vanish completely. Finding those patients matters because they may avoid major surgery. The team compared physical exam, endoscopy, and two kinds of MRI scans.

Fifty patients were checked six to eight weeks after treatment, and results were judged against tissue tests or a year without regrowth. Seventeen patients had a complete response. The clinical exam alone was the most accurate single method. Adding MRI raised the combined accuracy further, reaching a near-certain call when all methods agreed. The authors recommend the combined approach for selecting patients for organ-saving care.
europmc-pmc4624425:
Simon Lewin and colleagues brought out a 2015 methods paper presenting GRADE-CERQual, a way to judge confidence in findings from qualitative evidence reviews. Interviews and similar studies increasingly inform health and social policy. Yet reviewers lacked a clear method to say how much trust a combined finding deserves. The paper appeared in PLOS Medicine.

CERQual rates each review finding on four parts: limits of the studies behind it, how relevant those studies are, how coherent the finding is, and whether enough data support it. The approach comes from a subgroup of the GRADE Working Group, whose system rates quantitative evidence. By making confidence judgements open and structured, CERQual aims to help decision makers use qualitative evidence with the same care as trial results.
europmc-pmc4663725:
A 2015 study using RNA-guided Cas9 editing to create targeted, heritable mutations in barley and Brassica oleracea came from Tom Lawrenson and colleagues. Gene editing promises faster crop research, but performance in these species was unproven. They aimed the system at genes present in several copies. The work appeared in Genome Biology.

In barley, mutations appeared in twenty-three and ten percent of first-generation lines for the two gene copies targeted. In Brassica, ten percent of screened plants carried edits, and a visible dwarf screen confirmed the knockout effect. Edits passed stably to later generations without the delivery construct. Off-target edits occurred despite sequence mismatches, which the authors flag as both a hazard and a tool for editing gene families.
europmc-pmc4754625:
Nasim Mavaddat leads a large group in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute in 2015 on whether common gene variants can sort women by breast cancer risk. Single variants shift risk only slightly. Combined into one score, they might flag who needs closer watch or early checks.

The team built a score from 77 variants in more than 33,000 cases and a like number of controls, all of European origin. The variants acted on their own, with no strong pair effects. Women in the top slice of scores faced about triple the risk of those in the middle. Lifetime risk ran from about one in twenty at the low end to about one in six at the top. The authors say such sorting could guide screening plans.
europmc-pmc4766925:
F. L. Greenway, writing alone in the International Journal of Obesity in 2015, reviews why lost weight so often returns. Diet and exercise can take weight off, yet most people regain it over time. The review asks what the body itself does to pull weight back, apart from habit and willpower.

After weight loss, hunger hormones shift toward eating more, energy use drops, and the brain's control center reads the new weight as too low. Sleep debt and some drugs push the same way. Holding the loss means fighting those shifts daily, which the author calls hard for behavior alone. Drugs and surgery change the body's settings themselves, so he rates them the best long-term bet, and urges more study of the regain machinery.
europmc-pmc4806325:
Binsheng Zhao and six co-authors test the stability of radiomics in Scientific Reports in 2016. Radiomics mines routine tumor scans for hundreds of measured features, hoping the pattern betrays the tumor's type and likely course. A feature that shifts with scanner settings, though, is worthless as a medical marker, and little was known about that risk.

The team used a rare same-day repeat scan set from lung cancer patients. Each scan was rebuilt at six settings, mixing three slice thicknesses and two sharpening styles. Most features repeated well across settings, which supports the field's promise. One limit stood out: scans rebuilt with smooth versus sharp styling should not be mixed in one study. The paper urges scan settings be fixed and reported in radiomics work.
europmc-pmc4893825:
William McLaren and co-authors presented the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor in Genome Biology in 2016. Genome studies pour out DNA variants, and each must be judged: does it change a protein, sit in a control zone, or do nothing? The predictor annotates variants in coding and non-coding regions alike, drawing on the deep Ensembl data stores.

Web, script, and offline routes suit casual and high-volume users, and settings can be tuned or extended. The tool is open source and free, and it logs choices so results can be repeated exactly. Fast, shared judgment of variants speeds gene hunts in research and care, where one missed call can hide a diagnosis.
europmc-pmc4931325:
Xue Gao leads a large team showing that acetate, a simple carbon source, also acts as an epigenetic signal in cancer cells low on oxygen. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. Tumors often use acetate to build fatty acids and grow. How acetate helps beyond raw material was unclear. The team worked with hypoxic cells, which mimic the low oxygen zones inside tumors, and traced acetate into histones, the spools DNA wraps around.

Acetate raised chemical tags on histone H3 that switch genes on. Two fat building genes, ACACA and FASN, turned up, and cells made more new fat. Enzymes named ACSS1 and ACSS2 ran the process. Human liver tumors high in those enzymes showed the same tag and gene pattern. The authors conclude acetate both feeds fat making and, by tagging histones, orders more of it under stress.
europmc-pmc4938625:
Lei Yu and five co-authors test a circular RNA called Cdr1as as a driver of liver cancer growth. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE in 2016. Circular RNAs are ring shaped RNA molecules that can bind microRNAs and blunt their action. Cdr1as was known to bind miR-7, a microRNA that restrains tumors. The team measured both molecules in liver tumor tissue and in healthy tissue beside the tumors.

Cdr1as ran high in tumors while miR-7 ran low, and the two levels moved in opposite directions. Cutting Cdr1as slowed cancer cell growth and invasion in dishes. Adding miR-7 did the same, and it lowered two growth genes, CCNE1 and PIK3CD. Cutting Cdr1as also lowered those genes, working through miR-7. The authors conclude Cdr1as acts as an oncogene, a growth promoter, in this cancer by soaking up a protective microRNA.
europmc-pmc4963825:
Frantisek Malir and four co-authors mark fifty years of research on ochratoxin A, a mold toxin that contaminates food and feed worldwide. Their review appeared in Toxins in 2016. The toxin harms kidneys above all. It causes kidney disease in pigs, damages poultry, and is tied in people to Balkan endemic nephropathy and to kidney tumors in the Balkan Peninsula. It also forms DNA adducts, chemical attachments that can drive cancer.

The review weighs two routes to harm, direct DNA damage and oxidative stress, plus epigenetic effects. The authors conclude the cancer effect in rodents rests on those routes combined. They describe the toxin as one of the most potent kidney carcinogens ever tested in rodent programs. The same combined mechanism, they argue, can plausibly act in people. The review closes with the need for strategies that cut exposure through food and feed.
europmc-pmc4978925:
William Chow and five co-authors present gEVAL, a web browser for checking the quality of genome assemblies. Their paper appeared in Bioinformatics in 2016. Nearly all genome research leans on a reference assembly, a stitched genome map. Local errors in that map are hard to spot and fix. G EVAL lets a user open any region and compare the assembly against many data types at once: sequence alignments, rival assemblies, and physical maps.

The browser flags allelic differences, low complexity stretches, odd coverage, and likely sequence or assembly errors. It also suggests fixes for the faults it finds. Public sites cover human, mouse, zebrafish, and chicken assemblies for the Genome Reference Consortium. A downloadable version works for any organism. The authors describe gEVAL as a working tool of reference genome teams, already used by pig, chicken, and mouse consortia.
europmc-pmc5065525:
Thorold W. Theunissen and a large co-author group set criteria for naive human pluripotent cells in Cell Stem Cell in 2016. Human stem cells in the dish sit in a primed state, a step beyond the embryo's earliest inner cells. Several recipes claim to push them back to that naive state, but no agreed test existed to judge the claims. The team compared converted cells directly with the human embryo across several molecular yardsticks.

They propose that the activity of transposable elements, jumping DNA stretches switched on in early embryos, is a sensitive gauge of true naivety. Conversion also wiped most DNA methylation genome-wide, reversibly, sparing imprinted genes, and the X chromosome took the state seen before implantation. Yet the naive cells would not join mouse embryos, the classic mouse test. Different recipes scored differently against the criteria, giving the field a shared backdrop for judging future claims.
europmc-pmc5087825:
Jacob Kjell and Lars Olson review rat models of spinal cord injury in Disease Models and Mechanisms in 2016. Repairing the injured cord is a longstanding goal, and rats are the workhorse mammal for testing how. The review weighs the injury types used, from contusion to compression and cuts, and what each has taught about the damage that follows impact.

Rat work mapped how the injured cord's circuitry rewires, built sturdy tests of walking and sensation, and showed where recovery can be coaxed. The levers are calming harmful inflammation, managing scarring, protecting myelin, and replacing lost tissue with grafts and bridges. Several candidate treatments now in human trials began in these models. The authors are candid that rat pathology is not human pathology, but they judge few neurological models as robust or as transferable, and they see genetically modified rats widening the model's reach.
europmc-pmc5126725:
Moez Hanin, Chantal Ebel, Mariama Ngom, Laurent Laplaze, and Khaled Masmoudi reviewed plant salt tolerance in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2016. Salty soil is a growing threat in dry regions, where scarce water and poor drainage leave salt behind. Salt starves plants of water and poisons leaves with sodium.

Plants cope in two broad ways: keeping salt out at the roots, or controlling where it goes and how much builds up inside tissues. The review covers the transport genes behind both strategies and how they could be bred or engineered into crops for salty fields. It also discusses pairing crops with nitrogen-fixing bacteria and root fungi as a greener way to hold yields on salt-damaged land.
europmc-pmc5140425:
J. W. D. Megaw examined what causes heart and aorta disease in Europeans living in India, in The Indian Medical Gazette in March 1910. He analyzed cases from the Calcutta General Hospital, whose patients were mostly Europeans or Eurasians long resident in India, plus newcomers such as sailors.

Megaw warns that the records rarely stated the underlying cause, so he re-read each case's notes and judged the cause himself, accepting that the figures claim no great accuracy. He used two sets: three years of hospital cases and nine months of his own patients, where direct inquiry was possible. The analysis sorts cases into groups such as rheumatic and syphilitic disease, seeking patterns in how heart disease arises under Indian conditions.
europmc-pmc517825:
Patrick Eichenberger and ten co-authors mapped the gene program of a single cell type in PLoS Biology in 2004. When the bacterium Bacillus subtilis forms a spore, it divides unevenly, and the mother cell follows a five-hour differentiation program. The team charted every gene switched on or off in that cell.

The program runs through a chain of transcription factors. The first factor turns on 262 of the 383 genes involved, including two repressors that then switch off nearly half of them again. Later factors add pulses of 75 and finally 36 genes, each wave partly repressing the last. The authors describe the logic as linked feed-forward loops producing successive pulses, a circuit design they suggest may recur in other developing cells.
europmc-pmc5222725:
Joseph T. P. Yeeles, Agnieska Janska, Anne Early, and John F. X. Diffley rebuilt the eukaryotic replisome from purified parts in Molecular Cell in 2017. The replisome is the machine that copies DNA, pairing an unwinding helicase with the enzymes that build the two new strands. In living cells it copies at one to two thousand bases per minute, and the team wanted to learn which parts set that speed.

Starting from controlled assembly and activation of the helicase, the rebuilt machine matched natural behavior only when helper factors Mrc1 and Csm3/Tof1 were present, since they are crucial for full-speed travel. The fastest copying came when polymerase epsilon built the leading strand together with its clamp PCNA. Polymerase delta could build the leading strand more slowly, is required for the lagging strand, and also helps set up leading-strand synthesis before polymerase epsilon takes over.
europmc-pmc5222925:
The Japan Esophageal Society published parts two and three of the eleventh edition of its esophageal cancer classification in the journal Esophagus in 2017. A shared classification lets doctors describe tumours of the esophagus, the food pipe, in the same terms, so staging, treatment records, and research can be compared across hospitals.

Part two gives detailed explanations of the descriptive rules: tumour location, visible tumour type, and depth of invasion, plus how spread to lymph nodes and distant organs is recorded. Part three works through findings by method, including endoscopy. One worked example defines the junction between esophagus and stomach by the lower edge of fine palisading vessels seen through the scope, with the stomach's fold margins as a backup landmark. Gaps between that junction and the cell-type boundary are diagnosed as Barrett esophagus.
europmc-pmc5273325:
Byrom Bramwell presented four cases of acute fatal cirrhosis of the liver in one family in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1916, the tenth of his clinical studies. The patients were children aged nine, ten, fourteen, and fourteen. Bramwell sets the cases beside a disease his former house-physician Kinnier Wilson had defined in 1912: progressive lenticular degeneration, a familial nervous disease always paired with liver cirrhosis.

Wilson's disease strikes young people with tremor, slurred speech, swallowing trouble, weakness, stiffness, and wasting, and it ends in death. Under the microscope its mark is decay of the lenticular nucleus, a deep brain structure, while the cirrhotic liver rarely causes symptoms in life. Of Wilson's twelve analyzed cases, eight were familial. Bramwell weighs Wilson's conclusions: the disease looks acquired rather than inborn, probably toxic in origin, possibly brewed in the liver itself, with the poison acting on the motor system.
europmc-pmc5304225:
Yuko Ueda and nine co-authors published a cancer study in Scientific Reports in 2017. The work centers on ALKBH3, a protein that removes methyl marks from RNA. Such marks can block the reading of genetic code. The team asked what this removal does inside cancer cells.

Tests with a pure form of the protein showed it can strip a methyl mark from transfer RNA, the helper RNA that builds new proteins. Cleaned transfer RNA worked better in a test tube system and made proteins faster. When the team lowered ALKBH3 in human cancer cells, the cells grew more slowly and made less new protein. The results link RNA cleaning to tumor growth.
europmc-pmc5353725:
Thomas Maes, Rebecca Jessop, Nikolaus Wellner, Karsten Haupt, and Andrew G. Mayes devised a fast screen for tiny plastic bits in Scientific Reports in 2017. Plastic waste breaks down in seas and soils into microplastics, scraps too small to see with ease. Counting them in field samples is slow, since the gold test needs costly scans of each grain. A cheap first pass could sort the bulk fast.

Their trick uses a dye called Nile Red, which clings to plastic and glows under blue light. After a density float-off and filtering, a plain photo through an orange filter shows the glowing specks for counting by software. Fine zoom shots can catch bits a few micrometers wide. The dye's hue shifts with the plastic's surface traits, which may even sort types. In sea mud tests, the glowing count matched the slow scan count speck for speck.
europmc-pmc5360725:
Dmitry Petrov, Colin Mansfield, Alain Moussy, and Olivier Hermine reviewed twenty years of failed ALS trials in Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience in 2017. ALS, a nerve disease that wastes muscle, kills tens of thousands of people a year across the world. Most patients live two to four years from first signs. One drug, riluzole, cleared in the mid nineteen nineties, gives a mild gain and stands alone.

More than sixty drug hopes have been tested since, and near all failed to show real gain in people. The team works through more than fifty trials to sort why. Two late hopes get close care. One is a pill, masitinib, tested in a wide, true-to-life patient set. The other is a drip drug, edaravone, whose one win came in a narrow slice of patients. The pair may soon join riluzole, but on unlike proof.
europmc-pmc5373125:
Christian K. Tamnes led a team that tracked teen brain growth across four study sets, in the Journal of Neuroscience in 2017. Before brain change can be tied to thought, mood, or illness, the normal path must be mapped with care. The team pooled brain scans from late childhood to early adult life, ages seven to twenty-nine, with close to four hundred people and more than eight hundred scans in all.

Each set was cleaned and read the same way, but kept apart so the patterns could be checked for true repeat. Across all sets, the brain's outer layer shrank in volume and thickness along curved paths, with the pace split by region. Surface area fell more mildly and steadily. Thinning drove most of the volume loss. Links between area change and thickness change formed rich local patterns, strong in the folds of the front and side brain.
europmc-pmc5385025:
Rasnik K. Singh and his co-authors review how food shapes the gut microbiome in a 2017 paper in the Journal of Translational Medicine. The gut holds vast numbers of germs that affect health. Diet can shift those germs fast, with changes seen within a day. The review weighs what is known about common parts of the diet and the germ shifts each one tends to bring.

Some foods lead to clear, repeatable shifts in gut germ groups. Those germs in turn affect the immune system and body chemistry, with links to bowel disease, weight gain, diabetes, heart disease, and cancer. The authors say knowing these links can help doctors and patients use diet with more care.
europmc-pmc5399825:
Marc Miravitlles and Anna Ribera review how symptoms shape the burden of COPD in a 2017 paper in Respiratory Research. COPD is a long-term lung disease whose signs include breathlessness, cough, mucus, wheeze, and chest tightness. The authors gathered studies, mostly from real-world care, that link those signs to quality of life, daily activity, sleep, mood, flare-ups, and outlook.

Symptoms change across the day, often worst in the morning, and that pattern shapes what patients can do. Breathlessness in particular tracks with less movement, poor sleep, and more anxiety and low mood. The review ties symptom load to flare risk and to how the disease unfolds. The authors say spotting and easing symptoms early is key to lifting the daily weight of the disease.
europmc-pmc5412925:
Pereira and Berry review how nutrient niches shape the gut microbe community. Their review appeared in Environmental Microbiology. Hundreds of microbe species share one gut. Why rivals do not wipe each other out is unclear. An old theory by Rolf Freter offers one answer. A species survives by using some scarce nutrient best. The gut, though, is no steady soup. Food supply shifts across place and time.

The authors argue the theory needs widening. Species can share the same nutrient in different sites. They can also take turns across time. Flexible metabolism is a second survival strategy. Many gut microbes burn mixed substrates at once. Host diet sets much of the nutrient map. Host secretions add to it. Immunity filters which niches stay open. The review ties these strands into one frame. It aims to explain community assembly and stability.
europmc-pmc5439125:
Maria and co-authors review the painful mouth injury that radiation therapy causes in head and neck cancer care. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Oncology. The injury is called radiation-induced oral mucositis. Radiation inflames the mouth, tongue, and throat lining. Sores then break the surface barrier. Eating and drinking can become near impossible. Severe cases risk sepsis and weight loss. Treatment breaks follow, and tumor control suffers.

The injury strikes up to 80 percent of these patients. With altered dose schedules, it reaches all of them. United States costs were put near 17,000 dollars per patient. The review walks through the five stages of damage. It covers scoring scales and look-alike conditions. Risk factors include added chemotherapy, poor oral hygiene, and smoking. Prevention and treatment options fill the later sections. Stem cell approaches appear among the newer ideas. The piece serves clinicians who manage this dose-limiting harm.
europmc-pmc5440625:
Zhang and co-authors survey drug-resistant gut bacteria across hospitals in China. Their research article appeared in EBioMedicine. Carbapenems are reserve antibiotics for hard infections. Bacteria that resist them leave doctors few options. Such strains were spreading in Chinese hospitals. The team collected 1,105 resistant strains from 25 locales. They then read the genes behind the resistance.

Two carbapenemase genes explained 90 percent of cases. The gene blaKPC-2 covered 58 percent. The gene blaNDM covered 32 percent. A few clone types drove much of the spread. They include ST11 in Klebsiella pneumoniae. E. coli types ST131 and ST167 also stood out. The genes ride on plasmids that pass between bacteria. The NDM plasmids shared a tight common core. KPC plasmids were more varied. A fosfomycin resistance gene was common. The colistin resistance gene mcr-1 stayed rare.
europmc-pmc5476625:
Xie and co-authors report a nanoparticle study in Scientific Reports. Gold nanoparticles are promising carriers for drugs inside cells. How their shape affects entry into cells was little tested. The team made three shapes of like size: stars, rods, and triangles. All wore the same neutral coating to keep the test fair. Mouse macrophage cells served as the test bed.

Triangles entered the cells most readily, they report. Rods came next, and stars entered least of all. Each shape leaned on different entry routes into the cell. The ranking gives designers a clear guide. Flat triangular carriers may deliver drug loads best.
europmc-pmc5487525:
Dykes and Emanueli present a review in Genomics, Proteomics and Bioinformatics on long non-coding RNA. Most of the genome is copied into RNA that never makes protein. These long transcripts were long dismissed as noise. Disease-linked gene variants cluster in their regions, though. That hint says many of them do real work.

Some long RNAs act as decoys that soak up microRNAs. Others guide protein complexes to exact spots on chromatin. They can loop distant DNA regions together as scaffolds. Such moves switch genes on or off with fine control. The review sorts the best-proven cases from the speculation.
europmc-pmc5498525:
Ramirez and co-authors present a review in Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience on microglia in the retina. Microglia are the immune sentinels of the brain and spinal cord. The retina is an outpost of the brain, so the same cells guard it too. In health they protect neurons, but runaway activation can kill them. Three age-linked diseases frame the survey.

Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and glaucoma each harm the retina. Protein deposits tied to these diseases appear in retinal tissue. Activated microglia gather near those deposits and release inflammatory signals. Those signals can spread damage to neurons, they report. The authors map this shared pathway across all three diseases.
europmc-pmc5501725:
Parsons and co-authors present a systematic review and meta-analysis in Behaviour Research and Therapy. It covers home practice in two mindfulness programs, MBCT and MBSR. Both programs assign daily meditation practice at home for eight weeks. How much practice people truly do was unclear. Whether more practice yields better results was also unclear.

Across 43 studies with 1,427 people, practice averaged 64 percent of the assigned amount. That equals about 30 minutes a day, six days a week. More practice linked modestly to better outcomes across 28 studies, they report. The link was small but statistically firm. Teachers can cite it to support steady home practice.
europmc-pmc5509825:
Hull and co-authors report a qualitative study in the Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders. It examines social camouflaging by adults with autism spectrum conditions. Many autistic adults hide their traits to pass in social settings. Little was known about how that masking feels or why people do it. The team gathered accounts from 92 adults.

Wanting to fit in drove much of the masking, they report. Techniques mixed hiding traits with rehearsed social workarounds. The payoff included wider contact with other people. The costs included exhaustion and strain on self-image. Camouflaging may also delay diagnosis, above all in women. A three-stage model sums up the process.
europmc-pmc5512625:
Kanisicak and co-authors report a lineage-tracing study in Nature Communications on scar cells in the heart. After a heart attack, fibroblasts switch into myofibroblasts that build the scar. Where those cells come from was long disputed. The team engineered mice where a marker gene, periostin, tags them for tracing. Heart attacks were then induced in the animals.

Nearly all heart myofibroblasts carried the tag, they report. Tracing showed they stem from resident fibroblasts of one lineage. Vessel, immune, and muscle cells did not contribute. Deleting the tagged cells shrank collagen output and scar size. Once healing ended, the cells settled back down.
europmc-pmc5557425:
Hassoun, Linden, and Friedman present a review in Critical Care on MRSA bloodstream infection. MRSA is a form of Staphylococcus aureus that resists key antibiotics. When it reaches the blood, illness and death rates are high. It can also seed infections in the heart and bones.

The review tracks how common this infection is across patient groups. It stresses fast identification of the strain and its source. First-line drugs such as vancomycin have real limits, from slow action to rising resistance. New rapid tests can name the germ within hours, not days. The authors also cover prevention. Readers get a current guide to a hard-to-treat infection.
europmc-pmc5640425:
Himmelstein and co-authors built a knowledge network to rank drugs for new uses. Their research article appeared in eLife. The project is called Project Rephetio. It models drug effects from 755 known treatments. Their network, Hetionet, links many data types. It joins compounds, diseases, genes, and pathways. Data came from 29 public resources.

The network holds about 47,000 nodes. It holds over two million relationships. The team found patterns that mark real treatments. They then scored about 209,000 compound and disease pairs. External checks supported the predictions. The scores gave fresh leads for epilepsy drugs. The whole study ran in the open. Community members gave feedback during the work.
europmc-pmc5658625:
Wei and Zimmermann present a review in Microbial Biotechnology. It surveys microbial enzymes that attack petroleum-based plastics. Such plastics resist breakdown and persist in landfills and oceans. Growing waste volumes make that trait a global concern. In recent years, researchers found enzymes that modify or degrade these polymers. They could anchor greener recycling processes.

Coverage spans polyethylene, polystyrene, and polyurethane. Polyethylene terephthalate, or PET, gets close attention. Polyester hydrolases can recover PET building blocks for reuse. The authors weigh how far such biocatalysts have come. They also set out hurdles for real recycling plants. These include polymer traits that block enzyme action.
europmc-pmc5810025:
Cregger and co-authors chart microbes living in and on poplar trees. A tree hosts microbes in its soil, roots, stems, and leaves. Together they form one unit, the holobiont. Little was known about how each niche's microbes differ.

The team sampled 30 tissue niches in two poplar types. Gene surveys profiled bacteria, archaea, and fungi. Habitat class shaped the microbes more than tree genotype. Leaves were the exception, where genotype mattered most. Two likely fungal pathogens marked the hybrid trees. Diversity rose from leaves down to soil. Readers get a detailed atlas for a bioenergy tree.
europmc-pmc5824125:
Rebelo and co-authors build a single PCR test for colistin resistance genes. Colistin is a last-resort antibiotic for stubborn infections. Resistance genes called mcr now ride on plasmids between bacteria. Labs need a fast way to spot all five known types.

Their multiplex test reads mcr-1 through mcr-5 in one run. Bands land about 200 base pairs apart for easy reading. Checks on 49 farm isolates from four nations matched genome data fully. One new variant, mcr-4.3, turned up along the way. Readers get a cheap surveillance tool for labs without sequencers.
europmc-pmc5831225:
Sosna and co-authors test whether wiping out microglia early can slow Alzheimer's disease in mice. Their study appeared in Molecular Neurodegeneration. Microglia drive brain inflammation, yet their part in plaque formation stayed unclear. The team used the 5XFAD mouse model.

They fed young mice the CSF1R blocker PLX3397 for three months. The drug nearly erased microglia from the brain. Intraneuronal amyloid then fell sharply, and neuritic plaques formed far less. Toxic pre-fibrillar oligomers dropped in brain and blood. Treated mice also scored better on fear conditioning. The authors argue microglia help start the amyloid buildup itself.
europmc-pmc5832425:
Filadi, Pendin, and Pizzo review mitofusin 2, a protein that keeps mitochondria connected and well placed. Their review appeared in Cell Death & Disease. The protein sits in the outer mitochondrial membrane. It fuses mitochondria together and tethers them to the endoplasmic reticulum.

Those jobs shape energy output, organelle traffic, and quality control. Faulty copies cause Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A, a nerve disorder. Changed levels also appear in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. Metabolic disease, heart muscle disease, and cancer show links as well. The authors close with open questions, including how its tethering works and which lost job drives illness.
europmc-pmc5835025:
Vogel and co-authors compare two RNA vaccine platforms against influenza in mice. Their study appeared in Molecular Therapy. Both platforms deliver genetic instructions for a flu protein. Self-amplifying RNA also carries the machinery to copy itself inside cells.

That copying paid off in protection. The self-amplifying vaccine matched plain messenger RNA at a 64-fold smaller dose. It guarded mice against H1N1, H3N2, and B strain challenges. A three-strain mix protected against back-to-back infections. The authors pitch the platform as a fast answer when a new virus emerges.
europmc-pmc5940825:
Barbeira and co-authors extend the PrediXcan gene mapping approach so it runs on GWAS summary data alone. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. PrediXcan links genetic variants to traits through predicted gene expression. The new method, S-PrediXcan, computes those results from summary statistics. The authors show it is accurate and robust. They apply it across 44 GTEx tissues.

They test more than 100 phenotypes from GWAS and meta-analysis studies. The result is a public catalog of expression and trait associations. Most associations were specific to one tissue, they report. Some strong signals turned up in unexpected tissues. Genes for monogenic diseases were enriched among related traits. Small changes in such genes may cause milder traits, they suggest.
europmc-pmc5987925:
Shaw and co-authors show that a group of intestinal macrophages is long lived and marked by Tim-4 and CD4. Their study appeared in The Journal of Experimental Medicine. Gut macrophages were thought to follow an old model of constant renewal. Blood monocytes were said to replace them without pause. The intestine was the last tissue held to fit that model. The team tested the idea directly in mice.

They found a population that maintains itself over long periods, they report. It does not depend on monocyte replenishment to persist. These resident cells support gut balance and defence. Their work redraws how gut macrophage origins are understood.
europmc-pmc6030625:
Bruijn and van Dieën review how foot placement steadies human walking. Their article appeared in the Journal of the Royal Society Interface. During walking, the body's center of mass sits outside support. That makes each step a balance challenge. Yet most people walk without major trouble.

Models predict where a foot should land to stay stable. Concepts include the capture point and extrapolated center of mass. Experiments show people largely follow those predictions. Foot placement tracks body motion from the step before. Vision, balance organs, and body sense all feed the estimate. Hip muscles adjust the swinging leg in flight. The review also covers aging and illness effects. Readers get an integrated account of gait control.
europmc-pmc6115425:
Wang and co-authors present a research article in Cell Death and Disease on how breast cancer spreads. The work centers on macrophages, immune cells that sit inside tumors. Such cells release signals that can help cancer grow. The team asked which signal matters most.

A screening test found CXCL1 was the signal these cells release most. CXCL1 made breast cancer cells move and invade more, in mouse and human cells. It acts by switching on a gene called SOX4. Blocking CXCL1 in the immune cells shrank tumors in mice. High CXCL1 also tracked with worse survival in patients. The authors propose it as a treatment target.
europmc-pmc6212925:
Maggini and co-authors review immune needs across the human life course. Immune strength changes as people grow and age. Diet shapes that strength at each stage. Poor diet weakens defences and raises infection risk. The review appeared in Nutrients.

Key nutrients include vitamins A, C, D, and E. B vitamins, folic acid, iron, selenium, and zinc also matter. Lack of these nutrients is a world health problem. The authors cover immune traits at each life stage. They link each stage to infection risk and nutrient needs. They review trials of nutrient supplements. Topping up a true lack can improve defence. Needs differ by age, so doses should be tailored.
europmc-pmc6240225:
Moossavi and co-authors review the NLRP3 inflammasome in cancer. Inflammasomes are large protein complexes inside cells. They form in response to danger signals. They activate enzymes that switch on inflammation. The review appeared in Molecular Cancer.

The complex pairs a Nod-like receptor with adapter and caspase proteins. Its activation releases active IL-1b and IL-18. Faulty control of NLRP3 is linked to tumour growth. Yet study findings on its role conflict. It may promote cancer in some settings. It may restrain cancer in others. The authors sum up current knowledge on both sides. They also cover its promise as a therapy target. Clarifying this dual role is a key next step.
europmc-pmc6247925:
Min and co-authors present a software package for very large DNA methylation data sets. Their paper appeared in Bioinformatics. The package is called meffil and runs in R. Methylation data sets keep growing in size and genome coverage. Standard tools struggle with the memory load. Meffil was built to check quality, clean, and analyse data from Illumina chip arrays.

A rebuilt cleaning method cuts memory use without slowing the work. The method can also absorb group effects and batch effects in one step. Settings that once needed hand tuning are now estimated by the program. Data split across sites can be cleaned without sharing private records. That feature helps joint studies across many centres. The code is free online for other teams to use.
europmc-pmc6250425:
Zivanov and co-authors describe the third major release of the RELION software. Their paper appeared in eLife. RELION builds three dimensional structures from electron microscope images. The method is called single particle cryo-EM. Version 3 adds speed from standard computer chips as well as graphics cards. That mix frees users from memory limits on one card type.

New tools pick particles from images with no starting template. Jobs can run from scripts while images are still being collected. Fine corrections handle particles sitting at varied depths in ice. Curvature of the imaging sphere is also corrected for large particles. Tests on public data sets gained clear gains in detail over older versions. The gains ranged from 0.2 to 0.7 ångströms. Such steps help labs reach atomic level models faster.
europmc-pmc6268925:
Bassolé and Juliani review essential oils used in combination against microbes. Their review appeared in Molecules. Single oils kill bacteria, fungi, and viruses in lab tests. In real foods, far higher doses are often needed for the same effect. Strong doses can spoil taste and raise cost. Pairing oils offers a way around that problem.

Pairs can add their effects or multiply them through synergy. The review gathers tests of oil pairs and of single oil parts paired together. It also surveys how labs measure whether a pair truly helps. Proposed ways the pairs attack microbes are laid out. Food safety drives much of this work. Spoilage organisms and food poisoning germs are the main targets. The authors argue that smart pairing can bring lab strength closer to kitchen use.
europmc-pmc6273625:
Mlcek and co-authors review quercetin, a plant compound with anti-allergy effects. Their review appeared in Molecules. Quercetin is a leading member of the flavonol group. It is rich in onions, apples, berries, tea, and wine. Allergy rates have climbed worldwide over three decades. Immune overreaction sits at the heart of that rise.

Quercetin calms allergy on several fronts at once. It cuts histamine release and lowers inflammatory signals. It also restrains allergy antibodies and rebalances immune cell types. Enzymes that drive allergic inflammation are blocked as well. In lab tests it beat a standard allergy drug on one key signal. Uses in asthma, hay fever, and peanut allergy are discussed. The review gathers the mechanisms behind those effects. It points to quercetin as a base for new allergy products.
europmc-pmc6306025:
Polinder and co-authors review lasting symptoms after mild brain injury. The review appeared in Frontiers in Neurology. Most patients recover from mild traumatic brain injury. A subset keeps somatic, thinking, and emotional problems. These are often grouped as post-concussion syndrome. That label itself is debated.

Reported rates of lasting symptoms range widely. Estimates run from 11 to 82 percent. Somatic, mental, and social factors interact in complex ways. Inconsistent labels and tests have slowed progress. Treatment now targets symptom relief, not root causes. The authors urge standard measures in long-term studies. Better imaging and team-based care also feature in their outlook.
europmc-pmc6318225:
Jackson and co-authors report a large trial of maintenance therapy in myeloma. The phase 3 trial appeared in The Lancet Oncology. Patients had newly diagnosed multiple myeloma. After first treatment, they were assigned by chance. One group took lenalidomide daily in each cycle. The other group was simply observed. The trial ran at 110 hospitals across Britain.

About 1,900 patients joined this stage of the trial. Median time without disease progress doubled with the drug. It reached 39 months, against 20 with observation. Three-year survival was similar overall between groups. Transplant-eligible patients did gain a survival edge. Benefit on progress held across all subgroups. The drug thus delays relapse after initial therapy.
europmc-pmc6324425:
Gomes and co-authors chart the burden of opioid deaths in the United States. Their study appeared in JAMA Network Open. It covers fifteen years of national death data. Opioid deaths have risen fast across North America. Young and middle-aged adults face the steepest rise. The team measured both death share and years of life lost.

Opioids caused 0.4 percent of all deaths in 2001. By 2016 that share had reached 1.5 percent. That is a rise of almost threefold in share. Opioid deaths cost about 1.68 million years of life in 2016 alone. The burden hit adults in their twenties and early thirties hardest. In 2016, one in five deaths in that age band involved opioids. Early death on this scale shapes whole communities.
europmc-pmc6325125:
Groth and co-authors review myeloid-derived suppressor cells in tumor growth. Their review appeared in the British Journal of Cancer. These cells, called MDSCs, come from immature bone marrow cells. Chronic inflammation in cancer blocks their normal maturing. They pile up in mice and patients with tumors. Once present, they strongly damp immune attack.

MDSCs release signals that quiet defense cells. They starve T cells of nutrients those cells need. They block lymphocytes from reaching the tumor. They also boost other suppressive cells and harmful reactive species. That makes them a wall against many immunotherapies. The review covers their origin and ties to other cell types. It surveys drug plans to stop them, some now in trials.
europmc-pmc6325825:
Yang and co-authors study a circular RNA that drives triple-negative breast cancer. Their paper appeared in Molecular Cancer. This cancer type lacks the usual hormone drug targets. It tends to spread early and fare poorly. The team screened tumor and nearby tissue from patients. One circular RNA, circAGFG1, stood out as raised.

High circAGFG1 levels tracked with later stage and worse outlook. Lab tests showed it speeds cell growth and movement. It also helped tumors grow and spread in mice. The ring works by soaking up a small RNA, miR-195-5p. That frees a cell-cycle gene, CCNE1, from restraint. More CCNE1 then pushes the cancer forward. The authors present circAGFG1 as a possible marker and target.
europmc-pmc6327425:
