Suárez-Calvet and co-authors test a fluid marker of microglia in Alzheimer's disease. Their study appeared in Molecular Neurodegeneration. Microglia are the brain's own immune cells. A receptor on them, TREM2, affects disease risk. A soluble piece, sTREM2, can be measured in spinal fluid. The team asked what its rise really reflects.

They studied 1,027 people in a large imaging cohort. Raised sTREM2 appeared early in the disease course. It tracked with tau-linked nerve cell damage. It did not track with amyloid buildup itself. Some participants carried rare TREM2 gene variants. Their data added a genetic angle to the picture. The marker thus seems to flag a specific process. It points to tau-related degeneration rather than amyloid load.
europmc-pmc6336925:
Pinti and co-authors review how brain imaging studies clean their signals before analysis. Their paper appeared in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy tracks blood flow in the cortex. Papers in the field use widely different cleaning steps. Many also describe their methods incompletely.

The team reviewed 110 papers from 2016 on cognitive neuroscience. They found large gaps in reported detail. That makes replication and comparison hard. They then tested filtering methods on synthetic data. The goal was a sound filter step before standard analysis. The work argues for a shared pre-processing standard. It gives the field a common ground for future studies.
europmc-pmc6365925:
Kolodziejczyk and co-authors present a review in EMBO Molecular Medicine on gut microbes and fatty liver disease. Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease is now the most common liver disease worldwide. A minority of patients progress to NASH, an inflamed form that can cause cirrhosis and liver cancer.

The review traces how gut microbiota shape liver fat and sugar handling. Microbe-derived compounds also tip the balance between inflammatory and calming signals in the liver. The authors survey evidence on the gut-liver axis and on diet and genetic risk. They close with open questions about how microbes might be targeted to slow the disease.
europmc-pmc6381325:
Best and co-authors report a blood test study in Cancer Cell on lung cancer. Platelets that meet a tumor change their RNA, becoming tumor-educated platelets. Those RNA patterns may reveal cancer without a biopsy.

A swarm-based method picked the best RNA marker panels from platelet samples. The test found late-stage lung cancer with eighty-eight percent accuracy in a validation group. Early-stage cancer was found with eighty-one percent accuracy. Results held across age, smoking, and storage time. The authors present platelet RNA as a real path toward early lung cancer checks.
europmc-pmc6401825:
Sun and co-authors review a gelatin-based hydrogel in Polymers. GelMA is made from gelatin that can harden under light. It suits biomedical use because it fits well with living cells and its traits can be tuned.

The review explains how GelMA is made, with the light-based method in detail. It compares ways to measure the gel and its starting fluid. Uses in cell culture and tissue building follow, with bone and cartilage in focus. Those tissues bear load, so a gel must be strong as well as kind to cells.
europmc-pmc6436925:
Pärnänen and co-authors ran the first Europe-wide check of drug resistance in city sewage, comparing what flows into treatment plants with clinic data. Sewage mirrors the people it serves, germs and all, since residents shed resistant germs into it. If sewage tracks clinic numbers, it could give cheap, broad tracking between formal surveys.

The sewage pattern did mirror the clinic one. Resistance rose from north to south across Europe, in step with the rates clinics report. Resistant germs and their genes also passed through treatment and out with the cleaned water in the countries sampled. The team weighs which genes make the best warning signs, and argues that sewage can flag resistance trends in a whole community early.
europmc-pmc6507025:
Guo and co-authors test whether baicalin can ease depression-like behavior in mice. Their study appeared in the Journal of Neuroinflammation. Baicalin is a plant compound taken from Radix Scutellariae. It is known for strong anti-inflammatory action. The team links that action to toll-like receptor 4, or TLR4.

They used a chronic mild stress model in mice. Baicalin at 60 mg/kg eased the animals' depressive-like symptoms. It also cut levels of IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-α in the hippocampus. The drug lowered TLR4 by acting through the PI3K/AKT/FoxO1 pathway. Blocking that pathway with LY294002 removed the benefit. Cell tests in microglia backed the same account.
europmc-pmc6605025:
Trunk, Khalil, and Leo review bacterial autoaggregation. Their article appears in AIMS Microbiology. In autoaggregation, bacteria of one type clump together and settle. Self-recognizing surface molecules, called autoagglutinins, drive the clumping. The trait is widespread but still poorly understood.

The authors first sort out rival terms such as flocculation and co-aggregation. They then survey classes of autoagglutinins. Proteins, pili, flagella, and sugars can all serve. Extracellular DNA can act as glue as well. Clumping often protects cells from stress or host defenses. It is also an early step in biofilm formation. Worked examples show how aggregation aids infection and persistence.
europmc-pmc6608625:
Kidmose and co-authors introduce Namdinator, a pipeline for fitting structural models. Their article appears in IUCrJ. Cryo-EM and crystallography produce density maps of molecules. Atomic models must be flexed to fit those maps well. The standard method, MDFF, has a steep learning curve.

Namdinator runs the whole MDFF process in automated form. Users supply a model and a map, online or locally. The pipeline prepares files, adds missing atoms, and runs the simulation. Harmonic restraints guard against overfitting and distortion. A Phenix refinement round then polishes the model's geometry. Benchmarks show excellent fits with no manual steps. The tool can also fix errors late in model building.
europmc-pmc6610925:
Akella, Ciraku, and Reginato review a nutrient pathway that feeds cancer growth. Their article appears in BMC Biology. The hexosamine biosynthetic pathway turns sugars and other nutrients into one key product. That product, UDP-GlcNAc, supplies the sugars that coat and tag proteins. Such tags are widely altered in tumors.

The pathway draws on glucose, glutamine, fatty acids, and nucleotides. Cells may use it as a sensor of energy supply. Its end product drives two kinds of glycosylation. It also feeds the O-GlcNAc tag on nuclear and cell proteins. These changes tune signaling, gene control, and cell movement. The authors link the pathway to the epithelial-mesenchymal transition. They argue it helps explain how tumor metabolism drives cancer traits.
europmc-pmc6657025:
Charlson and co-authors update WHO estimates of mental disorders in conflict settings. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appears in The Lancet. Older WHO figures were over a decade old. They lacked modern methods and uncertainty ranges. The team searched three databases plus grey literature. Studies covered depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress. Bipolar disorder and schizophrenia were included too. Bayesian meta-regression produced the new point estimates.

About 22 percent of conflict-affected people had a disorder. That figure counts any point in time. Mild forms made up about 13 percent. Moderate forms added about 4 percent. Severe disorders reached about 5 percent. The authors urge scalable mental health interventions. Humanitarian need, they argue, is urgent and large.
europmc-pmc6683325:
Gehrig and co-authors test gut microbe directed foods in animals and undernourished children. Their study appears in Science. Malnourished Bangladeshi children carry immature gut microbes. Standard treatment foods ignore that immaturity. The team studied children moving from severe to moderate malnutrition. Plasma and stool tests mapped their state. Test foods then entered germ-free animals. Mice and piglets carried defined sets of bacteria. The foods targeted missing weaning-phase taxa.

A blinded feeding trial came next. One lead food beat the other test foods. It raised the targeted bacteria as designed. Plasma markers of growth also rose. Bone formation and immune mediators rose. Brain growth markers rose as well. The results support a causal gut-growth link.
europmc-pmc6773825:
Aiello and co-authors review immunosenescence and how to oppose it strategically. With age, the immune system remodels and weakens. Older people face more infections, weaker vaccine responses, and more inflammatory disease. Two changes stand out: naive immune cells dwindle, while memory cells grow in share. Together with chronic low-grade inflammation, these are the hallmarks of immune aging.

Aging is plastic, so interventions may slow it. Diet, supplements, and immune-modulating treatments are the main levers. Dietary strategies chiefly target the chronic inflammation of aging. Drugs also show promise. Interleukin-7 can grow fresh naive T cells. Checkpoint inhibitors may restore tired T cell responses. The review clarifies the options for fighting immune decline.
europmc-pmc6885225:
Nandi and co-authors review the enzyme catalase, in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity. Normal cell work leaks harsh molecules that can scar DNA, proteins, and fats. Cells hold defences that disarm them. When the balance tips, the result is oxidative stress, tied to ageing and disease. Catalase is one of the chief guards.

Its job is narrow and vital: it breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. When catalase is missing or faulty, peroxide builds up and damage follows. The review links that failure to diseases from diabetes to nerve decay. It also covers diabetes in pregnancy and its risks for mother and child. The authors survey what might restore the enzyme's guard.
europmc-pmc6893625:
Verderosa and co-authors review agents that eradicate bacterial biofilms, in Frontiers in Chemistry. Most bacteria can settle on surfaces and build biofilms, layered communities wrapped in self-made slime. Biofilms shrug off antibiotics that kill free-floating cells. They drive stubborn, returning infections by organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus.

Most drug work aims to stop biofilms forming or to break them apart. Neither directly kills an established film. This review covers the rarer class that does: eradication agents meant as stand-alone treatment. Halogenated phenazines and quinolines lead the field, with strong action against staph species and low cell toxicity. None, the authors note, has yet been tested in a living body.
europmc-pmc6909825:
Mejzini and co-authors review ALS genetics and treatment, in Frontiers in Neuroscience. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis destroys the motor neurons that move muscles. Its causes remain largely unexplained despite decades of work. More than 50 genes have now been tied to risk or to the disease process itself. Yet most patients still have few treatment options.

The review walks through the most commonly mutated genes and how each may injure neurons. It also asks why so much of the inheritance stays hidden, pointing to gene-environment interplay and patient subgroups. Several cellular processes recur across genetic forms, from protein clumping to faulty RNA handling. Sorting patients by subtype, the authors argue, is the path to personalised therapy.
europmc-pmc6930825:
Calderón-Ospina and Nava-Mesa review three B vitamins that keep nerves healthy. Their review appeared in CNS Neuroscience and Therapeutics. Thiamine, pyridoxine, and cobalamin are vitamins B1, B6, and B12. Each works as a coenzyme in nerve cells. Shortages cause well known nerve diseases, yet the vitamins can help some conditions even without a proven shortage.

The pair map what each vitamin does in central and peripheral nerves. Roles include energy production, antioxidant defence, and making myelin and neurotransmitters. They then examine synergy: how the three vitamins support each other's pathways. Combined use against peripheral neuropathy serves as the clearest example. Their shared chemistry, they argue, explains why the trio works better together.
europmc-pmc6951025:
Zuo and co-authors identify a long RNA that drives fat making in liver cancer, then target it. Their study appeared in the Journal of Hematology and Oncology. Long non-coding RNAs regulate many body processes, and faulty ones appear in cancer. In liver cancer, their roles and treatment uses stayed unclear.

One such RNA, LINC00958, ran high in tumour tissue and cell lines. Patients with high levels fared worse. The RNA soaks up a small RNA, miR-3619-5p, freeing a growth factor that boosts fat production and tumour growth. A chemical tag added by the enzyme METTL3 kept the RNA stable. The team then built nanoparticles carrying a silencer of LINC00958. The particles homed to tumours, released slowly, and fought the cancer well in tests.
europmc-pmc6970225:
Rudd and co-authors produce the first full global count of sepsis cases and deaths. Their analysis appeared in The Lancet. Sepsis is organ failure driven by a disordered response to infection. It is a major cause of health loss, yet standard global burden estimates omit it, since an underlying infection is always the listed cause.

The team mined 109 million death records and 8.7 million hospital records from the Global Burden of Disease 2017 study. In 2017 they estimate 48.9 million sepsis cases worldwide. Sepsis-related deaths reached 11.0 million, about a fifth of all deaths that year. Rates fell sharply from 1990, with standardised incidence down by more than a third. Burden varied widely by place, age, and sex. Sound counts, the authors argue, should guide policy and resources.
europmc-pmc7075525:
Studer and co-authors improve protein model quality estimation in the journal Bioinformatics. Predicting a protein's shape is half the task; judging whether a model is trustworthy, with no experimental structure to compare, is the other half. Single-model methods grade one structure alone, while consensus methods need a whole ensemble. The QMEAN score is a leading single-model approach based on statistical potentials and agreement terms.

The new version adds a distance constraint score, DisCo, which borrows distance distributions from experimentally solved relatives of the modelled protein. A neural network learns how to weigh that consensus-flavoured evidence against the classic QMEAN terms. QMEANDisCo keeps the broad reach of single-model grading with accuracy closer to consensus methods. It ranks among the top performers in the CAMEO benchmark and in CASP13, with fast response times. A side finding: contest models are not ideal training data for such graders.
europmc-pmc7093825:
Benítez-Páez and co-authors link missing gut bacteria to inflammation and insulin resistance in obese children, in mSystems. Child obesity raises the risk of insulin resistance, which can lead to type 2 diabetes in adulthood. The team examined the gut microbes of obese children and compared species levels with metabolic measures.

Two species, Blautia luti and Blautia wexlerae, were depleted in children with insulin resistance. The authors present evidence that these bacteria may help lower the inflammation tied to obesity complications. Childhood offers a window to act before damage settles. The findings point toward future microbe-based strategies for preventing obesity-related disease early in life.
europmc-pmc7145525:
Deutsch and co-authors report the 2020 state of the ProteomeXchange consortium, which standardises sharing of proteomics data worldwide, in Nucleic Acids Research. The consortium has coordinated submission and distribution of mass spectrometry proteomics datasets since 2012. Two new member archives, iProX in China and Panorama Public in the United States, joined the original four.

By the end of June 2019, more than 14,100 datasets had been submitted, over 9,500 of them in just three years, showing the field embracing open data. Reuse of shared data is growing fast and enabling big-data studies and new resources. Updated submission guidelines covering all six members are described, along with plans for the coming years.
europmc-pmc7196825:
Rezai and co-authors report an early trial using focused ultrasound to open the blood-brain barrier in Alzheimer's disease. Their study appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The barrier blocks most drugs from reaching the brain. The hippocampus, vital for memory, is a prime treatment target. Animal studies showed ultrasound can open the barrier briefly and safely.

The trial treated the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex in patients with early Alzheimer's. Ultrasound was guided by magnetic resonance imaging. The team checked whether the opening was safe, workable, and reversible. The barrier closed again after treatment, as hoped. Opening it could let antibodies and other drugs reach memory circuits. The authors present the results as a first step toward delivery-based therapies.
europmc-pmc7237725:
Gaudreault and co-authors review African swine fever virus, a deadly virus of pigs with an unusual life cycle. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Veterinary Science. The virus is the only known DNA virus spread by arthropods. It was identified in Kenya in 1921 and remains entrenched in Africa. Soft ticks and warthogs maintain it in the wild without getting sick themselves.

Domestic and feral pigs, by contrast, suffer devastating disease. No vaccine exists against it. Control rests on strict quarantine and culling of herds. The virus is tough and spreads through infected animals, pork products, and contaminated objects. Research on how it enters cells has overturned early assumptions. A receptor once thought essential proved dispensable in gene-edited pigs. The review surveys biology and the hard road to a vaccine.
europmc-pmc7254925:
Greenwood and co-authors test whether an online food questionnaire measures diet accurately enough for large health studies. Their validation study appeared in the American Journal of Epidemiology. The Oxford WebQ asks people to recall everything they ate in the past 24 hours. It is used in big studies such as UK Biobank and the Million Women Study.

The team recruited 160 participants in London and measured their biomarker levels at 3 separate time points. Blood and urine markers for protein, potassium, and sugar, plus movement-based energy estimates, served as the standard. WebQ results matched those markers about as well as a traditional interviewer-led recall, which takes far more staff time. Accuracy improved when answers from repeated rounds were averaged.
europmc-pmc7260225:
Chia and co-authors checked hospital rooms for traces of SARS-CoV-2 in air and on surfaces. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Samples came from isolation rooms in an intensive care unit and a general ward in Singapore. The aim was to learn how much virus patients leave around them, and at what stage of illness.

The team took 245 surface samples from 30 rooms. More than half of the rooms had at least one positive surface. Floors, bed rails and air vents were often positive. High-touch surfaces were most often positive in the first week of illness. Air tests found viral RNA in two of three rooms sampled. The authors say airborne spread needs more study.
europmc-pmc7273325:
Rima and co-authors summarize the official taxonomy of the virus family Paramyxoviridae. Their profile appeared in the Journal of General Virology. It sums up a longer report by the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses. The family holds large enveloped RNA viruses. Members infect mammals, birds, reptiles and fish.

Human diseases in the family include measles, mumps and several parainfluenza infections. Nipah and Hendra viruses are also members. The profile sets out virus structure, genome order and how copies are made. It then sorts the family into four subfamilies with their host ranges. Readers get the standard reference layout for this virus group in a few pages.
europmc-pmc7360025:
Percie du Sert and co-authors explain the ARRIVE 2.0 reporting guidelines item by item in PLoS Biology. Animal studies often omit details that readers need to judge reliability or repeat the work. This companion document was developed alongside the revised guidelines themselves.

For each of the 21 items in ARRIVE 2.0, the authors give the reasoning, the supporting evidence, and the exact details to report. Examples of good reporting show what each item looks like in practice. The Essential 10 and the Recommended Set structure from the main guidelines carries through. Researchers writing up animal experiments get a practical manual, and reviewers get a yardstick for what a complete methods report should contain.
europmc-pmc7402625:
Deng and co-authors test reinfection in monkeys in Science, asking whether a first bout of SARS-CoV-2 protects against a second. Recovered patients worldwide feared catching the virus again, and the answer shapes vaccine hopes. The team built a rhesus macaque model of the infection.

The monkeys developed interstitial pneumonia and virus spread mainly through the airways and gut. Rechallenged with the identical strain during early recovery, they showed no detectable viral spread, no symptoms, and no tissue damage. Antibody and cellular responses were notably stronger after the second exposure than the first. Primary infection, the authors conclude, protects macaques against reinfection, at least in the short term. Early human fears of instant reinfection eased on this evidence.
europmc-pmc7416625:
Luo and co-authors publish the genome of Aegilops tauschii in Nature, the wild goatgrass that donated the D genome to bread wheat. Wheat is a hybrid of three genomes, and the D donor's own sequence is a key reference for breeders. The team combined several advanced sequencing and mapping methods.

The assembly was built in stages, starting from 42,822 cloned DNA fragments and merging shotgun and long-read data, then checked against optical maps. Errors were hunted down and scaffolds joined into a reference-grade sequence. With the progenitor decoded, researchers can trace which wheat traits came from this wild relative and mine its diversity for disease resistance and hardiness. A crop's family history, written in DNA.
europmc-pmc7426425:
Yu and co-authors improve a search tool that finds modified peptides in proteomics data. Peptides are short protein pieces read by mass spectrometry. Chemical changes on them can shift their mass and hide them from standard searches.

Their tool, MSFragger, uses an open search that allows unknown mass shifts. The new version also indexes shifted fragment ions, so it can pinpoint where a change sits. A fast calibration step tunes mass limits and other settings. Tests show the updated tool finds modified peptides with better sensitivity and accuracy. It held up well against pFind3, MetaMorpheus, and TagGraph. The work speeds the study of protein changes in cells.
europmc-pmc7429125:
Sperotto and co-authors review heart problems in a COVID-linked illness of children. The illness is multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children, tied to SARS-CoV-2 infection. Early reports said children were mostly spared severe COVID-19, so this syndrome was a surprise.

Affected children often show lasting fever, gut symptoms, rash, red eyes, and mouth changes. Blood tests show strong inflammation. Some develop low blood pressure and shock from weak heart muscle or wide blood vessel dilation. Coronary arteries can widen, and rhythm problems occur. Care rests on heart support, immune-calming drugs, and drugs that prevent clots. Long follow-up is vital, since the risk of lasting heart harm is not yet clear.
europmc-pmc7440125:
Kim and co-authors report COVID-19 hospital rates for children in 14 states. The COVID-NET system tracked lab-confirmed cases from March 1 to July 25, 2020. Most child cases seem mild, so severe illness needed a closer look.

The total rate was 8.0 hospital stays per 100,000 children. Rates were highest in children under 2 years, at 24.8 per 100,000. Hispanic and Black children had far higher rates than White children. Among 208 children with full chart reviews, one in three went to intensive care. A small share needed breathing machines, and one child died. Weekly rates rose over the period. The authors stress steady tracking and strong prevention in schools and childcare.
europmc-pmc7482825:
Wu and co-authors test rhein, a rhubarb compound, against chronic colitis in mice through the gut microbiome. Rhein absorbs poorly by mouth yet calms inflammation. Gut microbes are a new target for bowel disease care.

Mice with colitis from repeated dextran sulfate sodium rounds got daily rhein. Their colitis eased in clear terms. Metabolic scans named uric acid as a key driver that rhein lowered. Rhein shifted gut microbes, and Lactobacillus helped tune host purine metabolism. Uric acid weakened the gut barrier, and rhein undid that harm. Transplants of rhein-shaped microbiota alone relieved colitis in fresh mice. The study marks a microbe-first route to colitis treatment. It may guide new care for ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease.
europmc-pmc7483525:
Bolte and co-authors show that weak meningeal lymphatic drainage worsens traumatic brain injury. These vessels drain fluid and waste from the brain's coverings. The team used a mouse model of mild brain trauma.

Even mild injury caused severe drainage deficits within hours. The problems lasted at least one month after injury. Raised pressure inside the skull helped drive the failure. Mice with poor drainage before injury had more brain inflammation and worse thinking outcomes. In aged mice, restoring drainage eased injury-linked gliosis. The findings tie vessel health to recovery after head trauma. Drugs or other care aimed at meningeal lymphatics may offer a new way to treat brain injury, the authors argue.
europmc-pmc7497325:
Gires and co-authors review EpCAM, an epithelial cell adhesion molecule, 40 years after its discovery. It was first found as a tumor antigen on colorectal cancers. High levels on cancers and their spread made it a marker and target.

EpCAM helps run cell adhesion, growth, movement, stemness, and shape change in carcinoma cells. Whole protein and its cut fragments both send signals inside and between cells. It works with claudins, CD44, E-cadherin, and growth factor receptors. These acts shape tumor variety and partial shape change, which steer patient outcomes. EpCAM marks the epithelial state of tumor cells in the body and in blood. It also gauges the spread power of roaming tumor cells. The review weighs its value as a forecast marker and drug target.
europmc-pmc7503625:
He and co-authors review short-chain fatty acids and their signaling paths in inflammation and metabolism. Gut microbes make these acids by fermenting food in the gut. Acetate, propionate, and butyrate are the main three.

These acids help run energy balance and keep the gut setting stable. They act mainly through two routes: G-protein-coupled receptors and histone deacetylase effects. Through those routes they shape inflammation in the body. They also sway glucose and lipid handling in tissues. New work keeps finding fresh effects on absorption and gut function. The review sums up recent gains on their biology. It maps where these small acids may matter for metabolic and inflammatory disease care.
europmc-pmc7524325:
Mukherjee, Lordan, Ross and Cotter review gut bacteria in the genus Eubacterium. These microbes form part of the core human gut microbiome. The genus is diverse, which makes it hard to classify.

Several species make butyrate in the gut. Butyrate supports energy balance and gut movement. It also helps calm inflammation. The review covers bile acid and cholesterol changes by these bacteria. It tracks how levels shift with diet and age. Lower or altered levels have been linked to disease. Readers get a map of species and their roles in gut health.
europmc-pmc7536225:
Lee and co-authors link gut microbes to liver scarring in non-obese fatty liver disease. Fatty liver is often tied to obesity. It also occurs in people who are not obese.

The team profiled 171 Asian patients with biopsy-proven disease. They also studied 31 controls without the disease. Sequencing used 16S rRNA from stool samples. A Western cohort served for outside validation. Microbe diversity shifted with fibrosis severity in non-obese patients. Two families, Ruminococcaceae and Veillonellaceae, stood out. Stool bile acids and propionate were higher in severe cases. Mouse tests then checked four species for liver effects.
europmc-pmc7561225:
Morris and co-authors describe multisystem inflammatory syndrome in adults linked to SARS-CoV-2. A similar syndrome had been reported in children first. Adult cases began to appear from June onward.

The case series covers 27 adult patients in total. Nine were reported direct to CDC by clinicians. Seven came from published case reports. Eleven came from three published case series. Patients had heart, gut, skin and nerve symptoms. Severe respiratory illness was not a feature. Tests showed current or recent SARS-CoV-2 infection. Antibody testing helped confirm past infection in some cases. The authors urge clinicians to consider this syndrome in adults.
europmc-pmc7616025:
Pennington, Bell and Hill appraise a systematic review on laryngoscopy choice for pre-hospital intubation in adults. Tube placement by paramedics is debated in the UK. Safety gains from new tools need solid proof.

The review under appraisal was done by Hansel and colleagues. It compared video and direct laryngoscopes in practice. Video tools add a camera for a better view. That view may raise success rates for the procedure. This commentary checks the methods of that review. It then expands findings for clinical practice use. Skill, training and rare exposure shape the debate. Most UK paramedics seldom do this procedure in the field. The authors weigh whether video tools should enter routine pre-hospital care.
europmc-pmc7712525:
Mokkink and co-authors build a tool to judge studies of test reliability. Health scores vary with the tool used, the setting, and who gives or scores the test. Studies of reliability and measurement error must be sound to be trusted. Past tools left gaps for some instrument types.

A panel of 52 experts worked through three Delphi rounds. They agreed on design standards and on the best statistics for such studies. Ratings run on a four-point scale. The new COSMIN tool covers clinician reports, performance tests, and lab values. It aims to let any trained user grade a reliability study with care.
europmc-pmc7762425:
Vigata and co-authors review how to test hydrogels that deliver drugs. Hydrogels can be tuned, break down in the body, and shield fragile drugs. Labs use unlike methods to measure drug release from them. That makes results hard to compare and slows fair judgment of new systems.

The review lists the main methods to detect and count drugs released from gels. It shows how test fluid and setup choices sway the readings. Math and statistical models for release curves get full treatment. The authors also cover diffusion measures and test models in dishes and in animals. Their aim is shared, harmonized practice for the field.
europmc-pmc7891125:
Dejnirattisai and co-authors report a structural study of antibodies that bind the SARS-CoV-2 spike. Antibodies are central to protection against the virus. Some are used as treatments. The team focused on the receptor binding domain, the part of the spike that latches onto human cells.

They gathered 377 human monoclonal antibodies that recognise the spike. Of these, 80 bind the receptor binding domain. A competition method sorted their binding sites across that domain. Nearly all strongly blocking antibodies stopped the spike from meeting its receptor. The team solved 19 structures of antibody fragments bound to their targets. Some strong antibodies used unusual binding modes. The best of them protected animals when given before or after infection.
europmc-pmc7939325:
Brown presents an English translation of De Venenis, a Latin work on poisons by Petrus Abbonus. The text follows the edition of MCDXCVIII. Brown opens with a wry defence of his labour. Years of medical practice, he says, taught him that the only tasks worth doing are the seemingly worthless ones. Translating this old book of poisons is his chosen example.

He warns the reader that the work may hold mistakes. The Latin of its century is rough, and many words appear in no dictionary he could find. He leaves sharp critics to enjoy their edge in knowledge. The laughter the task gave him is his reward, he writes. Behind the humour sits a real scholarly gift. The translation opens a medieval treatise on venoms to English readers. Brown's preface alone shows the spirit of the early medical historians.
europmc-pmc7997025:
Gray and co-authors report a cohort study of COVID-19 vaccine response in pregnant and lactating women. These women were left out of the first vaccine trials. That gap left them to decide without data. The team enrolled 131 women of childbearing age at two academic centres. Most were pregnant or breastfeeding; a small group was neither. Blood and breast milk were tested across the vaccine course.

Vaccine-driven antibody levels matched those in the nonpregnant group. Levels also topped those seen after natural infection in pregnancy. Antibodies reached the umbilical cord blood of babies delivered in the study window. Blocking power was confirmed in a subset of samples. Side effects after the shots were gathered by questionnaire. The study gives this group the direct evidence the trials had skipped.
europmc-pmc8005925:
Page and co-authors explain the PRISMA 2020 reporting guideline item by item in this companion paper. The main statement sets out what systematic review reports should include. This longer document explains why each recommendation matters. It pairs the guidance with worked examples drawn from published reviews.

For each checklist item, the authors give bullet points that detail what to report. They walk through the changes made since the 2009 version. The update reflects new methods for finding, selecting, and combining studies. The examples show good reporting in practice. The authors hope wider uptake will make review reports more open and accurate.
europmc-pmc8048825:
Muyldermans gives a practical guide to generating and designing nanobodies. Nanobodies are single-domain antibodies drawn from camelid immune systems. Their small size solves problems that plague full antibodies. Researchers clone nanobody repertoires from camelid B lymphocytes. Those libraries may be immune, naïve, or fully synthetic. Selection then fishes out the binders for a chosen target.

The guide walks through each generation route in turn. Phage display pannings and yeast surface display anchor the selection step. Synthetic libraries randomize the antigen-binding loops of a scaffold. After a lead nanobody is found, engineering can refine it further. Muyldermans surveys where the finished molecules end up. Research tools, diagnostic tests, and therapies all use them. The guide stresses matching library type to the job at hand.
europmc-pmc8080625:
Jo and co-authors review the prion-like spread of TDP-43 in diseases of the aging brain. TDP-43 normally works in the nucleus, tending RNA. In disease, it clumps in the central nervous system. Such clumps mark amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia. They also appear in Alzheimer's disease and in LATE, a dementia of the very old.

Evidence now suggests the clumps travel from cell to cell. A bad seed templates fresh clumping in each new host cell. That pattern mirrors prions and the spread of tau and amyloid. The review gathers the clinical signs of staged spread in patients. Lab studies that pass seeds between cells get equal weight. The authors then unpack how the seeds form and move. Blocking the hand-off, they argue, could slow many diseases at once. The idea reframes these illnesses as disorders of propagation.
europmc-pmc8088725:
Gong and co-authors review how to design and build CAR natural killer cells for cancer therapy. Natural killer cells spot and burst malignant cells on their own. Arming them with chimeric antigen receptors could sharpen that gift. Getting genes into NK cells long proved hard. New expansion methods, CRISPR editing, and better delivery have changed the odds.

The review starts with CAR design for NK biology. It then covers the vehicles that carry the receptor gene in. Viral transfer and electroporation get compared in detail. Ways to detect the finished receptor follow. Cell sources and growth protocols round out the build. Early studies show target killing without the worst CAR-T side effects. Cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity have not appeared. Lessons borrowed from CAR-T work thread through the survey. The authors look ahead to off-the-shelf products.
europmc-pmc8139425:
Stamatatos and co-authors show that mRNA vaccination supercharges the antibodies left by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Infection alone teaches the immune system one version of the virus. Variants then test how broad that lesson runs. The team studied people who had recovered from infection. It measured their neutralizing antibodies against several variants. An mRNA vaccine dose entered the picture next.

After vaccination, neutralization rose and widened at once. Antibodies that infection had primed now covered variant spikes better. The boost crossed variant lines that infection alone handled weakly. Hybrid immunity, part infection and part vaccine, proved the stronger shield. The editors' summary frames it plainly: boosterism could save lives. For the recovered, one dose may not be a mere top-up. It can complete an education the virus started badly. The finding shaped early booster debates worldwide. Breadth, not just height, is what vaccination added.
europmc-pmc8234625:
Fu and co-authors review the spatial layout of the tumour immune microenvironment. A tumour is an ecosystem, not a mere lump of cancer cells. Its immune parts shape growth, return, and spread.

Older studies flattened that layout and missed much of its order. New high-throughput tools now map where each cell type sits. Those maps show how position governs immune attack. They also help explain why therapy response varies so much. The review gathers the new mapping methods and findings. It ties spatial patterns to treatment choices for patients. Position, in short, turns out to carry real biological meaning.
europmc-pmc8263825:
Lam and co-authors introduce Kleborate, a genomic surveillance tool for Klebsiella pneumoniae. This bacterium drives resistant hospital infections and newborn sepsis. Its diversity makes genome data hard to read.

Kleborate covers the species and its close relatives in one framework. It checks the traits of proven clinical weight in a single pass. Those include resistance and virulence markers. The team tested it on public genome sets. It serves research, clinic, and public health users alike. Shared outputs should make outbreak data easier to compare across labs. Public genome collections supplied its demonstration data.
europmc-pmc8329225:
Pan and co-authors show that the SARS-CoV-2 N protein fires the NLRP3 inflammasome. Excess inflammation marks severe COVID-19. Inflammasome activity tracks with that severity.

The N protein pushed cells to mature inflammatory cytokines. It did the same in mice. The protein binds NLRP3 directly. That binding helps NLRP3 join ASC and assemble the inflammasome. In animals, the protein worsened lung injury. It also sped death in sepsis models. The work names a viral trigger for hyperinflammation. Blocking the pairing could calm severe disease. Assembly of the inflammasome is the turning point shown.
europmc-pmc8423625:
Kerimov and co-authors build a shared catalogue of gene expression and splicing QTLs. Such QTLs link gene variants to changes in gene activity. Many studies had published their own results, but format gaps blocked easy joint use.

The eQTL Catalogue re-computed results from 21 studies in one uniform way. Quality checks were applied across the whole set. For matched tissues, effect sizes matched well between studies. Most QTLs were shared across tissues, yet purified cell types showed more unique ones. Some of those fresh QTLs matched disease signals. The summary data are free for anyone to use in reading genome-wide study results.
europmc-pmc8431625:
Molnar and co-authors analyze the cytokines and chemokines that drive osteoarthritis. This joint disease is a common cause of disability around the world. It harms all joint tissues, not cartilage alone. Low-grade inflammation sits at the center of the process.

Inflammation tips the balance between tissue build-up and break-down. Signals that raise or calm inflammation both shift with disease stage. The review takes each cytokine in turn and sets out its job in the joint. Chemokines that draw immune cells in get the same treatment. The authors also weigh these signals as biomarkers. Their account maps the network that steers this slow joint decay.
europmc-pmc8481125:
Robichaux and co-authors sort EGFR mutations in lung cancer by protein shape to predict drug response. These mutations drive non-small cell lung cancer. Drugs exist for the classic forms, but many rarer forms lack proven treatments. Their drug sensitivity was largely unknown.

The team mapped mutations in 16,715 patients with EGFR-mutant disease. They tied each mutation's shape change to drug sensitivity. Four subgroups emerged from that structure view. The groups predicted patient outcomes after inhibitor treatment better than the old exon-based sorting. The authors argue this shape-first scheme can guide care and trial choices. It may extend to other cancer genes with many mutation types.
europmc-pmc8486125:
Delahaye and Nicolas chart the errors and biases of nanopore DNA sequencing. Oxford Nanopore sequencers read longer DNA stretches than older machines. The trade-off is a higher error rate. Fast shifts in chemistry and software made error maps go stale quickly.

With the MinION platform now more stable, the authors give a fresh view. They studied errors in bacterial and human DNA reads. GC content proved a crucial factor, though nanopore reads were thought free of GC bias. Low-GC reads held fewer errors than high-GC reads. Repeated stretches caused about half of all errors, mostly deletions. Read quality scores still help predict error levels.
europmc-pmc8601625:
Robeson and co-authors introduce RESCRIPt, a software tool for building sequence reference databases. Such databases are key for microbiome work, diet studies, and environmental DNA surveys. Making them by hand is slow and hard to repeat. Poor database choice can also skew study results.

RESCRIPt is a Python package and a QIIME 2 plugin. It builds databases from sources such as SILVA, Greengenes, and GenBank. It can also rate and compare databases by set traits. Worked examples span gut microbes, diet traces, and genome checks. The authors show that bigger databases are not always better. Clean taxonomy and type strains gave stronger results.
europmc-pmc8604725:
Nassif and co-authors test the drug dapagliflozin in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. People with this form of heart failure face heavy symptoms and poor quality of life. The drug blocks a kidney protein that moves sugar and salt. The trial asked if it could ease symptoms and raise daily function.

In total, 324 patients were assigned to the drug or a placebo. After 12 weeks, the drug group gained 5.8 points on a heart failure health score. Walking distance in six minutes rose by 20.1 meters on average. Symptom and physical limit scores both got better. The authors report gains that patients can feel in daily life.
europmc-pmc8863725:
Negrini and co-authors review Sjögren's syndrome, a systemic autoimmune disease. The disease attacks the glands that make tears and saliva. Dry eyes and dry mouth are its hallmarks. It can also strike almost any organ system. Symptoms vary widely between patients. It may occur alone or beside other autoimmune diseases. Its root cause remains unclear.

The review covers how the disease likely develops. Genetic and environmental factors both play a part. Faulty B-lymphocytes and autoantibodies sit near the center. Diagnosis rests on symptoms, gland tissue tests, and antibody tests. New classification criteria and activity scores are explained. Treatment ranges from local dryness relief to immune drugs. Biologic medicines close the survey. The authors aim to update clinicians on a shifting field.
europmc-pmc9018425:
Dizman and co-authors tested whether a live bacterial product could boost immunotherapy for kidney cancer that had spread. Thirty patients received nivolumab plus ipilimumab, with most also taking daily CBM588, a product that feeds Bifidobacterium. The trial's main goal, a rise in those bacteria by week 12, was not met. Stool tests showed no clear shift in the gut community.

Yet patients on CBM588 went far longer without their cancer growing, 12.7 months against 2.5 months. Response rates were also higher, 58% against 20%, with no extra side effects. The authors call for larger trials to confirm the effect.
europmc-pmc9161525:
Dhyani and co-authors assess plant alkaloids as anticancer agents, with focus on six named compounds. The six are colchicine, vinblastine, vincristine, vindesine, vinorelbine, and vincamine. Alkaloids are plant chemicals that have shown real power against tumors. Several already serve as standard cancer drugs.

For each compound, the review gives medical uses old and new. It explains how the drug attacks tumors, often by blocking cell division machinery. It also covers efforts to scale up production in the lab. The authors argue these agents can support cheaper, effective cancer care. Readers get deep profiles of a proven drug family and its future scope.
europmc-pmc9223325:
One Health High-Level Expert Panel and co-authors set out a new definition of One Health for a sustainable future. The COVID-19 pandemic again showed how human, animal, and environmental health are linked. Four global agencies formed the panel in May 2021 to turn the concept into action. A shared definition was its first task.

One Health is defined as an integrated approach that balances the health of people, animals, and ecosystems. It mobilizes many sectors and communities to work together. Core principles include equity, inclusivity, and stewardship of nature. The approach also addresses clean food, water, energy, and air, plus climate change. The panel presents four keys to practice: communication, coordination, collaboration, and capacity building.
europmc-pmc9298325:
Berek and co-authors update the care of cancers of the ovary, fallopian tube, and peritoneum. A 2014 staging revision treats the three sites as one system. Most of these cancers are high-grade serous carcinomas. Evidence suggests many begin in the end of the fallopian tube, not the ovary.

The update restates the revised stage groups in detail. Stage IC splits by spill, rupture, or malignant washings. Node-only spread is split by the size of the deposit. Genetics, surgery, and chemotherapy are summarized for epithelial cancers. Targeted therapies are covered as well. Germ cell and stromal tumors of the ovary get their own treatment sections. The piece serves as a compact reference for clinicians.
europmc-pmc9349325:
GBD 2019 Hepatitis B Collaborators estimate the world burden of hepatitis B from 1990 to 2019. They modeled chronic infection, deaths, and disability for 194 WHO member states. Sources included population surveys, hospital data, cancer registries, and death records. Results were checked against WHO elimination targets.

In 2019 about 316 million people, 4.1% of the world, lived with chronic hepatitis B. Prevalence had fallen 31.3% since 1990, and 76.8% in children under five. Still, hepatitis B diseases caused 555,000 deaths that year. Death counts rose as populations grew and aged, even as rates fell. Only 15 countries hit the target cut in new cases. The team urges faster vaccination, testing, and treatment to reach 2030 goals.
europmc-pmc9387425:
Richardson and co-authors set out a framework for equity in digital health. Care is digitizing fast, and tools built without care can widen health gaps. Their framework names the digital determinants of health at four levels: individual, interpersonal, community, and societal. It extends a leading disparities framework with a digital domain.

Digital access alone is not the whole story. Skills, broadband supply, and design choices all shape who benefits. Over 95% of US hospitals now run certified electronic records with patient portals. Telehealth gaps during the pandemic showed the stakes clearly. A worked case study shows how to apply the framework. The authors urge a root-cause, multi-level view for builders and health systems alike.
europmc-pmc9837825:
Aggarwal and co-authors review the human microbiome and health, from current knowledge to engineering tools. Microbial communities live at many sites across the body. They evolved with us and now support core body functions. Upsets in those communities can start or worsen disease.

The review tours microbiomes by body system in turn. Digestive and breathing tracts get deep coverage first. Urinary, reproductive, and skin communities follow in the survey. It then gathers ways to reshape the communities for therapy. Diet, transplants, and engineered microbes all enter the frame. Enabling technologies close the review's arc. Multiomics readouts map the communities at fine grain. Reprogramming microbes turns them into living tools. Over 130,000 bacterial genomes now back this science. The authors frame engineering as the field's next leap.
europmc-pmc9871625:
Zhang and co-authors review how inflammation, immunity, and oxidative stress drive hypertension. Hypertension is a leading risk factor for cardiovascular disease, a major cause of death. Recent work links chronic inflammation to the rise of blood pressure. Both innate and adaptive immunity can take part.

The review describes how macrophages, neutrophils, and dendritic cells release inflammatory signals. It also covers T cell products such as interferon-gamma and interleukin-17, which promote oxidative stress. Regulatory T cells and M2 macrophages may protect against pressure rise. The authors map these pathways in disease onset and growth. They close with new ideas for treatment targets in hypertension.
fbi-vault-special-counsel-mueller-invest: The largest withholding log in this set of Federal Bureau of Investigation releases belongs to release 25 of the Special Counsel Mueller investigation records. Its deleted-page sheet counts 433 pages withheld in full. Long runs of pages are marked with a single word: Duplicate. Those pages are treated as copies of pages freed elsewhere in the case. Other runs carry the b5 mark, tied to the Justice Department, with privacy marks beside it. The part tells how much of this release was held back, and on what grounds.
fitzgerald-great-gatsby-1925:
F. Scott Fitzgerald published The Great Gatsby in 1925, his novel of Jay Gatsby's green-light pursuit of Daisy Buchanan. The tale moves through the glitter and rot of 1920s Long Island,. It sold modestly then and rose after Fitzgerald's death to near the summit of American novels.

Nick Carraway, a bond salesman from the Midwest, rents beside Gatsby's mansion and is drawn into his parties and past. Gatsby, born Gatz, built a bootleg fortune to win Daisy, now wed to brutal Tom Buchanan of East Egg. A hit-and-run, a garage killing, and Gatsby's own murder drain the dream of its gold in the end at summer's close. Nick's narration weighs the careless rich and the dreamer who outshone them in a prose of rare lyric polish throughout. The green light across the bay remains America's emblem of longing.
ford-no-more-parades-1925:
No More Parades, published in 1925, is the second volume of Parade's End and its great war book. Christopher Tietjens now serves as an officer in France, holding a draft of men together under shelling, mud, and absurd orders.

Sylvia follows him to the front, trailing scandal, while his mind keeps returning to Valentine Wannop and the England that is vanishing. Ford, who served himself, writes battle as confusion, noise, and moral pressure rather than glory. The trenches are rendered as a modernist time-piece, memory and terror interleaved. Many judge this the finest volume of the four.
frus-1861-d125:
On 30 May 1861, William H. Seward wrote to William Dayton, his minister in France. The letter is document 125 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's end of May orders to Paris matched his stern line to London that month. Both envoys were told to block any step toward the South. The letter shows one policy worked through two capitals at once, each with its own risks. The stern May line worked, and neither capital took the step the South craved. The step the South craved, recognition, stayed unmade in both capitals all year.
frus-1861-d225:
Writing home was Mr. Fay's duty, and his letter of 7 June 1861 went to Seward. Congress received it as Document 225 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The date falls in the opening months of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d25:
On 6 May 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Henry Sanford at the Brussels post. The letter is document 25 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's May orders went out as the Union blockade of Southern ports took shape. Envoys had to explain that step and defend its force in law. A letter to Brussels put those points in Sanford's hands, ready for use with the Belgian court and press. The blockade had been declared in April, and its law was now the front line of the paper war. Law, argued well, could hold a blockade that ships alone could not.
frus-1862-d125:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 8 August 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 125 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d225:
William Stuart wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 August 1862, and the letter is printed as Document 225 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was acting for Lord Lyons at the British legation in Washington.

August opened with the war's center shifting back to northern Virginia, where a new campaign was gathering. Stuart's letters to Seward carried British requests and protests in the formal manner of the legation. Read with Seward's replies around it, this letter shows the two offices grinding through wartime business. They ground on even as armies moved within a few days' ride of the capital.
frus-1862-d25:
Washington's orders went out to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London in a dispatch dated 28 February 1862. Congress received it as Document 25 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It belongs to the winter of the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d325:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 12 September 1862 in a letter printed as Document 325 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Five days later the armies met at Antietam, but in Paris the talk was of mediation drafts and Mexican reinforcements. Dayton's job was to keep those two files separate in French minds, so Mexico would not buy the South a friend. His report from this week sits in the file just before the battle news broke the pattern. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d425:
Horace J. Perry sent this report from the Madrid legation to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 16 August 1862. It is Document 425 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Mid-August 1862 found the Madrid mission in transition, with Gustav Koerner arriving to take over as minister while Perry stayed on as secretary. Perry's reports bridged the change, keeping Washington informed about Spanish policy without a gap. Spain still held the keys to Cuba's ports, and its stance in Mexico was settling into watchful distance from France. A reader gets from letters like this the steady, factual feed on which Seward built his Spanish policy.
frus-1862-d525:
On 5 November 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to James Shepherd Pike. It is Document 525 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record laid before Congress.

November brought the dismissal of McClellan and France's proposal for joint mediation in the war, which the Union refused. Seward's orders that month repeated the refusal to every post, great and small, The Hague included. Pike's Netherlands had no part in the mediation scheme, but a single line held everywhere was the policy's strength. The dispatch is part of the late-autumn file of that year. In it the Union, bloodied but standing, told Europe plainly that the war was an American question. It said the war would stay one.
frus-1862-d625:
On 1 April 1862, the day after his previous order, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a further instruction to Edward Joy Morris at Constantinople. It is Document 625 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Back-to-back orders to the farthest post in Europe suggest an enclosure or a second subject that could not travel in the same letter. The Ottoman file's business ran to the protection of American citizens and commerce in the Levant. There, consuls did the daily work. They did it under the minister's eye. Seward's paired instructions gave Morris the Department's mind on that business in full. Together the two letters show the care Washington took with a mission three months' post from home.
frus-1863p1-d125:
Charles Francis Adams dated this dispatch 12 March 1863, though the printed volume sets it after letters of 19 March. Adams was the American minister in London, writing to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The letter is document 125 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Stray dates are a quirk of these printed files, where late or loose sheets were set where they fit. The work in the letter is Adams's own: a report from the post that tracked Britain's mind on the war. Read on its true date, it fills a gap in mid-March. Read in its printed place, it is a small lesson in how the record was built.
frus-1863p1-d225:
The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 July 1863. It is document 225 of the 1863 volume of diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Confederate agents were busy in Britain buying ships, arms, and supplies. Reports from the London legation fed Washington's protests against that trade. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d25:
This second letter of 5 January 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams in London. It is document 25 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. Paired letters like these are a mark of the exchange all through the volume.

Seward often split his orders so each sheet held one clear point. Adams, in turn, could act on each as its matter ripened in his talks with the British. This letter is the mate to document 24, written the same day. Together they open Washington's side of the London file for 1863, in the week the war took on a new cause.
frus-1863p1-d325:
To Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this formal note on 24 November 1862. It appears as document 325 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada, then a British colony, shared a long border with the Union. Worries about raids, plots, and smuggling across that line sit behind part of this correspondence. It comes from the autumn after Antietam, when Lincoln's first emancipation order had just raised the stakes for Britain. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d425:
Secretary of State William H. Seward received a letter dated 26 March 1863 from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d525:
Document 525, dated 22 May 1863, records a letter from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d625:
From Britain's chargé d'affaires William Stuart to Secretary William H. Seward: a letter dated 29 September 1863. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. Stuart was holding the British legation in Washington while Lord Lyons was away on leave, so the channel ran through him that season.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d125: Harriman wrote to Hopkins again on November 13, 1943, a day after his previous letter in this series. The new message is Document 125 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Back-to-back letters from Moscow in the summit fortnight suggest fast-moving news, though the record names no subject. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series, among the last Moscow reports before Tehran.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d225:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff sent President Roosevelt a secret memorandum aboard the Iowa on 17 November 1943 about command of British and American forces fighting Germany. It carries two draft plans, Enclosure A and Enclosure B, and states plainly that the chiefs judge Enclosure A the sounder plan.

That plan argues the war in Europe has outgrown committee control. Operations in the Mediterranean, in northwest Europe, and the strategic bombing of Germany are tied so closely that a single commander should direct all three, under the Combined Chiefs of Staff. The chiefs urge an immediate appointment, warning that even a commander named now could not be working before the end of January 1944, and that delay risks confusion at a critical time.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d25: Roosevelt and Churchill signed a joint message to Stalin on August 18, 1943, in the middle of their Quebec Conference. It is Document 25 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. A letter in two names carried extra weight in Moscow, where Stalin had long complained of fighting the Germans nearly alone. The record names the three leaders and the date. The message is printed in the Foreign Relations series as a marker of allied unity that August.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d325:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 400/1 at Cairo on 26 November 1943, on control of strategic air forces in northwest Europe and the Mediterranean. It answers the American plan to place the Eighth and Fifteenth Air Forces under one headquarters in the United Kingdom.

The British grant America's right to organize its own forces, but record their view that the plan's drawbacks far outweigh its gains. A big day-bomber mission needs up to twenty-four hours to prepare. European weather allows a launch decision only hours ahead. Attacks from bases as far apart as Britain and Italy therefore cannot truly be combined in detail. Switching forces between theaters would also demand duplicate airfields, runways, and depots, locking up men and gear. General coordination, they conclude, can be had under the present organization.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d425:
The Log of the President's trip resumes with the second Cairo stay, covering 2 to 7 December 1943, kept hour by hour by Lieutenant William Rigdon. It opens with the flight back from Tehran on 2 December.

The President's plane reached Cairo West airfield at twenty-five minutes past two, Cairo time, after a 1,290-mile flight, and Roosevelt returned to Ambassador Kirk's villa in the Mena district. That evening word came from Ankara that President Inönü would arrive on Saturday 4 December for talks with Roosevelt and Churchill. The next day's entries show the machinery turning. Major Boettiger flew to Adana at noon to meet Inönü and bring him to Cairo. The President signed a batch of bills and a Day of Prayer proclamation. He lunched with Marshall, Leahy, McCloy, Winant, and Hopkins. He met his Joint Chiefs at ten past five.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d525:
Ambassador John Gilbert Winant wrote to Secretary of State Hull from London on December 22, 1943. Winant was deeply trusted in Britain, where he had stood with Londoners through the Blitz. The State Department printed his message in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Winant's reports carried a feel for British opinion that few envoys could match, because the British treated him almost as one of their own. A late-December message belongs to the period when London was digesting the Tehran and Cairo decisions and looking toward the invasion year. For readers, it offers the alliance's most sensitive listening post reporting home at Christmas time.
frus-1944-quebec-d125:
H. Freeman Matthews, deputy director of the Office of European Affairs, wrote to General McFarland of the Joint Chiefs on September 9, 1944. He enclosed a British Foreign Office telegram instructing London's ambassador in Moscow on a joint approach to the Russians. The subject was Allied plans for occupying northern Norway if German forces withdrew.

The British wanted Moscow told the plans were old, not improvised to block Soviet troops entering Norway. Norwegian pressure on Eisenhower's headquarters, help for Norwegian resistance, and a naval base for Russia convoys were the stated reasons. Matthews suggested similar instructions go to Ambassador Harriman, so General Deane in Moscow would have the political background.
frus-1944-quebec-d225:
Hopkins telegraphed Roosevelt on September 11, 1944, after discussing the Poland cables with the State Department and General Marshall. Warsaw's garrison was fighting on as the Soviet agreement to cooperate opened a narrow chance of relief. Hopkins proposed three coordinated steps for the president to set in motion at once.

First, a message to Poland's prime minister assuring him every possible step was being taken to bring Allied assistance speedily to Warsaw. Second, a message to Marshall asking that General Deane in Moscow explore the matter fully and urgently with British and Russian officers. Third, a State Department reply to Harriman, coordinated with Marshall's instructions to Deane. The Map Room corrected Hopkins's draft in one respect: the message went to the prime minister, not the president, of Poland.
frus-1944-quebec-d25:
President Roosevelt wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on August 11, 1944. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume, in the correspondence leading to the September conference.

Mid-August brought the invasion of southern France within days and the liberation of Paris within weeks. Roosevelt's letters then balanced the final campaigns against the approach of the Quebec meeting, where lend-lease and Germany's future awaited decision. For readers, this message shows the President steering the alliance toward its autumn summit while the greatest pursuit battle of the war ran its course in France.
frus-1945-50-intel-d125:
Admiral Leahy, the president's chief of staff and a member of the intelligence authority, wrote to Director Vandenberg on 12 August 1946. Leahy spoke with the president's nearness behind him. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

A letter from Leahy in the middle of the August ruling week carried weight beyond its words. As the authority's presidential member, he linked the board to the White House that had created it. Vandenberg, pressing his group's claims hard that summer, had to heed the channel. Readers should place this paper among the settlement papers of the dispute. The board ruled, the bureau protested. The president's own man wrote to the director who had forced the question.
frus-1945-50-intel-d225:
On 26 September 1947 the First Meeting of the National Security Council sat, and the minutes of the session survive here. It survives in print as document 225 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. A new law was about to remap the whole field: the armed services, the National Security Council, and the CIA all hung on it.

The record runs item by item, the way the meeting itself ran, with each topic closed by the group's choice on it. Read with the papers before and after it, the record shows a policy taking shape one meeting at a time. The Council had been created by law only weeks before, and its first meeting set the pattern for how it would work.
frus-1945-50-intel-d25:
Admiral Ernest King, chief of naval operations and commander of the fleet, wrote to Secretary Forrestal on 9 October 1945. King was the Navy's top officer and a formidable voice in any council. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

A paper from King carries the weight of the wartime fleet behind it. The Navy's intelligence, above all its code-breaking and its Pacific networks, was a prize in the postwar argument, and King guarded naval prerogatives jealously. Readers meet the service chiefs' level of the fight here. Not drafting details, but fixed positions from men who had won a war and meant to keep their tools. Forrestal received few papers with more authority behind them.
frus-1945-50-intel-d325:
The title "National Intelligence Authority Directive No. 11" heads a text dated 16 September 1947. The State Department prints it as document 325 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The Central Intelligence Group knew its days were short, since the National Security Act would soon set up the CIA in its place.

Once a directive went out, staff worked to its terms, and later papers cite its number as their warrant. Staff could be held to each line, which is why the words were fought over before issue. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d425:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 2 was issued on 13 January 1948. It appears as document 425 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The low number with a later date tells its own story. The Council revised and reissued its early rules as the new system settled. Directives like this one set who did which work across the government. They are dry reading, but they map the real lines of power in early Cold War intelligence. A revised base rule shows the Council learning from the first months of joint work.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d125:
Secretary of the Treasury Morgenthau sent Stettinius a sharp critique of British planning on 3 November 1944. His letter, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, forwards a memorandum on the British draft of a policy directive for Germany. A copy had gone to Lord Cherwell, with the War Department's approval, he says.

The enclosed critique finds the British draft wanting either way. If it is a long-range program, Washington is not ready to decide such issues. If it is an interim one, it prejudges them. Its ninety-seven pages of detailed instructions mix principles with office detail, and so give no basis for high-level decisions. Morgenthau urges talks confined to the major interim questions, leaving detail to staff work.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d225:
“Russian Request for Financing of Acquisitions of Capital Equipment During and After the War” is a briefing book paper of 26 January 1945. Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It states what Moscow asked, and the answer the State Department proposes.

The Russians seek a credit of six billion dollars at two and a quarter percent, with repayment ending in the thirtieth year. It would cover gear for now and for true postwar needs alike. The Department would answer through Harriman in set steps. No long-range equipment can go into production until the 3-C lend-lease terms, under talk since May 1944, are settled. Action on 3-C should come before the Fourth Protocol is signed, though Washington should not stand too hard on that point. Postwar credits are a separate matter.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d25: On 26 November 1944 Roosevelt wrote to Churchill again, continuing the near-daily rhythm of their fall correspondence. The message is document 25 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. By then the two governments were deep in preparation, and even short presidential notes could settle questions that lower officials had left open for weeks.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d325:
Settling two points before the afternoon's big meeting drove this Joint Chiefs session at Yalta on February 4, 1945. Admiral Leahy said the chiefs wanted Stalin to order his General Staff into full, free, and frank talks with the American and British staffs. They also wanted a direct channel for matching moves between General Eisenhower, Field Marshal Alexander, and the Soviet command.

General Marshall backed the plan, urging that the field commanders deal with each other through the Allied military missions in Moscow. The minutes show the chiefs rehearsing their asks hours ahead of the first plenary. Coordination with the Red Army was still more hope than fact.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d425:
Churchill urged patience in Hiss's notes of the plenary of February 9, 1945. Molotov had offered amendments to the American proposal on Poland. Churchill said he was glad to see advance, but he had something to say before the report went on. He referred to private talks about the Lublin government.

This matter cannot be hurried, he insisted. A complete meeting of minds might still be reached in the time left. Only 48 hours remained, he noted, and a day's latitude might be taken if needed. To leave without agreement on Poland, he warned, would mean failing on the most dangerous and tiresome matter of all.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d125:
Secretary Byrnes invited Robert Murphy to Berlin and listed his full party in a telegram dated July 5, 1945. The message is document 125 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Murphy, the political adviser in Germany, was asked to see that proper arrangements were made for the group, due to arrive July 13.

The party totals thirty-six people. Below Byrnes stand Harriman and Murphy, plus Assistant Secretaries Clayton and Dunn. There are also specialists for every region on the agenda. They range from Bohlen and Thompson for Russian questions to Vincent for China and Dooman for the Far East. A staff of twelve handles administration and secretarial work. The roster shows the State Department arriving at Potsdam staffed for any subject the leaders might raise.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d225:
Ambassador Kirk relayed Churchill's dark mood about Russia in a telegram from Caserta on July 12, 1945. The message is document 225 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Field Marshal Alexander had confided what he had heard from the Prime Minister.

Churchill is very ill at ease about the Russians, Alexander said. Reports from Ambassador Clark Kerr's talks with Soviet officials left no doubt in Churchill's mind about Russia's ultimate intentions. Stalin was being amiable now to sweeten the atmosphere before the meeting, but several unpleasant things would likely be tabled, and even a fait accompli or two should not be ruled out. Alexander urged knotting together at once what could be salvaged of the Western way of life in Europe, Germany included.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d25:
Stalin listed his grievances at the second Kremlin conversation, on May 27, 1945, in Bohlen's memorandum. Hopkins opened by recalling that the Marshal had hinted at questions about the United States that worried him. Would he care to begin with them?
