Stalin said he would not hide behind Soviet public opinion. He would speak of the feeling created in Soviet government circles by recent American acts.

His concerns, as listed, ran wide. They covered Argentina's invitation to San Francisco, the reparations commission, and the Polish question. The curtailment of Lend-Lease and the disposal of German naval and merchant ships followed. Poland drew a heading of its own. The memorandum shows the mission turning, on its second night, into an accounting.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d325:
Soviet views on freezing enemy assets in neutral countries are reported in a Washington cable to Ambassador Winant of June 30, 1945. Moscow's embassy messages had described the Soviet stand on assets held in Switzerland, Spain, Portugal, and Sweden. The assets belonged to Finland, Rumania, Hungary, and Bulgaria.

Because those states had declared war on the Axis, Moscow argued, their resources should go to rebuilding, so state assets should not be blocked. Private assets, the Soviets said, should be blocked, with control in the hands of the Control Commissions. The Department agreed on the private assets, but parted from Moscow on the state holdings.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d425:
British proposals on the coal famine come in an aide-mémoire from the British Embassy dated July 3, 1945. It refers to the recent exchange of messages between President Truman and Prime Minister Churchill on steps in Germany to relieve Europe's threatening coal famine. London's first point concerns consultation.

Procedure should at once be concerted, the Embassy says, for consulting the Soviet government on the question, as well as the French, whom Washington had already approached. It is common ground, London adds, that Germany should be administered as a whole, under policies agreed by the four controlling powers. The note then turns to amendments in the draft directive the President proposed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d525:
Russian absence from Europe's economic bodies is the problem in a briefing book paper dated July 3, 1945. Its recommendation matches its title. It would obtain Soviet agreement to take part fully in four bodies. They are the Emergency Economic Committee for Europe, the European Coal Organization, the European Central Inland Transport Organization, and the United Maritime Authority.

The discussion admits how far matters stand from that goal. The Soviet Union has declined to participate in the first three bodies, all temporary advisory organizations for urgent continental problems. Negotiations to establish them began in the fall of 1944, and every effort was made to obtain Soviet participation. Failing that, the three were set up during May 1945 without Moscow.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d625:
From Moscow on July 10, 1945, reparations chief Edwin Pauley sent an urgent secret wire to Ralph Davies. Davies was deputy head of the Petroleum Administration for War. The wire is document 625 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam, with a copy to the White House.

Pauley asks Davies to rush him two sets of figures. First, the tanker needs for supplying Western and Mediterranean Europe from Anglo-U.S. oil sources. Second, the rough tanker saving if Austrian, Hungarian, and Rumanian sources could be used in full. He refers to Davies's letter of June 29, which had set out the western oil needs. The short wire is a working step in the push, seen across this file, to free East European oil for Allied use.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1025:
Philip Mosely wrote to William Clayton on July 21, 1945, about a Soviet proposal by Ivan Maisky. Maisky had urged immediate internationalization of the Ruhr. Mosely warns that the plan would revise the agreed occupation zones at Britain's expense. It would strip the larger part of the British zone's resources. That would come only weeks after America honored the zone lines.

He recalls that Truman refused Churchill's plea to hold the May advance line as a bargaining chip. America withdrew on its pledged word. Mosely's advice is to press Russia instead to start the agreed Control Machinery at once. Experience with that machinery, he argues, will teach more about lasting Ruhr control than a sudden new scheme.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1125: Acting War Shipping Administrator Conway wrote this internal note to Morse, aide to the War Shipping Administrator, on 20 July 1945. It belongs to the office that ran America's merchant fleet in wartime. The note is short staff business between two men in the same agency. Morse served as chief aide to Administrator Land, and Conway held the acting post under him.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1225:
Sato, Japan's ambassador in Moscow, replied to Foreign Minister Togo on 18 July 1945. His seat gave him the hard side of the errand: Soviet doors were not opening. Moscow stalled, smiled, and said little that Tokyo could use.

Sato's reports home carried that cold news in careful words. He dealt with Soviet officials face to face and read their delays for what they were. Washington read his cables too, through its codebreakers, and learned that Japan's peace feelers were failing. This dispatch is the Moscow end of a dying hope, written by the man sent to keep it alive.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1325:
The Economic Subcommittee issued its report of 1 August 1945, the summit's last full day. By then the money terms of the peace were nearly fixed. A closing report from the experts summed up the economic brief at the point of decision.

The group's work had run through the whole conference: German industry, food, reparations, and trade. Its reports gave the ministers agreed facts to bargain over. This final one belongs to the endgame. It shows the staff layer finishing its task as the leaders finished theirs, and it closes the subcommittee's run in the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1425:
The Soviet delegation put a proposal before the conference on 23 July 1945, in the run of late papers printed near the volume's end. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

By the second week at Potsdam, proposals were no longer opening bids; they were moves in a closing game. Each side knew the others' lines and drafted to shift them by inches. This Soviet proposal can be read against the final protocol of 1 August to see what those inches came to. The editors chose to print the drafting trail, not just the results. That choice makes the volume a record of negotiation rather than a trophy case.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-125:
Another staff memorandum from the United States delegation bears the date July 27, 1945. Two memos from the team on one day reflect the conference's late pace. Each handled a strand of business that could not wait. The paper joined the files later printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

What such a memo offers is a fixed point. It states what its writer held to be true or needed on that day. Later events can be measured against it. Readers tracing a topic through the volume will find these memos useful mileposts. They mark where thought stood before the final bargains were struck.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-25:
No official record survives of a garden talk on July 19, 1945, and the editors print a diary entry instead. The talk is covered by an editorial note in volume two of the Potsdam papers. Secretary Stimson's diary for that day supplies the only account.

Stimson writes that Lord Cherwell called at noon. The two men, with Harvey Bundy, sat out under the trees and talked over S-1. Cherwell was very reasonable on notifying the Russians, Stimson records. He felt about as doubtful on that question as the Americans did. Cherwell also reported Churchill much pleased with their luncheon together that week. The talk, he said, had much cheered the prime minister. The diary fragment is the only trace of a key side discussion on the atomic project at Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d725:
Samuel Reber, special assistant to the director of European affairs, wrote this memorandum on July 18, 1945. Document 725 dates from the Potsdam Conference's second day. Reber was a career officer with deep European service. His memos carried the working knowledge of the Department's Europe hands. The paper joined the second Potsdam volume.

Staff memoranda like Reber's formed the briefs behind the briefs. Leaders read summaries; men like Reber wrote the layers beneath. Readers find in such papers the facts officials trusted. The memo shows the conference's first days being fed by quiet, expert work done far from the cameras.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d825:
The Acting Secretary wrote to Melbourne in Rumania on July 28, 1945, in document 825. Washington answered its acting representative in Bucharest in the conference's last days. The letter carried guidance from the home office. It was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

Guidance sent this late had to reckon with the summit's results. Melbourne would soon work inside the settlement's terms. Readers see Washington preparing its man for that change. The document closes a circuit opened by his many reports. Facts had flowed up for two weeks; now direction flowed down, shaped by Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d925:
The United States submitted this final Pauley version of its reparations position to the Economic Sub-Committee on July 24 or 25, 1945. It presents a plan for exacting reparations from Germany in a practical way. The program of removals would run through the occupation machinery already set up in Germany.

The plan allows removals to start at once, as an interim scheme. It pairs west and east in a swap. Steel equipment from the Ruhr would go to the Soviet Union. In return, farm goods, fuels, timber, and potash from the east would flow to western Europe. The attached proposal text repeats the zonal removal rules, with imports paid before other removals.
frus-1955-57v25:
Eastern Europe fills Volume XXV of the 1955–1957 set, with Romania, Bulgaria, and Hungary in the main blocks. The Hungarian revolt of 1956 stands at the center. Refugees, relief, and the world's response fill long runs.

Trade and aid questions with the satellite states run alongside. The papers show free-world hopes raised and then checked by Soviet tanks. Refugee files run to thousands of names and camps. Each policy choice was weighed in public and in private, and the two records read very differently. The revolt's files close on trials and quiet reprisals.
frus-1961-63v25:
Volume XXV of the 1961–1963 set gathers the machinery: foreign policy's organization, information policy, the United Nations, and scientific matters. White House coordination and State Department reform lead. Intelligence files follow.

Information policy takes the next block. The UN run is the longest, with votes and funds in the files. Human rights, refugees, and narcotics take short runs. Space closes the volume, with Soviet-American space talks. The set ends at the switchboard. These papers show how the machine itself was rebuilt while the crises ran. Refugee and narcotics files sit between the larger blocks.
frus-1964-68v25:
Volume XXV of the 1964-1968 series is devoted to South Asia. The bulk of the volume covers India and Pakistan together, in 526 documents. A short closing chapter covers Afghanistan. The papers follow food aid to India, arms for both states, and the 1965 war between them. They also trace U.S. efforts to restart aid after that war.

Cables from New Delhi and Karachi mix with memos from Washington. Presidents Johnson, Ayub Khan, and Prime Minister Nehru all appear in talks on aid. The records show Washington trying to feed India while keeping both states from war. Food, in the end, mattered as much as weapons.
frus-1969-76v25:
Volume XXV of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1969-1976, is devoted to the Arab-Israeli crisis and war of 1973. Its 425 documents run in one sequence. They open with the surprise attack of October 1973. They follow the U.S. airlift to Israel and the push for a cease-fire. The nuclear alert of late October appears in the records. Shuttle talks in November close the main run.

Meeting records show Kissinger pressing the military chiefs on supply flights. Cables from Cairo, Tel Aviv, and Moscow fill the war chapters. The papers trace how the war reshaped U.S. ties with both sides. Oil and the Arab embargo form the backdrop throughout.
gao-gaoreports-b-297225:
Information Ventures protested the terms of a Navy call for toxic study help in GAO decision B-297225, dated December 1, 2005. The user was the Navy Environmental Health Center. The call asked for nine sample study reports. The firm said that count was too high. It also hit the post note and the trade tag for the work.

GAO denied the protest. The record backed a need for just one sample report. The call did ask for too much on that point. But the firm did not show it could meet the need for one. With no proof it could meet one, the high count did it no harm. No harm means no win, even when a term is too broad.
gao-gaoreports-b-297425:
Prudent Technologies protested a Housing award for lead checks in GAO decision B-297425, dated January 5, 2006. The winner was Tidewater. The region was the Denver region. The work was lead tests on single family homes held by the agency. The firm's bid was ruled not fit on tech grounds.

GAO denied the protest. The bid lacked facts the call asked for. That lack was clear on the record. Marks fit the scheme in the call and were sound. A bid that skips asked facts can be cut as not fit. The firm had to give the facts in the bid. It could not cure the gap in a protest. The award thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-297825:
Allied Protection Services protested the terms of a Defense call for guard work in GAO decision B-297825, dated March 23, 2006. The user was the Pentagon Force Protection Agency. The call required a secret site pass before bids were due. The agency would not back new firms for that pass. The firm said those terms shut out fair play.

GAO denied the protest. The pass term tracked a real need. Work had to start on the set date with no delay. A firm with no pass could not start on time. The choice not to back new firms fit that need. Strict guard terms can stand when start time is key.
gao-gaoreports-b-310725:
Fraud case cash may not be kept by a watchdog office in this GAO decision, B-310725, dated May 20, 2008. The National Science Foundation's Inspector General wins cash back in False Claims Act cases. Part of that cash stands for the cost of the probe. The office asked if it could add that part to its own funds. Congress sets the office's funds as a fixed sum each year.

GAO held that it may not. The cash is no true repayment of the office's funds. That slim carve-out does not fit here. Adding the cash would swell the fixed sum with no leave in law. The cash must go to the Treasury as the law directs.
gao-gaoreports-b-310825:
DRSC3 Systems, LLC won part of its protest. GAO ruled in B-310825 on February 26, 2008. The firm raised five claims in its fight. One said a rival had set the gauge for the goods and thus held a head start. One said talks were thin on its weak spots. Two hit the tech scores of the bids. The last hit the past-work score of the winner.

GAO split its ruling. Gains from past work for the state are not unfair gains. Talks flagged the key weak spot in plain terms. The tech scores held up as fair. But the past-work score was flawed. Its notes clashed with the facts they drew on.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1025:
The Kennedy Center's federal building work is rechecked in GAO-06-1025, a report dated September 15, 2006. In April 2005, GAO urged tighter oversight of federal funds. It also urged better fire code compliance and sound project management. This report grades progress on those calls. It covers the state of federally funded projects and planned spending. It also tests the board's oversight role.

GAO found steps taken, with more work to do. The center hired the Smithsonian's inspector general to audit federal funds on building projects. A peer review of its fire study led to changes in that study. Rules for contracts, money, and project control were written. The 2005 building plan shows renovations will miss the planned 2008 finish and budgets, GAO found. Costs for the remaining projects have risen.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-125:
Navy Reserve staffing needs are reassessed in GAO-06-125, a report GAO issued on October 18, 2005. In 2004 the Navy studied how many selected reserve members it needs to back the active force. The 2005 defense law ordered GAO to judge that study. GAO reviewed the criteria and process the Navy used.

The Navy ran a structured review but skipped a key test. It never weighed the cheapest mix of active and reserve staff, though defense rules demand that test. Some units also worked from outdated mission papers. The approved changes would cut over 16,000 reserve posts. They would add about 880 active posts and about 450 civilian posts. The Navy first estimated savings near $283.5 million a year. GAO urged cost checks and fresh data before such shifts are locked in.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-25:
Teacher qualification rules under the No Child Left Behind Act are tracked in GAO-06-25, dated November 21, 2005. The 2001 law told teachers of core subjects to meet set standards by the end of the 2005-2006 school year. Congress has given about $3 billion a year for teacher improvement under the law. GAO checked how states were doing against the deadline. It traced how chosen districts spent the federal funds. It also judged how the Education Department watches and helps the states.

GAO reviewed data from 47 states and visited 6 states and 11 high-need districts. One snag was simple: key facts on the department's Web site were hard to find. GAO urged the Secretary of Education to make that guidance easier to reach. A clearer link to state teacher efforts and a better search tool were the fixes. The department agreed and said steps were already under way.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-425:
Junk faxes waste paper and toner and tie up fax machines. Report GAO-06-425, issued April 5, 2006, reviews how the ban on junk faxes is enforced. A 1991 law barred faxes that send ads to homes and firms without consent. A 2005 law made clear when a past business tie counts as an exemption. It also set opt-out steps for people who get such faxes.

The 2005 law told the Federal Communications Commission to report to Congress each year. It also told GAO to report on the agency's work. GAO checked the agency's steps and results and weighed their strengths and flaws. Weak steps and weak handling of performance hinder enforcement, GAO found.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-525:
Taxpayers who cannot pay in full may offer to settle for less. Report GAO-06-525, issued April 20, 2006, reviews the Internal Revenue Service's offers in compromise program. Under such an offer, a taxpayer pays what they can afford. The agency writes off the rest of the tax owed. In 2005, the agency accepted over 14,000 offers. A new type of offer based on exceptional circumstances raised concern.

GAO described trends in program performance and their causes. It judged whether rules for the new offers fit the statute. It examined timeliness, quality, access, compliance, and cost. Performance has been mixed, GAO found. Better data and simpler rules could help.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-625:
Grant management at the Environmental Protection Agency is the subject of GAO-06-625, a report GAO issued on May 12, 2006. Grants make up over half of the agency budget, about $4 billion a year. The agency awards grants through 93 programs to states, tribes, universities, and nonprofit groups. In 2003, the agency set out a five-year plan to fix long-running grant problems.

GAO found that the award process had grown stronger, but key paperwork was often missing. In-depth checks on grantees had improved, while routine monitoring and grant closeout still lagged. Work to show what grants achieve was not yet complete. Staff and resource management also faced major problems. GAO urged the agency to finish its reforms and tighten accountability.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-825:
The fight against human trafficking abroad is assessed in GAO report GAO-06-825, issued on July 18, 2006. Trafficking buys, sells, and holds men, women, and children against their will. Beyond the harm to victims, it fuels criminal networks and public health costs. A 2000 law set the United States on a global antitrafficking course. GAO reviewed the data, strategy, and reporting behind that effort.

GAO found that estimates of global trafficking are questionable. United States data collection on the crime is fragmented across agencies. No overall strategy or performance measures exist to judge success abroad. The State Department's yearly report ranks foreign governments on their efforts. GAO said that report has limited credibility and uneven influence. Better data and strategy, GAO urged, are basic needs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-25:
Air travel could triple by 2025, and the old control system cannot stretch that far. GAO assessed the rebuild in GAO-07-25, a report dated November 13, 2006. Congress created a joint planning office in 2003 to design the next system. Seven agencies share the work, led by the aviation agency. GAO reviewed the plan's status and the hurdles ahead. It also convened a panel of experts.

The planning office had built a sound framework, GAO found. Partners agreed on a vision and eight strategies. An integrated plan and progress reports were in place. Work had begun on a system blueprint and cost figures. But roles stayed fuzzy, GAO said. Procedures for settling disputes and tapping partner funds were unwritten. The space agency's research budget was set to fall 30 percent by 2011. That shift could leave new technology half-developed. GAO listed five steps to firm up the joint effort.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-425:
Hiring and keeping skilled tech staff at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is covered in GAO-07-425, dated September 10, 2007. A fiscal year 2006 spending law told the DHS chief information officer to file an IT workforce plan. The law also told GAO to review that plan. GAO matched it against 27 proven workforce practices.

The plan fit federal guidance in most respects, and a sound base existed. Some key practices were still thin, though. Actual rollout had barely begun across the department. GAO blamed blurry roles and low priority next to rival tech demands. Three component agencies were checked for early action. GAO pressed DHS to sharpen the plan and push it out in full, so the staff who run its systems stay strong.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-825:
Chemical safety rules in the United States and Europe are compared in GAO-07-825, dated August 17, 2007. The Toxic Substances Control Act of 1976 guides U.S. policy. The European Union's new system is called REACH. It stands for Registration, Evaluation and Authorization of Chemicals. GAO set the two side by side on three points. It asked who must produce safety data, how risks get curbed, and what the public learns. GAO made no recommendations in the report.

REACH forces firms to gather and share data on their chemicals' effects. It covers old and new chemicals made in set volumes. Under the U.S. law, the burden sits on the Environmental Protection Agency. It must prove data are needed before firms must test. Firms need only notify the agency before making a new chemical. REACH treats data duties as the maker's job. That split shapes how fast risks come to light.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-925:
Asian American and Pacific Islander students are profiled in GAO-07-925, dated July 25, 2007. The group holds about 8 percent of college degrees. It makes up about 5 percent of the population. Nearly half of its adults held a four-year degree in 2005. Incomes lead all other groups on average. Group averages hide wide subgroup gaps, though. Asian Indian and Chinese adults hold degrees at high rates. Vietnamese, Cambodian, Laotian, and Hmong adults lag far behind. Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander incomes sit lowest.

Entry education and immigration status explain much of the spread. Students from poorer subgroups face cost and language hurdles. Colleges with many such students use targeted aid and outreach. Good practices stay locked inside single campuses, though. GAO urged the Education Department to spread what works. Sharing should cover recruiting, retention, and graduation tactics. Outreach to poor high school students matters too. The department broadly agreed with the advice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-125:
Complaint handling at the communications regulator is reviewed in GAO report GAO-08-125 (February 15, 2008). The Federal Communications Commission gets about 100,000 complaints a year. It may probe them and act when telecom laws are broken. Those laws guard access to services such as 911, among other aims.

From 2003 through 2006, one bureau logged 454,000 complaints. About 95 percent were closed with a letter or a referral to the firm involved. Formal actions were few. GAO found that weak data systems and few performance goals make the program hard to judge. It urged better data and clearer measures of results.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-25:
In GAO-08-25, dated October 19, 2007, GAO examined the energy futures watchdog and the markets it guards. Prices for crude oil, heating oil, gasoline, and natural gas have climbed steeply since 2002. Some blame shifts in supply and demand. Others point to heavier futures trading. GAO opened the study on its own authority.

The report traces trends in both physical and derivatives markets. It maps the legal reach of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission over them. It then tests how well the agency spots and acts on abuse. Trader data and talks with market players and six agencies ground the work. Its title warns that oversight questions remain.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-325:
GAO report GAO-08-325, dated April 30, 2008, reviews the Department of Defense's global strike concept. Global strike aims to hit high-value targets fast, at long range, with precision weapons. GAO assessed how well the concept is defined, what capabilities exist, and how funding needs are set.

GAO found that combatant commanders read the concept in different ways, and that outreach, doctrine, and joint training lagged. The department had studies under way on strike weapons, including prompt global strike options for sometime after 2018. But it had not fully assessed the support capabilities that strikes need. GAO made eight recommendations to tighten communication and build a prioritized investment strategy. The department agreed with the report and all eight recommendations.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-525:
In GAO report GAO-08-525, issued June 27, 2008, GAO looks at encryption of federal data. Breaches at many agencies have raised fears about sensitive data on laptops, handheld devices, and portable media. Encryption scrambles data so only key holders can read it.

GAO found strong commercial tools exist to lock files, folders, and whole drives, and to guard data moving across networks. Poor setup, weak key care, or untrained users can still leave data exposed or lost for good. The Federal Information Security Management Act of 2002, the Privacy Act of 1974, and health privacy law frame the duties. GAO urged the budget office to sharpen its guidance and picked agencies to plan better. Both generally agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-825:
A mock cyber attack called Cyber Storm tested how agencies and firms fight back together. The first drill ran in February 2006. GAO-08-825, dated September 9, 2008, lists the eight lessons the homeland security department drew from it and grades the fixes since.

Lessons covered teamwork, planning, shared data, public messaging, and tools. The department lined up 66 fix tasks and finished most of them. A full 16 tasks are still under way and 7 are only planned. The second drill in 2008 echoed many of the same points. GAO urges the department to set dates and finish the rest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-925:
Federal technology projects often reset their goals, and GAO-08-925, a July 2008 report, asks how often and under what rules. The government planned to spend about $70 billion on IT in fiscal year 2008. Resetting a project's cost, schedule, and performance baseline can reflect real change, but it can also hide overruns and delays. GAO surveyed managers of 180 projects drawn from 778 major projects at the 24 biggest agencies.

About 48 percent of major projects had been rebaselined, and of those, 51 percent were reset twice or more and 11 percent four times or more. Changed requirements drove 55 percent and funding changes 44 percent. Every big agency has a rebaselining policy, but none fully matches best practices, and the budget office has issued no guidance on what policies should contain.
ginza-rba-lidzbarski-1925:
The Ginza Rba, the Great Treasure, is the holy book of the Mandaeans, a small faith that survives in Iraq and Iran. Mark Lidzbarski's German rendering of 1925 is the standard scholarly version. The Mandaeans prize John the Baptist and hold light and life as twin first powers.

The book holds their tale of creation, hymns, prayers, and the soul's road through the worlds of dark and light. It tells how the soul must pass guards and rivers to reach its home on high. Lidzbarski spent a life on the Mandaean tongue to make this version. His work opened a whole scripture to the learned world.
gitlow-v-new-york-1925:
Gitlow v. New York, decided by the United States Supreme Court on June 8, 1925, is hosted here as the Court's official syllabus, the numbered summary of its holdings. Benjamin Gitlow, a socialist leader, had been convicted under New York's criminal anarchy law for a manifesto urging mass strikes to overthrow the government.

The syllabus records two holdings that pull in opposite ways. The Court upheld the conviction, saying a state may punish speech that urges the violent overthrow of government. Yet it also assumed, for the first time, that free speech and a free press bind the states through the Fourteenth Amendment. That second point later became the base for most modern speech law.
glasgow-barren-ground-1925:
Ellen Glasgow considered Barren Ground, published in 1925, her best novel. Glasgow wrote it after years of success with Richmond society stories. This time she set her story on worn-out Virginia farmland and made a working woman its hero.

Dorinda Oakley is betrayed in love as a young woman and flees to New York. She returns home determined to restore her family's ruined farm by science and sheer will. Across thirty years she drains, plants, and prospers, while love offers her a second, harder choice. Glasgow reverses the usual plot: the land, not a husband, is the prize worth winning. Barren Ground is a landmark of American regional fiction.
hemingway-in-our-time-1925:
Ernest Hemingway published In Our Time in New York in 1925, his first book with a major American publisher. Hemingway had built the collection from stories written in Paris, where he worked among the modernist writers of the Left Bank. The book made his reputation.

Nick Adams grows up across the stories: fishing in Michigan, wounded in the war, drifting through Europe after it. Between the tales, short brutal vignettes show bullfighters, soldiers, and refugees. Hemingway's style, short sentences and telling omissions, changed American prose at a stroke. Stories like Big Two-Hearted River and The Doctor and the Doctor's Wife remain classics. In Our Time is the founding book of his career.
history-of-egypt-chald-a-syria-babylonia:
Gaston Maspero's fifth volume carries on the Eighteenth Theban Dynasty. Thutmosis the Third stands at its center, as empire builder. His taking of Qodshu in his forty-second year is retold. Tribute from the south and the triumph song of Amon follow.

Amenothes the Third and the worshippers of Aton close the volume's arc. Vassal kings, royal gifts, and marriages bind the Syrian provinces to Pharaoh. Foreigners' standing in Egypt is set out with care. A later section shows Ramses the Second at war in the south. Readers get Egypt at its widest reach, ruling by sword, gold, and letter.
holdsworth-history-english-law-vol7-1925:
The seventh volume of Holdsworth's History of English Law appeared in 1925. Holdsworth's project, pursued at Oxford over decades, aimed to record the whole growth of English law. By the seventh volume the story had passed the age of revolution and entered calmer waters.

Volume 7 covers the eighteenth century, the age of Mansfield in the courts and Blackstone in the study. Holdsworth describes a law polished into system: commercial law modernized for a trading nation, and the great commentaries giving the whole a shape students could learn. It was the law's Augustan age, elegant and confident. Holdsworth treats it with the respect of a man who loved the tradition he chronicled. The volume remains a standard guide to the century that made the common law a world system.
holdsworth-history-english-law-vol8-1925:
Holdsworth issued the eighth volume of his History of English Law in 1925. The history had grown from medieval beginnings through revolution and Augustan polish. Its author, by now the dean of English legal historians, turned to the century of reform.

Volume 8 covers the first half of the nineteenth century. Bentham's fierce attack on the old law opens the story, and the great reforms follow. Courts were rebuilt, procedures simplified, and whole fields of law cleaned of archaic clutter. Holdsworth tells of the law's modernization with the zeal of a historian who had lived to see its results. The old order is swept away in these pages, reform's triumph recorded act by act. The volume is essential reading on how Victorian England remade its law.
homer-odyssey-pope-1725:
Homer's Odyssey came to Augustan England in Alexander Pope's version of 1725 to 1726. Pope's Odyssey was the companion piece to his Iliad of the decade before in couplets. He shared the work with two helpers, Fenton and Broome, though his name crowned the title.

Odysseus sails through monsters and tempests toward Penelope and his rocky isle of Ithaca. Pope's couplets give the sea tale a smooth, bright, and courtly English polish and grace. The suitors' slaughter and the test of the great bow close the homecoming plot in Ithaca. Notes by Broome filled out the learning that Pope's verse wore so lightly for readers. Together the Pope Homers fixed Augustan taste for classical epic in English verse.
james-warning-to-the-curious-1925:
Late ghost tales by M. R. James fill A Warning to the Curious, his set from 1925. The lead tale warns a man who digs for a lost crown on the coast. Old lore guards the crown. Theft wakes a thin, grim shade that will not rest.

Each tale is lean, clear, and full of dread. James wastes no word. A small wrong step leads to a vast price. Fans treat the set as his ripe best work. It is the yardstick for the short ghost tale. The coast tales use flat sands, grey seas, and lone paths to fine effect. Place does half the work of fear in James's late craft.
jaufre-occitan-breuer-1925:
Jaufre is the great Arthurian romance of the troubadour lands, written in Occitan, the old tongue of the south of France. Hermann Breuer's 1925 critical edition prints the full poem, 10,955 verses in all. Its hero is a young knight who comes to Arthur's court seeking deeds.

Jaufre rides out to face giants, enchantments, and a proud foe who shames the court. The tale mixes high adventure with the wit and grace of the southern courts. No other Occitan romance of Arthur survives at this scale. Breuer's edition is the scholar's door into that lost shelf of song.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-25:
Death comes for Jogues in Volume 25, published by Thwaites in 1898. The book covers the years 1644 and 1645 across Iroquois and French lands. Mohawk men kill the peacemaker who had come to save them.

Fellow priests tell of his death with heartbreaking, plain simplicity. They count him a saint even as they write the sad news. Grief runs through the reports, yet the mission work goes on. Baptisms, burials, and brave journeys fill the months that follow. His blood, in their eyes, seals the mission he loved and served so well. Sorrow and pride fill the closing reports of this book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-cupino-or: Aaron Cupino, also spelled Kupino, taught Talmud and headed a school at Constantinople. He flourished about the close of the seventeenth century. He had studied under Ḥayyim Shabbethai at Salonica, then moved and founded his school. Its graduates included Aaron ben Isaac Sason and Isaac Raphael Alfandari. Cupino also wrote letters on learned questions to R. Benveniste and other scholars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-b-abina-12: Abba ben Abina was an amora who flourished in the third century. Born in Babylonia, he was a pupil of Rab. He moved to Palestine and became known in tradition chiefly for his haggadic sayings. One piece of his is singled out for praise. It is a confession he wrote for the Day of Atonement. In it he admits his sins, vows not to repeat them, and asks God to blot out his wrongs and pardon all his sins.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abelard-peter-2:
Peter Abelard was a French schoolman, thinker, and divine, called the boldest mind of the twelfth century. Born in 1079 near Nantes, he died in 1142 at the priory of St. Marcel. At the height of his fame as a teacher he fell into a love affair with Heloise, niece of Canon Fulbert. He wed her in secret, and her kin took revenge by maiming him.

The entry centers on his "Colloquy" among a thinker, a Jew, and a Christian. The Jew there defends the Old Testament from the charge of being a creed of flesh and gain. Abelard, the entry notes, spoke against the harsh rules that had penned Jews into trade and money-lending. Those rules, he held, made or swelled the very traits men blamed in Jews. He longed for leave to think, and seems to have wished that leave for all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abiob-simon-b-d: Simon b. David Abiob was a cabalist of the seventeenth century. He moved to Hebron, described as one of the chief gathering places for Jewish mystics of his day. His work "Bat Melek" (The King's Daughter) dealt with cabalistic questions. Solomon Altaras edited that work at Venice in 1712. The short entry gives no birth or death dates and names no other writings, so its record rests on the move to Hebron and the one book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-eli:
Polish preacher Abraham ben Eliezer ha-Kohen flourished in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. He was a great-grandson of Issachar Baer, the Rabbot commentator. At Amsterdam in 1673 he edited his grandfather's work Mareh Kohen and added a preface.

Later he went blind. Forty years on, well advanced in years, he published Ori we-Yish'i at Berlin in 1714. The book holds chosen sermons on repentance, prayer, and charity. Its title, My Light and My Salvation, points to two events: he regained his sight, and he escaped a dangerous fire unharmed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-de-meyr: Abraham de Meyrargues was a physician who lived in Marseilles, France, during the first quarter of the fifteenth century. Town records of trade and office name him for the years 1405-13. That is the whole of his record in the text provided. No family, work, or death date is given, and the entry rests on two French sources on doctors at Marseilles and on Jewish life in France.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abramowitsch-so:
Solomon (Shalom) Jacob Abramowitsch was a Hebrew and Judæo-German writer born at Kopyl, Lithuania, in 1836. He is also known as Mendele Mocher Seforim, or Mendele the Bookseller. He studied Talmud as a boy. After his father died in 1849, he wandered between towns. He learned in Slutsk and Wilna. Later moves took him through Volhynia and Podolia. Those travels taught him how Russian Jews lived.

Abramowitsch became a teacher in 1856. That year his first essay, "On Education," ran in "Ha-Maggid." He wrote on politics and science in Hebrew. His books include "Mishpaṭ Shalom" in 1860 and "'En Mishpaṭ" in 1866. His 1868 novel "Ha-Abot we-ha-Banim" shows old and young Jews in conflict. His tales of common folk, in Judæo-German, shaped the style of Yiddish writing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-accusatory-and-:
Accusatory and inquisitorial procedure are two ways to try a man charged with a crime. In the first, a charge is put in writing. The state or the harmed side must prove it with witnesses. If proof fails, the man goes free. In the second, judges grill the man and press him to confess. In past days they used the rack or thumbscrew.

Britain and the United States use the first way only. Both bar confessions won by playing on hope or fear. The entry says the Jewish sages built a like system from the written law. It goes one step more. It makes no use at all of a man's own confession. Two or three witnesses must set the facts. A man can not make himself out guilty by his own mouth. Sages asked for a confession only near the end.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adler-liebmann-:
Liebmann Adler was an American rabbi born at Lengsfeld, in Germany, on January 9, 1812. He died in Chicago on January 29, 1892. He trained in Bible and rabbinic lore at Lengsfeld and Gelnhausen. He also studied at the Talmud school in Frankfort. He then took a course for teachers at Weimar. His first post was as teacher in his home town.

In 1854 he sailed for America. He soon won a post at Detroit as teacher and preacher. In 1861 the Anshe Ma'arabh flock of Chicago called him. He stayed with that flock to his death. In his last years it freed him from most duties of the post. He was a mild man who shunned all strife. In faith he held a careful line, with mild reform in rite. In 1890 he put out three books of sermons. A choice of them in English came out in 1893 as "Sabbath Hours."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aguilar-aguylar:
Moses Raphaelde Aguilar was born probably in Portugal. He died in Amsterdam on December 15, 1679. At Amsterdam he served as hakam. He was also principal of the Talmud Torah. In 1642 he sailed to Brazil with Isaac Aboab da Fonseca. He went as hazan and stayed for years. The Portuguese reconquest then sent him back to Amsterdam. There he took up his former post again.

At the school he taught Talmud and Hebrew grammar. His Hebrew was so fluent that he spoke it with pupils. He stayed in office for forty years. He wrote an approbation for Abraham Israel Pereyra. He published works on Hebrew grammar and ritual law. He also left about twenty works in manuscript. They were written in Spanish, Portuguese, and Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-akdamut-1025:
Akdamut is a mystical poem in Aramaic by Meir ben Isaac Nehorai. In Ashkenazic use it is sung on the first day of the Feast of Weeks. It comes just after the opening verse of the lesson from the Law. Two traditional melodies go with it, of very different ages.

The older tune is a chant in the eighth, or hypomixolydian, mode. It also serves for calling up the bridegroom of the Law on another feast. The later tune came from a cantor in Middle Germany, in the eighteenth century. It grew into a theme for the whole festival. Its finest setting, the entry says, is by J. L. Mombach, written about 1870 for the Great Synagogue of London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alhadib-alchadi:
Alhadib is the name of a family traced from the early 1300s to the late 1600s. The entry lists its known members one by one. A judge sat in Corfu in 1530. Others lived in Lepanto, Venice, Cairo, and Safed. The name itself means hunchback, the entry notes.

One member stands out for his learning. Isaac ben Solomon was a noted astronomer in Castile and Sicily. He wrote a work on reckoning time with tables from older masters. He also made new star tools of his own. A hymn for Esther bears his name in its first letters. Short notices fill the rest of the list.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-altaras-jacques:
Jacques Isaac Altaras built ships and gave to good causes. He was born in Aleppo in Syria in 1786. He died in France on Jan. 30, 1873. He left Jerusalem in 1806 for Marseilles. There he built ships and traded with the Levant. He did well in that trade.

Mid-century he took up a bold plan for Russian Jews. He sought leave for 40,000 families to move to Algeria. He went to St. Petersburg in 1846 to press the plea. The czar's terms called for a hard cash payment. Altaras saw the plan could not stand and dropped it. He led the Marseilles Consistory for thirty years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anglo-jewish-as:
Anglo-Jewish Association names a body formed by Jews of the British empire. Its aims were to lift the social, moral, and mental progress of Jews. It also sought protection for anyone who suffered for being a Jew.

The idea had been aired years before by men such as Dr. Benisch and Dr. A. Löwy, on the model of the Alliance Israélite Universelle in Paris. The Franco-German war of 1870-71 gave the push to found it. That war had stalled the Alliance's work and split French and German Jews. English Jews, prosperous and free, were urged to stand beside them and share the task.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antunes-1625: Antunes is the family name of several noted Jews, and the entry sketches them one by one. Aaron Antunes, hakam of Amsterdam about 1715, wrote to many rabbis of his day and left two works in manuscript. Luis Antunes, born in 1672, drew a life sentence from the Inquisition at Coimbra for professing Judaism. His kin Manuel, Raphael, Clara, and Beatriz met the same fate. The entry also names David, a poet on two martyrs, Gabriel, who settled in Barbados in 1680, and Aaron de Solomon, an Amsterdam printer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arbues-pedro-17:
Pedro Arbues was a Spanish canon and inquisitor, born about 1441 at Epila in Aragon and dead on September 17, 1485. Certain Jews, the entry says, called him the creature and darling of Torquemada. He became canon of Saragossa in 1474. Ten years later Torquemada made him inquisitor for Aragon.

In his first month, Arbues held two autos da fe at which several Maranos were executed and others lost property or did penance. Maranos, enraged and unable to buy limits on the Inquisition, plotted his murder. The entry names two rich Maranos who hired an assassin for the deed. It follows the plot hatched with highly placed converts, including the king's treasurer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-artaban-v-1825:
Artaban V was the last king of Parthia. A son of Volageses V, he took the throne about 216 after a struggle with his brother Volageses VI. For years he fought Rome with success, beating both Caracalla and his successor Macrinus. He died in 227, killed in his wars with the Persians, and the house of the Arsacids ended with him.

Toward the Jews he was well disposed. Abba Arika, head of the academy at Sura, received clear marks of his friendship. The king once sent him a gift of valuable pearls. Abba Arika sent back a mezuzah, a door-post inscription, with word that God's word outvalued all the gems of earth. At the king's death, Rab cried out that the bond of friendship had been sundered.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asher-ensel-b-j:
Asher Ensel ben Judah Loeb was chief of the bet din, the rabbinical court, at Slonim in Lithuania at the start of the eighteenth century. Two books of his are recorded. Otot le-Moadim, Signs for the Feasts, holds new readings on a chapter of tractate Pesahim and the laws of the festivals and half-festivals.

His second book, Baruk mi-Banim Asher, takes its title from Deuteronomy chapter 33: Blessed be Asher above sons. It is a sermon-style commentary on the Pentateuch. The two books came out at Zolkiev, the first in 1749 and the second in 1752, both after the author's active years. The entry cites Walden's Shem ha-Gedolim and Benjacob's book catalogue, and adds no personal details.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asriel-2025: Asriel is the ancestor named for the family of the Asrielites, in the genealogy of Manasseh. Numbers chapter 26 names him, and Joshua chapter 17 names him again. In First Chronicles chapter 7 the older version reads the name as Ashriel. The entry gives those references, the family that carries his name, and the spelling difference, and states nothing further about the man.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baer-beer-behr-: Baer, also written Beer or Behr, is treated here as a Jewish first name and family name. The entry derives it from the German word for bear. German Jews, it says, took names from their neighbors, above all when a like name could be found in the Bible. Jacob's words about his sons, set beside animals, made names like Baer, Wolf, and Löwe welcome. Among Polish and Russian Jews the name shrank into forms such as Baeril and Baerke, all rendered in Hebrew as Dob or Issachar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bamberger-bela-: Béla Bamberger was a Hungarian lawyer and writer on political economy, born at Szegedin in 1854. He studied law at Vienna and Budapest. The entry is brief. It calls him an authority on the currency question. Two of his works are named: one of 1890 on the background and money results of the North American currency question, and one of 1895 on the exchange tax. Both, it says, were awarded a prize by the Royal Hungarian Academy of Sciences.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bari-or-bari-de:
Bari, a seaport town in Apulia on the Adriatic, was a center of trade with Triest, Corfu, Messina, and the Orient. Yet information on its Jews is very scant. Tradition ties the settlement of Jews in southern Italy to the captives Titus brought after the sack of Jerusalem. On that account Bari must early have become a seat of Jewish influence, like Naples, Venosa, and Otranto.

When Oria was taken in 962, many of its people fled to Bari. A rabbinical school or famous teachers of the Law stood there by the twelfth century. Rabbenu Tam quotes the saying: "From Bari shall the Law go forth, and the word of the Lord from Otranto." Ibn Daud connects Bari with the four teachers who set out from its port in 960. The entry also retells the legend of Bari's people clothing the naked Babylonian exiles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-basilea-basila-:
Basilea, also spelled Bassola, was a family that came from Basel in Switzerland. Its members lived in north Italy and in Palestine from the fifteenth to the eighteenth century. The entry follows rabbis, printers, and scholars across those lands.

One early member corrected proofs of Talmud tracts at Soncino in 1489. His son Moses led an academy at Ancona, backed printing of the Zohar, and later traveled to Palestine. Later pages trace Mantua rabbis, a calendar maker, and work on the Hebrew Bible text. Moses was welcomed with great honor by the scholars of Safed after his long journey to Palestine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bat-kol-hebrew-:
Bat Kol means a heavenly voice that declares God's will, judgment, deeds, and commands. It may speak to one person, to rulers, to groups, or to whole nations. The entry first clears up the term itself, arguing it means sound or reverberation, not a simple echo.

Most of this very long entry gathers cases from Talmud and Midrash. Voices approve offerings, warn kings, settle disputes, and speak at Sinai. Later sections weigh how such a voice could guide law after prophecy ended. A full list of sources closes the piece. The bibliography points to Talmud and Midrash indexes for readers who want every passage traced.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belleli-lazarus:
Lazarus Menahem Belleli was a Greek writer on language, born in Corfu on Oct. 31, 1862. At fifteen he edited a Hebrew and Greek vocabulary for Genesis, with a sketch of Hebrew grammar. He wrote for Italian Jewish papers while studying at Athens.

Hostile attacks on Jews pushed Belleli to Italy, where he led Jewish schools at Leghorn. He gave up that post in 1890 for study in Paris. Later he reported trials after a riot at Corfu and rendered a history of the Jews into Greek in 1895. In 1899 he spoke for the Greek government at a great congress of Orientalists held abroad.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benedict-xiv-pr:
Prospero Lambertini, Benedict XIV, was born at Bologna in 1675, elected pope on Aug. 17, 1740, and died on May 3, 1758. Gracious toward heretics, he still pressed hard for the conversion of the Jews. His bull of 1747 let children over seven be baptized without parental consent.

Yet the entry notes he defended Jews against persecution in Poland and ordered a fair report on a blood charge in 1756. That report led to an acquittal in 1758. In Italy, though, he backed seizures of banned Hebrew books and strict ghetto rules for Rome. When Rome's Jews asked in 1751 to use the market and live outside the ghetto, he refused and renewed a harsh plan drawn up years before.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berachah-the-he: Berachah, called the Hero, was a Polish Jewish soldier killed in battle near Moscow in 1610. He was the son of Aaron the Martyr of Tishovitz and served in the cavalry. His bravery won the respect of the Cossacks, who gave him his surname. A bold rider, he charged the enemy line again and again until a bullet killed him. The facts came out later through witness testimony in the legal case of his widow, heard before the rabbis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernhardt-sarah:
Sarah Bernhardt, born Rosine Bernard, was a French actress born at Paris on Oct. 22, 1844, of Dutch Jewish parentage. Raised in a convent school, she entered the Conservatoire at fourteen. Her debut at the Comédie Française in 1862 brought only mild success, and more study followed.

From 1872 she rose at that house, winning her greatest triumphs in Phèdre and the classic plays of Racine and Corneille. A break in 1879 cost her heavy damages in a civil suit. Tours to London and America with her own company followed, and she took charge of Paris theaters herself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bethphage-3225: Bethphage was a town named in the New Testament. Matthew, Mark, and Luke all mention it. They link it with Bethany and the Mount of Olives. It stood on the Jericho road near Jerusalem. It lay outside the city wall. Talmudic passages call it the Sabbath distance limit. Some texts describe it as walled. That detail fits no known nearby site. The entry ends with a plain admission. Bethphage's exact location has not been determined.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-birzhi-polish-b: Birzhi is a district town in the government of Kovno. Its Polish name is Birze. Of its 1,500 people, 600 are Jews. Most of them work in handicrafts. The entry praises local Jewish charity highly. A hospital serves the community there. Clothing and loan societies are named. A Talmud Torah teaches eighty-eight children. Jews nearby farm rented land as well. Some work it themselves, some with hired help.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blumenfeld-beri: Berish Blumenfeld was a Galician Hebraist. He flourished in the early nineteenth century. Wealth let him serve Hebrew learning freely. Such scholars spread knowledge among their brethren. His work was a true labor of love. In 1826 he published a Job translation. It carried his Hebrew commentary alongside. His views on Job's date stirred debate. S. D. Luzzatto insisted Job was ancient. Their letters on it survive. He also aided Levinsohn's works' spread. Simson Bloch dedicated a translation to him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-boundaries-1192:
Boundaries are the limits of a tract of land. When Hebrew tribes settled in Palestine as farmers, fixing clear lines between tribal and family lands mattered most. The Book of Joshua records those lines in care.

Biblical law forbids moving a neighbor's landmark in set terms. It does not give the detail found in Talmudic law. Rabbis treated removal of a mark as theft as well. They set surveyors to guard the lines of each estate. Rules govern measuring land, dividing fields among brothers, and building shared walls. Each side had to give half the strip on which a dividing wall stood.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bramble-3625: Bramble is a prickly shrub, and the entry warns that the word covers three terms loosely. Atad appears in Jotham's parable in Judges, where trees seek a king. That plant belongs to the rhamnus group. Hoah is rendered bramble only once and thorns elsewhere. The Greek batos is rendered bramble once in twelve uses, in Luke. The entry sends readers to Thorns and Thistles for the fuller treatment of all three terms in Scripture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brociner-josef-:
Josef B. Brociner was president of the Union of Hebrew Congregations of Rumania. He was born in Jassy in Oct., 1846. He studied law there from 1864 to 1866 and helped found a Jewish defensive society.

Brociner settled at Galatz as a merchant in 1867. He rose in Masonry to the thirty-third degree, a first for a Rumanian Jew. From 1873 he led the local Alliance committee at Galatz. He represented Rumanian Jews at Paris conferences in 1876 and 1878. In 1878 he went to Berlin to press their cause at the Congress of the powers. The Union of congregations was his idea, and its members chose him first president by a unanimous vote.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bun-3825: Bun is treated here as a short personal name, not as a word for bread. The entry calls it a dialect shortening of Abun, also given as Abin or Rabin. It appears only in Palestinian sources. Several teachers cited under the short form show up in the Babylonian Talmud under the full name. One Palestinian scholar of the fourth century is cited once as Bun and once as Abun, with his father's name spelled two ways. The entry is a compact name study built from Talmud citations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-califs-3925:
Califs treats the first Muslim rulers and their stance toward Jewish subjects. The entry says policy followed need as much as faith. Mohammed let subdued Jewish tribes of Arabia stay for half their harvest, since their farming fed his armies. Abu Bekr kept that bargain. Omar then moved Jews to his new town of Kufa in Iraq.

Under Omar, Jews paid special taxes and wore a set garb to mark them apart. They had to host traveling Moslems for three days and could not ride horses. Later califs swung between favor and pressure. One Fatimid ruler made a Jew governor of Damietta district, and that man built a canal that kept his name. The entry ends as Saladin ends the Fatimid califate in 1171.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carcassonne-dav: David Carcassonne was a French physician born Dec. 20, 1789, at Remoulins in the Gard. He died at Nîmes on Nov. 15, 1861. Son of a purveyor to Napoleon's army, he joined the Grande Armée as a surgeon at twenty three. He marched with the emperor to Russia in 1812 and was taken prisoner there. Back at Nîmes he quit medicine and made carpets instead. He sat on the town council from 1837 to 1848. His one book treats the medicine of the Hebrews, old and new.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-castello-castil:
Abraham Isaac Castello, a rabbi, preacher, and poet, was born at Ancona in 1726. He died at Leghorn on Aug. 1, 1789. He reached Leghorn at age thirteen, poor and alone, intending to become a mechanic. A fine voice led him toward the cantor's post instead. He married the daughter of cantor Adam Bondi and later succeeded him.

Hard study of Hebrew, Spanish, and rabbinical science raised Castello to rabbi and preacher. Christian scholars sought him out for talks on religion and philosophy. He may be the scholar with whom Lessing conversed on a scientific tour. His writings, all printed at Leghorn, include an allegorical drama from 1765, a doctrinal address from 1753, and a memorial sermon on Francis I of Germany. Hebrew poems of his also appeared in later collections.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chambery-4225:
Chambéry is the capital of the department of Savoy, in France. When Philippe Auguste drove Jews from France in 1182, many took refuge at Chambéry and nearby towns. They paid heavy taxes, set at 75,374 francs in 1300 and lower sums in later years. Amadeus V granted them privileges, confirmed on Nov. 17, 1323.

In 1348, during the Black Death, Chambéry Jews were accused of poisoning the wells. Many were killed at Chambéry and in towns round about. A further persecution came in 1394. In 1417 two converted Jewish physicians were set to examine Jewish books for blasphemies against Christianity. In 1430 a converted Jew from Chambéry examined Hebrew books for a duchess at Trévoux. He ordered the books of the Jews of Savoy burned, the entry reports.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chigirin-4325: Chigirin is a town in the government of Kiev, in Russia. In 1897 it held 9,870 people, including about 3,000 Jews. Trade and handicrafts were the chief Jewish work, with 551 artisans in all. Tailoring led, with 204 persons at it. About 200 families asked yearly for Passover aid. Schools included a government school with 300 pupils, 120 of them Jews, about 30 ḥadarim with 230 scholars, and a Talmud Torah with 45 pupils.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cloud-pillar-of:
Cloud, Pillar of, guided Israel through the wilderness, as Exodus xiii. 21 tells it. By day the Lord went before the camp wrapped in cloud to show the way. By night the pillar turned to fire. Once, the entry notes, it moved behind the people to shield them from the pursuing Egyptians.

A natural root is proposed first. Armies on the march often carried fire ahead, smoke marking the route by day and flame by night. Alexander and Thrasybulus used the trick, and Arab caravans still did. Rabbinic lore then expands the tale: seven clouds of glory ringed the camp, and strips of one cloud bore glowing letters from the patriarchs' names above the tribal standards.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohn-ludwig-ado:
Ludwig Adolf Cohn, a German historian, was born in Breslau on May 22, 1834, and died in Gottingen on Jan. 13, 1871. A childhood illness left him deformed, and his mother taught him past the age of eight. He entered Breslau University in 1851 and Berlin in 1853, taking his degree at Breslau in 1856 after a long sickness.

He embraced Christianity and taught at Gottingen from 1857 until his death. The entry praises his wide reading, sharp criticism, and fair spirit. His books include the Pegau annals of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, a study of the Thirty Years' War, and a life of Emperor Henry II. His chief work, family tables for the history of the German states and the Netherlands, appeared in 1864-65.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-constanza-until: Constanza, called Custendje until 1878, is a Rumanian town in the Dobrudja province. Its Jewish story starts with the Russo-Turkish campaign of 1828. Jewish purveyors came with the Russian army then and stayed, forming the seed of a small community. Sephardic Jews from Asia Minor later founded a separate body. The war of 1853 swelled the numbers again, and a cemetery was laid out. Sir Moses Montefiore, passing through in 1868, gave 200 pounds toward a synagogue. By 1902 about 1,000 Jews lived there, some 400 of them Sephardim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-4925:
The David family played an important part in the early history of the Jews in Canada. Its founder there, Lazarus David, was born in Swansea, Wales, in 1734 and settled in Montreal in 1763. He helped found the Spanish and Portuguese Congregation Shearith Israel and was an active organizer of the young community. He died in Montreal in 1776.

The entry gives short lives of his sons and grandson. David David was a founder of the Bank of Montreal and gave land for Canada's first synagogue, built in 1777. Samuel David served with distinction in the war of 1812. Aaron Hart David became a noted Montreal physician and dean of a medical faculty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-abu-sulai:
David ibn Marwan al-Muḳammaṣ, a native of Rakka in Mesopotamia, was a philosopher and controversialist of the ninth and tenth centuries. The entry calls him the father of Jewish philosophy, yet he stayed almost unknown until the late nineteenth century. Scholars still debate reports that he studied under a Christian teacher or changed his faith.

His main work, the "'Ishrun Maḳalat" (Twenty Chapters), survives in fifteen chapters found at St. Petersburg in 1898. Its topics run from the creation of the world and the unity of God to prophecy and the commandments. David followed the Motazilite kalam, a school of rational theology. He also wrote on Genesis, Ecclesiastes, and the Jewish sects.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-debir-5025: Debir names two things in the Bible, and the entry treats both. First, Debir was a king of Eglon. He joined four other kings against Gibeon and was crushed by Joshua, then caught and put to death. Second, Debir was a city in the south of Judah, earlier called Kirjath-sepher. Joshua is said to have conquered it, though another passage names Othniel as its captor. It ranked among the Levitical cities. Its site is not certain, but the entry suggests a large hill village southwest of Hebron.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dispeck-david-b:
David ben Joel Dispeck was a Talmudic scholar and homilist born about 1744. He studied in a yeshibah under Joshua Cohen. In 1771 he became rabbi of Mering in Bavaria. Later posts took him to Metz in 1778 and to Beyersdorf and Baireuth in 1785.

At Beyersdorf, Dispeck gathered his homilies into a book called Pardes Dawid. The homilies follow the order of the weekly Torah portions. The same book holds 365 solutions to hard passages in Maimonides' Yad ha-Hazakah. It was printed at Sulzbach in 1786. One of his responsa also appears in Jacob Berlin's Be'er Ya'akob.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-duran-durand-or:
The Duran family was a wide-spread Jewish house first rooted in Provence. A Mosse Duram appears in a Tarascon list running from 1350 to 1487. The family moved first to Majorca. From there many members settled in Africa. Descendants still appear late in the eighteenth century.

The entry walks through the family's leading men one by one. Aaron ben Solomon served as a dayyan at Algiers in the fifteenth century. Profiat Duran, called Efodi, won fame as philosopher, grammarian, and controversialist. Simon ben Zemah Duran anchors the middle with his great work Magen Abot. A family pedigree, drawn from Steinschneider's catalogue, closes the long account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-edelmann-hen-to:
Hirsch Edelmann, called Hen-Tob, was an author and editor born in Swislocz, Russia, in 1805. A rabbi's son, he had a strong Talmudic schooling. He widened it with old and new Hebrew literature. He died at Berlin on Nov. 20, 1858.

Edelmann's first work, notes on a legal commentary, came out at Wilna in 1839. At Danzig and Königsberg he ran printing houses and issued prayer books. He spent about ten years in England. There he was among the first scholars to work through the Oppenheim collection at Oxford. With Leopold Dukes he published its treasures as Ginze Oxford in 1851.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eleazar-abraham: Abraham Eleazar is the false author named on an old work on alchemy. The book came out at Leipsic in 1760. Its title calls it an ancient chemical work by Rabbi Abraham Eleazar. The entry holds that the real author was Julius Gervasius of Schwarzburg. The preface claims Abraham took his ideas and pictures from copper tablets of Tubal Cain. A second part adds a further claim. It says the matter was first cut on tablets by a Jew named Samuel Baruch.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-embroidery-5725: Embroidery is fancy needlework done upon cloth. Linen is its most common ground in the old world. Egypt and Assyria raised the art to a high pitch. Bible texts name the craft in many a place. A Babylonian mantle that tempted Achan was worked in gold. Ezekiel speaks of fine stitched linen from Egypt. The hangings of the Tabernacle show the Hebrews' own skill. Aaron's coat and girdle were worked the same way. Egypt and Babylon both have their backers in the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-epstein-or-epps:
Epstein, or Eppstein, is one of the oldest Jewish family names in the Slavic countries, the entry says. Rabbis and printers with the name appear in records from the fifteenth century onward. One line ran through Brest-Litovsk and Grodno to Aryeh Lob Epstein, rabbi of Konigsberg. The entry warns that many later families simply took the name. More than two hundred Epsteins appear in the New York directory alone.

After the family survey, the entry gives short lives of notable Epsteins one by one. They include physicians, rabbis, bankers, and writers across Europe. Alois Epstein of Prague is covered for his many books on child illness. Aryeh Lob Epstein is covered for his works on the 613 commandments and the Sabbath. Jacob Epstein of Warsaw appears as a banker and giver to charity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-evreux-hebrew-o:
Evreux, capital of the department of Eure in France, was a medieval center of Jewish learning. Its scholars are quoted across the Tosafot and in the Kol Bo. Samuel ben Shneor, called the Prince of Evreux, ranked among the most famed tosafists of his age. His brother Moses wrote the Tosafot of Evreux.

Other names fill the entry: Isaac of Evreux, Judah ben Shneor with his liturgical poems, and Meir ben Shneor. Nathan ben Jacob's son Jacob copied the five Megillot with the Targum in 1357 for Moses ben Samuel. The entry gives no account of the community's size, taxes, or later fate. Its focus stays on the scholars and their books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-farjeon-benjami: Benjamin L. Farjeon was an English-Jewish novelist born in London in 1833 and dead there on July 23, 1903. He went out to New Zealand and helped run that colony's first daily newspaper. His first book, Grif, came out in 1870 and drew Dickens's notice. Many novels followed, among them London's Heart, Great Porter Square, and The House of White Shadows. Four books treat Jewish scenes and figures with sympathy: Solomon Isaacs, Aaron the Jew, Miriam Rozella, and Pride of Race. The entry lists titles only, with no plots.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-finzi-felice-61: Felice Finzi was an Italian scholar of Assyria born at Correggio in 1847. He died at Florence in 1872. While he read law at Bologna, he gave his time to languages. He worked most on the Assyrian language and its writings. He lectured on those subjects at an institute in Florence. With Paolo Mantegazza he founded a journal of ethnology and anthropology. He also helped found the Italian Oriental Society. His works include a study of Etruscan finds and a language essay printed at Florence in 1870.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fontanella-isra: Israel Berechiah ben Joseph Jekuthiel Fontanella was an Italian rabbi and cabalist. He lived at Reggio Emilia, later at Rovigo. His years run from the end of the seventeenth century into the first half of the eighteenth. He was also a noted Talmudist, the entry adds. As a skilled cabalist he edited a twofold index to the Zohar. It was printed at Venice in 1744 and is ascribed to a certain Samuel. The first volume indexes subjects. The second indexes the Bible passages quoted in the Zohar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-franks-6325:
Franks is an American Jewish family whose members served as officers on both sides in the Revolutionary war. The earliest known member was Jacob Franks, a merchant who settled in New York early in the eighteenth century. His son David was a loyalist, born in New York in 1720. David supplied the army in the French and Indian war. In the Revolution he acted for the British side in prisoner exchanges. Congress jailed him twice as an enemy of the cause.

David Salisbury Franks took the American side. He was a merchant at Montreal and headed its congregation in 1775. He advanced money to the American army there and served as paymaster. Later he served as a diplomatic agent. Isaac Franks enlisted at seventeen and fought at Long Island. Rebecca Franks was famed for her wit and her letters. In 1782 she married a British general and settled at Bath.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fundao-6425: Fundao is the chief town of its district in Beira, Portugal, where more than a third of 27,000 people in the wider council were of Jewish origin. For over two hundred years the Inquisition cut down that group. Its first victim there was Gracia Henriques, burned at Lisbon on April 1, 1582. Many Marranos left early in the seventeenth century. Some reached London by about 1656. A few families still kept Yom Kippur in secret.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gastfreund-isaa: Isaac Gastfreund, a Galician rabbinical scholar born about 1845, died in Vienna after 1880. He wrote a life of the tanna Akiba ben Joseph, printed at Lemberg in 1871. A German work on Mohammed in Talmud and Midrash came out in parts from 1875 to 1880. In Hebrew he wrote lives of the Konigswarter family and of Adolph Jellinek. A joint volume gives short lives of Jonathan Eybeschutz and Solomon Munk.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gerson-felix-na: Felix Napoleon Gerson, an American poet, writer, and newsman born in Philadelphia on October 18, 1862, was schooled in that city public schools. From 1880 to 1890 he worked for the Philadelphia and Reading Railroad. He helped end the rail strikes of 1887 in Philadelphia and New York. In 1891 he became business manager of The Jewish Exponent. His book of poems, Some Verses, came out in Philadelphia in 1893.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gottheil-paul-e: Paul Eduard Gottheil was a German Protestant missionary. He was born at Fraustadt on April 5, 1818. He died at Stuttgart in 1893. A convert to Christianity, he entered mission work in 1848. His employer was the British Society for the Propagation of the Gospel Among the Jews. He kept that link to the end of his life. He served at Cannstadt's English church and at Stuttgart's Diakonissenhaus. The entry calls him very successful as a missionary. Several of his converts became ministers or missionaries themselves. He was a brother of Rabbi Gustav Gottheil.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gueterbock-karl:
Karl Eduard Gueterbock was a German jurist. He was born at Königsberg, East Prussia, on April 18, 1830. He studied history, then law, at four universities and graduated in 1851. He joined the bar in 1859 and became a judge in his home town. He taught Prussian law there from 1861. He rose to assistant professor in 1863 and professor in 1868, then gave up his judgeship. The entry notes that he embraced the Christian faith.

His books cover English company law of 1856 and 1857. He wrote on flaws in Prussian bankruptcy practice. He studied Bracton and his tie to Roman law. He also traced the origins of the Carolina, the old German criminal code.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hagenau-7025:
Hagenau is a walled town of Alsace on the Moder, sixteen miles north of Strasburg. Jews settled there soon after its city charter of 1164, drawn by the rights Frederick Barbarossa granted. A synagogue stood by 1252. In 1262 Richard IV confirmed that the town's Jews answered to the imperial chamber alone.

Hard years followed: houses and synagogue seized, Jews plundered and banished in 1346, then readmitted to pay the city's debts. For centuries only six families held a firm right to live there. After France took Alsace in 1648, rules eased, then tightened again in 1714 and 1720. The entry closes with the town's rabbis and a count of 695 Jews in a population of 17,958.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hamath-7125:
Hamath was a city and district on the northern frontier of Palestine, set at the foot of Mount Hermon. Amos calls it "the great Hamath." Its people, the Hamathites, are counted among the descendants of Canaan. The kingdom first appears in David's time, when King Toi of Hamath warred with Hadadezer of Zobah and sent his son to greet David on Hadadezer's defeat.

Solomon held Hamath as a tributary and built store-cities there. After his death it won back its freedom, then fell by degrees to Assyria. Tiglath-pileser III took tribute and annexed nineteen districts in 730 B.C. Sargon settled 4,300 Assyrians in the land, and Shalmaneser moved Hamathites to Samaria. Greeks and Romans knew the city as Epiphaneia. Burckhardt found it in 1812 under its old name, Ḥamah, on the Orontes, with 30,000 people and Hittite stones in relief.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hannaux-emmanue: Emmanuel Hannaux was a French sculptor born at Metz in 1855. He began at Strasburg, returned to Metz in 1870 when war broke out, then moved to Nancy to stay in France, carving pipes to fund his studies. In Paris from 1876 he entered the Ecole des Beaux-Arts. The Salon of 1889 gave a third medal for "Le Bûcheron" and a second for "Le Drapeau"; in 1894 the first medal for "Orphée Mourant." Chevalier of the Legion of Honor in 1900 and won the Médaille d'Honneur in 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-head-dress-7325:
Head-dress surveys what the ancient Israelites wore on the head, and it admits how little is known. Bible sources say almost nothing on the topic. Stone carvings show Israelites bare-headed or in foreign dress. One early verse names cords worn with sackcloth around the head.

The entry guesses that the common form matched the Bedouin wrap. A folded cloth guarded the neck, held by a thick wool cord. In later times a turban-like dress took over, built on small caps. Priests wore special forms, such as the high priest's miter. Crowns and circlets named in the Bible are also discussed, with honest gaps noted.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-helena-7525:
Helena was queen of Adiabene, wife of Monobaz the First and mother of Monobaz the Second. She was likely of Greek origin. About the year 30 she became a convert to Judaism. In a famine at Jerusalem she sent to Alexandria for corn and to Cyprus for dried figs, to feed the hungry.

The Talmud tells of her gifts to the Temple. She set a golden lamp over its door whose flash at sunrise marked the hour for the Shema. She also kept a Nazarite vow for many years after her son came home safe from war. Her bones were moved to Jerusalem and laid in a tomb she had built. She died about 56.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herz-henriette-:
Henriette Herz, born in Berlin on Sept. 5, 1764, led Berlin society from her home with her husband, physician Markus Herz. They married in 1779, when she was fifteen. Her learning was wide. She knew many languages, read the Bible in Hebrew, and judged literature for noted authors.

Her salon drew figures such as Schiller, Mirabeau, Humboldt, and Schleiermacher. Close friendship with Schleiermacher drew public talk, yet the entry calls it platonic. Widowed in 1803, she taught to support her family. She refused offers tied to accepting Christianity until after her mother died, then was baptized in 1817. She died in Berlin on Oct. 22, 1847.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirsch-august-7:
August Hirsch, born at Danzig on Oct. 4, 1817, was a German physician and medical history writer. After a few years in commerce he studied medicine from 1839. He took his degree at Berlin in 1843. He practiced at Elbing, then Danzig.

Hirsch's studies of disease by place led him to historical pathology. His handbook on that subject became key for military and tropical doctors, the entry says. Berlin called him to its medical history chair in 1863. He reported on epidemics in Prussia and Russia for the government. He also helped found a public health society in the Franco-Prussian war years. He died at Berlin on Jan. 28, 1894.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-holon-sandy-pla: Holon, glossed as sandy place or halting place, names two cities in this entry. The first was a city of Judah in the Hebron hills. It was given, with its suburbs, to the priests, in Joshua. A parallel passage in Chronicles calls that city by another name, given here in two forms.
