plos-pone-0350325:
Meenu Mariya James and colleagues mapped dengue fever across Indian districts from 2010 to 2022 by climate zone. Dengue has grown steadily in India, yet district level climate patterns were unclear. Districts were grouped into climate types, trends were fitted over time, and map tests hunted for clusters and hot spots of cases.

Spread varied sharply between districts. Fastest growth appeared in some cool zones, including tundra like and mild summer zones, with yearly rises near or above doubling in the steepest fits. Warm tropical zones kept high burdens too. Dengue pushing into cooler districts, the authors warn, means control plans built for hot lowlands alone will fall behind.
plos-pone-0350625:
Isa Spiero and colleagues compared Dutch language models for pulling signs and symptoms from primary care notes. Health records hold rich detail in free text, but hand coding is slow. Two local models were trained as direct classifiers on hand labelled notes about chest infections, with training sizes varied to find how much labelled data is enough.

Direct classifiers scored well, led by the medical tuned model. Prompt style use scored poorly for both models. Rare symptoms and missing mentions dragged scores down. About eight hundred labelled examples marked the floor for solid results. Local language models, the work shows, can unlock Dutch record text for research when labelled data are sufficient.
plos-pone-0350825:
Lauren Wakefield and co-authors built a computer tool for a hard problem on deer farms. A wasting disease spreads fast among penned deer. Once it takes hold, it is nearly impossible to remove. Testing only part of a herd can miss it in the early stage. A clean test result can leave false comfort.

Their tool works backward from a farm's own records. It uses herd makeup, animal movements, and past test results. From these it estimates the chance that disease hides in the herd unseen. That turns a bare negative result into a graded risk judgment. Farmers and officials can then decide about sales and movement with clearer eyes.
plos-pone-0350925:
Yisheng Yang and colleagues offer a smarter design method for the heavy pressure vessels inside wind tunnels. Tunnels that test aircraft at high speed need vessels that hold huge pressure without needless weight. Older design leans on habit and heavy safety margins, while pure data models falter when conditions change. Their method blends written design rules into a layered prediction model.

On a real tunnel section, the method cut vessel weight by about one quarter while keeping strength, and ran each design loop vastly faster than full simulation. Rule guided sampling and mixed quality training data drove the gains. Builders of test rigs and other pressure gear could design lighter, faster, and with more confidence.
plos-pone-0351125:
Msila and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask small-scale farmers in South Africa's Limpopo Province what would move them to change how they use water as the climate shifts. Most of the surveyed maize growers farm for their living, many are older, and most have some secondary schooling. Intentions were read through a standard behavior model with three drivers.

All three drivers mattered. A positive attitude toward adapting was the strongest push, followed by social norms, meaning what farmers believe people around them expect. Feeling able to adapt helped too, but less. In plain terms, farmers who saw adaptation as wise, felt backed by their community, and believed they could manage it were the ones planning to change. The authors advise climate programs to work on attitudes and community backing, not only on handing out technology, since intention is the doorway to action.
plos-pone-0351425:
Retirement reshapes health, mood, friendships, money, and purpose all at once. Yasin M Yasin and colleagues lay out a plan, in PLOS One in 2026, for an umbrella review that gathers earlier systematic reviews on what shapes well-being among retired older adults.

No findings are reported, because this is a protocol. The team will search five major databases for reviews published since 2015, then check their quality with an established checklist. Two reviewers will screen and extract data separately. The finished synthesis aims to show which factors and which kinds of support most deserve attention from planners and communities.
plos-pone-0351625:
Luca Alessandri and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One archaeology study dating an ancient salt production site near Rome by reading the magnetism locked into its kiln and pottery. Radiocarbon dating fails at this site because its age falls on a flat stretch of the calibration curve, and its plain jars offer few clues. Magnetic measurements gave two possible windows in the early first millennium BCE.

Combined with pottery styles and radiocarbon results, the magnetic dates let the team split the site's main area into three occupation phases spanning roughly two centuries. The authors argue that archaeomagnetic dating deserves wider use at sites where radiocarbon goes blurry, especially when several methods can be cross-checked against each other.
plos-pone-0351725:
Hamidreza Farzan and Maryam Koushkie Jahromi test a single dose of a medicinal mushroom extract on young men's brains and bodies around hard exercise, in this 2026 PLOS ONE trial. Twelve recreationally active men cycled to exhaustion twice, once after a gram of Cordyceps militaris extract and once after a starch placebo, in random order a week apart. Reaction time on a colour-word task and oxygen use were measured before and after each ride.

After exercise, reaction times were significantly faster on the mushroom day, while accuracy stayed at ceiling in both. Resting oxygen uptake also ran higher with the extract, though peak exercise values did not change. One dose, the authors conclude, sharpens the post-exercise mind without touching endurance itself.
plos-pone-0351925:
Jiale He and colleagues simulated what happens when farmers water dry fields with groundwater rich in arsenic, a poison that builds up in soil. Their test soil came from the Kuitun River Basin in Xinjiang, China. By changing evaporation, acidity, and salt in the water, they watched how arsenic moved through the soil profile, using special membranes to picture its spread.

All three water traits steered the arsenic. Under weak evaporation it traveled farther, both down and sideways, through the topsoil. More alkaline and saltier water pushed it deeper from the surface layer. For dry regions that must irrigate with tainted groundwater, the results flag which water conditions let arsenic sink toward roots and groundwater, and argue for managing water chemistry, not just water quantity.
plos-pone-0352025:
Sue Jordan and co-authors study in 2026 whether children in Europe born with major birth defects die more often when their families are poorer. Linked records from registers in seven countries covered tens of thousands of such children, followed to age one and to age ten. Social position was measured by mother schooling or by area hardship, depending on country.

Death was more common among the most deprived than the least deprived at both ages, and the gap was stronger after infancy than in the first year. Clear gaps reached statistical strength in only some registers. Children of mothers from outside the European Union also died more often. More support for the poorest is urged.
plos-pone-0352325:
Nana Zhou and four colleagues teach ground robots to label scenes they have never been trained on. Their 2026 study targets unstructured environments: rubble, scrub, disaster ground. Ordinary segmentation models need retraining for each new setting. Their framework instead leans on a vision-language model that already links images to words. Deep prompt tuning nudges the image encoder toward rough terrain. The zero-shot ability of the base model survives the tuning.

An ensemble of text prompts, tailored to wild settings, sharpens the matching. Global and local features from both encoders are combined to align words with the right pixels. Vehicles that can segment an unseen hillside into rock, brush, and path without new training data are far more deployable. The design aims squarely at rescue and exploration robots, which never know what terrain waits around the next bend.
plos-pone-0353125:
Hadj-Abo and colleagues, in a 2026 mixed-methods study, compare people with type 1 diabetes who use automated insulin delivery with those who do not. These systems link a glucose sensor to a pump that adjusts insulin on its own. Research has often checked blood sugar outcomes while asking less about daily distress.

About one hundred seventy people answered a survey on blood sugar control and diabetes distress, and twelve were interviewed in depth. Users of the automated systems had lower long-term blood sugar readings and lower distress on every scale measured. The biggest gaps were in feeling burdened by daily management and feeling powerless. Interviews suggested the systems ease the constant mental work of dosing. Distress about low blood sugar differed less, which the authors link to wide use of glucose sensors in both groups. They argue that judging diabetes technology should weigh peace of mind alongside numbers.
plos-pone-0353525:
Wang and colleagues tested a drug for sepsis-linked lung injury in rats in a 2026 study. Sepsis, a runaway response to infection, often floods and scars the lungs. Rats given the drug at three dose levels were compared with untreated sick rats and healthy controls.

Treated rats survived at higher rates, and the benefit grew with dose. Lung swelling, injury scores, and inflammatory signals fell at medium and high doses. A cell-death pathway driven by iron also weakened, tied to a protective gene chain the drug switched on. Low doses helped only a few measures. The dose pattern supports further study of the drug for this lung complication.
plos-pone-0353725:
An editorial note from The PLOS One Editors in 2026 addresses a cancer study about a platinum drug and cell death in a rare chest cancer. Readers should note this flag before trusting the original findings. After publication, concerns were raised that several figure panels seemed to overlap with one another or with panels in related papers.

Editors reviewed the original underlying images supplied by the authors. Following that review, the journal states that it considers the concerns resolved. The note also records that raw data files were not shared as the article's data statement had promised. Readers get the full list of questioned panels, so they can judge the record for themselves.
plos-pone-0354125:
Emily Eichenlaub and co-authors test in 2026 whether neck posture and neck braces change how young healthy adults keep balance while walking. A stiff or forward bent neck is common in an ageing spine disease that also harms walking. Volunteers walked in braces set to different neck shapes while a treadmill jolted them or while they stepped sideways to a target.

Jolts shrank stability in all conditions, but only braced walking tipped into measured instability in one direction. Side stepping stayed accurate except when the brace bent the neck forward and the target lay far away. The authors advise fall risk teaching for people given neck immobilisation.
plos-pone-0354425:
Fumiyo Nakagawa led a team of eight authors mapping how people who live with HIV in Britain use health services, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. With good treatment, HIV is now a long-term condition, but not everyone uses services equally. The team compared use across social and demographic groups.

Nakagawa's patterns reveal who is underserved, by age, background, or circumstance. Unequal use can mean missed chances to keep the virus suppressed and catch other illnesses early. The NHS aims for equal care, so maps like this show where outreach must reach further. The study gives service planners UK-specific evidence instead of assumptions imported from other health systems.
plos-pone-0354525:
De Herdt and colleagues, in 2026, study a drug target that may help repair myelin, the coating that speeds signals along nerve fibers. Loss of myelin is a core harm in multiple sclerosis. A receptor called GPR17 stays switched on in young myelin-making cells after injury, and that may block them from maturing.

The team first checked human brain tissue from people with multiple sclerosis and found more of these receptor-marked cells near damaged areas. They then gave mice with toxin-caused myelin loss a new drug that blocks GPR17 by mouth. Treated mice showed faster repair in key brain and optic nerve areas. Their memory and visual signals also recovered. The results point to blocking this receptor as a possible route toward repair-focused treatment, though the work is still in animals.
plos-pone-0354725:
Mushuai Hao, Haonan Qi, Liang Zhao, and Wei Han published this 2026 training study on how the lowering speed of a squat shapes strength gains. Thirty sports students trained twice weekly for eight weeks at one of three tempos: a slow four-second lowering, a two-second lowering, or a self-chosen rhythm. Strength, sprinting, and jumping were tested before and after.

All groups grew stronger, and the two-second tempo showed the friendliest trend, boosting explosive jumping most. The slow group actually lost some spring-based explosiveness despite gaining strength. Hao advises matching tempo to the quality being trained.
plos-pone-0354825:
Uchhwas Banik and five colleagues published this 2026 study turning waste plastic into fuel in Bangladesh, where plastic use keeps climbing. They heated four common plastics without oxygen, a process called pyrolysis, and tuned the temperature for each type to draw off the most liquid oil and char.

Polypropylene gave the richest oil yield, and the liquids resembled familiar fuels in their carbon makeup. The leftover char was checked for industrial uses as well. Banik presents tuned pyrolysis as a practical route for cutting plastic waste while recovering energy from it.
plos-pone-0354925:
Lixia Lin and five colleagues published this 2026 plant study on a valued Chinese medicinal herb that wilts in heat. They grew the plant at four temperatures, from mild to severely hot, and tracked leaf health, chemistry, and protein changes to see how it copes and where it fails.

Heat cut photosynthesis, lowered green pigment, and raised signs of cell damage. Hundreds of proteins shifted, including ones for daily rhythms, antioxidant defense, and the cell's recycling system, which seemed to protect tissue. Lin's findings give breeders and growers a starting map for raising heat tolerance in a crop that warming summers now threaten.
plos-pone-0355125:
Victoria Ballén led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of drug-resistant E. coli in Barcelona's water treatment plants. They collected well over a hundred resistant strains across two wastewater plants and one drinking water plant, then read their genomes and tested drug resistance, film-forming ability, and virulence genes.

Treatment lowered bacteria counts, yet most strains still resisted several drugs, and some dangerous clones survived into reclaimed water. One resistant strain even appeared at the drinking water plant's inlet. Ballén argues water systems belong inside resistance surveillance, not outside it.
plos-pone-0355625:
Masaaki Kuwajima and colleagues built a new lab animal for brain research: a rat missing a protein called synaptopodin. Their 2026 paper explains that the protein helps organize tiny structures inside nerve cells that support learning signals. Mice without it existed already, but rats offer steadier timing for when learning circuits switch on, which can make experiments cleaner.

The engineered rats lived and kept normal kidney function, though they grew slightly smaller than usual. Under strong microscopes, their brain cells lacked two small internal structures that depend on the protein, and a key learning signal in the memory region ran weaker. Kuwajima and co-authors present the rat as a shared tool for studying growth, behavior, and memory.
plos-pone-0355725:
Li-Feng Hung and four colleagues track drug-resistant gut bacteria in emergency department patients across the rise and fall of Taiwan's COVID-19 Omicron wave, in this 2026 study. Their hospital's records covered more than eight hundred adults with bloodstream infections from a bacterial family that includes E. coli, about a third of them multidrug-resistant. The team divided the year into pre-peak, peak, and post-peak stages and searched broadly for stage-specific risk factors.

Which variables accompanied resistance changed with the stage: advanced age and red-cell measures early on, liver and platelet values at the peak, and white-cell measures afterward. Resistance trends also split by species, one notorious pathogen gaining ground against a key antibiotic while E. coli's resistance eased against several drugs. The authors argue stewardship and risk checks should adapt as a pandemic moves through its phases.
plos-pone-0356725:
Dipo Aldila and coauthors published a 2026 mathematical modeling study in PLOS ONE on hepatitis B and D, two linked liver viruses. Hepatitis D cannot spread on its own; it infects only people already carrying hepatitis B, through what is called superinfection, and it makes outcomes far worse. Their model splits a population into susceptible, vaccinated, infected, recovered, chronic, and doubly infected groups, with vaccination and liver transplantation as controls.

The analysis shows familiar threshold behavior: when the basic reproduction number sits below one, the disease-free state is stable and infection dies out. Above it, two kinds of settled states appear, with and without hepatitis D. A global sensitivity analysis found vaccination coverage and vaccine strength dominate that threshold number. Transplantation does not move the threshold, but it shrinks outbreaks and delays their peaks. Vaccine effort, they argue, is the master lever, with transplantation buying time and sparing severe cases.
plos-pone-0356825:
Ravian Wettstein and colleagues follow adults with attention deficit disorder for years. Their trial had added talking therapy to medication and education. The question now is whether the therapy pays off late, in quality of life. Early results had shown no added benefit right after treatment, but coping skills might ripen slowly. From the original cohort of several hundred, about a quarter completed the long follow-up survey several years later, rating life quality on a standard scale.

Life quality rose sharply by the end of the original treatment in both groups, then eased back over the years while staying above the starting point. No measure separated the therapy group from the education-only group at any point. Wettstein and colleagues conclude this dataset gives no sign of a delayed therapy dividend, though early gains themselves partly lasted.
plos-pone-0357025:
Marjolijn Carolien Sales and colleagues published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on predicting right heart failure after a patient receives a durable left ventricular assist device, a heart pump. When the heart's right side fails after surgery, patients can crash, so surgeons lean on risk scores rarely validated head to head. They applied six established scores to just over a hundred patients at one center, using a standard registry definition.

About one patient in five developed moderate-to-severe right heart failure. The established scores discriminated weakly to moderately; one scored worse than chance, while a postoperative version performed best of them. An exploratory five-variable model built by the team, using sickness level, liver markers, and pressure measurements, appeared much stronger, and held up after internal bootstrap checks. Derived and tested in the same small cohort, it needs outside validation before any clinical use.
plos-pone-0357125:
Hanizah Mohd Yusoff and coauthors published a 2026 nationwide survey in PLOS ONE on how Long COVID harms the working lives of factory workers in Malaysia. Close to eight hundred workers who had previously caught COVID filled in questionnaires on lingering symptoms, quality of working life, productivity, and safety. The authors then looked for which personal, symptom, job, and workplace factors tracked with poor work outcomes.

About a quarter of workers with Long COVID reported poor quality of working life. Roughly two in five admitted working while sick, about one in eight had taken sickness absences, and a small share reported safety problems. Risk rose with older age, smoking, more symptoms, shift work, chemical handling, confined spaces, noise, and manual lifting. Factories without a sickness absence policy fared markedly worse. The authors argue employers need formal absence policies and hazard controls aimed at this group, not just general wellness advice.
plos-pone-0357625:
Anqi Hu and seven colleagues compare gut microbes in giant pandas that pace and sway repetitively with those that do not, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Such stereotypic behavior troubles captive pandas, and gut microbes are known to influence the brain in other animals. The team watched fifteen captive pandas, then sequenced the bacteria in their droppings using two methods to build both a species list and a functional profile.

Pandas showing the behavior carried a distinctly different gut community, a pattern the authors describe as imbalance. One Serratia species was far more common in them, several Clostridium species trended upward, and a friendly Enterococcus species went the other way. Some of the shifted bacteria touch pathways that make brain signaling chemicals. The panda findings cannot prove cause, but they open a new angle on managing a stubborn welfare problem in zoos.
plos-pone-0357725:
Carla Blázquez-Fernández, Paloma Lanza-León, and David Cantarero-Prieto published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on social isolation and health behavior across generations in Europe. Isolation is a known health risk in old age, but its effects on the young are barely studied. Using the latest European Social Survey from twenty-four countries. The authors related five isolation measures, from rarely meeting others to lacking emotional support, against inactivity, smoking, drinking, and body weight. They did this generation by generation.

Isolation tracked with worse health behavior in every generation. Rarely meeting socially, for instance, raised the odds of physical inactivity across all ages. Generation X appeared as a bridge group, mixing traditional and modern patterns of connection and habit. Anti-isolation policy, they argue, should be age-specific and start young, because disconnection's health costs accumulate across a lifetime; social connection itself is preventive medicine.
plos-pone-0358125:
Jingwang Liu led a team of eight authors testing a drug's protective effect in mice, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. When blood flow returns to a limb cut off from circulation, the return itself injures muscle, a harm called ischemia-reperfusion injury. The team tested esketamine, a drug already used in clinics, against that injury.

Liu's group found that esketamine protected skeletal muscle in the mouse model. They linked the effect to regulation of autophagy, the cell's cleanup and recycling process. A drug already in human use is an attractive candidate, since its safety record is known. Much testing remains, but the finding hints that surgical patients could one day get muscle protection from a familiar drug.
plos-pone-0358225:
Asha Z Goodman, Winston T Stauffer, and Philippe A Gallay test a two drug bet against the worst outcomes of fatty liver disease, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The logic pairs correction with repair: semaglutide, the metabolic drug, against weight and sugar, plus a cyclophilin inhibitor aimed at the inflammation and scarring that become self sustaining. Their mice developed the disease on a Western diet with sugar water and a liver toxin. Then each group received one drug alone, or both together.

The pairing's effects diverged by outcome, as the design half expected. Semaglutide clearly cut body weight and shrank the liver tumor burden, the cancer endpoint that matters most. Scar tissue, measured by collagen staining, did not differ significantly between the treatment groups. The authors report the split honestly: metabolic victory, fibrosis stalemate. Advanced liver disease may need the scar targeted earlier, harder, or by other means than these.
plos-pone-0358325:
Yeliz Yilmaz Bozok and three colleagues compared two AI chatbots answering breast cancer questions, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Patients increasingly ask chatbots about their disease, so the quality of those answers matters. The team put patient-oriented questions to both ChatGPT and Gemini and scored the replies.

Bozok's head-to-head comparison tells patients and doctors which system gave safer and more accurate answers in this test. It also shows where both systems fell short, which is just as useful. Clinics fielding patient questions about AI use gain grounded advice here. The wider lesson is that chatbot answers on cancer should be checked, and studies like this show how to check them.
plos-pone-0358425:
Rebaka Pradhan and Onn Shehory review what computing research has done about labor trafficking online, in a 2026 PLOS ONE article. Traffickers now recruit and coordinate through digital platforms, while traces of offline exploitation also sit in online records. The authors separate those two settings and ask which machine learning and analytics methods have been tried in each, and where the gaps lie.

Following standard scoping review practice, they searched six databases plus extra sources and screened more than two thousand records down to twenty-one articles worth mapping. Work clusters around online recruitment fraud, illicit massage businesses, supply chains, and high risk industries such as fishing. Case studies, readable classifiers, and topic modeling appear often. Their closing agenda points future researchers toward the neglected settings and data types.
plos-pone-0359425: Cao and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on reading feelings from behavior signals. Their method joins two ideas: injecting extra hub nodes into a graph as behavior unfolds, and fusing the streams with graph attention. The task is multimodal sentiment analysis, judging mood from several signal types at once. Systems that read mood well could support mental health tools and more responsive machines.
plos-pone-0359525:
Zena Abdul-Ameer Mahdi and seven colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It investigates plant chemicals from Rhizophora mucronata, a mangrove tree. The question is whether these phytochemicals can block proteins linked to lung cancer, acting as inhibitors that slow the disease's machinery.

The approach is computational, using multiscale and in silico analyses, meaning computer simulations at several levels rather than wet-lab tests. Screening mangrove compounds on a computer is a cheap first pass for drug hunting. If any candidate looks strong, laboratory teams can test it in cells. Natural product researchers are the readers for this early-stage evidence.
plos-pone-0359625: López-González and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on spotting risky drinking in Guaviare, Colombia. They adapted the AUDIT, a standard alcohol screening survey, for primary care with mixed cultural groups. The team checked that the adapted questions read clearly and made sense to local users. A screening tool that fits local speech can catch alcohol harm earlier across Latin America.
pmc-13197425:
Jacob L Bongers and colleagues used ancient DNA to trace migration on Peru's Pacific coast in a 2026 study. Genome data came from twenty-one people buried in the Chincha Valley of southern Peru. The valley was ruled by the Chincha Kingdom from the thirteenth century until the Inca takeover in the fifteenth.

The DNA shows shared ancestry with groups far to the north. Early migrants carried pure northern ancestry, while later generations mixed with nearby coastal people. Kin buried in a shared family tomb married within the group. A dating model handled diet effects that blur age estimates on this coast. Customs such as skull shaping and red pigment use persisted across those centuries.
pmc-13200325:
Shunsuke Mori and colleagues present a 2026 report on two cases of an abnormal lung artery supply, with a literature review. In this rare condition, a body artery feeds the base of a lung instead of the usual lung artery. Saving lung tissue is favored now, but kept lung can die if mishandled, and selection rules were vague.

Detailed scans guided tailored care for each woman. In one, an aberrant artery held a large clot and the normal artery was undergrown, so surgeons removed just that lung segment by robot. She left hospital on day six. In the other, normal branches were intact, so a coil block of the aberrant artery sufficed. She went home on day three. Neither had complications.
pmc-13202125:
Permanent organ damage accumulates quietly in Sjögren's disease, and a 2026 cohort analysis authored by Onorina Berardicurti charts that accrual over five years. The research article follows 429 adults in an Italian multicentre research network, measuring irreversible damage across eye, mouth, and systemic domains with a validated damage index.

Nearly half the patients already had some damage at baseline, and the share rose to about two thirds after five years of follow-up. Higher baseline disease activity predicted damage in every domain, while an abnormal tear test specifically forecast eye damage. Antibodies, inflammation markers, and repeated mouth infections added domain-specific risks, pointing to earlier monitoring for high-risk patients.
pmc-13202525:
Quieting microbe chatter instead of killing microbes is the strategy in a 2026 study by Kosana Sai Chaitanya against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The research article designs triazole-linked compounds carrying a thiolactone unit to block quorum sensing, the chemical chatter that builds biofilms and drives toxin making.

A library of thirty glycinate and propanoate derivatives was modeled against the LasR regulator protein, then synthesized and tested on a reporter strain. Blocking was strongest at high doses and faded as doses dropped across the tested range. One nitrophenyl compound stood out, disrupting biofilms and cutting output of the pigment pyocyanin, which supports anti-virulence therapy as a complement to antibiotics.
pmc-13204325:
Snacking has quietly replaced meals for many young adults, and a 2026 longitudinal study authored by Mariëlle Tamara de Vaal follows that habit through a phone app. The FOODLOOP study tracked 264 Dutch millennials on twelve nonconsecutive days spread across four seasons, logging each snack's product, setting, and motive.

Participants averaged about four and a half snacks daily, and most choices were relatively healthful items like coffee, tea, fruit, and bread products. Liking, appetite, hunger, convenience, and pleasure drove most snacking, which clustered at home, with other people, and in the afternoon. Millennials with children snacked more than those without, and older millennials snacked more than younger ones.
pmc-13212725:
Fernando Cornet-Gomez and co-authors assess in 2026 how sharply present and future particle colliders can probe possible new physics hiding in the top quark. Their framework adds one extra interaction at a time to the standard model, rather than fitting everything together at once.

Data came from past American and European colliders plus the Large Hadron Collider, with projections for its high-luminosity upgrade and future lepton machines. Testing single effects separately reveals which measurements pin down which interaction most tightly. Global fits can hide that detail through cancellations between effects. The authors expect future facilities to improve sensitivity greatly, giving experimenters a map of the most valuable measurements to pursue.
pmc-13215525:
Tuodi Zhang and co-authors present a 2026 optimization study of a treatment system that couples a constructed wetland with a microbial fuel cell for rural sewage. The work focuses on winter, when cold weather weakens wetland performance.

Using response surface methods, the team tuned three electrode settings: plate projection, electrode spacing, and external resistance. The coupled system produced effluent chemical oxygen demand between about 19 and 54 milligrams per litre, all within the strictest local discharge class, while the wetland alone failed that class. At the best settings the system removed about 89 percent of the pollutant load, matching the model's prediction. The authors see the design as suited to scattered rural households.
pmc-13218525:
Obi Peter Adigwe and Godspower Onavbavba survey Nigerian healthcare professionals about artificial intelligence and machine learning in a 2026 cross-sectional study. AI promises help with everything from drug therapy fitted to the patient to faster research, and Nigeria's system struggles with staff shortages and thin infrastructure. Whether the workforce trusts and accepts these tools is a practical question for rollout.

A structured questionnaire reached professionals across Nigeria's six geopolitical zones through layered sampling, with pharmacists, doctors, and nurses the largest groups and most respondents under thirty. Two thirds agreed that machine learning can improve research, and a similar share thought AI could speed drug discovery. Two thirds also said the tools can support doctors by handling unstructured data, and more than three quarters expected gains in drug manufacturing. The authors read the positive views as a sign that the workforce is ready for large-scale adoption of these tools.
pmc-13222325:
Yaxel Levin-Carrion and co-authors review skull-removal surgery on both sides of the head for children with uncontrolled brain pressure, in a 2026 systematic review. Pressure that resists medical treatment after brain injury can kill, and surgeons use several decompressive patterns. Four databases were searched under PRISMA rules for patients aged twenty-one or younger.

Only five studies fit the strict pediatric synthesis, including one small randomized pilot trial. Reports centered on severe traumatic injury and widespread brain swelling. Timing, pressure thresholds, technique, and outcome measures varied so much that pooling was impossible. The authors describe an evidence base too thin and uneven to settle when this last-resort surgery helps children most.
pmc-13224725:
Justine Revel and co-authors compare a 2026 pair of mosquito-borne viruses, West Nile and Usutu, focusing on a protein they release called NS1. Both viruses can invade the brain, and NS1 helps them spread while weakening blood vessel walls. Lab, animal, and patient data were combined to see whether the two versions of the protein behave alike.

West Nile NS1 left infected cells in far larger amounts, survived heat better, and disrupted the blood-brain barrier in culture. In mice, West Nile infection also produced higher blood levels of the protein and stronger inflammation. Patient samples matched that split, since the protein appeared mainly in West Nile cases with neurological symptoms and never in Usutu cases.
pmc-13229925:
Dioselina Lanzagorta Ortega and colleagues report in 2026 a rare nerve variant found during thyroid surgery with nerve monitoring. The left laryngeal nerve did not loop down into the chest as usual. Instead it left the vagus nerve in the neck and ran straight across toward the voice box.

Such a non-recurrent nerve is uncommon, and a left-sided one is rarer still because it usually needs an unusual aortic arch layout. Injury to this nerve can harm voice, swallowing, and airway protection. Monitoring signals alerted the team during the operation, which helped them protect the nerve. Awareness of the variant, the authors argue, should shape how surgeons search and dissect in the neck.
pmc-13230325:
E Ram and D Carter propose in 2026 a new way to handle fading benefit from sacral nerve stimulation for bowel problems. The implanted device helps many people with fecal incontinence or bowel trouble after rectal surgery. When benefit fades, clinics often blame device mechanics first and may escalate procedures too quickly.

Their service model starts by confirming real loss of benefit against set thresholds, then rules out technical faults step by step. Next comes a structured check of nerve function, followed by reprogramming matched to the patient pattern. Fixed review intervals and clear cutoffs for revision or removal complete the pathway. Ideas such as nerve adaptation drift are offered as hypotheses, not proven causes.
pmc-13231725:
Elisavet Efthymiou and colleagues survey in 2026 Greek rheumatologists about food and nutrition in systemic sclerosis care. Gut symptoms weigh heavily in that disease, yet doctors lack agreed diet guidance for patients. Seventy-four specialists answered a questionnaire built for scleroderma care and nutrition education.

Doctors said patients most often ask for diet help to control symptoms, above general knowledge or special diet plans. Reflux topped the list of food-related worries, with bloating, heartburn, and swallowing trouble also common in their patients. Specialists backed structured support, favoring face-to-face diet visits and adding dietitians to care teams. Pain and finger ulcers were also reported in more than half of patients by most doctors.
pmc-13232625:
Akihiro Yamashita and colleagues report in 2026 a young woman whose hip bone broke through a benign cartilage tumor, then healed for good. She was nineteen when a minor injury snapped her femoral neck, already weakened by a large chondroblastoma reaching from the ball of the hip into the neck. Such tumors can return or kill the hip ball when surgeons scrape them out.

Her first surgery fixed the fracture with hardware, which stayed in place for the second operation. Surgeons then opened a window at the head and neck junction, scraped the tumor clean, and packed the space with graft bone. Ten years on, she shows no tumor return and no death of the hip ball. Careful scraping can give lasting control even after a fracture.
pmc-13233625:
Pupa U P A Gilbert and colleagues released a 2026 study of tooth enamel at the nanoscale across primate evolution. Enamel is built from thin hydroxyapatite crystals bundled into rods, and the slight angular mismatch between neighboring crystals was poorly understood. Using an imaging method called PELICAN, the team measured crystal orientation in twelve teeth from nine primate species spanning about eighteen million years.

Mismatch between adjacent crystals grew as food got harder in apes and monkeys, past and present. In the human line, mismatch rose over the past 1.6 million years, especially when meat eating and stone-ground grain entered the diet, but not with industrial food processing. The authors suggest small misorientation angles help enamel resist cracks, a trick materials designers could borrow.
pmc-13233725:
Vladimir Bozhdansky, Eran Bacharach, and Marcelo Ehrlich published a 2026 perspective on turning cancer's own survival programs against it. They use the idea of a frenemy pathway, a biological program that protects healthy tissue yet also helps tumors, creating weaknesses that treatment can exploit. Their focus is the tug-of-war between apoptosis, orderly cell suicide, and type I interferon signaling, the alarm system that summons immune attack.

Oncolytic viruses, engineered to infect cancer cells, sit at the center of the argument. By disturbing the balance between cell death and interferon defenses, a virus might force tumor cells into immunogenic death, the kind that trains the immune system to hunt remaining cancer. The authors frame this as synthetic lethality at the level of whole pathways rather than single genes.
pmc-13234125:
Hui Qi and colleagues released a 2026 study on computer diagnosis of brain tumors from MRI scans. Reading such scans by hand is slow, and nobody had compared the leading model families fairly under one strict protocol. Using 4,264 images from 333 patients, the team benchmarked convolutional networks and vision transformers with patient-level validation, so no person's scans leaked between training and testing.

A classic network, DenseNet-121, offered the best balance of accuracy and computing cost when no outside pretraining was allowed, while pretrained transformers stayed competitive when such data was available. The authors then upgraded DenseNet with coordinate attention, which tracks position along both image axes, and a hybrid image augmentation scheme. Their CAHA-Net topped the variants tested, reaching a macro F1 score near ninety-four percent with very few false alarms.
pmc-13234625:
Odinaka C. Iwuozo and co-authors fed in 2026 broiler chickens diets containing either poultry fat or olive oil and examined their brains. Olive oil is rich in monounsaturated fat, which can influence serotonin, a chemical messenger tied to behaviour and wellbeing. Two serotonin-rich brain regions were sampled, along with blood plasma. Chicks received the assigned diets from hatching to day twenty.

Birds on olive oil showed higher serotonin levels in both brain regions than birds on poultry fat. Thousands of small molecules differed between groups, and several hundred could be identified by name. Patterns pointed to changes in amino acid handling and energy-related pathways across blood and brain. Some compounds rose in one tissue while falling in another. The authors conclude dietary fat type reshapes metabolism inside serotonin circuits of young chickens.
pmc-13234825:
Müjgan Yilmaz Altun and co-authors followed in 2026 bone density around replacement knee joints in a randomized trial's secondary analysis. Sixty-three patients received either a cemented or an uncemented knee implant with an asymmetric shinbone part. Density was scanned at several points over two years in three zones of the thighbone and shinbone. Changes within patients and differences between groups were tested statistically.

Bone density fell around both implant types, most clearly in the front zone of the thighbone. That zone lost about a third of its density with uncemented fixation, notably more than with cement. Other thighbone zones lost less, and between-group gaps there were not clear. Shinbone changes stayed small, with only one clear decline under cemented parts. The authors judge the shinbone findings to be of uncertain importance for patients.
pmc-13236625:
Lijie Yang and a large team surveyed in 2026 more than four thousand Chinese children and teenagers about loneliness, stress, and taking drugs properly. Data came from a national medication literacy project run through children's hospitals in eighteen provinces. People aged eight to eighteen answered questionnaires on all three topics. Statistical mediation modelling tested whether stress carries part of loneliness's effect on habits.

The remaining link acted directly, beyond the stress pathway measured in the model. Chronic illness care in children depends heavily on steady medication habits at home. The authors, reporting a first such test in Chinese youth, urge programs that ease both loneliness and stress together.
pmc-13236725:
Salim and colleagues ask whether blood-thinning drugs raise bleeding risk in people with cavernous malformations in the brain. These tangled vessel clusters can bleed into the brain, so doctors often fear prescribing antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs to patients who have them. Hard evidence for that fear has been lacking, leaving hard calls in stroke and heart care.

Using a large health records platform, the team matched patients with these malformations who took blood thinners against similar patients who did not. None had bled before. Comparing later brain bleeds between matched groups gives the fairest test short of a trial, and the answer can free needed treatment.
pmc-13237925:
Huston and colleagues test whether stimulating nerves through the ear can prime the blood to clot faster. In animals, vagus nerve stimulation reduces bleeding after injury. The signal runs through immune cells in the spleen, which raise calcium inside platelets, readying them to activate the moment tissue is torn and clots are needed.

Healthy volunteers received ear-based vagus stimulation, alone or combined with trigeminal nerve stimulation. The team then measured platelet function and standard clotting tests. A safe, wearable way to prime clotting could matter in surgery and trauma, where minutes of bleeding decide outcomes. First, though, the effect must be shown in people, as here.
pmc-13238925:
Handke and colleagues ask whether obesity helps or harms patients treated for advanced urological cancers. Extra weight is reshaping outcomes across oncology in surprising ways. Their study covers metastatic bladder, kidney, and prostate cancers, the three big cancers of the urinary and male reproductive systems, in patients given systemic drug therapy at one high-volume centre.

Looking back over cases treated from 2017 to 2025, the team compares survival between patients with and without obesity. Cancer doctors know this as the obesity paradox question: heavier patients sometimes live longer on modern drugs. A centre-level answer helps clinicians counsel patients honestly instead of assuming weight only ever works against them.
pmc-13239325:
Reeju Maharjan and team reported in 2026 a case of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy triggered by opioid withdrawal, paired with a review of the published papers. In this stress cardiomyopathy the heart's main chamber weakens suddenly and balloons at its tip, looking like a heart attack while the coronary arteries stay clear. Withdrawal's surge of adrenaline-like chemicals is the suspected trigger.

The syndrome can bring chest pain, heart tracing changes that imitate a heart attack, and modest rises in heart injury markers. Treating the withdrawal itself with methadone or buprenorphine is central to recovery, the authors stress. With opioid-related harms climbing, they urge emergency clinicians to keep this diagnosis in mind when withdrawal patients present with cardiac symptoms. Early spotting changes care and outcome.
pmc-13240025:
Tania Biswas and team describe good results in treating a pigmented mouth condition in a 2026 case report. Pigmented oral lichen planus is a long-running immune disorder of the mouth lining. It leaves dark brown or black patches next to the usual white or red changes, and it often resists standard care.

The patient took mycophenolate mofetil by mouth, a drug that quiets the immune system and is kept for stubborn cases. Symptoms eased a great deal, and the dark patches faded with them. The authors offer the drug as a safe and sound systemic choice when plain treatments fail for this form. Their case adds one more documented success to a thin proof base.
pmc-13240825:
Mariko Saito and colleagues publish a 2026 mouse study on alcohol exposure shortly after birth and brain signaling tied to retinoic acid. This vitamin A related signal guides brain development. The newborn mouse stage models the final trimester of human pregnancy, when alcohol can cause lasting harm.

Using reporter mice whose cells glow where the signal is active, the team mapped activity across several brain regions. Activity was strongest in parts of the hippocampus and appeared in certain neuron types and support cells. Alcohol given on day seven reduced signaling in several regions, and it cut signal-carrying inhibitory neurons even more sharply than those cells were lost. The authors suggest weakened signaling may disturb neuron maturation.
pmc-13241925:
Wissam Arab and co-authors present a 2026 case report with literature review on ovarian cancer that had already spread to the brain at diagnosis. Brain spread in this cancer is rare, since cells usually travel through the abdomen. A patient with a BRCA1 mutation was found to have brain lesions shortly after her first surgery.

Her care combined several approaches across the disease course, and she survived long term on maintenance treatment with a PARP inhibitor drug. These drugs pile up DNA damage in cancers with faulty repair systems like hers. The authors also review published cases, noting how few involve brain spread found at the start. Their report supports considering targeted maintenance therapy in this difficult presentation.
pmc-13242125:
Schöneberg's team in Frankfurt sequenced every type specimen of a Bolivian frog whose home was logged before it was named. Oreobates chiquitanus survives at three sites in the Chiquitano Dry Forest, all near active logging. A base genome came from one paratype; side genomes covered all types. The museum stores became a genetic time capsule.

History rebuilt from genes shows the population rebounding from a dip some three hundred thousand years ago. Gene variety suggests a still-healthy gene pool. Every known population sits beside logging sites all the same. The genomes now anchor a starting line for tracking future genetic erosion.
pmc-13242325:
Hyera's team at the Western Cape bathed fat cells in gold specks to block lipid storage. The work stayed in cell dishes. Citrate-capped particles of fourteen nanometres were made by simple chemistry. Mature mouse fat cells received rising doses. Staining, survival assays, and gene activity arrays tracked the response.

The particles spared cell survival while cutting cell lipid build-up dose by dose. 35 genes shifted, clustered around fat formation and lipid handling. Networks centered on PPAR signaling and fat-cell hub genes. Hyera pitches the gold particles as an obesity play awaiting animal tests.
pmc-13242825:
Craig Mortimer and co-authors present a 2026 observational study of nebulised salbutamol effects in ambulance-treated asthma attacks. Guidelines have urged less reliance on this reliever drug over possible side effects, yet it remains frontline care. The team tracked heart, breathing, oxygen, and blood sugar changes around treatment.

Among well over a hundred eligible patients, heart rate and breathing rate eased modestly while oxygen saturation improved slightly. No overall worrying heart rate rise appeared. Blood sugar was measured in only a small prospective subgroup, where it rose a little, reaching significance only after removing one atypical case. The authors say the data are too thin to change glucose monitoring practice and call for larger prospective studies.
pmc-13245025:
Jingchi Wen and co-authors dissect what drives carbon emissions in Lithuania under the European Green Deal in 2026. Energy use dominates the country's emissions, and links with growth and policy shift over time. The team used wavelet tools that track ties at different time scales.

Data ran from 1996 to 2024 on energy intensity, research spending, waste handling, legal compliance, growth, and trade. Energy intensity proved the strongest and most lasting driver of emissions. Growth added upward pressure as well. Research and strong institutions cut emissions only at some times, and waste policy mattered least. The authors put energy efficiency and green innovation first for policy.
pmc-13245525:
Nicola Pugliese and a large group of colleagues review how to find liver scarring earlier in fatty liver disease in 2026. Fatty liver disease now leads chronic liver disease in Europe. Scarring, called fibrosis, best predicts who will fare badly, yet it often goes unseen until late.

Blood markers, scans, lab algorithms, and AI tools can now grade scarring without biopsy. Use stays patchy because of low awareness, uneven access, split referral paths, and uneven payment. The authors favor joined models that link primary care with specialists in one pathway. Such models could speed referral and fair access, above all for people with diabetes or obesity.
pmc-13246525:
Smith, Jin, Miller, and co-authors built reference samples for testing milk for bird flu, in this 2026 Food and Environmental Virology paper. With highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 turning up in dairy cattle, laboratories need to detect the virus in milk, and proficiency exercises check whether labs get the right answers. That requires spiked milk samples whose virus levels are known precisely and stay uniform.

The team used digital PCR to count viral genomes in their stock and samples exactly, then confirmed the standard USDA detection assay read them consistently. Replicate samples barely varied, no milk-matrix interference appeared, and levels stayed stable over time. Such well-characterized samples, they argue, make nationwide lab evaluations trustworthy.
pmc-13246925:
Pelzer, Werthmann, and Svaldi piloted mirror exposure therapy for teenagers with anorexia nervosa in this 2026 Eating and Weight Disorders study. Distorted body image drives the illness, and guided sessions viewing oneself in a mirror reduce that distortion in adults, but evidence in adolescents was thin. Twenty-four female inpatients were randomized to twelve mirror sessions over four weeks or to usual treatment alone.

Mirror exposure added no measurable benefit on overall body image or eating-disorder symptoms; both groups improved during inpatient care anyway. Exploratory analyses hinted the mirror group reduced body-checking and avoidance behaviors, and eye tracking confirmed patients fixated on body parts they disliked, though that bias did not shift. The authors say larger trials must find which patients benefit and when.
pmc-13248325:
Ramadanov and colleagues built a prediction model for blood transfusion around hip replacement surgery, reported in 2026. Transfusions after this operation link to worse outcomes and higher costs, yet clinics lacked a tool built for this procedure. The team drew on a registry from one certified German arthroplasty center covering 2016 to 2023.

Of six hundred forty-eight patients, about one in six needed a transfusion. Low starting hemoglobin, longer operating time, greater blood loss, and lower body weight each raised the risk, while male sex lowered it. The model sorted patients accurately, and the authors ask for testing at other hospitals before routine use.
pmc-13248825:
Silveira and a Brazilian team built an antibacterial wound dressing, reported in Small Science in 2026. Infection is the most common reason skin wounds stall, so the team made zinc oxide nanoparticles using moringa leaf extract as fuel. They spun those particles into a membrane of two biodegradable plastics using an electric field method called electrospinning.

The best membrane, holding five percent nanoparticles, soaked up more than three times its weight in fluid and stayed friendly to skin cells in culture. It also held back two common wound bacteria, Staphylococcus aureus and E. coli. The authors propose the dressing for infected and slow-healing wounds, pending further testing.
pmc-13249725:
Valentine, Zhang, and Liu measured how attention treats shapes, in a 2026 perception study. When people attend to a simple feature like color, nearby feature values get a boost that fades with distance, a pattern called similarity gain. The team asked whether the same holds for shape, using a circular shape space where forms morph gradually into one another.

Volunteers watched two target shapes and ignored overlapping distractors, reporting brightness changes in the targets only. Accuracy peaked when the two targets matched and fell steadily as their shapes diverged, across two experiments with different shape ranges. The authors read this as shape-similarity gain: attention boosts look-alike shapes, suggesting the brain keeps an inner similarity map for objects.
pmc-13250225:
Iwu-Jaja and colleagues map research on fighting drug-resistant infections across the World Health Organization's African region. Their 2026 BMJ Public Health scoping review sorts interventions against the five goals of the global action plan on antimicrobial resistance. The team searched four databases, plus grey sources, in late 2025.

Forty-nine studies qualified, clustered in South Africa, Ethiopia, Kenya, Ghana, and Nigeria. Most tested stewardship programs or awareness training in large hospitals and showed better prescribing or knowledge, but few tracked long-term change. Prevention, vaccination, animal-health links, and full cost studies were all scarce in the literature. The authors call for longer implementation research, wider country coverage, and economic analysis to guide the region's response.
pmc-13250325:
Martin Larisch and colleagues tell a cautionary trauma story in this 2026 case report. A 57-year-old woman was in a car crash and developed a severe tear in her small bowel, but since she was stable, she chose treatment without surgery.

Scans three weeks later suggested the tear had healed. At 21 weeks she returned with worsening belly pain, nausea, and vomiting, and imaging showed a new hole at the same spot. Surgery found a three-centimetre tear beside a scarred, narrowed section, and part of the bowel was removed. The authors warn that a healed-looking scan can hide slow blood-starvation damage, so long follow-up is vital.
pmc-13250425:
Matsumoto and colleagues check whether adding bone cement makes hip fracture nails hold better in older patients. Their 2026 Geriatric Orthopaedic Surgery and Rehabilitation study followed three hundred patients at several Japanese centers. All had upper thighbone fractures fixed with a nail inside the bone, with or without cement support.

No screw cut-out, the main failure being tracked, occurred in the cement group, while four cases appeared without cement. Excess sliding of the screw and overall complications were also numerically less common with cement. No cement-related harm was seen during the study period. Differences were not statistically firm, so the authors call the approach promising for high-risk elderly patients and ask for randomized trials.
pmc-13250625:
Ashish Sapkota and colleagues report an unusual concealment case in this 2026 paper. A 28-year-old man was brought from police custody with rectal pain, and after first denying it, he admitted he had hidden six glass drug ampoules inside his rectum.

Examination and imaging confirmed the objects were there. Glass drug vials are fragile, so leakage was a real danger, and surgery was planned. Before it happened, the ampoules passed out on their own with no harm, confirmed by later imaging. The authors note that in stable patients, laxatives and watchful waiting can sometimes avoid surgery, though this lucky ending is not a care plan.
pmc-13250825:
Tachikawa and colleagues report an elderly woman whose colon cancer triggered a dangerous immune overreaction called hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Their 2026 Surgical Case Reports paper covers a syndrome where a cytokine storm drives immune cells to devour blood cells. It usually follows blood cancers, and solid tumors like colon cancer rarely cause it.

The eighty-three-year-old woman arrived with a month of appetite loss, lasting fever, and mental decline. Scans and biopsy found an advanced cancer of the ascending colon, and surgeons removed the right side of her colon robotically. Fever and swelling returned after surgery, and a blood smear on day twenty-five confirmed the syndrome. Stronger steroid treatment failed to help, and she died on day forty-six, leading the authors to urge vigilance for this complication.
pmc-13251825:
Kai Kopecky and a large team study how dead giants shape living ecosystems in this 2026 paper. Foundation species such as trees, grasses, corals, and oysters build whole habitats, and their remains keep working long after death.

The team drew on experiments and records from ten sites across the United States research network. Five sites were on land and five were marine, and the records spanned two to 32 years. The dead routinely changed the life rates of their living kin. Effects ran from halving growth to a twelve-fold rise. The authors call this material legacy a hidden layer of ecosystem memory. They see it as a practical tool as climate-driven die-offs grow.
pmc-13252725:
Calvin Teahan, Enda Whyte, and Siobhán O'Connor survey Gaelic games coaches on injury prevention in this 2026 study. Ireland's fast, evasive field sports injure legs often, and warm-up exercise programmes proven to cut injuries exist, yet word was that few coaches used them.

Of 342 adult coaches answering an anonymous online survey, about six in ten used some form of prevention routine, but only 44 percent knew the formal programmes. Elite coaches used them more than others. Many coaches built or tweaked their own versions. Attitudes were positive, but four in ten admitted they did not know how to run a programme, and a third said no training was available. Education is the fix proposed.
pmc-13253325:
Sakshi Ghai and colleagues measure technology-facilitated sexual exploitation and abuse of children across Africa and Asia in a 2026 population study. Digital access is expanding fast among children in low- and middle-income countries, yet evidence on online grooming, sexual solicitation, coerced image sharing, and sexual extortion there has stayed thin. The team analyzed the Disrupting Harm project's nationally representative surveys from 2020 and 2021.

The data covered 11,912 children aged twelve to seventeen in twelve countries across eastern and southern Africa and Southeast Asia. One in six internet-using children reported at least one such experience in the past year, which scales to more than ten million children. Most experiences were never disclosed to anyone. Older children disclosed less, while active parental involvement online and knowing where to seek help both raised disclosure. The authors press policymakers and technology companies to act together.
pmc-13253825:
Akira Shinaoka and co-authors test a citrus compound on lymph flow in a 2026 trial. Monoglucosyl hesperidin, from citrus peel, aids blood flow and cuts swelling in earlier work. Thirty healthy adults took 300 milligrams a day or a placebo, swapping over in a crossover design, while scans measured the main lymph duct.

No effect showed in the full group. Among people with no exercise habit, though, the duct widened clearly after intake, matching higher lymph flow seen in animal studies. The authors also propose duct scans as a painless marker for future lymph studies.
pmc-13254625: Viet Thuc Dang and co-authors issued a 2026 correction to their paper on a bis-macrocyclic peptide ligand designed to mimic the active site of multicopper oxidase enzymes. The correction fixes two errors. One is the affiliation listing for author Andy Nguyen, which should be only the University of Illinois Chicago. The other is a misspelling of the word macrocyclic in the original title. The publisher apologizes for the errors, and no findings of the study are changed in this notice.
pmc-13255825:
Avni Bhatia and co-authors present a 2026 interview study of shelter workers in the United Kingdom about unowned cats living freely outdoors. Overpopulation, untreated illness, missed routine veterinary care, and cruelty topped the welfare worries. Workers blamed tight funding, staff shortages, poor facilities, and cats unsuited to home life inside their own organizations. Outside pressures included weak government backing, low public awareness, and inconsistent community care. Fuzzy labels like stray and feral also muddied decisions. Participants urged wider trap-neuter-return programs, better staff training, shared standards across charities, and stronger laws with real enforcement.
pmc-13256125:
Bibiana Sgalletta and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of iron's double role in the brain: essential nutrient and potential toxin. Neurons need iron for development, insulation of nerve fibers, and making chemical messengers. The brain guards its supply tightly through the blood-brain barrier and specialized support cells.

Too little iron early in life leaves lasting harm to thinking, movement, and behavior. Too much promotes oxidative stress, a form of cell death called ferroptosis, and inflammation, and abnormal deposits appear in Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and several rarer diseases. The review moves from whole-body iron handling to cell-level control inside the brain, then to disease links. Inflammation is highlighted as the main channel through which excess iron injures neurons.
pmc-13257025:
Carl P. Herbort Jr. and a large co-author group argue in a 2026 review for renaming a family of eye inflammations. The older label, white dot syndromes, grouped diseases only by pale spots seen in the eye. Those diseases differ sharply in cause and in where inflammation starts.

Multiple evanescent white dot syndrome and related disorders fall in the second. The authors propose non-infectious choroiditis, split by mechanism and location, as the cleaner umbrella term. pmc-13257725:
Mickael Soued and co-authors test an oral kinase blocker against early nerve pain and inflammation in rats in a 2026 study. Losmapimod blocks p38 MAP kinase, a signal involved in pain processing. Nerve ligation created acute neuropathic pain, while a paw injection model tested inflammatory pain over several days.

The drug eased heat and touch sensitivity from the first days after nerve injury. Its effective dose beat gabapentin's on a weight basis, and combining the two added effects without synergy surprises. Against inflammation, the drug shrank paw swelling as strongly as a standard anti-inflammatory medicine. Prior human work suggests good tolerance of the compound. Surgeons face pain that mixes nerve and inflammatory parts after operations, and the authors propose this drug as a candidate worth clinical testing for that window.
pmc-13257825:
Ralf Stroop and colleagues pilot a mini ultrasound probe inside the spinal canal during lumbar surgery in a 2026 feasibility note. A slim linear probe linked to a standard ultrasound system did the scanning.

Insertion and imaging succeeded in both cases without complications. The dural sac and nerve roots appeared in high resolution, letting surgeons check decompression completeness before closing. Handling and rotation needed no force, and operating time did not grow. Spine surgeons gain a real-time view from inside rather than outside the canal. Larger series must prove that the extra sight changes decisions and outcomes, not only pictures.
pmc-13259425:
J. Alkabli, Naif Abdullah R. Almalki, and Yaaser Q. Almulaiky anchor an enzyme onto copper treated acrylic textile in a 2026 study. The fabric was chemically fitted with amine groups that grow copper hybrid structures in place. A plant extract route produced a more uniform composite than the standard chemical route.

Enzyme loading reached over nine tenths on the green made textile. Bound enzyme reacted nearly twice as fast as free enzyme in solution. The bio textile removed most of a target pollutant within ninety minutes. Activity survived heat that nearly destroyed the free enzyme. Wastewater treatment gains a reusable cloth catalyst with strong heat tolerance.
pmc-13259525:
Anderson de Santana Botelho and coauthors test pepper plant oils against dengue mosquito larvae in a 2026 study. Oils from three Piper species and their blends were chemically profiled first. Larvae of the third growth stage faced graded oil doses in the assays.

One species oil killed half the larvae at the lowest dose among the pure oils. Blends were gentler on a brine shrimp safety screen than pure oils. One blend paired the weakest and strongest oils into a cooperative effect. Computer docking suggested the active compounds block a nerve enzyme in larvae. Public health programs gain plant based larvicide candidates with early safety data.
pmc-13260025:

pmc-13260125:

The authors explain routes by which microbes and their products shape a child's risk and disease course. They also cover new treatment ideas, including helpful live microbes, bacteria-killing viruses called phages, and antimicrobial peptides. The review aims to guide more precise care for sick children.
pmc-13260625:
David M Williams, Clifford L Norman, and Lloyd P Provost presented in 2026 a method for making quality the strategy of a whole healthcare organization. They then plan improvement and manage the resulting efforts across the organization. Healthcare examples show the activities aligning vision, strategy, and culture while keeping learning continuous. The authors argue this shift lets organizations chase strategic aims and hold performance gains over time, not just finish single projects.
pmc-13260725:
Unnur Gudnadottir leads a 2026 cohort study of antibiotics given in pregnancy for Group B Streptococcus, a common bacterium that can harm newborns. pmc-13262925:
Elaynne Silva de Oliveira and colleagues audit street-level surroundings for walking and activity in São Paulo, Brazil, in a 2026 journal article. Homes in the Central-West region had the best overall surroundings. Adults with more schooling, those identifying as White or Asian, and those aged 60 or older lived in areas with better scores for looks, trees, sidewalks, and crossings. Adults with less schooling and those identifying as Black or Brown lived near poorer sidewalks. The authors urge fairer urban planning.
pmc-13263125:

Dye levels after spraying were far above background air levels, with a clear statistical difference. Age, sex, and ethnic background did not significantly change how much dye became airborne in adjusted analysis. The authors conclude that nasal preparation sprays can generate aerosols. They advise clinicians to weigh that risk against the benefits and add protective steps where needed.
pmc-13263225:
Youngrok Park and colleagues describe a clever second transplant strategy after cord blood transplantation in a 2026 case report. With no matched donor for his own tissue type, he received cord blood from two donors, and unusually, cells from both persisted side by side.

When the cancer relapsed again and was beaten back, the team used the dominant cord donor's tissue type as the target for finding a new donor. A matched donor was found on that basis. pmc-13263325:
Celine Ransy and co-authors report a 2026 journal article questioning a standard lab test of how cells make energy. Using both tests on one plate improved accuracy, and they estimate about half of resting oxygen use is not tied to energy production.
pmc-13263425:
Xinjia Gu and colleagues charted in 2026 the toll of childhood hernias across low- and middle-income countries using Global Burden of Disease data. pmc-13263525:
Alessandra Imeneo and colleagues evaluate keeping infected vascular grafts quiet with long-term antibiotics when removing them would likely kill the patient. pmc-13264225:

The case shows a rare cause of failed drainage and a minimally invasive fix.
pmc-13264825:

pmc-13266125:

pmc-13287325:

pmc-13288025:

pmc-13288325:

pmc-13288725:
Zizhen Zhou and colleagues hunt sharper COVID-19 warning signs in blood in 2026. Standard clot markers sort severity poorly. The team profiled plasma by illness grade. Three grades were used. Proteins that rose with illness were clustered. Top picks were checked in a fresh group.

pmc-13289025:

pmc-13289225:

pmc-13289425: Bo Kim and Cara C Lewis are named on a short 2026 correction notice in Implementation Science Communications. The notice fixes only the competing interests statement of an earlier commentary on a paper by Austad and coauthors from 2025. No research data, methods, or findings are presented, so the record is genuinely thin beyond that single fix.
pmc-13289925:

pmc-13290325:
Nurgul Montayeva and co-authors review fungal toxins in poultry through a One Health lens in a 2026 article. pmc-13290525:

pmc-13290725:

pmc-13290825:

pmc-13291025:

pmc-13291225:
How well do classic life quality tools work in schizophrenia care? Max Wiessner leads a 2026 review of three interview-based scales. Good tools are vital to judge if care helps. The review used strict world standards for rating health measures.

That path may serve patients better than more work on old scales.
pmc-13291325:
City haze makes heat islands worse, but cool roofs can help. Minghao Dong leads a 2026 study of passive daytime cooling under haze. Such coolers shed heat to the sky without power. Dirty air changes how well they work.

The team tuned a clear film’s thickness for haze. Thick films won under haze, thin ones under clear skies. Tests backed the model’s odd prediction. pmc-13292225:
Yeyun Cai and colleagues review self-powered smart devices for personalized healthcare in a 2026 article. pmc-13292325:
Simon Herbel, Guillaume Dumas, and Tomas Urbina defend a 2026 exchange about whether daptomycin still belongs in treating Enterococcus faecium bloodstream infections in intensive care. pmc-13293425:

pmc-13293625:
Tomoyasu Kashiwagi and colleagues report, in a 2026 surgical case, a strangulated small bowel blockage tangled with a major pelvic artery after lymph node surgery. A 77-year-old man arrived with severe belly pain after earlier bladder surgery.

About 230 centimeters of bowel were removed, the artery was saved, and recovery was smooth.
pmc-13293725:
Wenwen Liang and colleagues model, in a 2026 study, what predicts recovery from depression after stroke, a common and harmful complication. Mood after stroke swings between recovery and relapse, yet what drives each shift was unclear.

pmc-13293825:
Led by Milena Wojciechowska, a 2026 study asks which mental traits shape daily life for people living with asthma. Patients were compared with healthy controls. pmc-13293925:

pmc-13294325:

pmc-13295925:
Takayuki Ando and co-authors examine, in 2026, why people with several chronic conditions end up attending many clinics in Japan, a pattern called polydoctoring. Using nationwide claims data, they track what changes when a new condition appears in the same person.

pmc-13296225:

pmc-13297325:

pmc-13297425:

pmc-13297725: Denis Bignotti and his co-authors issued a short fix to their 2026 case series on Class II bite care with bar devices and clear aligners. pmc-13297925:

pmc-13298225:

pmc-13298525:

pmc-13300225:

pmc-13300525:

pmc-13301025:

pmc-13301125:

pmc-13301925:

pmc-13302125:

pmc-13302325:

pmc-13302725:

pmc-13303925:

The authors warn against reading lab accuracy as proof of clinical value.
pmc-13304125:

pmc-13304525:

pmc-13304925:

pmc-13305325:

pmc-13307025:

pmc-13307725:

pmc-13307825:

pmc-13308225:
