Among 1678 unrelated mothers, 129 told of asthma, and 27 variants drawn from large global studies were checked one by one and as a joint score.

One variant in the SMAD3 gene passed the strict bar, with an odds ratio of 1.80 for asthma in this group. The joint score also tracked with higher odds, though the gain per step was small in size. Small numbers barred a full genome scan, so the authors call for more cohorts in groups that gene studies have long skipped over.
pmc-13308425:
Stephen Wiblin and colleagues analyse a 2024 survey of 5,177 Australian adults in 2026 to explain who takes COVID-19 boosters and virus drugs. The sample by design held many people with several chronic illnesses. Conduct was mapped with the capability, opportunity, and motivation framework, checked with strict models.

Booster uptake fell sharply between 2023 and 2024 in the responses. Older age, medical risk, and university education again and again flagged higher uptake and stronger plans. Renters and employed people showed lower uptake across vaccine results. Motivation scores were the strongest single flag once loop scoring was fixed. Among people who caught COVID-19, only about fifteen percent got virus-fighting treatment. The authors urge equity-focused campaigns that remove built-in barriers for renters and younger workers instead of rehashing knowledge ads.
pmc-13308725:
Chenyang Huang and co-authors test in 2026 whether a lower oestrogen dose can hold pregnancy rates in hormone primed frozen embryo transfer cycles. Records from 2022 to mid 2025 split 1955 high dose cycles from 202 low dose cycles, all with one blastocyst moved per cycle.

Raw rates favoured the low dose group, yet the groups differed in age and egg reserve at the start of care. After matching and model fixes, the gap shrank and lost firm standing in the final checks. Early loss rates also matched between groups. A gentler dose may suit younger women, yet forward trials must prove the trade is safe and fair.
pmc-13309525:
Shinji Futami and co-authors study harmful self-directed antibodies in a rare lung disease in a 2026 article. In autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, antibodies attack a signal the lungs need to clear fatty material, yet total antibody amount does not match how sick patients are. The team asked whether the exact target spot and grip strength matter more.

From 28 patients, 186 antibodies were sorted by which spot on the signal they bind. For one binding class, tighter grip meant stronger blocking, and patients with more of these antibodies were sicker. High-grip antibodies of that class alone caused disease signs in engineered mice. The authors say target spot plus grip, not amount alone, drives harm.
pmc-13309825:
Di Lian and colleagues ask in 2026 whether faster genetic testing changes outcomes for children hospitalised with community-acquired pneumonia in Fujian. Records covered 199 children whose lung washings were tested between 2021 and 2023, split into targeted sequencing and conventional testing groups. The sequencing group was further divided at forty-eight hours.

Sequencing found bacteria and viruses at rates several times higher than conventional methods and caught mixed infections in over half its cases. Children tested early improved their cough about three days sooner and cleared chest sounds a day sooner than late-tested peers. Treatment changes also came more promptly in the early group. Costs and stay length trended lower without reaching significance. The authors argue early sequencing belongs in routine workflow, shifting testing from mere identification toward outcome-driven care.
pmc-13310625:
Qi Zhang, Yu-Ting Qiao, and Shu Li review in 2026 the MARCH family of membrane-bound ubiquitin ligases, enzymes that tag other proteins for removal or rerouting. Each family member carries a signature ring-shaped catalytic domain anchored in cell membranes. The review gathers recent work on their structures, locations inside cells, and expression patterns across tissues.

MARCH proteins steer immune responses by controlling which signalling molecules persist on cell surfaces. They also maintain organelle balance and influence tumour growth by disposing of regulatory proteins. Different members attach different tag chain types, sending substrates down different disposal routes. Because these enzymes decide the fate of many immune and cancer proteins, they attract drug development interest. The authors call for mapping more substrates and interaction networks. Such maps, they argue, could open treatments for severe immune and malignant diseases.
pmc-13311125:
Carolynn Hare and colleagues test whether autistic and ADHD traits shape how senses combine in a 2026 study. Both conditions show sense processing differences, and they often co-occur, yet joint trait effects were unclear. A broad university sample did a fast detection task that measures gain from paired sights and sounds.

Ninety two young adults took part, with a mean age near 18 years old at testing. Trait scores showed no link to accuracy gain from paired senses. No added or joint effect of the two trait sets appeared either. When base sense sharpness is held equal, trait level alone may not drive sense combining in young adults.
pmc-13311325:
Visarat Palitnonkiat, Sirote Wongwaisayawan, and Tharin Thampongsa present in 2026 a case where appendicitis followed physical trauma rather than the usual internal blockage story. A 38-year-old man jumped from a second-floor height during a delusional episode and was transferred for psychiatric care after trauma checks found no major injury. Four days after the fall, right lower abdominal pain began.

Examination found localised guarding and rebound tenderness, and computed tomography confirmed acute appendicitis. An emergency appendectomy followed. Trauma is a rare but documented trigger for appendix inflammation, which is why the team pairs the case with a literature review. Appendicitis is the commonest cause of acute abdomen in emergency practice, so it belongs on the list even after injury seems to explain pain. Anchoring on the trauma, the authors warn, can delay a routine but time-sensitive diagnosis.
pmc-13311725:
Henry Badji and co-authors lay out protocols in a 2026 article for using genome sequencing to trace gut bacteria that cause diarrhea across Africa. The GETCampy-Africa study sits inside a One Health frame.

Standard lab work shows where these germs are but cannot resolve fine strain differences, drug resistance, or spread paths. The study uses a case-control design across several countries, sampling people, animals, and the environment. Genome data will pin down which sources feed human illness and how strains move. The protocols give other teams a shared method for high-resolution gut germ tracking.
pmc-13311925:
Seungyoon Roh and co-authors in 2026 present a study on how three Toll-like receptor paths shape the inflammatory output of chicken macrophages. The cytokine IL-1 beta sits at the center of the network.

The team stimulated a chicken macrophage cell line and blood-derived macrophages through the TLR2, TLR3, and TLR4 routes. Responses differed sharply by route, with the virus-mimic route raising IL-1 beta, IL-18, and interferon beta, while the bacterial wall route answered weakly. A gene-edited line lacking IL-1 beta let the team test how the cytokine steers each route's output. The work fills a gap in bird immunology with disease-control value.
pmc-13312025:
Peishuang He and colleagues use computer models and multi-omics data in a 2027 study to explain why retinol speeds cell growth at low doses yet harms cells at high ones. Retinol is a common anti-aging ingredient in skin products, but the switch behind this two-way behavior was unclear.

Working with human foreskin fibroblasts, the team combined gene, protein, and metabolite data with a genome-scale metabolic model. Low doses switched on retinoic acid signaling and rerouted cell chemistry in ways that favor growth. High doses instead brought oxidative stress, a build-up of harmful intermediates, and signs of ferroptosis, a form of cell death. The authors name control points such as DHRS3 and GCLM that could guide safer retinol products.
pmc-13312825:
Azadeh Rakhshan and colleagues present a 2026 case report of ossifying fasciitis in a man's hand, a benign growth notorious for impersonating cancer. The lesion mixes spindle-cell growth with stray bone formation and grows fast enough, with dense imaging, to be mistaken for a sarcoma. While it usually appears on the trunk or upper limbs, the hand is an exceptionally rare site.

Their patient, aged 34, developed a painless lump on the palm of his right hand over two months, sitting beside a flexor tendon on scans. Under the microscope the removed mass showed fibroblasts in bundles within loose stroma, bone rimmed by osteoblasts, and scattered giant cells, with no malignant features. Marker tests confirmed the diagnosis. The authors stress that knowing this entity, and matching tissue, imaging, and clinical clues, spares patients needless radical surgery.
pmc-13313525:
Luana Figueiredo and Makeda Smith host a conversation piece, published in 2026, on how Canada should think about national and human security. Experts in defense studies, foreign policy, law, and human rights weigh the costs of guarding sovereignty. They also weigh the weakness of shared alliances in a shifting world.

The piece weighs the risk of American indifference or hostility. It notes a turn toward ad hoc coalitions, whole-society defense models, and strength at home. It also shows how border rules and selective law use can repeat racialized harm and wear down humane norms. The authors argue that Canada cannot outsource its safety or rest it on arms alone. Real security must rest on justice, equity, and human rights. Guarding the state means little if people inside it are not safe and free.
pmc-13314325:
Diana L. Chávez-Aviña and colleagues examine, in a 2026 study, how an alcohol extract of the medicinal plant Tradescantia spathacea steers macrophage behavior, and whether the answer depends on mouse genetics. Macrophages from two strains, BALB/c and C57BL/6, run different metabolic programmes. The team exposed bacterially stimulated cells from each to the extract and measured toxicity, nitric oxide output, and genes for attack and calming signals.

The extract harmed neither strain's cells, though the dose benchmarks differed sharply. The half-maximal value was 4.76 micrograms per milliliter in one strain against 81.92 in the other. Nitric oxide responses ran in opposite directions between strains at that dose, inverting the pattern. Gene responses likewise diverged: one strain leaned toward a pro-oxidant yet regulated profile, the other toward a recruitment signal. The authors conclude the plant is a genuine immune shaper whose effects cannot be read off one model.
pmc-13314425:
Qingping Zhang leads a 2026 study of whether living high on a plateau dulls hearing. Long-term life at altitude has been floated as a factor in hearing, but proof from people who live high for years was limited.

The study drew 187 plateau residents aged 50 years or less at a Qinghai hospital health check. They were split by home altitude into three groups. The low group held 79 people at 2200 to 2499 meters. The middle group held 51 at 2500 to 3499 meters, and the high group held 57 at 3500 meters or more, by the report counts. Hearing was tested at six tones from 250 Hz to 8 kHz in both ears, with averages for low and high tones too. Early results showed the clearest group gaps at the high tones. The work weighs altitude as a quiet risk for the ears of plateau peoples.
pmc-13314625:
Ângela Alves, Rita Pombinho, and Didier Cabanes review how single-cell methods expose variety in bacterial virulence, in a 2026 paper. Cloned bacteria do not act as one uniform mass; during infection they split into unlike states across place and time.

That spread springs from random gene firing, shifting surroundings, gene change, and cell aging, the authors write. Tricks such as two-state switches, phase variation, dormant persistence, quorum sensing, and memory of past states let cells hedge bets and share labor. Groups gain fitness and staying power in hostile hosts by mixing bold and quiet members. Single-cell tools can now decode this patchwork gene by gene. Grasping it may explain why infections flare or linger and where new drugs could strike.
pmc-13315125:
Sydney Yearley and colleagues map, in a 2026 scoping review, how American health care screens patients for food insecurity and connects them to help. Hunger worsens nearly all health outcomes, yet implementation in clinics was poorly charted. Searching four databases through May 2025 for United States studies reporting both a screening process and a referral mechanism, the team synthesized 136 qualifying studies out of 11,406 records found.

Every study screened for food insecurity; none screened for the broader idea of nutrition insecurity. Screening usually rode inside social-needs questionnaires and electronic records, most often in outpatient settings, and methods were left unspecified in a fifth of studies. Referrals scattered across 39 strategies, led by community resources and clinic-embedded services, with food programmes and Food Is Medicine interventions behind. Only half of studies reported referral rates and a third reported whether referrals completed. The authors flag completion tracking as the field's biggest blind spot.
pmc-13315325:
C Parisi and a large oncology team report in 2026 on sex differences in side effects from new antibody-drug conjugates for lung cancer. Patients with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer got these drugs in early-phase trials at Gustave Roussy between 2018 and 2023, targeting proteins such as TROP2, HER2, and others.

Among 132 patients, about half women, three quarters had side effects of grade 2 or worse. Women had more such effects than men, with 82.8 percent affected versus 69.1 percent for men, and a higher median count of effects. Metabolic problems such as appetite loss and weight loss were also more common in women.
pmc-13316225:
Yi Lin sets out in 2026 a perspective on plant embodied intelligence, the idea that adaptive problem solving in plants emerges from the interplay of their spread-out structures with the environment. Intelligence is increasingly discussed beyond brains and nerves, and this branch of the idea was still undeveloped.

The review lays foundations and research paths, from shape change and growth to distributed memory, ecological signaling, swarm-like behavior, and decisions under risk. Global work spans plant neurobiology, systems biology, and bio-inspired materials. Mixing careful measurement, molecular tools, ecology models, and plant-inspired robots could advance both plant and intelligent systems science.
pmc-13316625:
Tristan N Samuels and colleagues built a 2026 human cell model for a rare inherited disease caused by faulty copies of NARS1, a gene needed to charge transfer RNA with asparagine. The illness strikes infants and children, hits the nervous system, and has no targeted treatment.

Two dominant faulty copies made cells sicken and switch on a stress program. Adding plain asparagine fully restored growth in patient skin cells and shut the stress signal off, a rescue the team also saw across protein patterns. A matching transfer RNA therapy and a stress-blocking drug each helped only in part. The simple nutrient result points to a low-cost treatment lead worth clinical testing.
pmc-13317125:
Evan Holmes and colleagues, in a 2026 primate cell study, examine lasting effects of repeated wood smoke exposure on airway lining cells. Wildfire smoke harms breathing and can worsen asthma and chronic lung disease, yet the molecular story of exposure and recovery is incomplete. Cells came from adult female rhesus monkeys and were grown in differentiated form.

Gene activity and chemical marks on DNA both shifted after smoke exposure. Affected networks involved immune responses, oxidative stress, cell death and the integrity of the airway barrier. One week after exposure stopped, clear gene changes persisted, enriched for inflammation, wound healing and repair pathways. Tissue appearance under staining, however, showed no significant change, suggesting molecular injury can outlast visible damage.
pmc-13317325:
Anne C. Madeo and a multi-site team describe, in 2026, work to help hospitals adopt a population health software platform called GARDE. The open-source system finds patients who may benefit from hereditary cancer services, then supports engagement, education and access to genetic testing. Adoption across sites has been uneven.

Using a framework for evaluating health technology through its life cycle, the team ran focus groups and interviews with seventeen people at five health systems. Barriers and supports centred largely on information technology needs for a platform linked to electronic health records. The group drafted responses to each barrier, then surveyed implementers on importance and feasibility. Eight strategies scored well on both counts and were chosen for an implementation toolkit.
pmc-13318725:
Ziyan Lyu and colleagues present a 2026 expert consensus on running combined cardio-oncology clinics. These clinics pair cardiologists with clinical pharmacists. Their shared task is safe, rational drug use in cancer patients. Heart damage from anticancer drugs is a leading cause of death in this group.

No established management systems existed for such joint clinics. Sichuan Provincial People's Hospital therefore led the effort, sponsored by the Clinical Pharmacy Branch. That hospital opened its combined clinic in March 2022. The consensus responds to national policy promoting pharmacist-led services and medication counselling. It aims to standardise workflows and pharmaceutical care for cardio-oncology patients. Single-discipline care, the authors argue, cannot meet these complex needs alone.
pmc-13319325:
Zeming Wu and co-authors propose, in 2026, viewing ageing through entropy, the physical measure of disorder. Evidence increasingly suggests ageing is not just accumulated damage but a system-wide drift toward disorder at every scale, from molecules to organs. The authors build a three-stage model of the lifespan.

Development builds order, adulthood holds order steady, and later life becomes dominated by disorder. Known hallmarks of ageing are reframed as connected nodes in one entropy-centred network. To make the idea measurable, the authors sketch a multiscale index that would combine disorder readings across biological levels. They present it as a proof of concept. If entropy reduction proves to be a shared mechanism behind effective interventions, the framework could guide new biomarkers and rejuvenation strategies.
pmc-13319925:
Erik Stuchlý and co-authors test how people guess the choices of others in a 2026 study of mental copying. When we forecast what a friend will pick, we may run our own choice process in our head as a stand in. If that inner process is skewed, the forecast should skew too, a claim the team tested by first bending risk tastes.

People were tuned to high or low chance settings, which shifted their own risk values, then asked to forecast picks by three stock figures with set risk styles. Their forecasts shifted for the average and risk shy figures but not for the risk seeking one. Own risk lean also tracked forecasts for the first two figures only. Copying seems real, but who the other person is sets its limits.
pmc-13320325:
Ben-Jian Zhong and co-authors name three new mushroom species from subtropical China in a 2026 taxonomy study. The trio belongs to a brittlegill group known for mild taste and varied cap colors, sorted here by both looks and gene proof. Field finds from the region were checked spore by spore and joined to gene trees built from four gene zones.

One new species wears a dark ruby grey cap with tight gills and flesh that stays white when bruised. The second wears a pale pink white cap and a stem that yellows with age or bruising. The third shifts from red grey to purple brown and its flesh browns when bruised. Gene trees back all three as fresh branches, and full accounts with photos fix their names for future finds.
pmc-13320425:
Yuan-Qing Luo and co-authors turn roasted sesame hulls into a flavor boost for sesame oil in a 2026 food study. Hulls are a thrown away part of the seed, yet roasting loads them with prized scent compounds. Soaking hulls in plain oil was tuned to draw that scent across while also testing whether the hull goods slow oil spoilage in storage.

The best soak used one part hull to five parts oil at mild heat for eight hours, in the trials reported. That oil gained balanced caramel, roast, and nut notes from hull aromatics. In fast aged storage its spoilage marks first rose faster, then after forty days climbed far more slowly than plain oil, and off scent build up stayed lower. Waste hulls thus serve twice, as flavor and as guard.
pmc-13320825:
Bo Pan leads a large expert group setting out a staging system for children's heart function in a 2026 guidance article. Heart failure in children is rising worldwide, and the group, from the Pediatrics Society of the Chinese Medical Association, wants care to start earlier in the disease course. The system applies to all children, not only those already ill.

Three stages are defined, from full heart function through early dysfunction to outright failure. For each stage, the article sets out how to recognise it and how to manage it, forming a full care pathway. The stated aim is to make childhood heart failure more preventable and treatable and to cut its long term burden.
pmc-13321125:
Liang Chen and his team present, in 2026, a way to estimate plant biomass in a famous Jurassic ecosystem from its fossil insects. The Yanliao Biota of China preserves rich insect fossils from about the Middle Jurassic. Plant mass underpins food webs and carbon storage, yet deep-time estimates have mostly been relative rather than counted.

Each insect's body mass was estimated from fossil measurements using rules calibrated on modern insects. Crowd densities followed from metabolic scaling rules. Herbivore biomass was then turned into plant biomass through a feeding transfer model, with all uncertainties explored by repeated random runs. Checks showed insect biomass dominated the uncertainty. The rebuilt values matched productive modern ecosystems with recognisable biome counterparts, and fossil insects seem to encode real energy limits of ancient landscapes.
pmc-13321225:
Alshaimaa Tarek and colleagues report a rare artery disease found before birth in a 2026 case report from Egypt. Generalized arterial calcification of infancy hardens and narrows large arteries very early in life, often causing breathing distress, heart failure, and high blood pressure. About 300 cases have been reported worldwide.

At 29 weeks of pregnancy, ultrasound showed valve narrowing, thickened heart walls, and heavy calcium in the aorta and ductal arch of the fetus. Gene testing found a homozygous harmful change in the ENPP1 gene, written as c.749C>T in the report. The authors call it the first gene confirmed Egyptian fetal case and stress expert heart scanning plus gene tests for counselling.
pmc-13322225:
Austin F Crossanoff and William L Balanoff report, in 2026, striking mood improvements after full dental implant rehabilitation in adults who had beaten addiction. It often wrecks oral health through acidity, poor nutrition and neglected hygiene, yet full dental repair is rarely part of recovery care. The study asked whether rebuilding teeth changes depression scores.

Records covered 101 treated adults in a row, all with verified long-term recovery. A changed depression survey was filled in before treatment and when the final prosthesis was delivered. Average scores fell from the severe range to near zero, and every patient improved. Four fifths began above the severe threshold, while over nine in ten ended in the minimal range. The authors argue implant rehabilitation deserves a place in full recovery care, not elective status.
pmc-13322625:
Taynara Gabriele Ribeiro Piano and co-authors test selenium and tellurium compounds against gut worms of farm animals in a 2026 laboratory study. Roundworm infections harm ruminant health, and heavy dewormer use breeds resistant parasites. Three compounds were tested on worm eggs and larvae from sheep and cattle, with cell safety checks alongside.

One selenium compound, diphenyl diselenide, stopped egg hatching best, while the tellurium compound AS-101 killed larvae best in the assays. Pairing the selenium compound with ivermectin gave a mild joint boost. That selenium compound was also gentlest on kidney cells in culture. The results mark a possible new family of worm treatments for livestock.
pmc-13322825:
Haoyu Wen, Weiwei Chen and Yuquan He explain how blood vessel walls harden with calcium, in a 2026 review of vascular calcification. The process is now seen as active, driven by smooth muscle cells in the vessel wall rather than simple mineral build-up.

Under strain from calcium and phosphate imbalance, sugar and fat toxicity, oxidative stress and long-term inflammation, those cells switch toward a bone-like state. They release tiny vesicles, break down surrounding matrix and switch on growth signals such as Wnt and BMP pathways. Other cell changes add to the effect. The authors discuss treatment ideas that target metabolic control points, block the cell switch, or alter gene regulation.
pmc-13323025:
Matteo Ricchi and a large team develop a counting method for Salmonella Infantis in poultry faeces, reported in 2026. This serovar dominates broiler production in the European Union and often colonises birds without signs, letting resistant strains spread quietly into meat.

Their method adapts a miniaturised most-probable-number approach and confirms results with a specific qPCR test. Performance checks used spiked and naturally contaminated samples, with matrix effects judged by Bland-Altman analysis and repeat testing across runs and operators. Applied to real samples, the method quantified bacterial loads well enough for risk assessment work. The authors present it as a monitoring tool for flock-level control in Italy and beyond.
pmc-13323125:
Huixian Xie and co-authors test a structured weight programme for psychiatric inpatients, in a 2026 study at Taizhou Second People's Hospital. Their 5-4-3 model joins five fields, four phases and three supports in one loop. Psychiatry, nursing, nutrition, rehab and pharmacy staff lead it jointly.

Inpatients with a body mass index of 24 or higher joined between November 2024 and April 2025. Care ran through stays of one to six months. A three-month follow-up came after discharge. Outcomes covered weight, body mass index and metabolic measures. They also covered patient knowledge and staff practice. Weight after discharge came mainly from self-report, which the authors flag as a bias risk.
pmc-13323325:
Rodolfo G Gatto, Hossam Youssef and Yuen Gao introduce a collection on imaging biomarkers for TDP-43 and tau protein diseases, in a 2026 editorial. The two abnormal proteins recur across many degenerative brain disorders and increasingly look like partners rather than separate problems.

Tau tangles and TDP-43 clumps can drive each other's build-up, harm synapses and disturb RNA handling, jointly speeding neuron loss in the editors' framing. Structural MRI shows shrinkage patterns while PET imaging traces molecular pathology in living brain. Featured work adds further clinical dimensions beyond classic symptoms. The editors argue that imaging both proteins together is key to earlier and sharper diagnosis of these mixed diseases.
pmc-13324625:
Felix Pius Omullo and team measured one-year survival among hemodialysis patients at a Kenyan county hospital. Their 2026 retrospective cohort covered all patients who started treatment for end-stage renal disease at Murang'a County Referral Hospital between January 2024 and January 2025. Routine outcome data from such county settings are scarce, even though county hospitals deliver most of this care in Kenya, and the team used Cox regression to find stand-alone signs of death.

One-year mortality reached 34.2%, a high rate the authors tie to systemic gaps in pre-dialysis care. Older age and central venous catheter use were the only stand-alone predictors of poorer outcomes, and tube use exceeded 89% of patients, a near-universal catheter-first pattern. The authors urge decentralized vascular access programs and earlier kidney-doctor visits, so more patients start with arteriovenous fistulas instead of tubes and outcomes improve in resource-limited settings.
pmc-13325125:
Soroush Torkamannejad, Hoi-ying Yip, and Bingyun Sun count heart ion channel proteins directly in a 2026 proteomics study. These large membrane channels set the heartbeat rhythm, and faulty levels can trigger dangerous arrhythmias.

Targeted parallel reaction monitoring with an in-sample calibration method measured copy numbers in human ventricle tissue. Extended digestion of the tough tissue fraction exposed proteins that broad surveys miss. The team quantified the main subunits Nav1.5, hERG, and Cav1.2, plus the helpers Cavβ1 and Cavα2δ1. Copy numbers let labs compare channel counts across studies and hearts on the same scale. The method should extend to systematic surveys of these hard-to-measure proteins.
pmc-13325625:
Daniele Midori Kakimoto Higa and colleagues review anesthesia for balloon heart valve repair in dogs in a 2026 retrospective study. Balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty eases severe pulmonic stenosis, but the strained heart makes anesthesia risky.

Records covered 21 dogs treated in 2024 and 2025, with a median age of 18 months. French Bulldogs made up 33.3 percent of cases, and fainting was the top sign at 42.9 percent of the dogs. Induction leaned on etomidate and midazolam in 95 percent of procedures. Low blood pressure struck 66.7 percent of dogs during surgery and often needed drug support. The balloon cut the valve gradient in 90 percent of cases.
pmc-13325925:
Shangjing Li and team built a pangolin-based smart skin that switches how it handles THz waves. Their 2026 paper addresses a conflict in wave defense: stealth, pass-through, and shielding demand different matter ways, while static materials cannot switch among bounce, soak-up, and pass-through states. The proposed skin blends flow-soft liquid metal, graphene sheets, and iron oxide nanorods into a three-part build.

Strain-driven microstructural change lets the skin switch back and forth among four states: bounce with 32.4 dB shielding, soak-up with 60.2 dB bounce loss, pass-through up to 76.7%, and secondary bounce with 50.8 dB shielding. It also senses with steady cycles, issuing shape-change instructions and checking the result in a closed loop that adapts function to external demands. The authors see uses in soft equipment armor and multifunctional wearables, for civilian and defense settings alike.
pmc-13326425:
Fatima Gul and colleagues relate blood branched-chain amino acids to body fat in visceral obesity in a 2026 study. Belly fat ties closely to insulin resistance, yet the place of these amino acids in that link is unsettled.

The study enrolled 105 people: 52 with obesity alone, 32 with obesity plus type 2 diabetes, and 21 healthy controls. Amino acid levels ran higher in both obesity groups, with valine up most, at 43.46 micrograms per mL in the diabetes group against 30.48 in controls. Levels tracked with visceral fat area, waist size, and insulin resistance scores. Valine showed the tightest links and stayed tied to waist size in joint models.
pmc-13327025:
Yunwei Long and colleagues report a 2026 surgical series for Kümmell's disease, where a spinal bone collapses weeks after injury and bends the back. Common cement procedures often fail in late stages, so the team tested short-segment fixation paired with a leverage method to straighten the spine.

Records covered 22 patients treated from 2020 to 2023, with pain scores, nerve function grades, and spinal measurements compared before and after surgery. Operations averaged about 100 minutes with modest blood loss, pain eased, and restored bone height reached 83 percent of expected values on average, alongside a mean angle correction of 19.32 degrees across the group. Nerve grades also improved, supporting the combined approach for advanced cases.
pmc-13328025:
Krystyna Kowalczuk and colleagues measure skipped nursing care across three countries in a 2026 survey. Care rationing, leaving needed tasks undone, lowers quality and raises error risk. Between March 2024 and March 2025, 610 hospital nurses in the Czech Republic, Poland, and Slovakia rated how often 32 nursing activities were omitted.

Age, family status, schooling, and years on the job showed no clear link to overall rationing levels, which differed only slightly between hospitals. Ward type mattered far more: emergency departments reported the most omitted care, and tasks needing long patient conversation were dropped most often. Staffing fixes should target the busiest wards and protect time for talking with patients, the authors imply.
pmc-13329325:
Alba García-Viola and colleagues set out a 2026 protocol for building a chatbot to support health workers who face aggression at work. Attacks on health staff have risen worldwide, yet reporting stays low and private support is hard to reach. The planned chatbot is called Sanidad Segura.

Work will run in two phases: first building and expert-checking content from reviews and local rules, then pilot testing with emergency and critical care staff in Almería, Spain. Ease of use will be scored with a standard scale, and reading ease with a Spanish scale. Interviews will probe user experience and barriers. Blending both kinds of evidence should show whether the tool is usable and welcome.
pmc-13329425:
Siyi Wang and co-authors describe three new goblin spider species from China in a 2026 taxonomic report. All three belong to Trilacuna, a genus found only in Asia. Two species come from Sichuan Province. The third comes from Chongqing and Hubei. Both males and females are described for each species.

Each account gives detailed body form, marks that separate the species from close kin, and photos of key parts. Names reflect their places: batang, kangding, and shennongjia, each paired with the genus authors Tong and Li. The genus held 55 valid species before these additions, the authors note. Careful form records help map spider diversity and guide later field surveys in the region.
pmc-13329725:
Kai Ting Mok and a large team describe building and testing a family health app for infants and parents in 2026. The app, FamNucleus, was co-built by clinicians using behaviour theory and a complex intervention guide. A test version ran for one month from December 2024 to January 2025 with 25 parents and 6 health professionals.

Users rated the app with standard experience and quality scales, and group talks probed views on adoption. Parents rated appeal and clarity above average, but scored speed and novelty lower in the summaries given. Professionals scored it higher overall, with top marks for appeal and novelty. Content checks were mostly strong. Ease of understanding fell from early version to test version, a point for redesign.
pmc-13330525:
Juseong Kim and colleagues present a deep learning tool for codon choice in human gene designs in a 2026 study. Messenger RNA drugs need codon patterns that boost protein output and keep the RNA stable. Older methods lean on frequency tables and miss wider sequence context. The new tool, COformer, blends convolutional and transformer networks.

Contrastive learning helps the model tie codon patterns to matching amino acids while reading both local and global context. Training used sequences tuned by commercial tools. In lab tests, designs from COformer raised protein output through better codon use and stronger RNA stability, the authors report. The approach may aid vaccine and drug design where output levels matter.
pmc-13331325:
Rahisha Maskey and team reported orbital myeloid sarcoma masquerading as orbital cellulitis. Their 2026 case paper presents a 24-year-old woman with two weeks of growing left orbital pain and swelling, first treated as orbital cellulitis. Myeloid sarcoma is a rare extramedullary manifestation of acute myeloid leukaemia, and orbital spread is rare and may mimic infection or inflammation.

Despite antibiotics, swelling, eye pain, and proptosis grew worse, prompting further tests. Imaging showed a retro-orbital mass pressing on the optic nerve, and blood film showed blasts. The patient carried an FLT3-ITD change and got chemotherapy plus orbital radiotherapy to 25 Gy in 12 fractions. Vision improved from 6/24 to 6/6, proptosis resolved, and remission was confirmed about four weeks after starting chemotherapy, with falling minimal residual disease. The team stresses early biopsy and blood workup for odd or stubborn orbital lesions, since prompt leukemia therapy improves visual and body-wide results.
pmc-13331425:
Pichatorn Suppakitjanusant and colleagues test a risk score for brain vein clots in a 2026 study. The 10-point CLOTS-EVT score bundles warning signs such as low awareness, low platelets and sodium, seizures, and wide clot spread to flag early decline and guide clot removal timing. Records spanned 12 centres from 2015 to 2017.

In total, 80 adults were scored. Headache was the top symptom, and most patients received blood thinners while 10 percent had vessel procedures in the reported care. A score of 4 or more predicted early decline with 82 percent sensitivity and 61 percent specificity in the validation values. Higher scores also tracked with worse discharge function and longer stays.
pmc-13333325:
Takashi Mikami and colleagues publish a step-by-step protocol in 2026 for profiling blood cancer samples with mass cytometry while tagging live cells so many samples can run together. The technique reads dozens of markers per cell, ideal for rare populations, but staining varies between runs and antibodies are costly.

Their workflow covers sample collection, live-cell barcoding with antibodies against β2-microglobulin and CD147, staining, data collection, and analysis for blood and bone marrow samples. Tagging living cells, rather than fixed ones, keeps surface markers in their natural state, a real concern for leukemia blasts that can look deceptively plain. The panel centers on T cell features and can include a CD19-binding fragment to spot CAR T cells when needed. Practical notes address signal spillover between mass channels and how to titrate many antibodies together. The authors aim to cut cost and technical noise for precious patient samples.
pmc-13333425:
Bora Moon and colleagues compared health curiosity across cultures in a 2026 study of Google search patterns in the United States and South Korea. Fresh starts such as New Year prompt waves of health goal setting, a pattern called the temporal landmark effect. Whether it plays out the same in individualistic and collectivistic societies was open.

Using Google Trends search data on health terms in both countries, the team found Americans showed the stronger landmark effect, with health searches clustering in the year's early periods. Korean searches instead traced an inverted U, peaking mid-year rather than at the start. The authors say the difference matters for anyone timing a health campaign: a January push fits the American rhythm, while Korean audiences may respond better later in the year. The study also stretches landmark theory by showing the fresh-start pull itself varies with culture.
pmc-13333525:
Yige Wang and Qiang Xiao argue in a 2026 review that viral pneumonia is, at root, a crisis of the body's fats as much as of its immune proteins. Severe lung infections end in respiratory distress and organ failure. The authors gather evidence that the lipidome, is remodelled along the way.

Their synthesis describes a metabolic crash: LDL cholesterol plunges, while HDL flips from shield into an inflammatory vehicle, and both shifts forecast who fares worst. Mechanistically, respiratory viruses hijack the SREBP-SCAP axis to stockpile lipid droplets for virus particles, and they exhaust the GPX4 defence system until lung cells die by ferroptosis. Gut-lung crosstalk and metabolic inflammation set the patient's threshold for barrier failure. Therapeutically, the pair back lipid-restoring strategies, pro-resolving mediators and metabolic stabilizers, and propose AI-driven typing to match treatment to the patient.
pmc-13333625:
Yuka Murofushi and co-authors built and tested an anti-doping education program grounded in values for university sport in Japan, reporting the work in 2026. The UNIVAS program aims to strengthen clean-sport decision making rather than only teach rules.

Three linked studies shaped the work. First, the team drafted 15 doping decision scenarios from theory, past literature, and Japanese disciplinary cases, then surveyed 1,000 student-athletes and support staff about them. Second, chosen scenarios became lecture slides, scripts, and worksheets, refined through five pilot classes. Third, a pre-post study checked short-term changes under two teaching formats. The process offers a tested model for universities that want ethics-based doping prevention.
pmc-13334125:
Mesud Fakirullahoglu and co-authors tested whether adenosine triphosphate can protect the stomach against damage from the cancer drug olaparib, in a 2026 rat study. Olaparib, a PARP inhibitor, causes gastrointestinal side effects that oxidative stress may help explain.

Rats were split into healthy control, olaparib-only, ATP-only, and combined groups. Stomach injury was scored by ulcer area and count, tissue slides were examined, and lipid peroxidation plus antioxidant defenses were measured. Olaparib alone produced marked mucosal injury, heavy tissue damage, and strong oxidative stress. Adding ATP shrank ulcers, preserved tissue structure, and restored oxidative balance across the measures taken. The findings suggest a simple energy molecule might shield the stomach during PARP inhibitor therapy, pending further work.
pmc-13334425:
Eduard Bezuglov and co-authors surveyed elite track and field athletes about intravenous therapy use in a cross-sectional study from 2026. IV infusions of legal substances sit in a gray zone of sports medicine, and how common they are was poorly documented.

An anonymous questionnaire drew 138 elite athletes, 73 men and 65 women, with answers collected between October 2020 and January 2021. Over half, 56.5 percent, reported receiving IV drugs not banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency, and 18.8 percent used them regularly. Actovegin led the substance list at 77.4 percent of users, followed by phosphocreatine and amino acids. International-level athletes reported IV use more often than national-level peers. The prevalence raises questions for team doctors and anti-doping educators even where no rule is broken.
pmc-13335025:
Feishen Lin and colleagues report a 2026 case of miliary tuberculosis complicated by acute respiratory distress syndrome, treated with high-dose glucocorticoid. A 25-year-old man in prior good health came in with a productive cough lasting two months and worsening breathlessness for one week. Chest scans showed widespread miliary nodules, ground-glass haze across both lungs, and fluid around both lungs, worse on the right.

Lab tests revealed type I breathing failure, elevated immune markers, low sodium, low protein, and raised tumor markers. Sputum acid-fast bacilli smears came back negative, but pleural fluid tests showed high ADA enzyme and immune signal gamma, suggestive of TB pleurisy. Lung biopsy confirmed granulomas with positive acid-fast staining, settling the diagnosis as miliary TB, TB pleurisy, severe lung infection, and acute breathing distress syndrome.
pmc-13336225:
Fernanda da Costa Ferreira, Mariana Miguel Vieira, and Ângela Maria Rosas Cardoso gathered nurses' perspectives on care at Child and Adolescent Psychosocial Care Centers in Brazil in a 2026 qualitative study. These community centers anchor mental health care for young people, and nurses' preparation for them is in question.

Semi-structured interviews with nurses from the Federal District health service and residents in a child and adolescent mental health program were analyzed thematically. Three axes emerged: mental health in academic training, continuing education, and whether the nursing role there is being dismantled or built. Nurses reported that university training still leaves them unready for the biopsychosocial model and broader clinical practice, producing insecurity. Continuing education stood out as the practical remedy already within reach.
pmc-13336425:
Xiao Xu and co-authors created microspheres that can carry many kinds of radiometals for liver cancer embolization in a 2026 materials study. Radioembolization works well against advanced liver tumors, but standard radioactive spheres pose material and handling problems.

Their spheres are built from a conjugated poly(imide dioxime) ligand forming an interlocked linked network. They accept lutetium-177, yttrium-90, rhenium-188, gallium-68, and technetium-99m at just 40 degrees Celsius, serving both imaging and therapy. Spectroscopy, computing, and stability tests in vitro and in vivo showed the metal complexes barely leak radiation carriers. Lutetium-labeled spheres foretold organ shunting and delivered radiotherapy in rat and rabbit liver tumor models. One all-purpose labeling platform could ease how hospitals prepare these treatments.
pmc-13336525:
Renata M M Pimentel and colleagues study 2026 COVID shots and their effects on new cases, lethality, and deaths in São Paulo, Brazil. This study tracked the effects of shots against SARS-CoV-2 on new cases, lethality, and deaths from COVID-19 in São Paulo from 2020 to 2022. It is a city-wide time series study with official public data.

City data came from the São Paulo Municipal Health Department, by Regional Health Coordination (CRS) zones. The Prais-Winsten regression model worked out the daily change rate (DPC). This let the team class trends in disease rates as rising, falling, or flat. São Paulo saw 17 percent of its people infected at least once by SARS-CoV-2, with a fatal outcome in 0.4 percent of its people. The North zone had a higher lethality rate at the start of the pandemic, falling much over the period.
pmc-13336625:
Pengfei Bai and co-authors report a 2026 light-driven method that makes hydrogen peroxide while also upgrading a plant-based alcohol. They joined zinc indium sulfide with carbon dots, forming a junction that splits light-made charges well. Furfuryl alcohol plays three roles at once: electron donor, starting material, and proton source.

In a very dry solvent mix, the system reached a peroxide rate of 24 mmol per gram per hour with high light use. The alcohol turned into furoic acid with 98% conversion and full selectivity for that product in the reported tests. Pairing a useful oxidation with peroxide output could cut waste in green chemical production.
pmc-13337025:
Yangyang Chai and co-workers designed a tumor-only delivery trick to beat resistance to anti-PD-1 immune therapy, in a 2026 study. Their carrier is a lipid nanoparticle tuned with a lysophosphatidylcholine lipid that cancer cells take up eagerly through their altered fat metabolism. It carries small interfering RNA against CD28, a protein that helps tumor cells hide by stabilizing PD-L1 messages.

In animals, the particles silenced about 80 percent of tumor-cell CD28 and cut PD-L1, while sparing T cells whose own CD28 is vital for immune attack. The treated tumors shifted toward an immune-friendly setting and responded again to checkpoint blockade. The approach shows how cell-selective delivery can unlock a target that would be unsafe to block body-wide.
pmc-13337825:
Huub C. Gelderblom, Glenda Gray, and Brian Kelley argue for fairer global access to antibody drugs in a 2026 perspective. Monoclonal antibodies are a major medical success, yet poorer countries get few of them. More than 130 are approved in the United States, while only sixteen sit on the WHO essential list as cited.

Long-acting prevention antibodies, starting with nirsevimab for RSV in infants, could join the essential list group and build momentum together. HIV treatment history shows prices fell a hundredfold through political action, not new technology alone. The authors frame combined demand as a wheel that could roll toward equal access.
pmc-13339225:
Yixin Chen and colleagues review contact-free detection tools for heart failure in a 2026 article. Heart failure disables and kills many older adults, yet early signs are vague and standard scans or blood tests need skilled staff and clinic visits. New sensor and algorithm systems promise continuous tracking at home.

Wearable fluid sensors and combined platforms that merge heart sounds, motion, and other signals are surveyed. Artificial intelligence and cloud tools turn those streams into risk alerts and personal plans. Policy support and industry teamwork have sped products to market as reviewed. The authors weigh promise against proof, urging validation before wide clinical trust.
pmc-13339625:
Nathalia S. de Oliveira leads a 2026 synthesis adding alkene arms to flavones at one chosen site. Flavones are plant pigments with many uses, and direct carbon-hydrogen editing avoids prebuilt handles. The flavone carbonyl itself guided a ruthenium catalyst to carbon 5.

Partners included acrylates, styrene, and vinyl ketones, giving yields up to 92 percent as reported. A carbamate group at carbon 7, normally a strong guide, did not divert the reaction. Theory showed lower energy paths for carbon 5 and a dead end at carbon 8. The work gives a clean route to 5-alkenyl flavones for further study.
pmc-13341225:
John W Seibert reported a giant second branchial cleft cyst in 2026 in a 24 year old woman with a year long painless, enlarging left neck mass. Such congenital lateral neck cysts rarely exceed 10 centimetres, and giant size near critical nerves and vessels creates diagnostic and surgical challenges. Imaging showed a large bilobed cyst deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle from skull base to below the collarbone.

Needle aspiration cytology excluded cancer, yet the cyst returned after ultrasound guided aspiration. Complete surgical removal preserved the spinal accessory nerve and all nearby neurovascular structures. The case shows that total excision, with careful nerve preservation, offers durable cure for giant branchial cysts.
pmc-13341625:
A word list for spotting cyberbullying victims online is built and tested by Xingyun Liu and colleagues, in their 2026 study. Self-reports skew victim counts, so the team mined Weibo posts, psychology lexicons, and questionnaires to construct a Chinese lexicon across methods, perceived harm, and coping responses.

The lexicon held 442 words, validated against expert ratings on 500 posts and checked for cross-platform fit on 3,442 RedNote posts. DeepSeek-R1 and GPT-4o were also made to repeat the construction steps under simple and complex prompts, their agreement with human judgments scored statistically. Machine help in lexicon building is itself part of what gets assessed.
pmc-13341925:
Macrophage metabolism is a battleground in tuberculosis, in a 2026 review by Xiaohe Lu's team. When the bacteria infect these immune cells, energy pathways rewire in ways that serve both host defense and germ survival.

Heightened glycolysis, normally a fighting trait, can be used by the germ. TCA cycle products such as itaconate nudge cells toward a permissive state, while competition over arginine and tryptophan decides nitric oxide output. Fat metabolism tilts the balance further by context. Mapping this tug-of-war names metabolic checkpoints that host-led therapies might flip against the germ.
pmc-13343325: Jiajun Sun and co-authors published a brief 2026 correction notice for their brain-wave study of face processing in schizophrenia. The notice itself carries no study findings. It only repairs the author list. Sun, Qing Liu, and Li Liu are now marked as equal first authors. Hongjun Sun is added as a third corresponding author. The original article has been updated.
pmc-13343425:
Xinyao Xie and colleagues studied desertification control in 2026 in the middle reach of the Yarlung Zangbo River, Tibet's breadbasket and primary grain region. Cold, arid climate plus human activity drive wind erosion that strips soil and vegetation, threatening farm output and ecosystem stability. China has launched large afforestation programmes there, including Grain to Green and the Two Rivers and Four Streams project.

The study assesses how those programmes affect aeolian desertification, soil retention, and vegetation recovery in a fragile high altitude landscape. Large scale tree planting can stabilise soil, yet species choice and water use decide success. The findings guide restoration in Tibet's grain heartland under a harsh climate.
pmc-13345825:
Weiwei Zhu and co-authors hunt risk factors for vein clots in preterm babies in a 2026 hospital study. Newborns clot more than any other children, and premature infants carry the highest risk. The team compared 94 clot cases with 188 controls from one Beijing neonatal unit's records across 2014 to 2025.

Clots struck 1.0 percent of hospitalized preterm infants, and 96 percent of cases tied to central lines. Leg PICC lines on either side independently raised risk at every prematurity level, and mothers' use of blood-thinning drugs during pregnancy also predicted clots. Portal vein clots followed umbilical lines while limb clots followed PICC placement. Line choices, the authors argue, deserve sharper scrutiny in tiny patients.
pmc-13348225:
Zesmin Akter and colleagues present a goatpox vaccine genome from Bangladesh. Their announcement came out in 2026. The genome is complete. Isolate LRIGP01 came from infected goat lung. That isolation took place in 1992. The virus was weakened over many passages. Forty-four passages in Vero cells did the work. The result became the master seed. The Livestock Research Institute holds that seed. Goatpox spreads fast among herds. No direct cure exists for it.

The genome runs 150,342 nucleotides in length. It encodes 151 genes in total. Its G plus C share is 25.3 percent. Family trees place it beside Indian isolates. Several goatpox isolates from India cluster with it. A vaccine seed genome supports batch checks. It also supports outbreak tracing. Vaccines and farm hygiene guard this disease alone.
pmc-13349825:
Hui Wang and fellow authors reviewed in 2026 how light quality and methyl jasmonate signalling jointly control betalain pigments in plants. Betalains give red-violet and yellow-orange colours in the plant order Caryophyllales and are valued as natural food colourants.

Light acts through photoreceptors and a COP1-HY5 module, shifting pigment build-up by wavelength and species. Methyl jasmonate, converted inside cells to an active form, frees transcription factors that switch pigment genes on. Both routes meet at R2R3-MYB factors that bind the promoters of key genes such as CYP76AD1 and DODA. Knowing how the signals converge could help growers and food makers raise natural pigment yields.
pmc-13349925:
Xingwu Xie and colleagues built imaging models in 2026 to predict an aggressive growth pattern in liver cancer from MRI scans taken before treatment. The pattern, vessels wrapping tumour clusters, signals strong blood vessel growth and immune activity in hepatocellular carcinoma.

Scans from 336 patients supplied both habitat features, describing tumour sub-regions, and deep learning features. Separate models were built from each feature type, then merged into a fusion model that performed best. A further group of 47 patients with matched gene data let the team link scan traits to immune cell patterns. A scan-based test could flag this dangerous subtype without a biopsy.
pmc-13350025:
Selina V. Haller and co-authors tuned hydrogen production by a heat-loving bacterium in a 2026 fermentation study. The microbe, Thermoactinomyces mirandus, makes hydrogen from biomass sugars in the dark, a renewable route whose yield depends heavily on conditions.

Grown at 52 degrees without oxygen, it was tested on five sugars and several nitrogen feeds. Yeast extract worked best, and fruit sugar, xylose, and lactose led the fuels. Holding acidity steady at 7.2 raised hydrogen yield about 4.2 times and let the bacteria consume nearly all the lactose. Small tweaks in feeding and acidity can turn a weak fermenter into a far more productive one.
pmc-13350325:
Cheng-Chun Peng and co-authors reported a surgical case in 2026 of spinal gout destroying part of a man's lower spine. Gout rarely reaches the spine, and deformity from crystal deposits there is rarer still; their patient was 59 years old.

Care came in two stages: a side-approach fusion between vertebrae first, then endoscopic decompression through two small portals plus screw fixation from behind. Afterwards the man walked normally and the joined segment fused solidly. The report lays out a minimally invasive, around-the-spine strategy for a condition few surgeons meet, and argues treatment should be tailored to the damage found.
pmc-13350625:
Diana Mendes and colleagues surveyed the burden of respiratory syncytial virus in Europeans aged 60 and over in a 2026 real-world study. Although RSV is a common cause of chest illness in older adults, its full toll was poorly measured.

Doctors reported on 1,581 patients, grouped by stage: acute, ongoing, recovering, or recently out of hospital. Symptoms, other illnesses, daily activity limits, and quality of life were captured, with patients also scoring their own recovery. That staged view shows the illness stretching far past the first weeks, informing vaccine and service planning for a virus long treated as a childhood problem.
pmc-13351925:
Kyle H Cichos leads a 2026 multi-centre study of whether bioglass bone graft lowers infection after lower back fusion surgery. The 45S5 bioglass material kills microbes in lab tests, but clinical proof was missing. Records covered open transforaminal lumbar fusion operations from 2017 to 2022 with at least 1 year of follow-up.

The final group held 1,376 patients, with 470 receiving bioglass and 906 receiving other grafts. Infection at the surgical site within 1 year was the main outcome. Adjusted models compared infection risk between graft types while accounting for patient and surgery traits. Use of bioglass linked to lower infection risk, supporting wider study of the material in spine reconstruction.
pmc-13352025:
Frida Lona-Durazo and co-authors probed in 2026 sex gaps in gene risk for blood in urine. The genes were type four collagen genes. This state is understudied and tied to kidney disease. Sex shapes many kidney traits through hormones and gene regulation. Yet sex-differential gene effects for blood in urine had not been fully probed.

Sex-specific genome-wide work in the UK Biobank was replicated in two cohorts. These were the Million Veteran Program and Geisinger MyCode. Loci were found where gene effects on blood in urine differ by sex. Tests used sex-by-genotype interaction work. Observational work linked blood in urine to estradiol and testosterone. The findings hint that collagen-linked kidney risk is not sex-neutral.
pmc-13352125:
Hussein Abu Rabia reports a 2026 case of gastric antral vascular ectasia, often called watermelon stomach, found after a fall. The condition widens small vessels in the stomach outlet that leak blood slowly over time. An 82-year-old patient arrived after an unwitnessed fall with low blood pressure on standing and haemoglobin of 90 g/L.

Camera study of the stomach showed the striped vessel pattern without active bleeding, and the patient also had a fragile pelvic fracture. Intravenous iron corrected severe iron lack, haemoglobin rose, and symptoms settled. Rabia stresses that hidden blood loss may show first as falls and weakness in older adults rather than gut complaints.
pmc-13352625:
Lillian M. Cool leads a 2026 study measuring how small drugs bind native kinases inside living cells. Flow cytometry with fluorescent dasatinib probes measured binding to untagged ABL1 kinase in living cells.

Dasatinib bound the native kinase 3 to 6 fold more tightly than tagged versions carrying NanoLuc or mVenus labels. Profiling extended to 25 native kinases and exposed controls such as SRC self-blocking and membrane-shaped states of DDR1, DDR2, and EPHA4. Probe acidity was tuned across a pKa span of 4.1 to 7.3, and a transporter boosted uptake of acidic probes. Calibrated beads fixed true inside-cell drug levels.
pmc-13353925:
Aya Ahmed Youssef-Gamal led a 2026 random trial comparing two items for full pulpotomy in mature molars with painful pulp swelling. Biodentine and Portland cement were tested head to head, with after-op pain as the main outcome. The team also checked matrix metalloproteinase-9 in pulpal blood, a marker of swelling, and related it to pain before care and bleeding time during the procedure.

Seventy-two molars were assigned at random to one of the two items, and bleeding colour, profuseness, and pulp attachment were recorded during care. Pain scores after care showed which item left people more comfortable. Dentists gain evidence for choosing a pulpotomy item that preserves the tooth while capping suffering.
pmc-13354025:
Shivraj Jadhav and co-authors surveyed colistin pushback in Klebsiella pneumoniae from a tertiary-care clinic, in 2026. This opportunistic bacterium causes pneumonia, urinary sickness, bloodstream sickness, and sepsis, and multidrug-tough strains have pushed colistin back into use as a last-resort drug. Pushback to that last resort now threatens care options.

The review covers medical and microbiological aspects of tough isolates, with how pushback emerges and spreads in clinic settings. It stresses the illness-control challenge when few drugs remain. Clinic teams gain a consolidated account of a growing threat and the care tests needed to slow it.
pmc-13354625:
Shengtao Wang and co-authors studied a protein called ANXA3 in osteosarcoma, a bone cancer found most often in young people, in 2026. They changed ANXA3 levels in cancer cells and in mice to see how it shaped stem-like traits. Stem-like cells can renew themselves and may drive spread and drug failure.

Raising ANXA3 boosted stem-like traits, cell spread, and resistance to a common cancer drug, while lowering it had the reverse effect. In mice, blocking ANXA3 slowed tumor growth and spread to the lungs. The work flags a chain of signals tied to ANXA3 as a possible target for new bone cancer care.
pmc-13355725:
Maneshka Vindesh Karunananda and others checked asthma, allergic rhinitis, and atopic dermatitis among schoolchildren in Sri Lanka, in 2026. Allergic ills are rising among children worldwide, but local rate and risk factors in Sri Lanka were partly documented. Without local numbers, school health and allergy services cannot plan effectively.

Schoolchildren were surveyed for the three problems, with risk factors tested across demographic, green, and family factors. The study provides rate estimates and names the exposures most strongly linked to each illness. Child and public health teams gain a baseline for allergy stopping and care in Sri Lankan schools.
pmc-13355825:
Harald Streicher and co-authors adapt a human safety frame in 2026 to judge the environmental risk of cosmetic ingredients without new animal tests. European rules bar animal testing for cosmetics, yet water safety data are still required. Using triclosan as a test case, they ran a full ten-step read-across process, borrowing data from like chemicals and lab-based methods.

Their approach paired cautious screening exposure guesses with sharper market-based ones, and set safe water levels from new non-animal methods. Results were checked against classic endpoints from animal-based studies. The authors present the case as a first full proof that the frame can work for environmental safety.
pmc-13356025:
Ana B García-Ruilova and others gave a massive arthropod barcode bank from the Neotropical Eastern Pacific, in 2026. Ten terrestrial sites across Costa Rica, Ecuador, Panama, and the Galapagos and Cocos Islands were surveyed over one to seven years, producing the first collection of its kind for this bioregion. Tropical arthropod diversity is vast and chronically under-documented.

Twenty-five banks jointly document 952,087 specimens and 45,812 barcode index numbers, spanning one phylum, seven classes, thirty-nine orders, 556 families, and 2,318 genera. The open banks support taxonomy, ecology, and conservation research. Biodiversity scientists gain an unprecedented baseline for a region where species loss may outpace discovery.
pmc-13356725:
Yaling Ma and co-authors fed laying hens mold-tainted diets in 2026 to test a combined detox agent against fungal toxins in feed. Eight hundred hens were split into five groups for about four months: plain feed, feed with moldy corn or moldy cottonseed meal, and the same tainted feeds plus the detox agent. Mold toxins are a known threat to egg output and bird health.

Moldy corn cut egg output, egg weight, and egg white quality and raised signs of oxidative stress, with like but milder effects from moldy meal. Adding the detox agent restored laying and antioxidant status and enriched helpful gut bacteria such as Lactobacillus. The authors back its use in commercial egg production.
pmc-13358825:
Emma Jacobs and Hiran C. Fernando trace the rise of keyhole esophagus surgery in a 2026 review. Removing the esophagus the open way caused heavy harm, so surgeons developed a minimally invasive route with small cuts and cameras. Over recent decades the method has spread widely. The authors ask how it grew and what it changed for patients.

Drawing on trials, pooled reviews, and recent studies, they find the keyhole route cuts lung problems and overall complications compared with open surgery. Robot help and better care around the operation mark the newest steps. The review also flags where proof is still thin, guiding what surgeons should study next.
pmc-13359925:
Paul Tunde Kingpriest and others scoped training for genomic and bioinformatic pathogen surveillance in Africa, in 2026. Pathogen surveillance is vital where disease burdens are high, and genomics enables early finding, pushback monitoring, and aimed step. Adoption, however, is hindered by limited training and educational stock.

The scoping review mapped current training plans across Africa, identifying gaps and opportunities in curricula, access, and room. It shows where training exists, where it is missing, and what new plans must cover. Public health planners gain an evidence base for building the workforce that genomic surveillance needs.
pmc-13360225:
Lingyun Wang and co-authors built a 2026 language model that grades cancer response from radiology report text alone. The model, WiNGPT-32B, is open source and runs on local machines, which keeps patient data in-house. It was trained with knowledge passed down from GPT-4. The team fed it reports from 258 patients with solid tumors, covering 2,065 scan time points.

The model works through four chained steps: pulling out lesion sizes, adding up the key diameters, classing the tumor response, and writing the report. This follows the RECIST rules doctors use to judge whether a cancer shrank, held steady, or grew. Its scores were weighed against GPT-4 and against a human radiologist. The authors aim to make response grading faster and more uniform across hospitals.
pmc-13362825:
Khairunnisai Tarimah and colleagues present a 2026 scoping review on magnesium sulphate given around surgery and whether it protects the brain. Brain injury during operations can arise from several paths at once, and magnesium touches many of them, from calming overexcited nerve signals to steadying blood vessels. The team screened four databases and sorted 18 studies into direct brain outcomes, side benefits, blood markers, and lab mechanisms.

Pain after surgery, opioid use, and shivering fell in a steady pattern, and recovery traits improved. Direct brain protection proof, on thinking, brain oxygen, and stroke-like events, stayed thin and mixed. The authors frame magnesium as a broad stress softener during surgery, not a proven brain shield, and urge trials that track many outcomes at once.
pmc-13363025:
Dong Shin You and a large team present a 2026 cell biology study on how cell size reshapes the cell's protein mix. Using human cells engineered to grow across a two-fold size range while still dividing, they measured gene messages and proteins genome-wide, plus how fast each turns over. Live imaging of fresh gene messages let them watch how the reading of genes changes as cells grow.

Turnover rates barely shifted with size, but message levels did, which pins the protein reshaping on gene control. Bigger cells held their gene-reading bursts open longer while keeping burst size the same, a neat way to scale output. The findings explain a basic puzzle of cell physiology and bear on cancer and aging, where cell size goes astray.
pmc-13363625:
Mengxuan Zhang and colleagues report a 2026 rat study on an extract of Scutellaria baicalensis, a skullcap herb long used for stroke, against brain injury after blood flow returns. This ischemia-reperfusion injury kills brain cells in part through ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death. The team blocked the main brain artery in rats, treated them with the extract, and probed tissue with protein maps, stains, and cell tests.

Treated rats scored better on nerve function and showed less brain damage. Iron buildup and power-unit harm in cells fell, and a key protective axis recovered. Blocking the PI3K/AKT pathway erased the benefit, in animals and in cells, which pins the effect to that path. Four active compounds were found absorbed in the blood.
pmc-13363725:
Seda Bodur, Rasit Asiloglu, and Keziban Yazici present a 2026 synthesis on how soil acidification reshapes the hidden food webs of tea plantation soils. Years of heavy nitrogen fertilizer leave tea soils strongly acidic, which filters which microbes can live there. Past work tracked bacteria and fungi, but this review spotlights protists, the tiny hunters that eat bacteria and release nutrients plants can use.

The authors argue that acid stress rewires who eats whom, not just who survives, and that this rewiring can shift nutrient cycling, disease suppression, and plant vigor. Direct proof in tea soils is still thin, since most of the chain rests on other soil systems. They frame tea fields as ideal test beds for joining stress and food-web views.

pmc-13401125:

pmc-13401625:

pmc-13402025:
