A tweaked Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient net, with fading learn rates, prized replay, and parallel training, eased wobble, trade-off skew, and slow replies. Tests on a two-axis rig with full-year 2024 field data from Xiaojin County, Sichuan, gave near twelve point three percent more power than PID, Q-learning, and plain DDPG. Wear fell by near eighteen point seven percent. Replies came in under eight milliseconds. Sun farms gain a smart tracker brain.
pmc-13454825:
Xiaokang Zeng and four colleagues report, in a 2026 mouse study, that a mitochondrial helper protein keeps natural killer cells numerous and sharp. These killer cells form a first line of defense against tumors and viruses. The protein, Hspa9, guards the energy hubs inside blood cells. The team deleted it only in blood-forming cells and watched the killer cells.

Killer cell counts fell sharply across the spleen, bone marrow, and liver in the altered mice. The remaining cells released less of a key attack signal and showed weaker killing marks. Surface sensors tied to growth and maturity shifted as well, suggesting stalled development. A central growth pathway, Akt with mTOR, ran quieter in the deficient cells. The authors name Hspa9 a promising handle for tuning killer cell strength in future immune therapies.
pmc-13455225:
Yan Zhang and others studied urinary and serum iodine in relation to children's iodine nutrition and lipids in 2026, in iodized salt regions of China. Iodine has a narrow safe intake range, and abnormal status may affect children's lipid metabolism through thyroid function. After widespread iodized salt use, urinary iodine in some regions exceeded appropriate ranges, yet the iodine-dyslipidemia link remained unclear.

Children and adolescents aged six to seventeen in iodized salt regions were studied, with urinary iodine, serum iodine, total cholesterol, and triglycerides explored by kernel density plots and chi-square tests. Logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index, with stratified and interaction analyses testing effect modification, plus restricted cubic spline models. The study clarifies how iodine status relates to childhood lipid profiles in a post-iodization setting.
pmc-13455325:
Jiaru Gao and colleagues warn that a common liver-protecting supplement may blunt breast cancer treatment in a 2026 cohort study. S-adenosylmethionine, often given during chemotherapy to shield the liver, can also alter gene activity through methyl marks, raising a question about its effect on cancer outcomes. The team reviewed 1,013 women treated at a Zhengzhou hospital between 2018 and 2020, matching treated and untreated patients on baseline traits and tracing survival by length of exposure.

Exposure for 14 days or more during post-surgery chemotherapy linked with shorter overall and disease-free survival than no exposure, even after adjustment. Tumour tissue from poor responders showed higher supplement levels, stronger m6A marks and higher METTL3 and METTL14 expression. The pattern is observational, so it cannot prove harm, but it urges doctors to weigh liver support against possible effects on treatment response.
pmc-13457125:
Ming Diao, Yaxi Zhu, and Hailing Tang compare, in a 2026 meta-analysis, artificial intelligence against the dermatologist's magnifier for judging whether a pigmented skin spot may be malignant. Sorting such spots well catches melanoma early and spares healthy skin needless cutting. The team searched four databases and kept ten studies with seventeen test arms.

Performance overlapped heavily. Dermoscopy sensitivity ranged from about 42 to 97 percent across studies, and AI landed in a similar span. AI specificity likewise overlapped the clinicians' range. In the single study of clinicians aided by AI, sensitivity was perfect and specificity solid, a hint that partnership may beat either alone. Spread between studies was wide, reflecting varied algorithms and settings. No publication bias showed. The authors conclude that today's AI matches standard dermoscopy on average, with consistency, not peak skill, as the open problem.
pmc-13457525:
Marga Giménez and colleagues report how an automated insulin delivery system performs in everyday Spanish practice. The MiniMed 780G adjusts insulin around the clock for people with type 1 diabetes, yet Spanish real-world data were missing. Their 2026 analysis pulls CareLink records for 16,392 users and compares age groups, life before and after starting the system, and a full year of use.

Users spent an average of 75.9 percent of time in the target glucose range, with 51.0 percent in the tighter range and only 2.2 percent below 70 milligrams per deciliter. More than three quarters cleared the international goal of 70 percent time in range, and those using the recommended settings did better still, reaching 79.8 percent. Among 4,294 users with before-and-after data, time in range jumped from 64.7 to 75.8 percent after the switch. In the 6,664 people tracked for twelve months, the gains held steady, which the authors read as durable benefit.
pmc-13457725:
Ya Liu and a large team sort Chinese college students by their beliefs about the HPV vaccine, which prevents cervical and other cancers yet sees patchy uptake in young adults. Their 2026 cross-sectional survey covered 2,755 students at five universities in Shandong and Guangdong, measuring beliefs across five health-belief dimensions and hunting for hidden subgroups with latent profile analysis.

Two clear profiles emerged. Three quarters of students landed in a high-barrier, moderate-benefit group, while the remaining quarter saw high benefit and low barriers. That quarter knew more, felt better supported, found services more reachable, scored higher on e-health literacy, and reported stronger intention plus higher uptake, 24.6 percent against 15.3 percent in the larger group. Being female, seeking information, and knowing more raised the odds of the favorable profile, with e-health literacy the strongest correlate. The authors suggest health education should attack barriers and digital skills together.
pmc-13458625:
Zizhen Xiao and colleagues re-engineer a nickel catalyst for cracking ammonia back into hydrogen, a leading plan for shipping clean fuel. Nickel is cheap but poisons itself: hydrogen atoms cling to its surface and block fresh ammonia, while the particles sinter at working heat. Their 2026 catalyst packs nickel nanoparticles at 66.5 weight percent inside an alumina framework, ringed by atomically dispersed cerium.

The cerium specks, single atoms and tiny clusters, act as hydrogen scavengers. Hungry for hydrogen, they form Ce3+-OH groups that pull adsorbed atoms off the nickel, freeing sites for the next ammonia molecule and speeding the cycle. The design sidesteps the usual activity-stability trade-off of ceria supports and sustains a hydrogen production rate of 324.0 millimoles per gram of catalyst per minute at 600 degrees Celsius. The authors present the scavenger concept as a general trick for catalysts suffocating on their own products.
pmc-13458825:
David Shin and colleagues test whether living in a blue zone, a longevity hotspot famed for low chronic disease, changes outcomes after kyphoplasty for spinal compression fractures. Their 2026 retrospective review covers 372 patients treated at one tertiary center between 2009 and 2025, sorted by postal code, then matched one-to-three. Just 190 patients remained, only 15 of them blue zone residents.

The lifestyle signal was clear: blue zone patients reported no alcohol use against 34 to 64 percent among others. Tobacco use was 7 percent against 43 to 47 percent, in both raw and matched comparisons. Outcomes, though, refused to follow the legend. No association emerged between blue zone residence and complications, readmission, or survival. The familiar villains ran the show: tobacco predicted 30-day readmission, while age, anesthesia risk score, diabetes, and blood loss lengthened hospital stays. Longevity habits may delay fractures, the authors conclude, but they do not rescue the operation's course once the fracture happens.
pmc-13459925:
Yanhua Luo and co-authors used single cell gene reading to watch how inhaled hydrogen gas reshapes immune signals in the gut during sepsis recovery. Sepsis, the body's runaway response to infection, damages the gut barrier early, and hydrogen has shown protective hints without a known mechanism. In their 2026 mouse study, animals with surgically induced sepsis received hydrogen or not. Gut tissue underwent cell by cell reading alongside barrier leak tests and inflammation measures.

Hydrogen significantly reduced gut injury and barrier leakage, shown by lower leak markers in blood, and calmed whole body inflammation in the treated animals. The reading revealed sepsis had expanded a non functional B cell population and skewed T cell development, and hydrogen restored both toward normal balance. Analysis of signals between cell types showed the gas reshaping the web that coordinates mucosal immunity. Hydrogen's gut effects can now be targeted more precisely, the authors argue.
pmc-13460225:
Xin Qiao, Jing-Jing Zhang, Bin Liu, and Jian-Wen Qin searched in 2026 for factors that predict survival in pleural mesothelioma patients. In this cancer of the lung lining, malignant fluid builds up around the lung. Their Tianjin cohort held 71 patients diagnosed between 2015 and 2025, followed by regular telephone checks. Survival averaged a median of thirty months, and models tested clinical and lab measures, especially tests on the pleural fluid itself.

Four routine measures stood on their own. High lactate dehydrogenase in the fluid and high fibrinogen each multiplied the death hazard several-fold. Larger average platelet size also worsened outlook, and a higher lymphocyte count proved protective. All four come from ordinary baseline testing, though the authors want confirmation from larger future studies before clinical use.
pmc-13461325:
Alexandra Grigoreanu and colleagues surveyed veterinary students and teaching staff in Romania on dog-assisted support programs for campus wellbeing. Such programs bring trained dogs into study settings to cut stress, yet their acceptance inside veterinary education was untested.

The survey drew 200 students and 99 staff, who answered questions on dogs, program knowledge, and their own mental health. Both groups liked dogs and strongly backed the programs, seeing gains for stress, mental health, and the learning climate. One in five students, 20.5 percent, reported a diagnosed mental health condition, underlining the need for support. Women answered more warmly and saw less risk than men, Grigoreanu notes, though logistics and anxiety concerns remained.
pmc-13461725:
Jingna Tao and colleagues built machine learning models that stage autoimmune gastritis from scope images and blood tests. Autoimmune gastritis is a slow stomach disease where the immune system destroys acid-making cells, and staging today depends on observer judgement.

The study enrolled 203 patients classed into three stages by how much healthy stomach lining remained. Seven algorithms were trained on five feature sets, mixing standard scope views, magnified imaging, and a serum panel. A random forest using scope plus blood features staged best, with a macro-AUC of 0.878 across the three stages. Lost stomach folds and two blood markers ranked among the strongest staging signals, Tao reports. Barrett's oesophagus, a risky throat-lining change, appeared in 66.8 percent of patients, backing routine checks in this group.
pmc-13461825:
Pastorino and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how to free natural killer cells, immune cells that can kill cancer without prior training, to attack solid tumors. Two braking systems dominate their control: KIR receptors and the NKG2A axis, which keep the cells tolerant of healthy tissue. Tumors exploit these brakes, in part by keeping or raising levels of a surface tag, HLA-E, that presses the second brake.

Pastorino notes that blocking either brake alone has brought only modest gains in most solid tumors, despite strong lab logic. The surrounding tumor tissue adds more blocks: physical barriers, low oxygen, metabolic stress, and suppressive networks that limit entry and staying power. Future plans, the authors argue, should combine brake release with hand-picked or engineered killer cells that resist exhaustion. Added treatments should remodel the tumor niche so the cells can reach it and keep fighting.
pmc-13462025:
Jie Ding and colleagues test whether top-down maps help people learn layouts from virtual navigation in a 2026 study. Maps present survey knowledge directly, yet navigation builds egocentric knowledge, and whether the two integrate was unclear. Three experiments had participants navigate virtual city and village environments to find target sequences, then complete pointing, direction-judgment and map-reconstruction tasks, with and without map viewing.

Map previews before exploration in city and village settings showed no overall accuracy gain, and even a detailed map shown repeatedly during exploration in a landmark-rich village gave no benefit. The authors speculate that translating between egocentric and allocentric frames blocks integration. Designers of navigation training gain a caution: map study alone may not improve learning from first-person exploration.
pmc-13462225:
Kanvinde, Khurana, and Mudaliar wrote a 2026 clinical guide to vitamin B12 deficiency in children, a common yet often missed nutritional disorder. Shortage can damage brain development for good, stunt growth, and disturb blood formation, above all where mothers are deficient or diets are vegetarian. Brain symptoms often appear before blood changes do.

Diagnosis blends the clinical picture with blood counts, blood film review, and B12 testing, Kanvinde explains. Extra markers such as methylmalonic acid and homocysteine sharpen the picture when results sit near the cut-off. Inherited faults in B12 handling can now be found by gene testing and need lifelong care. Oral B12 works for most diet related cases, while injections suit severe anaemia, nerve damage, or poor uptake from food. Delayed treatment may leave lasting nerve damage.
pmc-13463825:
Viraj Bandsode and ten co-authors read Salmonella genomes from soil and water to track virulence and drug resistance worldwide. Lab data skew toward rich countries, leaving wild strains from poorer regions poorly mapped. The team sequenced fifty-four fresh isolates from India and set them beside global collections.

The joint set held 1,399 genomes, and over half of the Indian isolates resisted many drugs at once. Rare genes for colistin resistance, a last-line drug, already circulate in wild strains. Core attack genes stayed alike across groups, while extra resistance and plasmid loads shifted by family line. Wild waters and soils, the authors warn, form one linked global pool of risk genes.
pmc-13464925:
Zhongsong Wang and colleagues reworked the mouse family tree in 2026 for Murinae, a vast rodent group that anchors ecology and medical research. Deep tribal ties stayed disputed, and no framework had joined genome comparison, selection pressure, codon use, and shape evidence. The team sequenced two new full mitogenomes and compared 117 species across 13 tribes and 50 genera.

Mitogenomes proved highly conserved in layout, with length shifts mainly in the control region, and all protein genes under strong purifying selection despite tenfold rate gaps. Codon bias tracked natural selection and family ties. Critically, the data reject a sister pairing of Micromyini and Vernayini, placing Vernayini beside all remaining Murinae except Hapalomys with maximal support.
pmc-13465125:
Mengying Guan and Hua Hao review CDK4/6 blocker drugs in hormone-driven breast cancer, where the drugs have redrawn the treatment map. Three drugs in the class serve both early and spread disease. The review weighs them side by side rather than as interchangeable copies.

Real gaps in benefit appear between the three drugs across trial settings. Resistance grows through two broad routes: loss of the drug's target machinery, or detours that bypass the block entirely. Sorting resistance that way can guide what to try next, the authors argue. Protein shredders, new hormone blockers, and antibody-guided drugs lead the next wave. Sharper patient picking may gain more than yet more drugs, they conclude.
pmc-13465325:
Haoqun Zhang and four co-authors pair eye tracking with taste panels for three red bean and coix seed drinks. Self-report scores can bend under memory and wording ease, so the team also logged where eyes lingered on the answer scale. Twenty-four volunteers rated scent, taste, feelings, and liking for each drink.

The score a person picked and the score their gaze held longest agreed strongly, and both ranked the drinks in the same order. Gaze scores, though, swung too widely person to person to swap for picked scores. Warmth and sweetness tracked with pleasant feelings and with liking across both read types. One feeling word, good-natured, clung most steadily to liking, which marks gaze as a helpful side channel.
pmc-13465925:
Root-Bernstein published a 2026 study linking two diseases long thought separate. People with type 1 diabetes face a higher risk of multiple sclerosis, and the reverse also holds. Both diseases involve immune attacks, but the shared trigger has stayed unclear. His work tests whether diabetes-linked immune proteins also target myelin, the nerve coating.

Lab searches matched immune receptor codes from patients with both diseases. Tests then showed diabetes-linked antibodies sticking to myelin basic protein in samples. Most patient blood samples reacted to myelin, while healthy samples did not. Certain gut bacteria proteins also mimic myelin, a fresh clue in the data. Such cross-reactions could explain nerve damage seen in long-term diabetes. More lab work is still needed to prove this chain of cause in patients.
pmc-13466425:
Ruixiang Yuan and eleven colleagues published this 2026 study of a gene that helps the fungus Verticillium dahliae attack cotton plants. This fungus causes Verticillium wilt, a serious cotton disease, and it uses secreted enzymes to break down plant cell walls. The gene, named Vdbgl1, makes an enzyme that digests glucan, a wall sugar, and it switches on strongly during infection. The team tested what happens when the gene is removed or silenced.

Deleting the gene slowed colony growth by about a fifth and cut spore production and germination. The mutant fungus was also more sensitive to wall stress and salt stress. On cotton, the mutants caused a disease index roughly 19 to 28 percent lower, and fungal biomass fell by 42.7 to 61.8 percent in the plants tested. Silencing the gene from inside the plant gave similar protection. The authors present Vdbgl1 as a promising target for wilt control.
pmc-13466525:
Yung-Yi Lan, Rujith Kovinthapillai, Andrzej Kędzia, and Elżbieta Niechciał review how to cut dangerous acid buildup at the start of type 1 diabetes in children, in a 2026 article. This crisis, diabetic ketoacidosis, often strikes because early symptoms get missed, and poorer or rural families face it more. Screening blood for early autoantibodies can flag the disease before symptoms begin.

The review gathers evidence on who faces the highest risk, how screening programs run, and which early treatments might slow the disease itself. Sources span trials, guidelines, and pooled analyses from 2011 onward, plus classic older work. The authors argue that finding the disease in its quiet stage is the strongest lever against a preventable emergency.
pmc-13466825:
Ziliang He, Junlong Ma, Yun Liu, and Zhanhong Du review how the body reacts against electrodes implanted in the brain, and how surface treatments might calm that reaction, in a 2026 article. Long-term implants power brain-machine interfaces and deep brain stimulation, yet the tissue response slowly degrades signals: resistance climbs, noise grows, and usable channels vanish.

The chain starts with insertion injury and protein coating, runs through barrier leakage, immune activation, and reactive support cells, and ends in scar tissue with lost neurons nearby. Countermeasures reviewed include non-stick coatings, helpful molecules fixed to the surface, drug-releasing designs, and interfaces that actively soothe immunity. The authors insist on linking each chemistry to the exact step it interrupts.
pmc-13466925:
Malak Ahmed Almalki and colleagues present two children with a rare bacterial infection of the middle ear that masquerades as ordinary chronic ear discharge, in a 2026 case report. Only about fifty such cases appear in the literature. The germ usually travels up the Eustachian tube from the throat and demands surgery plus long antibiotic courses.

The first child, a seven-year-old boy with Joubert syndrome, kept draining from one ear six months after a ventilation tube was placed; a second cleaning plus three months of antibiotics cleared it. The second, a ten-year-old girl, drained for four months despite several drug courses. Tissue from surgery gave the diagnosis in both, underlining that stubborn ear discharge deserves a biopsy.
pmc-13467125:
Abdulaziz Alshomrani, Anum Hussaini, and Elhadi Miskeen run a national survey of long COVID in Saudi Arabia, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. The team reached 1,790 adults with confirmed infections across all thirteen regions between mid-2023 and late 2024. Long COVID followed the World Health Organization definition: symptoms lasting at least three months with no other explanation.

About a third of respondents met that definition. Fatigue dominated the symptom list, followed by breathlessness and thinking problems. Being female roughly doubled the odds after adjustment, and a harder initial illness also predicted lasting symptoms. The study adds healthcare use and daily burden measures, giving planners the first nationally framed numbers for the kingdom.
pmc-13467525:
Isabella Peetz and colleagues review what the fruit fly brain teaches about repairing injured nervous systems. The fly, Drosophila melanogaster, offers a rich toolkit of genetic tricks for watching neurons and support cells regrow after damage.

Evidence from crush, cut, and stab injury models shows flies can regrow nerve fibres, support cells, and even neurons. New support cells clearly arise from existing ones in the central brain and the eye lobes. Where new neurons come from is murkier: in eye lobes they spring from sleeping stem cells, unproven for the central brain. Peetz frames these open questions as the manual's missing pages, guiding the next repair experiments.
pmc-13467725:
Sadaf Memon and colleagues scan the genome in 2026 for regions tied to grain protein content in hulless barley, a nutritious cereal grown in the Tibetan regions of China. Protein content decides much of the grain quality but shifts strongly with environment. The study grew 266 barley accessions in six environments between 2018 and 2021 and measured protein in the harvested grain.

Protein content ranged widely, from 5.02 percent to 18.31 percent, with moderate heritability and a clear interplay between genes and environment. Scanning nearly 169,000 genetic markers with three statistical models found no marker that passed the strictest threshold in the combined analysis, though 40 markers at 18 spots passed a looser one. Chromosome 7H carried the most consistent signal across models. Seven candidate genes were identified near the signals, giving breeders concrete leads for higher-protein barley.
pmc-13468025:
Xing Li and co-authors test in 2026 whether an extract of rooibos tea rich in the flavonoid aspalathin can undo liver fat problems caused by a high-fat diet. Male mice were fed a normal or high-fat diet, and some high-fat animals then received the extract. The team measured liver triglycerides and cholesterol deposits, read the activity of genes for fat making, burning, and transport, and sequenced the gut microbes.

High-fat feeding raised liver fat stores sharply and suppressed many cholesterol-handling genes. The rooibos extract counteracted those changes, pushing gene activity and fat levels back toward normal. The diet had also reshaped the gut microbial community, its diversity, and its metabolic pathways, which the extract partly corrected. The paired liver and gut results support the tea compound as a candidate for diet-related liver protection, at least in mice.
pmc-13468125:
Bai and colleagues compared tree plantations in subtropical China in 2026 to learn whether mixing a nitrogen-fixing tree into eucalyptus stands locks more carbon into soil, and in a steadier form. Plantations store carbon, but carbon that sits loose in soil can escape fast. Mineral-associated carbon, bound to soil minerals, lasts far longer.

After five years, mixed stands with the fixing tree Erythrophleum fordii held about a fifth more soil carbon than pure eucalyptus. The stable mineral-bound share rose even more in the top layer. Fungi played a key part: carbon left behind by dead fungal cells rose by about half, and modeling showed that microbe-derived carbon fed the stable pool directly, more than enzyme routes did. The authors present mixed planting as a practical way to make plantation carbon stick.
pmc-13469025:
Yu and a research team showed in 2026 how a protein called TRIM47 fuels nasopharyngeal cancer, common in southern China and Southeast Asia. The protein was sharply raised in tumor tissue, and lab and animal experiments tested what it does. TRIM47 tags a metabolic enzyme, SDHB, for destruction by the cell's disposal system; SDHB normally helps mitochondria burn fuel cleanly. The team measured growth, movement, and fuel use with TRIM47 raised or lowered.

Destroying SDHB rewired the cancer's metabolism: cells leaned on fast sugar burning, consuming more glucose and excreting more lactate, the classic Warburg pattern. Tumors grew faster, spread markers rose, and cell shape shifted toward invasion, while restoring SDHB reversed the damage. Adding succinate, the chemical SDHB processes, blunted the effect of removing TRIM47, and vitamin C suppressed tumors TRIM47 drove. The authors propose the pair as a drug target and vitamin C as a tailored therapy.
pmc-13469425:
Youmin Shin and seven colleagues published this 2026 study training models to pinpoint where seizures start in focal cortical dysplasia, a malformation of brain cortex behind epilepsy that resists drugs. Finding the seizure onset zone leans on expert reading and monitoring. From scalp EEG recorded during seizures in 69 patients, the team extracted shape-based and connectivity features across bands. They compressed them with principal component analysis, and let machine learning pick the classifiers for side and location of onset.

Before compression, connectivity features beat shape features: one set reached an area under the curve of 0.781 for telling left from right, and the full set reached 0.786 for location. After compression, energy features improved, reaching 0.811 for side and 0.829 for location in the window after seizure onset. The authors propose the framework as a decision aid for surgery planning, helping plan where invasive electrodes should go.
pmc-13470325:
K. Fathima Shadiya and colleagues track in 2026 how mercury contamination in Indian wetlands changes across places and seasons, using two fish eating birds as indicators. Droppings from little cormorants and oriental darters were gathered non invasively at six sites between 2022 and 2024. The sites spanned farm wetlands, salty fields, and mangroves on both fresh and coastal water.

Lab digestion and absorption measurements found total mercury levels shaped by year, species, and site together. Coastal wetlands showed the highest readings and a rising trend, reaching roughly forty nine milligrams per kilogram in cormorant droppings by 2024. Inland sites stayed comparatively clean, which the authors link to lower human inputs. Mercury in droppings rose nearly threefold over the study years. The team argues droppings offer a humane window on wetland pollution.
pmc-13471325:
Kyousuke Kamada and colleagues test in 2026 whether the timing of a brief brain stimulation pulse decides if it disrupts speech. Doctors mapping language areas before surgery normally stimulate cortex for several seconds, which can trigger seizures and gives varied symptoms. Recordings of fast brain waves, called high gamma activity, mark active language spots more steadily, peaking at a known moment during picture naming.

Two patients named pictures while the team recorded those waves, then delivered short stimulation pulses before or after each person peak. Early pulses caused frequent naming errors, up to ninety two percent in one patient, and slowed answers. Late pulses caused far fewer errors. The authors argue that aligning stimulation with the wave peak turns a blunt mapping tool into a precise probe of language timing.
pmc-13472325:
Tsutsui and colleagues built in 2026 a solid state nanopore that senses on its own, with no gates or pumps run from outside. A nanopore is a hair thin hole whose charge flow shifts as bits pass through. In most rigs the hole sits fixed and dumb. Here charge in the bath makes crust grow and melt in the hole in turns. Each turn sparks a spike of flow, and the hole's state holds a trace of what just passed.

Bits that slip through bend the spikes in set ways: height, span, and pace. A learner read those bends and told the four DNA letters apart. Blends of letters were counted in true shares, not just named. The trick stretched to seven amino acids, the blocks of proteins. The team frames the hole as sense, memory, and spark in one.
pmc-13472725:
Fang and colleagues built MoESurv in 2026, a computer model that predicts survival for rare cancers despite having no training cases of those cancers. Most deep learning models need large datasets, which rare cancers cannot supply. MoESurv instead learns shared patterns from many cancer types at once, using a mixture-of-experts design where separate sub-models handle common and cancer-specific signals.

Tested on seven rare cancer types from a large public atlas, the model beat the best rival method by about four points on a standard ranking score. It also held up in outside cohorts, including a Chinese brain tumor dataset and a rare subtype of glioblastoma, a fast-growing brain cancer. The model split patients into high- and low-risk groups and flagged genes tied to survival, which the authors say adds both clinical and biological value.
pmc-13478425:
Roberts and colleagues argue in 2026 that maternal health belongs at the center of the global justice agenda. That agenda was set by the United Nations Commission on the Status of Women at its 70th session. Their discussion frames preventable harm around pregnancy and birth as a measure of unfairness in health systems, not just a clinical problem. Disadvantaged groups, including Indigenous, immigrant, rural, and low-income women, carry the heaviest burden described.

The authors name practical strategies with evidence behind them, including community-based models of care near women's homes, midwifery-led care, and maternal mortality review systems. Their recommendations call for collaboration across sectors, stronger national accountability for outcomes, and investment in care that fits women's cultures and languages. Nurses, midwives, and birth support workers are cast as key policy voices, and the piece insists that treating maternal health as a human right is the route to equity.
pmc-13478525:
Mohamed Elnaggar and three colleagues designed in 2026 a cascaded controller to steady frequency and voltage together in linked power grids. Load swings, parameter drift, and the coupling between frequency and voltage loops strain older control schemes.

Their design pairs a two-degree-of-freedom proportional-derivative stage with a leaky tilt-integral stage, tuned by the Crayfish Optimization Algorithm against a time-weighted error score. Tests covered step load jumps, random load swings, generator limits, dead bands, voltage tracking, and parameter shifts up to 40 percent. It damped swings faster, shrank frequency and tie-line deviations, and held terminal voltage steadier than PID, TID, and fractional-order rivals.
pmc-13479425:
Saeed Anbari Moghadam, Elham Akhondzadeh Noughabi, and Shahideh Jahanian Sadatmahalleh present a 2026 study building a rule-based model that doctors can read, for sorting endometriosis cases. Endometriosis, where womb-like tissue grows outside the uterus, causes pelvic pain and trouble having children, yet naming it is slow. Earlier forecast models relied on opaque math that doctors cannot inspect or use at the bedside.

The team instead built plain rules from patient data, sorted by disease stage. Rules state their terms in plain if-then form, so a doctor can see exactly which findings drive each call. The authors argue this openness matters more than small gains in hit rate, because doctors must explain decisions to patients. Stage-by-stage rules also fit how the illness looks at each phase.
pmc-13479625:
Lauren Tostrud and coauthors published a 2026 records study of inherited gene testing in uterine serous carcinoma, an aggressive womb cancer where guidelines say testing should be considered. Real-world completion rates were largely unknown. The team reviewed every case diagnosed from 2019 to 2024 at one academic cancer center, 131 patients in all.

Only five patients had prior testing, and just forty-five, about thirty-four percent, were recommended testing or referred to cancer genetics. The study then counts how many referred patients actually completed testing and how many carried a harmful inherited variant. Referral patterns by patient characteristics are also examined. The gap between guideline advice and bedside practice is the paper's central finding, pointing to fixes in referral workflows.
pmc-13481325:
Takeuchi and colleagues compared in 2026 two routes for placing long-term central venous ports: under the collarbone or in the upper arm. The study covered 1,195 patients implanted from 2012 to 2021, with 706 subclavian and 489 upper-arm ports. Outcomes were tracked for up to five years across more than 600,000 catheter-days.

Complication-related removals occurred in about seven percent of the subclavian group and eight percent of the arm group. After adjustment, overall removal risk did not differ between routes. Profiles differed, though: infection-related removal was more frequent with arm ports, while catheter fractures occurred only in the collarbone group, at about two percent. Infection-free and fracture-free survival also differed. The authors conclude route choice should weigh which complication a patient can least afford.
pmc-13482325:
Lou and co-authors mine the published record in 2026 for operating rules for anammox wastewater treatment, a process where bacteria convert ammonia and nitrite straight to nitrogen gas. Anammox promises big savings for city sewage plants, and the introduction cites cuts near 60 percent in aeration energy and 90 percent in sludge, but plants lack clear guidance on settings. The team fed a large dataset from prior studies into automated machine learning and then opened the models up for interpretation.

Two boosting models built by the automated system predicted nitrogen removal outcomes with accuracy scores between 0.814 and 0.993 across the response measures tracked in the dataset. On fresh data the team collected themselves, the models still generalized respectably, scoring between 0.725 and 0.945 on the same accuracy scale used. Dependence plots then mapped the operating ranges and incoming-water traits linked to the best removal, turning the black box into practical guidance for plant operators.
pmc-13482825:
Heidarpanah and colleagues schedule a hydropower reservoir like a battery in 2026, pairing a price-forecasting neural network with an evolutionary optimizer for Iran's Karun-IV plant. Water released at the wrong hour sells cheap, so their hybrid first predicts next-day peak electricity prices with a convolutional memory network. The NSGA-II optimizer then trades revenue against a guaranteed minimum of daily generation. The planning horizon covered a 10-year operational record.

Run against history, the strategy worked as designed arbitrage, holding water back through low-demand hours and releasing it when prices and demand peaked in the market. Total plant income rose about 10.5 percent over the historical record under the optimized schedule, while the daily generation floor kept the plant dependable for the grid. The authors present the coupling of forecast and optimizer, rather than either alone, as the source of the gain for reservoir operators.
pmc-13483125:
Jin and colleagues reviewed trials of pain-relieving creams and gels placed on skin graft donor sites in burn patients. When surgeons take a thin layer of skin for grafting, the spot it came from often hurts more than the burn itself. Their 2026 review searched four databases and gathered ten randomized trials comparing medicated dressings or anesthetic creams against placebo or standard care.

Pooled results showed no clear difference in pain scores between topical treatment and comparison care. Patients using the topical options did need rescue pain medicine less often, suggesting some real benefit beyond the score sheets. Data for several outcomes stayed thin, with few trials reporting them. Jin concludes topical anesthetics can serve as a useful add-on that trims systemic drug use, but larger trials must confirm the effect and settle the best protocol.
pmc-13483425:
Arthur Dubech and co-authors offer a 2026 review of ways to cut catecholamine drug exposure in septic shock. Noradrenaline remains the first drug for holding blood pressure when infection crashes circulation, but long, heavy dosing strains the heart, metabolism, and immune system. The review weighs early dosing, pressure targets set by skin blood flow, and non-adrenaline stand-ins.

Vasopressin trims catecholamine need and lowers the odds of a racing, uneven heartbeat. Angiotensin II helps when standard drugs fail, perhaps most in kidney injury. Steroids restore vessel grip and speed weaning off the drip. Short-acting beta blockers, blue dye targeting vessel relaxation, and immune-calming add-ons each show narrower, mixed promise. The authors favour a personal, layered plan that guards tissue blood flow while shaving the adrenaline burden.
pmc-13483525:
Esmaeil Teymoori and co-authors survey perfectionism among operating theatre nurses in Tehran in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Theatre work demands urgent, flawless performance, and chasing perfection can feed both rumination and job stress. Questionnaires reached 202 nurses across three public hospitals between mid-2024 and mid-2025.

Average scores showed moderate-to-high perfectionism, middling rumination, and high job stress. Perfectionism rose in step with both rumination and stress, with correlation values near 0.47 and 0.45. Nurses with degrees and permanent posts also scored higher on perfectionism. Together the measured factors explained about a third of the spread in scores. The authors suggest hospitals treat perfectionism itself as a mental-health target for theatre staff, through training and support that loosen unrealistic standards.
pmc-13483625:
Zhipeng Xue and co-authors test whether skipping a tourniquet helps recovery after a modified knee realignment operation. Their 2026 retrospective study covers 73 patients with inner-side knee arthritis treated at a Beijing hospital between January 2024 and January 2025. Thirty-five patients had surgery without a tourniquet and 38 had surgery with one, all under the same surgical team.

Visible blood loss during surgery was lower with a tourniquet, yet hidden blood loss afterward was notably higher in that group. Operating time and correction angle did not differ between groups. Recovery measures covering pain, function, and complications complete the comparison in the full report. The trade-off matters because total blood loss, not just what is seen in the operating room, shapes how patients feel and recover.
pmc-13484925:
Chang and Rangarajan applied artificial intelligence retrosynthesis tools in 2026 to covalent organic frameworks, porous crystalline materials built from organic building blocks called monomers. Only about thirteen hundred have been made, although the design space is vast, partly because proposed blocks may be impossible to make. Retrosynthesis software works backward from a target molecule to plan its synthesis, and this study used it on their building blocks for the first time.

Two known tools, ASCKOS and AiZynthFinder, together found synthesis routes for seventy-six percent of 359 reported monomers drawn from six hundred two-dimensional frameworks, evenly across structural types. The tools also found routes to eighty-three unexplored monomers that could form at least twelve hundred hypothetical ones. The authors say modern versions of the tools can remove a key bottleneck in turning computer-drawn frameworks into real materials.
pmc-13486925:
Eleanor Bray and others compare TikTok videos with teaching materials about unregulated vapes aimed at young people in the United Kingdom. In 2026, the content analysis codes fifty-eight TikTok videos found through eight illicit vaping hashtags, with educational resources gathered by web search. Youth vaping has risen sharply in Britain, and unregulated products add a new concern.

The most common video themes were indifference to the law, entertainment, and shared subculture, together drawing twenty-one million likes. Teaching resources scored as good overall but were weak on health risks from illicit vapes and on youth appeal, often feeling serious and disengaging. The authors argue that prevention matter must compete on the same terms of tone and relevance as the videos young people actually watch.
pmc-13487925:
Dongho Lee and colleagues search soybean DNA for natural tolerance to dicamba spray drift in a 2026 genetics study. Dicamba is a weed killer that can injure nearby soybeans lacking built-in tolerance. The team grew 188 related soybean lines in four settings and measured how each line handled unintended exposure, then scanned their genomes for linked regions.

Six regions on different chromosomes together explained a sizable share of the variation seen. Two regions stood out as major, holding candidate genes tied to detoxifying chemicals, including enzymes that help break down or move harmful compounds. One region also showed signs of diversity lost during domestication. The findings give breeders markers to select hardier soybean lines.
pmc-13488225:
Zuzana Rodova, Petra Petrova, and Vladimir Rogalewicz survey European occupational therapists about sensitive client activities in a 2026 study across thirty-two countries. The field uses the label dark side occupations for meaningful activities that carry ethical or social controversy, such as sexuality or addiction-related behavior. Therapists in four European regions answered closed questions about how often such topics arise, plus open questions about avoided topics and the label itself.

Sensitive topics came up far less in Central and Eastern Europe, and somewhat less in Southern Europe, than in Western and Northern regions. Many therapists avoided topics in advance rather than refusing them outright, shaped by culture, workplace climate, and professional boundaries. Views on the label split between useful and stigmatizing.
pmc-13489725:
Tomoki Nawashiro and colleagues report skull reconstruction in a young girl born with a giant pigmented birthmark in a 2026 surgical case report. The girl was aged six years and five months. She had a large scalp lesion slightly right of the midline. Early scans showed a wide gap in the skull running from frontal to parietal bone. A skin sample showed a blue nevus, a deep pigment cell growth. Development was normal and the gap stayed stable, so planned surgery came before school entry.

Plastic surgeons helped fit a custom artificial bone. Normal fatty tissue and the usual separation plane under the scalp were missing, with skin stuck directly to bone, membrane, and web-like tissue. Careful sharp dissection limited membrane injury, and later fluid buildup and small skin loss healed with local care and a swimming-cap pressure dressing.
pmc-13490525:
Małecki and team discovered a bacterial enzyme that slices the cell walls of staph bacteria even when those walls carry the modification that defeats the best-known enzyme drug. Lysostaphin kills Staphylococcus aureus by cutting wall cross-bridges, but resistant strains swap in serine-containing bridges it cannot cut. Their 2026 study cloned three versions of the new enzyme, LssR, from a related staph species, purified them, and tuned their working conditions.

All three versions, full-length, mature, and the catalytic core alone, dissolved live staph cells robustly in the reported assays. Crucially, they cut the serine-containing cross-bridges that confer lysostaphin resistance, a first for this enzyme family according to the authors. Each variant had its own optimal conditions, giving formulators choices. Małecki proposes LssR as a candidate antimicrobial for the day lysostaphin resistance spreads clinically.
pmc-13491425:
Canestrari and team mapped which genes a master switch protein turns on in Mycobacterium abscessus, a hard-to-treat relative of tuberculosis. The switch, sigma factor M, was suspected of commanding the bacterium's oldest secretion system, ESX-4, which helps it survive inside immune cells. Their 2026 study deleted the switch's gene locus in the bacterium, restored it in a comparison strain, and read all gene activity to catch what changed.

The comparison defined fifteen target sites transcribing fifty genes under the switch's control in the analysis reported. Promoter sequences at those sites shared a consensus pattern, evidence the switch binds and activates them directly. The regulon centers on ESX-4 machinery and its suspected secreted effectors, matching the pattern in tuberculosis and a harmless relative. Canestrari says naming the effector list is the first step toward learning how ESX-4 helps the bacterium endure inside phagosomes.
pmc-13491625:
Kaiwen Xiao and eight co-authors survey in 2026 how nanotechnology could sharpen both diagnosis and treatment of bladder cancer. The disease returns often, resists therapy, and lacks tools that detect and treat it in one system. Their review ties material design choices, such as particle size and surface chemistry, to performance inside the bladder's unusual environment.

Nano-sized sensors can pick up faint urinary biomarkers and support liquid biopsy, while engineered carriers hold drugs against the bladder wall despite constant urine flow. Platforms that merge imaging with therapy promise feedback during treatment rather than after it. The authors also weigh safety, reproducibility, and manufacturing scale, and they point toward artificial intelligence helping design future materials.
pmc-13492325:
Massimo Saviano and others report X-ray-free heart nerve burning in a pregnant woman with fainting from a too-active vagus nerve. In 2026, the case concerns a twenty-four-year-old with repeat fainting from a slowed heart and a noted long pause, for whom simple care had failed. The method targets calming nerve clusters that slow the sinus node and the lower heart node.

Using heart signal mapping kept to the right atrium, the team avoided X-rays wholly while keeping the method simple. Symptoms cleared through birth and into the after-birth period. The case offers a device-free choice instead of short-term or lasting pacing for well-chosen pregnant patients.
pmc-13493925:
Sara Coletta leads a seventeen-author team establishing in 2026 that an immune receptor called CD300e keeps fat tissue metabolically healthy during obesity. Twin studies had hinted at it: the heavier twin carried more of the receptor in fat, and weight loss lowered it. Mice engineered to lack the gene were fed a high-fat diet to test whether the receptor protects or harms.

Absence made everything worse: more weight gain, swollen fat cells, fatty liver, and poorer blood sugar control. Macrophages missing the receptor ate less fat and glucose and breathed more weakly through their mitochondria, a broad energy failure confirmed by protein profiling. Fat cells compensated by making more fat and releasing less. Silencing the gene in human cells reproduced the defect, nominating the receptor as a drug target.
pmc-13494025:
Parsa Iranmahboub leads a sixteen-author team comparing in 2026 two ways to translate prostate surgery pathology reports into summaries patients can actually understand. Since patients now see these reports instantly online, often before their surgeon calls, jargon-heavy documents breed anxiety and message traffic. One contender followed hand-written rules; the other was a large language model prompted with no examples.

Error-free summaries came from ninety-two percent of the rule-based attempts and ninety-seven percent of the language model's, a gap too small to call significant. On reports from a second hospital with different formatting, the language model held up untrained while the rule system needed only minor tweaks to match it. Institutions can pick either framework to fit their budgets and governance.
pmc-13494625:
Attila J Hertelendy, Nikki Romanik, and Gregory R Ciottone argue, in a 2026 commentary, that artificial intelligence should move pandemic readiness from reaction toward resilience. They open with outbreaks in May 2026. One was a hantavirus cluster on an Antarctic cruise ship that reached 13 cases with deaths. The other was an Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda, declared an emergency. Both, they say, exposed the same faults.

Detection lagged, with weeks lost before labs named the agent, and response stayed split across systems that share neither data nor pace. Germ jumps from animals are more common, yet watch efforts lag in the places at risk. The authors urge investment in three skills: prediction tools, AI, and map-based intelligence joined into command systems. Five years after a panel warned of being caught out again, they say the gap between proposed and working systems must close.
pmc-13495225:
Soon Lean Keng, Wong Mong Khim, and Azlina Yusuf measure, in a 2026 study, what nurses at a Malaysian teaching hospital know about maggot debridement therapy. The treatment places sterile fly larvae on chronic wounds to eat dead tissue and spur healing. It works well, yet wards rarely use it, and nurses, who lead wound care, had not been surveyed on it in Malaysia.

The team gave a tested questionnaire to 165 randomly chosen nurses. Most had heard of the therapy, and most held a nursing diploma. Still, over half showed low knowledge, and only about a quarter scored high. Knowing more tracked with having heard of the method and, more strongly, with having done it. The authors urge adding the therapy to nursing courses, ongoing training, and ward protocols so book learning turns into bedside skill.
pmc-13495325:
Yufeng Qin, Danli Song, and Ji Li review, in a 2026 article, low back pain in competitive gymnasts: how common it is, what drives it, and what gentle treatments help. Gymnastics loads the spine hard, yet the proof for this group had never been summed. The team searched five databases through early 2025 under standard review rules.

Ten studies with 736 gymnasts qualified. Back pain struck a quarter to a half of gymnasts depending on discipline, most in rhythmic gymnastics, and rose with age and weekly training hours. Core stability training cut pain by up to about three points on a ten-point scale. Posture retraining helped too, and mixing both gave the largest drops. No treatment hurt performance. The authors back eight to twelve weeks of such training, while flagging small studies and short follow-up as limits on the proof.
pmc-13495425:
Aadarsh Pandey and a large team profile, in a 2026 study, the diversity of citrus rootstocks in India using both looks and DNA markers. Rootstocks anchor citrus trees and shape yield and toughness, so knowing which lines truly differ guides breeding and saving of stock. The team scored seventeen rootstock types on twenty-seven fruit and seed traits and read them with nineteen targeted DNA primers.

Looks varied widely, with fruit weight and shape the most changeable traits. The DNA bands split the lines into four family groups matching their pedigrees, and pointed to two broad genetic pools. Looks and DNA told partly different stories, agreeing only moderately, which the authors read as the two lenses catching complementary sides of diversity. They name the most distinct rootstocks as prime parents for future citrus breeding and as stock worth conserving.
pmc-13495525:
Cristina Banella and a large team probe, in a 2026 study, a hormone receptor that may expose a weak point in childhood T-cell leukemia. This aggressive blood cancer relapses in about a quarter of children despite standard therapy, leaning on flexible fuel use to survive. The team profiled the beta3-adrenergic receptor in leukemia cells and tested a drug that blocks it.

The receptor ran far higher in leukemia cells than in healthy blood cells. Blocking it hit the cells' power stations, chiefly one core complex, and shut down fat burning, their backup fuel. Starved of flexible energy, the cells died by ferroptosis, an iron-linked death route, and iron-handling proteins in the blood shifted in step. The blocker also teamed up with a second energy drug to kill stubborn cells. The authors pitch the receptor as a target for high-risk disease.
pmc-13495725:
Sorasak Klinyod and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a pair of mirror-aware electrodes that amplify the signal of one handedness of a molecule. Many drugs come in left and right forms with very different effects, yet telling them apart sensitively is hard. The device faces two metal electrodes stamped with the same chiral pattern across a narrow channel, so a matching molecule bounces between them, reacting again and again.

Each round trip adds to the measured current, multiplying the signal more than tenfold for the favored form. Using DOPA, a Parkinson's drug, as the test case, the setup told the two forms apart with about nine tenths efficiency. The electrodes are porous platinum-iridium alloys imprinted with one DOPA form or the other. The authors see a route to cheap, sharp sensors for chiral drugs and chemicals.
pmc-13495925:
Md Saiful Alam and colleagues report in 2026 on cervical screening for women aged 50 and older, using data from the HPV FOCAL trial. Participants received either a test for human papillomavirus, a virus linked to cervical cancer, or standard cytology, which checks cell changes under a microscope. The question was which approach finds serious precancer changes more reliably near the age when screening often stops.

The analysis covered 6,471 women, split almost evenly between the two methods, with joint testing at a 48-month exit visit. Women who tested negative for the virus at the start later showed fewer serious lesions, and fewer cases were missed than with cytology. Adjusted results also favoured virus testing, supporting its use for this age group.
pmc-13499225:
Chew and colleagues review efforts to bring precision medicine to juvenile idiopathic arthritis in this 2026 article. This group of childhood arthritides is the commonest of its kind. Yet despite advanced drugs, many young patients still suffer flares. Lasting joint damage remains common too. Because children present and progress so differently, treatment chosen by biological profile would be valuable, but no biomarker yet predicts who responds to what.

Single-cell technologies can now profile genes and proteins in target tissues at fine resolution, revealing the disease's biological basis in individual patients. At the same time, machine learning methods make it feasible to combine those profiles with clinical outcomes across large, varied datasets. The authors summarize multimodal strategies for joining such data and set out research priorities for making tailored treatment real for these children.
pmc-13499325:
B Mothishwaran and co-authors compare in 2026 nurses' knowledge and daily practice on pressure injuries caused by medical devices, such as tubes and masks pressing on skin, across India and Europe. Turning knowledge into bedside practice is a persistent problem worldwide. A validated 20-point scale covering knowledge, attitude, and practice was given to 334 registered nurses working in the two settings, and gaps were examined by domain.

European nurses scored far higher overall than Indian nurses, with the widest gap in hands-on clinical practice. The differences did not track age, gender, or other personal factors in the analysis. Indian nurses more often held postgraduate degrees, which undercuts the idea that individual study alone explains the gap. The authors argue that ward routines, shared protocols, and staffing systems shape performance more than personal qualifications, so reform should target the clinical environment itself.
pmc-13500225:
Sebastian M Beller and co-authors measure in 2026 what a single-day dermatology workshop does for first-year medical students, whose skin training is often thin. Limited exposure can leave students shaky at recognising common skin conditions and unsure what dermatologists actually do. Their Dermatology Day mixed lectures, hands-on practice, and patient contact at one institution, with anonymous surveys, a ten-question knowledge quiz, and a scored lesion-description task before and after the event.

Twenty-seven students completed the opening survey and sixteen the closing one. Quiz scores did not change significantly, although lesion description accuracy trended upward without reaching significance in the small paired sample. Confidence rose significantly across several skills, from taking a skin history to knowing examination steps and biopsy basics, and awareness of diagnostic challenges in skin of colour also grew. Free-text answers prized meeting real patients with chronic skin disease.
pmc-13500425:
Dong, in a 2026 article, argues that biopiracy is better understood as epistemic colonialism. Biopiracy means companies taking indigenous plants and knowledge without fair payment. The theft, Dong says, is of knowledge systems, not just seeds. Building on Fricker's theory of knowledge injustice, Kuokkanen's idea of relational sovereignty, and Santos's call for Southern knowledge systems, the article proposes a three-stage story. It runs from biopiracy through epistemicide, killing knowledge traditions, toward rebuilt knowledge sovereignty.

Experiments in India, Brazil, and South Africa show how Western property law pushes aside communal, orally held knowledge. Benefit-sharing under the Convention on Biological Diversity still assumes Western rules. The TRIPS trade agreement comes in for sharp criticism as embedding that hegemony. Dong's remedy is plural: restore communities' control over their own knowledge, treat sovereignty as a web of ties rather than a fence, and build many-centred knowledge systems instead of one world centre.
pmc-13500725:
Luomeng Qian leads a nine-author team reporting a 2026 study of why liver cancer tumours stop responding to the drug sorafenib. Sorafenib blocks blood vessel growth, which leaves tumours short of oxygen. The team found that low oxygen makes hepatocellular carcinoma cells release more migrasomes, large vesicles shed by migrating cells, and that these vesicles carry the protein CD147 on their surface. Such vesicles were linked to tumours that resist the drug.

The vesicles enter other cancer cells by macropinocytosis, a gulping form of uptake that depends on a receptor called LPAR6. Once inside, the CD147-bearing vesicles switch on a PI3K/AKT/TWIST1 signalling chain. That chain pushes cancer cells to form their own vessel-like channels, a process called vasculogenic mimicry, which feeds the tumour and sustains resistance. Blocking both the vesicle uptake and the channel formation made sorafenib kill cancer cells more effectively.
pmc-13501625:
Kenan Qin leads a four-author team with a 2026 three-wave study of how everyday violence exposure may feed internet gaming disorder in Chinese teenagers. The sample held 386 junior high school students from Hubei Province, 47.9 percent boys, with a mean age of 12.23 years. Students completed surveys at six-month intervals covering violence exposure, peer bullying, negative emotion, and gaming disorder symptoms. The team then tested whether the earlier experiences predicted the later gaming problems directly or through middle steps.

Baseline violence exposure predicted gaming disorder one year later. An indirect path also emerged: exposure led to peer bullying at the middle wave, which fed negative emotion, which in turn linked to the disorder. The authors read the chain as a route by which harsh settings turn into compulsive gaming through social and emotional strain. They suggest the findings can guide prevention work aimed at peer relations and emotion control.
pmc-13501725:
Geetika Narang leads a four-author team with a 2026 analysis of the malaria parasite gene behind chloroquine resistance, called Pfcrt. The team assembled 979 Indian sequences of a key gene segment and 719 full-length sequences from around the world, then measured diversity, selection pressure, and population structure. In India, three major haplotypes dominated: CVIET, SVMNT, and CVMNK. CVIET prevailed overall, especially in the North-East, while the other two waxed and waned by region and period.

Diversity peaked between 2010 and 2019 even as malaria cases fell, implying drug pressure kept selecting variants. Mizoram showed the strongest statistical signature of that pressure, and North-East sequences carried a distinct structure likely imported from the Greater Mekong region. Worldwide, 65 haplotypes appeared, with Cambodia the most diverse and strong separation between countries. Six codons showed positive selection. The authors argue surveillance must stay regional to catch resistant lineages early.
pmc-13502925:
Larbi Ed Dafali leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 paediatric case that breaks two rules of Guillain-Barré syndrome at once: the paralysis came back, and it travelled the wrong way. A nine-year-old girl treated in Rabat had survived a classic ascending episode at age two. Fifteen days after an illness in July 2025, weakness began in both arms and descended, progressing within a day to flaccid tetraplegia with bulbar and breathing involvement.

Testing confirmed the diagnosis despite the geography: nerve studies showed demyelinating polyneuropathy, spinal fluid had the protein-cell dissociation, MRI lit up the cauda equina roots, and anti-ganglioside antibodies were positive. She needed ventilation and courses of intravenous immunoglobulin, a repetition whose benefit the authors note is uncertain. Recovery was substantial, reaching remission at three months. The case argues for keeping Guillain-Barré on the list even when paralysis descends or returns.
pmc-13503425:
Benneh and colleagues test a plant compound, deacetyl xylopic acid from the African spice fruit Xylopia aethiopica, as a helper for antidepressant drugs. Earlier work showed the compound family lifts mood-like behaviour in acutely stressed mice. Their 2026 study combined it with fluoxetine and other antidepressants in mouse despair tests. It then moved to a model where mice were restrained six hours daily for six weeks to produce chronic depression-like behaviour.

In the acute tests the combinations were synergistic: the mixture achieved the benchmark effect at doses below what simple addition predicted, across all four partner drugs on the interaction analysis. The chronic model proved tougher, since three days of the plant compounds alone did not reverse behaviour, while fluoxetine alone did, and a combined dose also worked. The authors read this as a fast-acting amplifier role for the compound.
pmc-13504825:
Shuenn-Wen Kuo and Pei-Ming Huang test a suction trick that speeds lung nodule mapping during keyhole surgery, in a 2026 study. Surgeons use a rotating scanner in the operating room to find small lung tumors, but the lung must inflate evenly for a clean read. Trapped air and sagging tissue slow the process.

The study covered 55 patients having wedge removal of small tumors through a single port. One group got gentle wound suction to aid lung expansion; the other did not. Mapping took about eight minutes less with suction. Poor expansion showed in half the standard group but only a tenth of the suction group. Adjusted models kept the suction group ahead. The authors say the cheap step could smooth this surgery's workflow.
pmc-13505025:
Fatemeh Boroomand leads a team reviewing how food compounds rewrite cancer-linked gene marks, in a 2026 paper. Genes carry chemical tags that tune their activity without changing the code; diet is one force that sets those tags. The review joins lab, population, and clinical threads into one map.

Compounds in green tea, grapes, soy, and cruciferous vegetables can block tag-adding enzymes, loosen packed DNA, and retune small RNA networks in lab models. Diets rich in such foods track with lower cancer rates, while diets heavy in red meat and added sugar track with damage-linked tags. Gut microbe products and fasting patterns also feed the tag system. Response varies with each person's genes, so the authors back biomarker-guided diet trials.
pmc-13505325:
Divya L C, Jaiprabu J, and Sridurga Mattyvanan studied kidney risk markers in 150 adults with type 2 diabetes at a South Indian hospital over one year. Beyond the usual urine albumin test, they computed a protein-creatinine ratio and several derived indices that set urine protein against kidney filtering function. Blood sugar control, diabetes duration, blood pressure, and body weight were recorded for comparison.

Forty percent of patients had normal urine albumin, while the rest split between mild and heavy albumin leakage. Every derived index rose step by step as albumin leakage worsened, and filtering function fell along the same path. The protein-creatinine ratio tracked urine albumin closely. Blood sugar level and the protein ratio each predicted kidney involvement on their own in adjusted analysis. The authors suggest these cheap urine-based indices can add useful detail beside standard tests when judging diabetic kidney disease.
pmc-13507025:
Qingmin Zhou, Changsheng Chen, Junyi Tong, and Peng Han map, in a 2026 study, a decade of research on executive functions in ADHD. Executive functions are mental skills for focus, memory, and self-control. Their count covers 2898 papers from 2015 to 2024 in a major citation database, charted by country, center, author, and journal.

The United States led in output, and King's College London led among centers, with Michael J Kofler the most published author. Seven topic clusters and five hot spots emerged from keyword maps. The authors point next work toward links between core symptoms and these skills, related conditions, and better diagnosis and treatment studies.
pmc-13507125:
Manmohan Sharma, Harshavarthini Shanmugam, and Soumya Ranjan Mahapatro present 2026 control methods that keep groups of moving agents in shifting formations on a preset schedule, even under denial-of-service attacks. Such attacks block messages between agents. Earlier methods settled too slowly or tied timing to starting states, which fails time-critical tasks.

Their first law uses timed triggers under attack, and a second self-triggered version predicts the next update from the last one, so constant watching is not needed. Math proofs back both laws, and simulations show they hold time-varying formations. Comparisons show the self-triggered version saves bandwidth on both sensing and control links. Exact preset timing also speeds recovery after attacks.
pmc-13507225:
Samsara W Upadhya, Nalin Ratnayeke, Katherine R Ferrick, David L Rosenthal, and Tobias Meyer show, in 2026 work, that human cells use two distinct gated routes to start DNA copying. Copying must begin once, on time, or genomes suffer damage. Prior models assumed fixed trigger levels for cell cycle regulators, which the new data contradict.

One route uses the CDC7 kinase to prime the copying machine, letting a partner kinase fire origins at low activity. The other route waits for shutdown of a brake complex, APC/Cdh1, and then needs much higher kinase activity through a different partner. Blocking S phase therefore requires closing both routes at once. Precise timing emerges from tunable thresholds, not a single switch.
pmc-13507325:
Miriam E Dillard leads a 2026 team that maps how a fat molecule fine-tunes Sonic Hedgehog signaling, a master patterning pathway in embryos, through the transducer protein Smoothened. Smoothened carries several pockets where fats and sterols dock, and combined docking may boost signaling in certain tissues only. The team pinpointed a pocket for arachidonic acid, a common fatty acid, atop the protein's membrane-spanning bundle.

Breaking that pocket weakened responses to both the Hedgehog signal and sterols. Mice engineered with the broken pocket often died around birth with heart defects and poor lung development, while brain development stayed normal. Tissue-selective tuning by local fats may let one pathway serve many organs differently.
pmc-13508225:
Liang Songlin and four co-authors report an elderly man's bladder-area cancer that vanished after a two-drug treatment, in a 2026 case report. The patient was 79 and had advanced urothelial carcinoma, a cancer of the urinary tract lining. He declined removal of the bladder, a major operation. His tumor showed only low levels of the HER2 marker that one of the drugs targets. The pair combined a drug-carrying antibody with an immune therapy drug, given every three weeks on back-to-back days.

After six rounds, scans showed the tumor had shrunk greatly. A follow-up procedure that sampled the old tumor bed found no cancer cells left, which counts as a complete response. Side effects stayed mild, limited to fatigue and nausea. The authors urge care in reading one case, and call for larger studies to test the pairing and to find markers that predict who benefits.
pmc-13508625:
Mohammad Barbati and five co-authors report clearing a blocked outflow tube on a heart pump without open surgery, in a 2026 case report. The patient was a 71-year-old man with a HeartMate 3 assist pump implanted more than three years earlier. The tube carrying blood out of the pump had narrowed over a long stretch. Redo surgery was judged too risky for him. Doctors instead threaded overlapping self-expanding stents through the vessel by catheter.

Imaging after the procedure confirmed the graft was open and flow had improved. A later clot-based narrowing at the far end was handled with stronger blood thinning rather than another procedure. The authors argue that catheter stenting, with safeguards tailored to the pump, can treat complex late blockages in chosen patients. This complication can hide behind normal blood tests and pump logs, they note, so scan imaging matters for spotting it.
pmc-13510125:
Naz and colleagues made copper nanoparticles using leaf extract of Grevillea robusta, a silky oak tree, in a 2026 lab study. The green route replaces chemical synthesis. Fresh and dried leaf extracts were mixed with copper sulfate, and profiling of the leaves found fatty acids among the compounds likely helping the particles form and stay stable. Five testing methods confirmed stable, crystalline, well-dispersed nanoparticles.

Naz tested the particles against bacteria and fungi that matter in clinics and on farms: E. coli and several crop-destroying molds. They worked strongly at low microgram doses across the board, with half-maximal doses in the single digits for bacteria. The particles also blocked biofilm and surface film growth, a key defense microbes use against treatment. Computer modeling suggested the leaf compounds bind target proteins in microbes well, backing the particles as eco-friendly antimicrobial options for medicine and agriculture.
pmc-13511625:
Rodriguez and colleagues ask whether brain scans can predict personality change in older people who still think clearly, in 2026 research on early Alzheimer's disease. Personality was tracked alongside amyloid PET scans, which reveal sticky protein deposits linked to Alzheimer's, and FDG-PET scans, which show how actively brain regions use sugar. Participants were followed for 55 months, and statistical models tested which baseline measures predicted later shifts in the Big Five personality traits.

A decline in openness, the trait covering curiosity and imagination, was tied to abnormal FDG-PET patterns in both simple and adjusted models. That single scan measure explained 15 percent of the variance in openness change over the follow-up period. Falling agreeableness was linked to lower baseline memory scores and to amyloid positivity, which together explained 11 percent and 8 percent of variance in their respective models. Other traits showed no clear link to the imaging markers.
pmc-13512025:
Cheon-Hwang Wi, Jun Hwang, Woo-Young Son, and Hyun-Wook Kim compare two food enzymes for cutting pig skin gelatin chains, in 2026 work. The aim is to tame gel setting for liquid foods. Gelatin sets firmly when cold, which helps texture yet blocks use in high-moisture products.
