Alcalase cut far more bonds than pepsin, judged by free amino group counts. The plain gelatin set into a stable gel, while both treated versions set weakly or not at all. The Alcalase product stayed fully fluid with no measurable thickness at a tested concentration, while the pepsin product kept notable thickness. Pepsin treatment gave the best oil uptake, emulsion stability, and a slight digestibility edge. Enzyme choice, the authors say, steers the balance between flow and function.
pmc-13512325:
Yuan Ren, Junwen Meng, Jin Zhang, Qijian Tian, Rui Huang, and Xin Liu track how pigment builds up in maize seedlings, in 2026 work. They join chemical and gene readings across five growth stages. Anthocyanin pigments color tissues and guard against stress, yet their control mixes metabolism with gene regulation in tangled ways. The team compared a pigment-rich maize line with a pigment-poor one to filter out noise from plain growth differences.

The two lines drifted apart from early stages onward in both chemicals and gene activity. Filtered candidates clustered in pigment-building routes, energy handling, and redox control. Two gene groups pulled in opposite directions against pigment content: one centered on MYB regulators long known to drive pigment pathways, and one rooted in basic metabolism and signaling. Integrated maps linked the MYB hubs to pigment building blocks, tying gene control to chemical output.
pmc-13518225:
Roberta Giusti Schran and three colleagues pool published results on pain relief for laboratory mice after surgery in a 2026 systematic review. Mice undergo countless operations, yet pain drugs are underreported and their benefit unproven as a whole. Forty-eight studies fed the review and forty-three the pooled analysis, spanning opioids, anti-inflammatory drugs, acetaminophen, and local anaesthetics.

Painkillers worked overall, with a moderate pooled effect. The relief was uneven: males benefited about twice as clearly as females, and mild surgery responded better than severe. Drugs eased provoked pain far better than the spontaneous pain animals feel at rest. Nearly every drug class failed against that resting pain. Most studies also carried bias risks. Giusti Schran's team concludes that standard practice leaves real gaps, especially for females and major surgery, and calls for better-designed trials to close an ethical hole in everyday lab work.
pmc-13518525:
Lubomir Skladany and others compare PEth testing with medical rules for spotting alcohol use relapse after liver transplant. In 2026, the forward-looking cohort studies 143 adults given new livers for alcohol-linked liver disease between 2008 and 2023. It checked relapse every three months since 2020 by both medical rules and blood PEth above 0.05 millionths of a gram per litre. Return to alcohol use lacks a neutral testing standard.

PEth found relapse in 32.2 percent of patients versus 48.3 percent by medical rules, with match in 68.5 percent of cases. Mismatch reached 31.5 percent, mostly doctor-plus but blood-test-clear cases. Every-three-months testing caught more severe relapse than semi-annual testing. Time since transplant on its own called marker relapse, hinting medical rules may rate relapse too high.
pmc-13518825:
Bing Li and five colleagues present LTPF in 2026, an improved particle filter for ultra-wideband indoor positioning. Radio-based indoor location serves robots and navigation, yet walls and obstacles scatter signals and inject wild errors. Standard particle filters lose accuracy when their particles cluster or get weighted badly.

LTPF spices the particle spread with chaotic sequences drawn from a reshaped logistic map, keeping particles diverse. A revised t-distribution, tuned by standardized residuals, builds the observation score so outliers sway results less. Against four rival algorithms, average accuracy gains ranged from about 40 to 50 percent. Computing cost stayed on par with the plain particle filter, keeping the method practical.
pmc-13520125:
Malek Marian and five colleagues review in 2026 how steering crop microbe communities on purpose could make farming greener and hardier under climate stress. Microbes living on and in plants shape growth, disease resistance, and stress tolerance. Tuning means adjusting the group's makeup, stability, and cross-talk rather than simply adding one strain.

Options surveyed span bacteria, fungi, protists, nematodes, and bacteria-infecting viruses, plus plant-derived compounds. Newer ideas include multi-level communities built from ecological traits, temperate phages, whole-community transplants, breeding for microbe-friendly plants, and synbiotic pairings of microbes with helpful compounds. Marian and co-authors flag knowledge gaps and urge plans mixing plant trials, simplified lab systems, computer modeling, and multiomics so gains last in the field.
pmc-13521225:
Yong Xiang and colleagues build in 2026 goose kidney organoids, miniature lab-grown kidney tissues, to study a goose astrovirus that causes fatal gout in goslings. No goose cell lines or standard lab animals existed for this disease, leaving its mechanism largely unexplored.

Organoids grown from embryo kidney tissue kept realistic structure and function. Virus infected several kidney cell types inside organoids, matching patterns in live birds. High viral dose sharply raised uric acid, mirroring disease severity, while flat cell cultures barely supported the virus. Gene and metabolite profiling showed disrupted purine handling, with three transporter genes tracking uric acid levels.
pmc-13522525:
Rebecca L Kelly and colleagues tracked mosaic chromosome changes in blood cells over time to learn what makes abnormal cell clones grow. Such changes, called mosaic chromosomal alterations, arise with age in white blood cells and can precede blood cancers.

The team scanned blood DNA from 56,324 adults in a US screening study and followed 1,746 repeat changes over time. A change's share of cells at one visit only modestly predicted how fast it would grow, so repeat sampling matters. Where in the genome the change sat drove growth most, with age, smoking, and other changes also shaping the pace. Changes already tied to blood cancers, above all myeloid ones, grew fastest, Kelly reports, marking them as risk signals worth tracking.
pmc-13523125:
Katherine E Bujold and colleagues test how positive charges on a DNA shell change nanoparticle uptake in a 2026 nanomedicine study. Spherical nucleic acids are particles coated with densely packed DNA strands that point outward, and cells absorb them efficiently through surface receptors. New DNA-like units carrying positive charges were inserted into the shell in varying numbers and positions.

Uptake rose as more charged units were added, but only when those units sat on the outer surface of the shell. Blocking experiments showed uptake depended on scavenger receptors and also on wider membrane composition. The results show that both chemical content and exact placement can be tuned to steer how these particles enter cells, informing the design of future nanoscale therapies.
pmc-13523325:
Sude Coşar and Merve Sarı compare two root canal medicaments in a 2026 laboratory study of extracted teeth. One hundred twenty-eight single-rooted teeth were prepared, filled for a week with either calcium hydroxide or N-acetylcysteine, and then cleaned out with plain needle irrigation or sonic activation. A calcium silicate sealer was placed, and a scanning microscope measured leftover medicament and sealer penetration into tiny dentin tubules.

Neither medicament type nor cleaning method changed how much medicament remained. Sealer penetration, however, was greater after the N-acetylcysteine medicament than after calcium hydroxide. Cleaning method made no significant difference. Penetration was deepest near the crown and shallowest near the root tip in all groups. The authors conclude that medicament choice, rather than activation, shapes sealer entry in this setting.
pmc-13523425:
Serim Lee and Allison A Appleton study combined pregnancy exposures and birth outcomes in a 2026 cohort analysis. Nearly three hundred diverse pregnant women from the Albany area contributed information on physical health, behaviors such as smoking and diet, psychosocial adversity, and environmental contaminants including lead. Statistical grouping sorted women into classes by their combined exposure patterns, and birth measures were compared across classes.

Three classes emerged: a low-risk group near half the cohort, a high-risk group across all domains at a similar share, and a small group high only on behavioral and environmental risks. Babies in the all-domain high-risk class were smaller on every measure, grew more slowly in the womb, and arrived earlier. Effects were strongest in male infants and in racially minoritized and less educated families.
pmc-13523825:
This 2026 letter by Prueksapraopong and Kohn replies to a comment on their article about lentiviral gene therapy for sickle cell disease. The exchange concerns what durability should mean for a one time genetic treatment. The authors agree that two measures differ: gene marking, the share of blood cells carrying the inserted gene, and protein expression, whether the gene still works.

In their study only one patient kept both marking and expression long term. One kept marking but lost expression, and two lost both over time. The authors contrast earlier trials in immune diseases where dozens of patients kept both. They suggest chronic marrow inflammation in sickle cell disease may shorten the survival of corrected stem cells. Prueksapraopong argues durability should mean lasting clinical benefit backed by both measures.
pmc-13525525:
Yan and colleagues combined a case study with a literature review on meningitis caused by Ureaplasma parvum, a tiny bacterium without a cell wall, in newborn babies, published in 2026. Their case was a boy born slightly preterm who arrived at seventeen days old with persistent fever. His blood tests looked normal, yet his spinal fluid resembled pus-forming meningitis, and standard antibiotics failed.

Yan reports that gene sequencing of the spinal fluid found the organism. Three weeks of azithromycin, an antibiotic that works without targeting a cell wall, cured the infection, though a language delay appeared by age two. Reviewing sixteen published cases for a total of seventeen, the authors found fever and seizures most typical, diagnosis resting mainly on sequencing. Treatment with macrolide antibiotics for three to ten weeks. Most babies recovered well, but brain complications such as fluid buildup occurred, and the best regimen remains unsettled.
pmc-13526525:
Jeong and colleagues trace a signal chain that drives harmful new blood vessel growth in low-oxygen eye tissue. A factor called HIF-2 alpha switches on genes that help cells cope with low oxygen. In sick eyes, that same switch helps leaky excess vessels grow.

In a mouse model of eye disease, the signal stem cell factor rose in support cells of the retina. Blocking that signal cut HIF-2 alpha levels and excess vessel growth in the mice. In human vessel cells, the factor raised HIF-2 alpha protein without raising its gene message. The boost ran through two known growth signal paths inside the cell. Blocking HIF-2 alpha wiped out the vessel growth push from the factor.
pmc-13526825:
Wenzhang He and others build, in a 2026 study, a machine learning model that shows its reasoning, to flag serious fungal infection early in pneumonia caught outside hospital. Such infections are risky and hard to confirm quickly. The model mines hundreds of texture features from chest CT, set beside usual medical factors.

The study took in 570 pneumonia patients from two hospitals, scanned between July 2022 and August 2024, split into training, internal test, and external test sets. Software outlined the infected lung regions on its own. The joint model reached areas under the curve near 0.81 on the inside set and 0.79 on the outside set. It beat versions that used medical factors alone or image features alone, and it gave better net benefit when weighed for real-world use. Age swayed the model's calls most, followed by fine texture details. Explanation tools made each single call open to checks by doctors.
pmc-13527925:
Sunita Gupta and nine colleagues present a 2026 case series on tuberculosis of the jaw and face bones. This rare form of TB often hides behind plain-looking swelling, ulcers, or a stiff jaw. Nine patients aged nine to 33 were seen at a center in a region where TB is common.

Scans typically showed eaten-away bone, breaks in the bone surface, or soft-tissue abscesses. Skin tests, cell samples, and standard staining frequently missed the diagnosis. A rapid cartridge-based genetic test or culture confirmed the germ in most cases. Every patient improved clearly on standard anti-tuberculosis drugs. The authors advise thinking of this disease in stubborn jaw lesions. They urge early testing with molecular methods.
pmc-13528325:
Rachel Lawrence and seven colleagues review ambient voice tools that listen to clinic visits and draft the notes in a 2026 paper. The tools aim to cut the paperwork load on clinicians. Searches in late 2025 covered four databases plus grey sources. Of 598 records, twenty-one studies qualified. Most measured user experience or counted time effects.

Some studies found lighter documentation and happier staff. Better perceived care quality was also reported. Nearly all proof came from short watch-and-see designs with self-reports. System-level gains, like safety or cost, were barely measured. Results swung with workflow fit, output quality, and setting. The authors say the proof does not yet back wide adoption. They call for longer studies with shared measures before health systems commit.
pmc-13528425:
Shirin Tarbiaat and colleagues tested arbutin, a plant compound, as a multi-target candidate against Alzheimer disease. Published in 2026, the lab study measured how beta-arbutin blocks two cholinesterase enzymes that break down acetylcholine, plus GSK-3beta, an enzyme tied to toxic tau tangles. Alzheimer disease brings memory loss with falling acetylcholine and tangled tau protein.

Applied alone to SH-SY5Y nerve-like cells, it did not harm viability. Docking simulations ranked its binding across the three targets in line with lab results. The authors present arbutin as a natural multi-target lead, still needing animal and human testing.
pmc-13528925:
Selvam Arjunan leads a large team tying a gut-made chemical to atrial fibrillation in a 2026 study. The chemical, TMAO, forms when gut microbes process foods like choline. Blood levels were measured in people having heart catheter tests. Higher levels tracked with having the rhythm disorder, even after risk factors were counted. Mouse work then tested cause.

Mice prone to the disorder developed it sooner on a TMAO diet. Normal mice showed more inducible episodes too. Extra choline sped onset, while a blocker that cuts TMAO slowed it. Gut microbe mixes shifted with choline and partly normalized with the blocker. Hearts remodeled badly, with wider left atria and slower electrical spread. TMAO jammed a muscarinic receptor, skewing nerve control of the heart. The authors name the pathway a drug target.
pmc-13531825:
Song-Ting Wei and colleagues chart a decade of infectious disease in Heilongjiang border towns during 2026 reporting. The province runs China largest land-port network along a long Russian border, with heavy cross-border movement complicating control. National reporting records covered all 18 port municipalities from 2014 to 2023.

Nearly 65,000 notifiable cases gave a yearly rate near 220 per hundred thousand people. Breathing diseases and blood or sex-spread diseases together formed over 70 percent of cases. Tuberculosis topped the list, followed by hepatitis B and influenza. Overall rates stayed stable while breathing diseases climbed.
pmc-13532825:
Elize W Lockhorst and colleagues review in 2026 a standard fitness programme before bowel cancer surgery at one centre. The programme bundles exercise, food advice, and mental support to build strength before an operation. Charts covered 401 people set for surgery from January 2022 to April 2024.

After the standard programme began in May 2023, uptake rose from 40 to 59 percent. Leg strength and cycling power rose clearly, and hospital stay after surgery fell from four days to three. Problem rates stayed alike across groups, even though the programme group had more other health issues. The findings support wider use of the standard programme in routine surgical care for similar patients.
pmc-13534225:
Ilgin Ozden and colleagues report in 2026 long-term results of a modified Nagoya surgical approach for bile duct cancer near the liver at a centre in Istanbul. Major liver surgery is the main chance of cure, and the Nagoya method is a careful bundle of steps. Records covered 53 patients operated from 2001 to 2012, each followed at least 12 years.

Death within 90 days was low, and survival reached one quarter at ten years. Thirteen patients lived past ten years, none with spread to lymph nodes or positive margins. Results matched global benchmark values for key outcomes and survival.
pmc-13534925:
Kelly A Meiklejohn and colleagues run in 2026 a global interlaboratory study of a proposed standard for image source opinions in forensic work. Labs compare faces, hands, and clothing in photos, yet opinion scales vary widely. Twenty image pairs of varied source and difficulty were judged by 38 practitioners and 44 laypersons.

Practitioners agreed with each other more than laypersons did across all three image types. Practitioners also judged true source more accurately for face and hand pairs. With a clear five-step opinion guide, both groups reached moderate agreement and high accuracy overall.
pmc-13536625:
Mohammad Daher and colleagues test in 2026 whether spine and pelvis measures alone can predict knee bending compensation in adults with degenerative spine disease. Bent knees are a common way patients offset a tilted trunk, and spotting them guides surgery planning. Records covered 201 surgical patients, with spine measures taken from standing X-ray images.

Knee measures were left out of the models on purpose to test true prediction. A support vector machine classified knee bending with fair accuracy and high sensitivity on test data. The authors say spine measures can flag compensation, though larger uniform groups should confirm the approach first.
pmc-13538525:
Claudia Novello and colleagues examine a chemical tagging process in post-mortem Parkinson brains in a 2026 imaging study. Tagging by the enzyme PARP1 adds chain-like marks linked in models to clumping of a key protein and neuron death. High-resolution imaging with three-dimensional rebuilding tracked mark buildup, stress granules, Lewy bodies, and cell death signs across affected brain regions from patients.

Marks gathered in cell bodies in affected regions before clumps of the key protein appeared. Marks plus stress granules fed into Lewy body formation, the hallmark inclusions of the disease. Marks also overlapped heavily with power units in the hard-hit midbrain zone, beside condensed DNA signs of dying neurons. The authors position the tagging pathway as a core driver and drug target.
pmc-13538725:
Fiona J Babir and colleagues test one-minute exercise snacks in adults with type 2 diabetes in a 2026 randomized trial. Sixty-nine inactive adults not on insulin were assigned to vigorous one-minute bouts or gentle mobility work, four times daily on at least five days weekly for twelve weeks, delivered remotely. Adherence and enjoyment led the outcomes, with fitness and metabolic measures trailing.

Both groups stuck to the schedule equally well and enjoyed it similarly, despite the snack group working far harder by effort and heart rate. Nearly all health measures changed alike between groups. The snack group alone gained extra sit-to-stand capacity by trial end. The authors judge brief vigorous snacks feasible in daily life, with modest fitness gains over gentle activity.
pmc-13539525:
Ben Johns and colleagues review strong light-matter coupling in hybrid polaritonic systems in a feature article. When light and matter excitations trade energy faster than they decay, they merge into polaritons, mixed states with new energy landscapes. Designs from mirrored cavities to metal nanostructures and open cavities are surveyed. Inorganic, organic, and hybrid materials reaching strong and ultrastrong regimes all feature.

Coherent motion, mixing with vibrations, dark state pools, and polariton-carried energy and electron flow get full treatment. Lab and theory tools for studying them are covered too. Cases where coupling reshapes charge transport, energy flow, and chemical change are highlighted. New middle and dark-strong regimes widen the field. The authors aim the review at energy and light-tech uses.
pmc-13539925:
Lu and co-authors propose a unified model of kidney damage in Sjögren's disease. Their 2026 review addresses renal tubular acidosis, where the kidney cannot acidify urine properly. This under-recognised complication often appears before the dry eyes and mouth the autoimmune disease is known for. Distal disease, the dominant form, stems from immune attack on the acid-secreting cells of the collecting duct.

The model links that distal injury to knock-on changes upstream. Damage to the proton pump and its partner proteins in intercalated cells blocks acid excretion. The resulting body-wide acidity drives the proximal tubule to reclaim more citrate. That starves urine of a natural stone inhibitor. That combination explains the kidney stones, calcium deposits, and potassium crises patients suffer. Current treatment replaces alkali and potassium but ignores the immune injury, and the authors argue response fades once scarring sets in.
pmc-13540225:
Liang Liu, Dong Wang, and Qidong Guo compare, in a 2026 cohort study, two operations for a shattered heel bone broken into the joint. Wide open plating rebuilds the shape well yet burdens the thin skin over the heel, while a locking nail slipped inside the bone promises a gentler route.

Ninety patients were compared after statistical weighting balanced the groups. Nail patients needed drains far less often, changed dressings fewer times, and scored much lower on a soft-tissue burden index the authors built. Pain at six and twelve weeks was lower, and foot function recovered faster. The authors argue early recovery, not just final scores, should guide choice.
pmc-13540825:
WeiWei Xu presents a 2026 computer study proposing a help tool for autism diagnosis from brain scans, since diagnosis still leans on clinical rating scales. Scarce scan data are a core obstacle, so the design manufactures extra examples before classifying.

Working from the public ABIDE collections, the model combined connection maps from resting brain scans with shape features from structural scans, after correcting for differences between scanning sites. A conditional generative network padded the smaller group, while attention-based fusion merged the two data types. Accuracy beat single-scan approaches in repeated testing, and performance held up across held-out centres. Highlight maps pointed to the default mode network and social brain regions.
pmc-13542025:
Lauriane Plouhinec and six colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether enzyme pre-treatment of soybean meal, a staple protein in chicken feed, disturbs the gut. Soy is rich in hard-to-digest plant fibres, and enzyme cocktails meant to unlock them might also shift gut microbes.

On intestinal cell lines, enzyme-treated soy left the gut barrier intact and triggered no inflammation. A commercial cocktail mainly boosted wheat fermentation. A pectin-focused fungal treatment, by contrast, raised gut-friendly acid production from soy and enriched the bacteria that make them. Tailoring enzymes to each feed ingredient is the lesson.
pmc-13542425:
DP Berry published a 2026 simulation study on dairy sire selection for farmers whose breeding goals are not simply the highest overall merit score. Standard mating recommenders maximise a total merit index and can miss such preferences, even when they already account for relatedness between animals.

Berry tested a recommender that penalises matings whose expected calf merit strays from farmer-set thresholds or target values for individual traits. The simulations showed herd programmes can indeed be steered to keep expected progeny close to those chosen limits. The cost was small: genetic gain on the total merit index slipped only slightly. The study supports digital mating tools that respect individual farm goals rather than pushing every herd toward the same maximum.
pmc-13543525:
Hooriehsadat Amini's team published a 2026 study on reusing approved medicines as blockers of BRAF. That growth-signal protein's V600E mutation drives several cancers, and current BRAF drugs often fail through resistance or side effects. The team built a shape-based search model from five known inhibitors and screened a library of approved drugs. They then narrowed hundreds of options through docking and molecular dynamics simulations against normal and mutant BRAF.

The heart drug ticagrelor emerged on top, binding the target about as stably as the reference inhibitor regorafenib. Lab tests in colorectal cancer cell lines of unlike BRAF status then tested ticagrelor, along with pioglitazone and nilotinib from the same screen. The drugs sharply slowed cancer cell growth and pushed cells toward death. A known, safety-tested drug turning into a cancer candidate is the appeal of repurposing, though clinical proof remains distant.
pmc-13543625:
Xing Chen and colleagues reported in 2026 on a long non-coding RNA called ACTA2-AS1 in bladder cancer, a molecule that does not build protein but regulates other genes. Mining public databases showed the RNA scarce in tumours, and the team confirmed the pattern in tissue from 132 patients alongside cell experiments. In cells, restoring it slowed growth, movement, and invasion while pushing cells toward death and cycle arrest; adding back the small RNA it absorbs reversed those benefits. A tumour-suppressing sponge lost in cancer, the authors argue, helps explain malignant behaviour and could anchor future tests or therapies.
pmc-13545325:
Rebekah A Jenkin and Kevin A Keay traced, in a 2026 history, how the University of Sydney obtained bodies for anatomy teaching across a century. Using institutional records, they documented 7,609 bodies received between 1883 and 1983, of which 4,084 arrived unclaimed from public institutions under an 1881 anatomy law. Asylums supplied most bodies until the 1930s, while donated bodies remained rare.

The people behind those numbers included former convicts, immigrants, miners, Chinese indentured laborers, and Indigenous Australians, many poorly placed to refuse. Poverty, isolation from family, and biased record keeping shaped who counted as unclaimed. Sydney shifted to a donation program in the 1940s, and the last unclaimed body arrived in 1961.
pmc-13546525:
Shan Liu and a large team set out in 2026 to create a laboratory model of colorectal cancer that resists both chemotherapy and radiation, a major reason treatment fails. They exposed two human colon cancer cell lines to repeated high-dose treatment, mimicking intensive clinical therapy, until resistant versions emerged. The surviving cells were then compared with their parent lines in dishes and in mice.

The resistant cells grew faster, formed more colonies, and invaded and migrated more strongly than the originals. In mice they produced tumors more readily and spread more often to liver and lung. The authors offer the model as a platform for studying how resistance develops and for testing ways to reverse it.
pmc-13546725:
Md. Tanks received salt, a commercial electrolyte saline, or methylene blue, alone and in combinations, in both controlled farm trials and real commercial journeys. Treated tanks held better water quality, built up less ammonia, and grew far fewer bacteria than untreated tanks. Blood sugar stayed lower in treated fish, a sign of less stress. Salt and saline at two parts per thousand, alone or with methylene blue, worked best. The authors give these doses as practical guidance for transporters.
pmc-13546825:
Alexeev and colleagues analyze what makes hospital readmissions for spinal surgical site infections long and expensive, in 2026 health economics research. The study included 123 readmitted patients with a mean age of 63.2 years, modeling how clinical and surgical factors predicted their readmission length of stay and direct hospital cost, two outcomes the authors show are tightly linked in this population.

Mean readmission stay was 15.9 days, and mean direct cost reached 25,713 dollars per readmission in the cohort. Stay length and cost correlated strongly, with a coefficient of 0.695 in the reported analysis. Each additional hospital day raised cost by 4.8 percent, adding about 1,207 dollars daily in the adjusted model. Staged index procedures were associated with 45.0 percent higher costs than single-stage operations. Private insurance, by contrast, was linked to lower direct costs than government coverage.
pmc-13547225:
Shwetakshi Mishra and Srikanth Mutnuri explored in 2026 whether microbes living in Arctic ice and water near Ny-Ålesund in Svalbard could make hydrogen fuel in the dark. Samples of glacial ice and surface water were held near freezing and at room temperature, with a chemical added to block methane makers. Gene checks tracked which organisms and pathways took over under each setup.

At the warmer setting with the blocker present, the cold-tolerant community pushed hydrogen to 85 percent of the gas produced, using an acetate-heavy route and several enzyme systems working together. Models of heat sensitivity suggested the microbes hold large untapped capacity. The authors see Arctic microbes as flexible helpers for low-temperature bioenergy systems.
pmc-13547325:
Nazanin Zamani and colleagues designed in 2026 an optical receiver chip meant to move forty gigabits per second while sipping power, built from carbon nanotube transistors instead of conventional silicon. Simulations gave the front stage a bandwidth above 28 gigahertz with very low noise, while the full receiver reached about 29.5 gigahertz and consumed roughly 1.4 milliwatts in total. Hand calculations matched the simulations closely, which the authors take as validation of their method. They position the design for future optical links inside data centers.
pmc-13548925:
Maria Abraham and colleagues built gene tools for a yeast group that mixes killers and harmless kin. Published in 2026, the study turned four Nakaseomyces species into a test system for gene-switch output. One species, N. glabratus, often infects people, while two appear in clinics without common disease and one lives on fruit.

The team built a CRISPR plasmid for fast guide-RNA cloning, made strains needy for amino acids and nucleotides, and ferried plasmids into each species. Gene-switch tests showed intact thiamine and phosphate signal routes in all four, with glabratus and bracarensis patterns closest. Three species survived a day inside mouse immune cells, while the fruit species did not. Readers get a toolkit for probing how yeast disease power evolved.
pmc-13549625:
Nicole Khezri and colleagues identify who bleeds into damaged brain tissue after a clot-removal procedure for stroke, in a 2026 global registry study. Hemorrhagic transformation worsens outcomes after thrombectomy, and its subtypes behave differently. The team analyzed 1,453 patients with blocked front-brain arteries treated in a first-pass device registry, comparing scans a day after treatment and modeling risk factors for each bleeding pattern.

Four in ten patients showed some bleeding on imaging, though only a small share, just over three percent, had symptoms from it. Diabetes, severe stroke scores, and high blood sugar at arrival raised the overall risk, while a healthy early scan score and having atrial fibrillation lowered it. Specific scan and sugar patterns predicted particular subtypes. The authors urge trials to report bleeding by subtype, since lumping them hides who is truly at risk.
pmc-13550025:
Morató, Peña-Salazar, Grande, and the STRESSURG group measure surgeons' trauma after patients die unexpectedly. Their 2026 paper reports the first international validated survey on this burden. Unexpected deaths during or just after surgery devastate operating teams. The psychological fallout was poorly quantified until now. A forty-two item questionnaire went to surgeons worldwide.

Three hundred fifty-four surgeons responded. The survey used the Impact of Event Scale-Revised instrument. Nearly half scored in the clinically relevant distress range. About twenty-nine percent met the threshold for probable PTSD. A quarter showed severe distress levels. Acting as the primary surgeon raised distress sharply. Mid-career surgeons suffered more than juniors or seniors. Only eight percent had received institutional psychological support. Over half believed such support should be mandatory. Structured support programs are urgently needed, they argue.
pmc-13550525:
Harriet L. S. Lawford and colleagues run a single blood survey that reads immunity to seventeen pathogens at once across Tonga, in a 2026 serosurveillance study. Dried blood spots from nearly eighteen hundred people aged five and up, collected in mid-2024 across three island groups, were tested on a bead platform carrying twenty-six antigens. Most pathogens clustered significantly by village. The authors argue the platform lets Pacific health teams aim campaigns precisely.
pmc-13551825:
ZhenKun Xiao, LiangJie Deng, YongHong Duan, Bing Wang, and AiHua Liu published a 2026 study pairing global burden estimates with individual cohort data on stroke tied to blood sugar and cholesterol dysfunction. Global Burden of Disease figures traced Chinese stroke deaths and disability from high fasting glucose and high LDL cholesterol between 1990 and 2023. A Chinese aging cohort served for discovery, with a United States cohort validating biomarker findings.

Age-standardized death and disability rates fell over the period, yet absolute numbers stayed large in 2023 in the reported estimates. A biomarker called eGDR, reflecting estimated glucose disposal, consistently tied to lower stroke risk and topped the predictor rankings in machine learning analyses. Adding it to standard risk models was tested for discrimination and clinical benefit.
pmc-13556025:
Yuanwu Zou and six colleagues studied in 2026 how eating patterns relate to chronic disease among people living at high altitude in Tibetan areas of China. National nutrition surveys rarely reach these regions, where food habits differ sharply. The team used food frequency questionnaires with 606 residents, extracted five dietary patterns statistically, and compared disease rates across low, middle, and high adherence to each pattern.

About four in ten participants reported at least one chronic disease. Patterns heavy in salt, carbohydrate, and fat, and a meat-heavy high protein pattern, both linked to more disease, as did smoking and local tea drinking. A traditional Tibetan pattern and regular physical exercise linked to less disease. The results give local health planners a picture of which habits to encourage and which to challenge.
pmc-13556325:
Qian Sun and ten colleagues found in 2026 that a widely used immune-suppressing drug, mycophenolate mofetil, also blocks poxviruses such as monkeypox. Approved antivirals for these viruses are scarce and resistance is a concern. Because vaccinia virus is a close, safer relative of the monkeypox virus, the team screened ten approved drugs that target nucleotide building enzymes in host cells, using vaccinia first.

The drug hit both viruses hard and acted after the virus had entered the cell. It works by stopping a host enzyme the virus needs for making DNA building blocks. The drug breaks that enzyme's partnership with a protective partner protein and forces it into inactive rod-and-ring bundles, draining the pool of building blocks. The authors propose this host-directed route as a template for broad poxvirus defences in future outbreaks.
pmc-13558625:
Monique Celeste Tavares and colleagues tested immunotherapy plus chemotherapy before surgery in early triple-negative breast cancer with inherited BRCA mutations, publishing the real-world cohort study in 2026. Trial evidence for this combination was strong, but data in BRCA carriers outside trials were thin. The multicentre cohort covered 726 patients who received at least one cycle of pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy and then had surgery.

Among 600 tested patients, 105 carried a pathogenic BRCA variant, mostly BRCA1. Complete tumour disappearance at surgery was more common in carriers than in others, at 74 percent versus about 62 percent. Survival looked favourable in both groups after a median 22 months, with a non-significant edge for carriers, especially those with residual disease. The findings support offering the regimen to BRCA carriers in routine care.
pmc-13559125:
Bowen Liang and three colleagues compare two open operations used to fix vesicoureteral reflux in children, a condition where urine flows backward from bladder toward kidney. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis weighs the Cohen technique against the Lich-Gregoir technique using only studies that compared them directly. Three databases were searched through March 2026.

Nine retrospective studies covering 655 children met the criteria. Persistent reflux after surgery, overall complications, reoperation, and later febrile urinary infection occurred at similar rates under both techniques. Lich-Gregoir operations finished faster and meant shorter hospital stays. Urinary retention after surgery, though, struck more often after Lich-Gregoir, while blood in the urine was more common after Cohen. The authors rate their certainty low to very low, weakened by retrospective designs and uneven complication definitions. Choice, they conclude, should weigh these trade-offs family by family.
pmc-13559625:
Ruizhe Yue, Zheng Wang, and Hao Zhang ask whether removing the primary tumor helps women whose triple-negative breast cancer has already spread to organs by the time of diagnosis. Their 2026 study uses the US SEER registry for patients diagnosed between 2010 and 2020 with metastases in liver, lung, or brain. Propensity matching paired operated and unoperated patients with similar profiles.

Of 1,827 patients, 543 had primary tumor surgery. After matching formed 507 pairs, median overall survival reached fifteen months in the surgery group against nine months without. Breast cancer-specific survival showed the same pattern. Adjusted models kept surgery tied to longer survival, and several sensitivity checks agreed. The authors caution that healthier patients may simply be chosen for surgery more often, so the link may reflect selection rather than a true treatment effect. They call their results hypothesis-generating.
pmc-13560125:
Virginia Vigiano Benedetti and colleagues profile the fibroblasts that surround breast tumors and uncover a previously unrecognized subset tied to immune suppression. Their 2026 study integrates three single-cell sequencing datasets from 29 patients and cross-checks patterns in cancer atlas bulk data. Cancer-associated fibroblasts shape progression and treatment response, but their flavors differ between breast cancer subtypes.

Alongside three known stromal populations, the team found a cluster they name metabolic stressed CAFs. These cells run programs for antigen presentation, stress response, sugar burning, and matrix remodeling. Their abundance rose as T cell presence and function fell. Triple-negative tumors held immune-infiltrated yet constrained environments rich in these cells, while Luminal A tumors showed weaker infiltration and mixed patterns. Several of the subset's genes predicted prognosis and chemotherapy response. The authors propose the cells as targets for improving immunotherapy.
pmc-13560425:
Yuqing Liu and three colleagues review how extracellular vesicles carry messages between the brain and the body's organs in Alzheimer's disease. Their 2026 article questions the brain-only picture of the illness, synthesizing evidence across six organ axes: liver, heart, gut, lung, bone, and fat. Vesicles move proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids across fluids and barriers.

Evidence runs strongest for the gut-brain, liver-brain, and fat-brain routes, while other axes rest mostly on animal models or engineered vesicles. Organ-derived vesicles may sway brain inflammation, blood vessel health, metabolism, barrier integrity, and amyloid or tau processes, and brain vesicles may in turn disturb peripheral organs. Translation faces stubborn obstacles: vesicle mixtures are heterogeneous, their organ of origin is hard to prove, and isolation methods lack standards. The authors frame vesicles as one signaling layer inside a wider systemic network.
pmc-13560625:
Svitlana Pidoprygora and three colleagues show how global comics made Ukraine visible yet distorted before 2014. Their 2026 article reads three case studies across comic traditions: Hergé's Tintin in the Land of the Soviets from 1929. The others are a 1976 Nestor Makhno comic by Spain Rodriguez and the Italian Ivan Karine series from the early 1960s. Visual and story analysis meets a postcolonial lens.

The authors name the mechanism distorted visibility: Ukrainian land, figures, and symbols appear, but folded into Soviet, Russian, or imperial stories. Hergé homogenizes Soviet space with Russian cultural markers. Rodriguez frames the anarchist Makhno through Russian Revolution mythology, leaving Ukraine a backdrop. Ivan Karine borrows Cossack imagery for a Russian imperial adventure. Naming, spatial framing, iconography, and narrative position each do part of the displacing work. The authors offer the case as a lens on cultural erasure in transnational storytelling.
pmc-13561225:
Angad Tiwari and five colleagues published this 2026 case report of one patient with mast cell leukaemia, the rarest and most aggressive form of systemic mastocytosis, a cancer of mast cells. Their patient was an 86-year-old man previously treated for a sinus lymphoma, in remission since 2017, and for prostate cancer in 2019. He arrived with acute pancytopenia, a drop in all blood cell types, first presumed to be lymphoma returning.

His serum tryptase, a mast cell marker, exceeded 11,999 nanograms per millilitre, and marrow sampling showed 20 percent abnormal mast cells, confirming the leukaemia. Gene sequencing revealed pathogenic variants in six genes, including TP53, plus a rare KIT variant; the usual KIT mutation was absent. He declined treatment with the targeted drug midostaurin, deteriorated and died two weeks later. The authors stress that unexplained low blood counts warrant suspicion of this disease, and that genomic profiling clarifies tangled cases.
pmc-13561725:
Hernandez and co-authors ask whether earlier injections change later surgery in this 2026 study of Peyronie's disease, the scarring condition that bends the penis and impairs sexual function. Collagenase injections dissolve plaque non-surgically, but clinicians worried that prior treatment might compromise the tunica tissue and worsen outcomes of plication, the tightening operation used when injections fall short.

From 926 men in their hospital series, 322 had received them, and 7.8 percent of those later needed plication against 5.6 percent of injection-naive men. Starting curvature was similar between surgical groups, and correction was near-identical, ending at 4.6 degrees against 3.0 degrees on average after surgery, both over ninety percent reductions. Early problems ran numerically higher after treatment, 20.0 versus 2.9 percent, without reaching that bar, and revision rates matched. The authors reassure that prior collagenase should not deter indicated surgery.
pmc-13562625:
Yifei Feng and six colleagues put a new surgical robot, the Carina platform, through preclinical trials for rectal surgery. Robotic help promises steadier work in the narrow pelvis, but each new system must prove itself before human use. The 2026 team first planned port and cart positions on three-dimensional reconstructions. Six pigs then underwent robot-assisted rectal removal, split into acute and longer-term groups. Working times, device errors, and complications were logged, and the longer-term pigs were examined after four weeks.

Every pig operation finished successfully with no device-related problems during surgery. The follow-up animals recovered well, and their joined bowel ends healed favourably by the 28-day check. Port and cart layouts were then confirmed on three human cadavers, where a full rectal resection could be simulated. The authors judge the platform feasible and safe at this stage, while noting that patient trials remain ahead.
pmc-13562725:
Saman Chalaki and four colleagues show that dairy cows which slim down too fast after calving are, at gene level, dismantling their own muscle. The weeks around calving push high-yielding cows into energy deficit, and they raid body reserves to fill the gap. The 2026 study followed 200 multiparous Holsteins giving at least 30 kilograms of milk daily, grouping them by condition-score loss to day 42. Muscle biopsies from 40 cows at days 21 and 42 measured genes for protein breakdown and building, while blood carried the chemical fingerprints of muscle loss.

Cows losing half a condition unit or more switched on the tagging machinery that marks muscle protein for destruction, including MuRF1 and Atrogin-1, and dialled down a synthesis regulator. Their blood held more creatinine and 3-methylhistidine, both in step with how much condition was lost. The authors urge tight condition management across the transition weeks to protect muscle and metabolic health.
pmc-13562925:
Wimalasena and colleagues present a systematic review, published in 2026. A bibliometric analysis accompanies it. The topic is research on micro-influencers. These are social media creators with small but engaged followings. Brands use them instead of celebrities. The team followed PRISMA methods. They analysed sixty-eight papers from the Scopus database. The papers ran from 2020 to 2025. Mapping software charted themes and connections.

The analysis maps how the field is structured. It shows which topics and methods dominate. It also shows where the gaps lie. Community-driven and authentic engagement distinguish these creators. The authors use the map to propose future research directions. Marketing scholars studying this fast-growing promotional channel are the audience.
pmc-13563725:
Congcong Yan and six colleagues trace molecular conversations between the meninges, the immune-active membranes wrapping the brain, and the hippocampus in Alzheimer's disease. How those membranes talk to the vulnerable memory region was largely unknown. Their 2026 study used two mouse models, one for amyloid disease and one for tau disease, layering bulk gene sequencing, protein measurement, and spatial gene mapping across disease stages. The design separated true disease signals from ordinary ageing.

A sturdy 19-gene hippocampal signature emerged, repeating in an independent dataset from each model. Spatial maps defined a progression axis along which meningeal spots clustered at the advanced end. Message-and-receiver analysis nominated signalling pairs between the tissues, tied to the states of microglia, the brain's immune cells. The authors are explicit that these computer-inferred channels, drawn from mice, are hypotheses. Human tissue checks and perturbation tests must come before any treatment talk.
pmc-13564125:
Shaun Shadaker and thirteen colleagues published this 2026 report of a population-based hepatitis C survey in Uzbekistan, carried out in 2022 to guide the country's national elimination programme. Earlier estimates of infection rates ranged wildly, up to 9.6 percent. The team sampled blood from adults and children across seven regions covering nearly 60 percent of the country. They measured both antibodies, which mark past exposure, and viral RNA, which marks current infection.

Antibody prevalence came out at 3.9 percent in adults and 1.1 percent in children, while active infection measured 2.0 percent and 0.5 percent respectively. Rates in Tashkent city ran higher, at 6.6 percent antibody prevalence among those surveyed there. Past surgery, invasive medical procedures and incarceration were tied to exposure, while invasive dental work and tattoos were tied to active infection. The authors present these as the most robust national estimates available, considerably lower than the older pooled figure yet above modelled estimates.
pmc-13569625:
Ashley Micuda and colleagues built a deep-learning system that outlines the inner ear on ordinary CT scans better than human experts, publishing the validation study in 2026. Inner-ear shape guides cochlear implant choice and tuning, yet hand tracing from clinical scans is slow, variable, and limited by resolution. The team trained the network on 4,784 paired datasets from 100 cadaver specimens imaged with high-resolution synchrotron scans and varied clinical CT machines.

On unseen scans, the network beat every individual expert, the expert average, and a consensus segmentation, reaching a Dice overlap of 0.922 against synchrotron truth at resolutions down to 625 micrometres. The authors present it as the first automated inner-ear segmenter to surpass experts, setting a new standard for surgical planning and implant fitting.
pmc-13570225:
Mingjun Rui and colleagues modelled whether adding blinatumomab to chemotherapy pays off for Hong Kong children with standard-risk B-cell leukaemia, publishing the cost-effectiveness analysis in 2026. The immune drug improved disease-free survival in a large trial, but its value from a public payer's view was untested. The team built a ten-year Markov model for average- and high-relapse-risk children, comparing chemotherapy alone with blinatumomab added first-line or second-line.

Both blinatumomab strategies fell below Hong Kong's willingness-to-pay threshold, with first-line use preferred in most probabilistic simulations. Drug cost and survival gains drove the results most. The authors conclude first-line blinatumomab appears cost-effective for newly diagnosed standard-risk paediatric B-cell leukaemia in this setting.
pmc-13572325:
Ravit Pertez-Machluf and colleagues ask, in a 2026 retrospective study, whether a past cesarean birth predicts failure of drug treatment for first-trimester miscarriage. Records covered 716 patients treated with mifepristone and misoprostol at a major center between 2019 and 2022, comparing those whose treatment completed against those needing further intervention.

Treatment failed in just under thirty percent. A prior cesarean nearly doubled the adjusted odds of failure, and each extra day of pregnancy age added a little risk. Failure rates ran higher still in the cesarean subgroup analysis. Among women without a cesarean history and earlier pregnancies, bleeding during treatment oddly marked lower failure. Counselors can now give cesarean-scarred patients a more honest estimate before choosing drug treatment.
pmc-13573425:
Hafiz Muhammad Obaid Kazmi, with 12 colleagues, reports a 2026 mouse study of glycine as a shield against brain harm from a cancer drug. Cisplatin cures many cancers but inflames the brain, above all the memory centre and the front cortex. Glycine, a simple amino acid, fights inflammation and oxidation and costs little.

Twenty-five male mice were split into five groups with varied timing of the drug and glycine over 14 or 28 days. Blood levels of a key inflammatory signal rose most in the long drug-only group. Glycine given alongside the drug held that signal lowest, and late glycine still helped. Brain slices showed nerve cells better preserved in glycine groups than in drug-only groups. The authors back wider preclinical tests of glycine as an add-on shield.
pmc-13575225:
Nebahat Sahin leads a 2026 hunt for drugs that block AXL, a protein found at high levels in many cancers and tied to poor survival. AXL helps cancer cells grow, spread, and resist treatment, and genetic studies support it as a drug target. The team screened compound libraries on the computer first.

Virtual screening, docking, and motion simulations narrowed the field, pinpointing contact spots inside the AXL binding pocket. Three lead compounds then went into lab tests on four breast cancer cell lines. Each slowed cancer cell growth, with the compound coded STOCK1N-80636 the strongest. One lead was nebivolol, a known drug from another field. The authors present the trio as starting points for AXL-focused drug development.
pmc-13576125:
Ji-Hyung Park leads a 2026 postmortem study of an Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin watched for years off Jeju Island, South Korea. The dolphin carried a mouth mass and a deformed jaw, noted over six years with three years of close monitoring. After death, the team combined scans, tissue work, microbe studies, and gene activity profiling.

Scans showed a jaw fracture at the mass site. Tissue checks ruled out viral growths and one tumour type, supporting a trauma-caused fibroma, a benign scar-like growth. Lung findings pointed to aspiration pneumonia as the main cause of death, with the bacterium Parvimonas micra dominant in a mixed infection. Chemical pollutant levels matched those typical of aged dolphins, with no sign they drove the final illness. The authors frame the case as a first for marine mammals.
pmc-13578325:
Prashantha Murahari and co-authors dope cadmium sulfide films with antimony to build a better ultraviolet light sensor, in a 2026 materials study. The films were sprayed onto glass by a mist based method. Crystal checks showed the same basic structure in every film, with the two percent antimony mix giving the cleanest crystals and the biggest, tightest grains.

That same mix soaked up more light and answered UV rays most strongly in current tests. Its response and recovery both landed near a second, and repeated cycles held steady over long runs. Too much or too little antimony did worse, so the middle dose carried the day. The authors offer the film as a durable pick for UV sensing in fields from flame alarms to space work.
pmc-13578425:
B Madhana and colleagues survey what builds trust in online banking in India, in a 2026 study of more than five hundred university students. Fast growth in digital banking has raised fears about fraud and data theft. The team asked how safety knowledge, felt threats, and teaching support from schools shape trust, then built predictive models on the answers.

Safety knowledge and school support both raised trust, while felt threats dragged it down. Knowledge also carried much of the effect of teaching, since students who learned more knew more and trusted more. A forest model predicted trust best among the tools tried. How students viewed AI tools strengthened the link from knowledge to trust, a point the authors press on banks and colleges alike.
pmc-13578725:
Deshraj Singh Thakur and Santosh Narayan Chadar turn teak wood waste into nano scale charcoal for cleaning dirty water, in a 2026 study. Plain charcoal from farm waste is cheap, yet it grabs only modest amounts of pollution. Shrinking the char to nano size after a controlled burn gave a far more porous material, rich in surface groups that can bind contaminants.

Lab checks mapped the pore web, surface chemistry, and charge of the new powder. Heavy metals and organic pollutants stuck through three routes at once: surface binding, charge pull, and filling of tiny pores. The authors present the teak char as a low cost, scalable option that gives sawmill waste a second life. Field scale proof and cost work remain ahead.
pmc-13579725:
Chiyoko Bando and colleagues report an 80 year old man whose fixed belief that mites infested his body traced back to a vitamin shortfall, in a 2026 case report. He misread lint and skin flakes as bugs, a visual illusion that fed the belief. Testing showed mild thinking decline and a marked lack of vitamin B12, and brain scans showed weak blood flow at the back of the brain. His wife had come to share the belief over time.

Care paired a low dose calming drug with the missing vitamin in its active form. The illusions cleared fast, the infestation belief faded after them, and the drug was stopped without relapse. Follow up scans showed better brain flow. His wife's shared belief eased as he improved and the pair spent time apart.
pmc-13582125:
Tsuyoshi Kobayashi and colleagues report an 83-year-old man whose emergency valve-in-valve procedure trapped a coronary protection balloon shaft between two valve frames. The first 23-millimeter SAPIEN 3 valve had been placed high, leaving a narrow sinotubular junction and risk of blocked coronary flow. After post-dilation, a leaflet stuck open and caused torrential aortic leakage with severe low blood pressure.

A second valve restored stable circulation, but its frame jailed the protection balloon shaft, which resisted inflation, catheter support, and snaring. Emergency surgery removed the balloon without removing either valve, and the patient went home without valve or coronary damage. The authors advise shielding the shaft with a guide-extension catheter and placing the second valve deeper.
pmc-13582225:
Ines Valenta and colleagues found a paradox in heart blood flow: faulty widening of large heart arteries was most common in patients whose small-vessel function looked normal. Flow-linked widening of large heart arteries as flow rises carries diagnostic and outlook weight, but its share across small-vessel states was unclear. Their PET/CT study covered 332 patients with symptoms, split by heart-muscle flow reserve.

Faulty widening affected 34.6 percent overall, but 46.2 percent of the normal-small-vessel group, versus only 13.3 and 17.9 percent in the two abnormal groups. Nearly half of patients with symptoms and normal global flow reserve may thus carry hidden artery impairment. The authors argue that checking this gradient could sharpen outlook and guide who needs further heart testing.
pmc-13582725:
Samantha Gaidula and colleagues build bite size nutrition lessons for medical students and test the reception, in a 2026 report from a Pennsylvania medical school. Doctors lean on food advice daily, yet training leaves most students unsure of their nutrition skills. The team's micro lessons, called Nutriments, slot food guidance into the case based frame students already learn in, so nutrition rides along with disease teaching rather than standing apart.

Students at the school reported a clearer grasp of nutrition in care after using the resource. They also backed wider adoption of the tool. The authors pitch the lessons as a portable patch any school can drop into its platform, while noting that survey warmth is a first step, not proof of bedside skill.
pmc-13586325:
Ilyes Abdelhamid and colleagues built Hyperpathway, a web tool that turns pathway-tagging tables into hands-on hyperbolic network maps. Tagging analysis of omics data flags which pathways a set of parts touches, but its tabular output hides systems-level patterns. Their 2026 tool converts results into a pathway-part network, links split parts lightly, and trims and puts back leaves to speed mapping without losing shape truth.

The network is drawn on a flat disk, with colours coding rank, links, weight, or user labels, showing working modules hidden in tables. Tests on gene, body-chemistry, and fat data backed its value. The authors present Hyperpathway as a general tool for any two-sided network, moving analysis beyond p-value lists.
pmc-13588925:
Watanabe Yoichi and six colleagues reconstruct how three rare herbs survived the ice ages in Japan's snow country. The plants are living relics, sole survivors of ancient lineages now confined to regions of heavy snowfall. Reading the full chloroplast genomes of many populations, the team traced each species' family history and past population swings in their 2026 study.

The three lineages split from their nearest relatives at wildly different depths, from about twelve million to about sixty-four million years ago, all long before the ice ages. Within each species, family trees stretched back anywhere from thirty thousand to three million years. Yet all three boomed in numbers between roughly one hundred thousand and ten thousand years ago, as the heavy-snow climate itself took shape. Present diversity patterns reflect each plant's powers of spread and where its refuges lay.
pmc-13592325:
Huihui Xu and seven colleagues bottle, in 2026, a boron vinyl anion carrying an unusually heavy negative charge. Such anions pair a boron carbon double bond with a vinyl anion, a pairing so charge rich that only one example had ever been caught. A phosphorus ylide arm steadies the center carbon here, letting the team isolate the species and test its temper.

The anion proved fiercely reactive, grabbing hydrogen gas within minutes and attacking a fluorinated ring in the cold. Its reactions with other partners install a bulky, strongly donating group that can calm wild intermediates such as germanium fragments. Carbon dioxide took a surprise path, inserting twice into the boron carbon bond to close a fresh ring, Xu and the team report.
pmc-13593725:
Vanessa Almonti leads a twelve-author team hunting for early warning signs that mineral fibers can set lung tissue on the path to cancer. Their 2026 study exposed a three-dimensional human bronchial model, grown to mimic real airway tissue, to crocidolite asbestos and to short and long chrysotile fibers, then tracked the tissue's responses.

Tests in the first two days showed only brief toxicity that the tissue shook off, which would make a poor early test. By twelve days, though, fiber-treated tissue showed lasting changes matching known hallmarks of carcinogens. Inflammatory signals kept firing. DNA break markers persisted without much cell death. Scarring and identity-shifting programs had begun in the cells. The authors propose these signatures, combined with physical fiber measurements, as a faster way to judge the cancer risk of inhalable fibers.
pmc-13595325:
Xiaoxu Na and colleagues test whether a mother's body fat during pregnancy relates to her newborn's brain cortex development. Their 2026 prospective study follows 169 mother and newborn pairs, measuring maternal fat directly rather than relying on body mass index.

Fat mass percentage was measured at 12 and 36 weeks of pregnancy using air displacement, a method that estimates body composition from displaced air. At about two weeks old, babies had brain scans during natural sleep. Higher maternal fat at both time points was linked to smaller cortical volume in memory-related regions, including the left entorhinal cortex and parahippocampal gyrus. Late-pregnancy fat was also linked to the right temporal pole. One region showed a sex-specific effect, suggesting boys and girls may be affected differently.
pmc-13596825:
Joon Sang Baek and co-authors asked tuberculosis patients and the professionals who treat them what a conversational agent, a chat-based digital assistant, should actually do. Their mixed-methods study surveyed 107 healthcare professionals and thirty-one patients, then interviewed ten patients in depth about treatment experiences and expectations.

Professionals named drug side effects as their top challenge, followed by drug-resistant disease, drug interactions, and poor adherence. Patients wanted side effect consultation most, then general information and diagnostic help, and a majority were willing to use mobile health tools. Interviews deepened the picture: patients asked for steady contact with providers, trustworthy information, emotional support, and services they could afford and actually operate. The authors convert these needs into design directions, from adherence support and visible treatment progress to psychosocial features, for a user-centered TB companion.
pmc-13599325:
Katarzyna Filip-Hutsch leads a ten-author team reporting in 2026 on germs carried by ticks and other biting insects in moose calves in Finland. Moose make good sentinels for these infections because they range widely across northern forests. The team tested blood from 23 calves in their first season of life, most taken by hunters, to see how early exposure begins.

At least one target germ appeared in 44 percent of the calves. Trypanosoma DNA showed up in 35 percent, and every find belonged to one known family line of that parasite, including three new gene variants. Anaplasma phagocytophilum appeared in 17 percent, and Bartonella bacteria in 9 percent. Family-tree analysis placed the finds within wide-ranging populations rather than local oddities. The authors say early infection is common in young moose, and they frame the work as a base for wider wildlife monitoring in northern Europe.
pmc-13600925:
Olayinka Oladosu and four colleagues report in 2026 a deep learning shortcut for detailed brain imaging in children. High angular resolution diffusion imaging reveals fine structure in the brain's wiring, but needs long scans that young children struggle to sit through. The team asked whether software could predict the richer dataset from a shorter scan, halving scan time.

Brain scans from 95 children aged 2 to 10 supplied the material. A model learned voxel by voxel to predict high-strength scan data from low-strength data. Bigger training samples, wider windows, and added tissue maps all improved accuracy. Eight white matter tracts in the remaining 71 children were then analyzed, and outcomes from predicted data followed the same age patterns as real data, including consistent sex differences in tract volume. The authors conclude that generated imaging is workable for studying how children's brains develop.
pmc-13602425:
George Triantafyllou and colleagues report a previously unrecorded artery variant found during routine cadaver dissection. In a 68-year-old male donor, the right colic artery, which normally feeds the ascending colon, branched instead from the right gastroepiploic artery near the stomach. Their 2026 case traces the 3.7-millimetre branch behind the transverse mesocolon toward the hepatic flexure and ascending colon, with no typical right colic artery present.

A literature sweep found no prior record of this origin in standard anatomy references or recent studies, with only one surgical report hinting at it without clear depiction. The authors explain the variant through embryonic vessel development and warn surgeons that colon surgery must allow for such detours. Triantafyllou and colleagues present the case as a first clear cadaveric record.
pmc-13602625:
Nadieh Rouhani and four colleagues describe in 2026 building and piloting a clinical dashboard for kidney inpatients in Iran. Kidney disease demands constant monitoring, and dashboards promise that picture at a glance. Working at Imam Khomeini Hospital in Urmia between 2022 and 2023, the team ran a two-round Delphi with 25 nephrologists to pick key performance indicators. They then built the system on common web and Android tools, with barcode access at the bedside.

The panel agreed on 58 indicators grouped into demographics, medical history, clinical and laboratory values, and discharge information, with electrolytes and blood pressure drawing the strongest consensus. Ten experts rated usability as acceptable on most principles, though orientation scored lower and was improved. After a three-month pilot, 40 clinical staff rated system quality, information quality, satisfaction, and net benefit highly. The authors conclude the dashboard is ready to support real-time monitoring and decisions on the ward.
pmc-13612225:
C D'Souza and a large Australian team report a single-cell study, published in 2026. It covers a rare lymphoma that can grow around textured breast implants. The team sequenced individual cells from these tumours. They asked where the cancer cells come from. They also asked what in their surroundings keeps them alive.

The cancer cells differed from patient to patient. They traced back to memory T cells. These are the long-lived immune cells that remember past infections. The surroundings held immune cells that appeared to support the tumour. Fluid around implants carried raised levels of immune messengers. A secreted form of the checkpoint protein PD-L1 was present too. Active immune suppression likely helps the lymphoma survive.
pmc-13612425:
Edukondalu Mullapudi leads a four-author team photographing a molecular machine that breaks the symmetry rules in 2026. Acyl-CoA carboxylases build fatty acid precursors, and every known version was a tidy, symmetric complex. Mycobacteria, wrapped in waxy mycolic acids, seemed to run something stranger. The team fished natural complexes out of Mycobacterium smegmatis cells and solved one's structure by cryo-EM.

The catch was a sixteen-subunit hybrid with two carboxyl transferase parts, one for short-chain and one for long-chain substrates. A two-layered transferase core wraps around a dimer of the epsilon subunit, whose folded segment builds an asymmetric nine-stranded barrel. On each face sits a tetramer of the biotin carboxylase part, able to rotate about ninety degrees. The architecture explains how one machine services varied chain lengths mycobacteria need. It also hands drug hunters a structurally distinct target in a pathogen family that includes tuberculosis.
pmc-13614125:
Cong Wang and colleagues review polymer carriers for cancer immunotherapy, their designs, and their roadblocks. Tumour immunotherapy mobilises the patient's own defences, yet uneven targets, exhausted immune cells, and hostile tumour surroundings blunt its power. Their 2026 review surveys how tunable polymer nanocarriers protect immune drugs, steer their release, and reprogram the tumour environment.

Carriers can boost antigen display, revive killer immune cells, and power vaccines, cell therapies, and tumour-killing viruses. Design rules, targeting tricks, and translation hurdles all get systematic treatment. Wang and colleagues close with AI-aided design plus humanised animal models as the next paradigm for smarter polymer immunotherapies.
pmc-13614425:
Stephen Bonett and colleagues report a 2026 survey of how well adults from racial and ethnic minority groups in Philadelphia know and use the city's community health worker program. Such workers help neighbours reach care, cut hospital stays, and support healthy habits, yet awareness of their services is uneven. Data came from a web health survey run in February and March 2024 with 522 participants, most of them Black and women, with an average age of 39.

Fewer than half, 44.6 percent, had heard of the program, and only 13.6 percent of all participants had used it. Among users, 80.3 percent were satisfied with the help they got. Some groups, including Asian and Hispanic residents and people with private insurance, were less likely to know the program exists. The authors say outreach, not service quality, is the weak link.
pmc-13615225:
Lu and colleagues examined in 2026 how brain age shapes the links among sleep quality, brain waste clearance, and thinking in healthy adults. Brain age estimates how old a brain looks on scans compared with the calendar. The glymphatic system flushes waste from the brain, largely during sleep, and a scan index called DTI-ALPS tracks how well it works. The data came from 582 adults aged eighteen to eighty-seven in a Cambridge aging project.

The clearance index leaned lower on the left side across groups. People whose brains looked older than their years showed a tighter link between the clearance index and sleep quality. Those with younger-looking brains showed the index tied more to thinking scores instead. Statistical modeling put brain age in the middle of the path from clearance to sleep efficiency.
pmc-13616125:
Singhal and colleagues present a 2026 scoping review of acceptability in dental care, . Canada's dental care plan, launched in 2023, cut cost barriers, yet only about half of enrolled people had used services by late 2025. The team reviewed existing reviews of barriers and aids to acceptable care, from both patient and provider views.

Findings were sorted by theme to build a framework. Cost clearly is not the whole story: trust, communication, cultural fit, and past experience shape whether people book and return. Providers' willingness to treat certain groups also matters. The synthesis gives the new national plan a map of the non-price problems to fix, and gives researchers shared terms for a concept that dental studies have used loosely.
pmc-13619325:
Lucas Rezende and six colleagues describe rebuilding a kneecap tendon that had failed twice before. Their patient, a forty-one-year-old farmer, first tore the tendon on its own after a period of tendon pain. Two repairs broke down, leaving the kneecap riding high and bone lost at its lower edge, a mix that makes standard fixes unreliable.

For the third attempt, surgeons combined suture anchors with a block of the patient's own shin bone and an added tendon graft taken from the lower leg. Twenty-six weeks later he could fully straighten the knee and bend it across a wide range, with kneecap height improved and function much better. The authors offer the combined bone-plus-tendon approach as an option when both tissue and bone are missing in hard revision cases.
pmc-13623425: Kathleen Fletcher and colleagues review skin small-vessel vasculitis marked by dominant IgM or IgG immune deposits. They ask what it means in practice and where it sits in the Chapel Hill vasculitis naming scheme. This IgM/IgG-dominant skin vasculitis recently joined the provisional single-organ subtypes, though in clinic it cannot be told apart from IgA vasculitis. Their retrospective review covers 14 patients seen at Mayo Clinic.
pmc-13623625:
Ramaditya Srinivasmurthy joins a large team pooling trial evidence on adding immune checkpoint inhibitors to standard chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma. The cancer sits in the upper throat and is most common in East and Southeast Asia. The immune drugs had already shown activity in this cancer, but their value alongside the standard combined treatment was untested as a body of evidence.

Three randomised trials covering 1,022 patients met the rules, with just under a thousand in the safety pool. Adding the immune drugs cut the risk of disease progression or return by roughly half on the combined measures. It also halved the risks of spread to distant sites and of local regrowth. Overall survival leaned the same way without reaching firm statistical ground. Immune side effects rose, while most chemoradiation harms did not. The authors say longer follow-up must show whether better disease control becomes longer life.
pmc-13623825:
Toby Hopkinson, Liam R Cox, and Andrew J Wilson review traceless ligand-directed labelling, a chemistry trick for tagging proteins inside living cells without leaving the tagging tool attached. A guide molecule homes to the target protein, hands over a small label to a nearby spot, and then floats away. That vanishing act lets researchers mark natural proteins in their real setting.

The review traces how the method developed, covering both direct transfer designs and catalyst-tethered designs where the guide carries a tiny chemical worker. Recent advances widen which proteins and label types the approach can reach. Working examples include watching proteins glow in live cells, mapping protein partnerships across the cell, adding natural-style chemical marks on demand, and even rewiring cell signalling. The authors also list what still blocks wider use, from delivery into cells to controlling exactly where the label lands.
pmc-13625025:
Miki Takahasi and Reiko Mazuka review how babies learn to time voice and breath together, a skill speech depends on. Babies babble in bursts of sound and silence, and those bursts must ride on steady airflow past the voice box. The authors trace two settings: solo babbling and face-to-face exchanges. They mark a shift in the second half of the first year. Timing then steadies with breathing, and later it turns flexible for social use.

To explain the shift, they compare songbirds and marmosets and weigh swallowing, which needs the same tight timing to keep food from the airway. Early spoon feeding and a sinking voice box may have raised the stakes for safe timing in human babies, laying groundwork for speech.
pmc-13626325:
Adam Viktorisson and colleagues chart sick leave around a transient ischemic attack, a brief stroke warning that clears within a day. Using Swedish registers, they followed 347 working-age adults treated in Gothenburg between 2014 and 2019 and 1,388 matched neighbors. Patients already took more sick days than controls in the year before the attack, a sign that ill health gathers before the event itself.

After the attack, sick leave jumped by a mean of thirty-nine extra days in the following year. Over a third were on leave two weeks out, with the attack itself, stroke, and mental health the top recorded reasons, and one in ten remained on benefit a year later. Higher income and holding a job predicted taking leave, a reminder that return to work after a warning stroke is a long road.
pmc-13627225:
Aysenur Pac Kisaarslan and five colleagues, publishing in 2026, probe a quiet arm of the immune system in children who carry two inflammatory diseases at once. Familial Mediterranean fever, caused by MEFV gene faults, often overlaps with spondyloarthritis, a joint and spine inflammation. The team compared blood and joint fluid cells from children with either disease, both together, or neither, counting innate lymphoid cells and reading the signals those cells make.

Cell counts looked the same across groups, so the difference lay in behavior. Cells from doubly affected children leaned hard into a type 2 program, raising two signature signals, while joint fluid in spondyloarthritis alone carried its own distinct signal mix. Overlap disease, the authors conclude, rewires what these cells do rather than how many gather.
pmc-13630225:
Nazia Thakur and thirteen colleagues screened bat sarbecoviruses, the family that includes the COVID-19 virus, for how widely they can use the ACE2 doorway protein across mammal species. Receptor breadth hints at spillover risk, and the team tested binding and cell entry against a panel of thirty-four ACE2 variants from bats, humans, livestock, and possible intermediate hosts.

Viruses from the SARS-CoV-2 branch behaved as generalists, entering through many receptors, while two other branches stayed specialists with narrow tastes, a split traced partly to specific spike residues. Generalists were also the most antigenically similar to SARS-CoV-2, showing strong cross-neutralisation by patient sera, though faint cross-reactivity spanned the whole subgenus. The authors link receptor generalism to pandemic potential.
pmc-13631225:
